The study specifically examines the relationship between Sabar drum strokes and the [ATR] (Advanced Tongue Root) feature of Wolof vowels. The findings reveal consistent patterns between Sabar drum strokes and Wolof syllables, indicating a significant correlation between the phonological properties of Wolof vowels and Sabar rhythms. This research contributes to the understanding of non-tonal drum languages and their role in cultural communication systems.
abstracts.009288: Typically, utterances of declarative sentences make assertions, whereas utterances of interrogative sentences ask questions. One popular idea about how to explain this is that the two clause types have denotations of different types (e.g. propositions vs. sets of propositions), which interact with a univocal context-update mechanism in a way that derives asserting and questioning from that denotational difference. This is a satisfying explanatory approach, because it proposes that interpretation is driven compositionally by the form of the sentence, and it refrains from construction-specific stipulations about context update. But there are many systematic exceptions to this typical association: for instance, rising declaratives and tag questions comprise askings despite their declarative form, and do so while signaling distinct varieties of bias. These observations have typically forced sacrifices of the properties that make the above style of explanation explanatory: either the connections between form and interpretation are weakened, allowing declarative sentences to sometimes share denotations with interrogative ones, or a univocal update procedure is jettisoned, bringing in construction-specific context updates to account for these ‘marked’ forms. In this paper I argue that neither sacrifice is necessary. If we treat some aspects of linguistic form as contributing meanings on the level of context update, and take seriously the idea that people make pragmatic inferences about the speaker’s choice to update the context in the way that they did, we can bring these constructions into the fold of well-behaved context updates. Question bias emerges as a consequence of pragmatic reasoning about the speaker’s context-update choices, without needing to be stipulated construction-specifically.
abstracts.009289: This paper discusses a special type of complement of perception verbs in Serbian, introduced by kako (‘how’). Via a parallel corpus analysis, I compare the distribution of Serbian kako-clauses and English -ing forms. I show that two types of non-interrogative kako-clauses can be used in translations of English -ing forms, distinguished based on their formal and interpretive properties: ‘eventive’ and propositional kako-clauses. Eventive clauses focus on directly perceived events and cannot be negated or combined with epistemic verbs, while propositional clauses express beliefs or judgments and have a truth value. At a formal level, eventive clauses feature a null subject, while propositional clauses feature an overt nominative subject. I argue that this distinction is captured syntactically through the notion of phasehood, with only propositional clauses merging a full CP domain. Adopting the Form-Copy operation, I propose that eventive clauses lack a phase boundary, allowing for the deletion of a lower subject copy and yielding the observed case alternation and null embedded subject. This analysis offers a unified syntactic account of kako-complements and contributes to the typology of perception-based clause embedding.
abstracts.009292: This dissertation investigates the morphosyntactic behavior of small nominals (SNs) — reduced nominal structures lacking certain morphosyntactic properties characteristic of full DPs — across languages. Based primarily on three detailed case studies — bare complements of Moksha postpositions, Moksha bare direct objects (DOs), and bare DOs in Hill Mari non-finite clauses, I propose diagnostics that can reliably identify small nominals cross-linguistically and explore their implications for syntactic theory, particularly regarding the structure of the extended nominal projection. The dissertation begins with a carefully delimited theoretical model of nominal phrase structure, emphasizing the role of functional projections in determining nominal size. Each nominal projection between NP and DP is examined in turn, with explicit predictions about its morphosyntactic reflexes. The core of the dissertation is dedicated to Moksha. I first provide an overview of Moksha nominal morphology and map its features onto a hierarchical DP structure, demonstrating how Moksha nominal phrases align with theoretical expectations. In the first case study, I analyze the contrast between genitive-marked and bare complements of spatial postpositions in Moksha, arguing that the former are full DPs, while the latter are SNs displaying reduced morphosyntactic marking and agreement capabilities. In the second case study, I examine genitive-marked vs. bare direct objects in Moksha. Although bare DOs superficially resemble bare postpositional complements, I argue that they are full DPs with null case marking rather than SNs. In the third case study, turn to related Hill Mari, analyzing the contrast between accusative-marked and bare DOs in non-finite clauses. I argue that bare DOs in Hill Mari are true SNs, with nominal size varying according to syntactic environment. Drawing on these case studies, I propose new cross-linguistic diagnostics for identifying SNs, addressing weaknesses in existing criteria. The refined diagnostics focus on definiteness, number, and possession-marking mismatches, improving the identification of SNs across languages.
abstracts.009293: Linguistics has always been a battlefield as the vision of language has always been the expression of the vision of human beings in any culture. Nowadays, neurobiological models and computational theories compete with linguistics towards the understanding of the origin, the function and the structure of human languages. These notes highlight two crucial points: first, these two competitors target two distinct and incompatible goals; second, there are aspects of human languages, like the systematic differences expressed within the boundaries of Babel and crucial notions such as “predication” which are unformulable outside linguistics theory.
abstracts.009294: English reciprocals (\textit{each other} and \textit{one another}) are generally classified as pronouns, but they are atypical and exhibit several characteristics of determinatives. As such, they exemplify a core problem in linguistic categorization: how to study boundary phenomena rigorously when the dataset consists of a small number of items that straddle categories. Rather than forcing a binary decision via selectively chosen diagnostics, I measure the stability of ambiguity. Using a comprehensive profile of 155 morphological, syntactic, semantic, and phonological properties, I locate the reciprocals in multidimensional grammatical space and apply five complementary lenses: distance measurement with permutation testing, a specification curve over metrics and feature blocks, comparison-group rotations, a simple mixture calibration, and calibration against known categories. Across these lenses, reciprocals consistently occupy a boundary position between canonical pronouns and compound determinatives, with mixture weights close to parity (approximately 0.53 and 0.49 for pronoun‑likeness) that remain stable across reasonable analytic choices. On a homeostatic property‑cluster view, this stability of ambiguity~-- together with cross‑dimensional tension (morphology pulling determinative‑ward, semantics pronoun‑ward)~-- is the expected signature of a genuine boundary. The framework generalizes as a template for transparent small‑$n$ categorization: it characterizes boundary behaviour without pretending to deliver decisive recategorizations. Within standard frameworks, reciprocals remain categorized as pronouns; the present results place them at the periphery, alongside morphologically complex items that realize fused grammatical functions.
abstracts.009295: We analyze a collection of long-distance assimilation patterns using Boolean Monadic Recursive Schemes (BMRS; Bhaskar et al. 2020, Chandlee & Jardine 2021). BMRS describe input-output maps as logical transductions using conditional IF…THEN…ELSE… syntax. These patterns emerge from varying the presence, type, and position of redundancy conditions within BMRS feature spreading functions. When potential targets fail to receive or propagate harmonic features, redundancy conditions override harmony by blocking feature reception, halting propagation, or preventing both, depending on their type and scope. This offers a unified computational account of variation in feature spreading and blocking without traditional representational assumptions.
abstracts.009296: This paper focuses on the peripheral hierarchy of Mandarin interrogatives. Based on question markers’ embeddability profiles in a series of nonquotational subordinating contexts, this paper argues for a three-way split in projections that contribute to the illocutionary force, attributing the non-co-occurrence of question markers to their semantics. Specifically, we propose that (i) LowIForceP houses the most embeddable meiyou , Op wh , and A-not-A; (ii) PerspP houses question markers restrictedly embeddable like bu and ma ; and (iii) HighIForceP houses the unembeddable ba . Looking deeper into the embeddability patterns of bu and ma , we argue that our PerspP should be interpreted à la Dayal 2023 in the sense that it introduces a not-at-issue requirement for the embedded question to be potentially active for the matrix subject. We explicate that the embedding of bu and ma is restricted by two constraints: (i) the embedded clause size must satisfy the syntactic selectional requirement of the embedding context; and (ii) the overall interpretation must be compatible with a not-at-issue requirement lexically introduced. Our proposal calls for a theory of selection that manifests a conspiracy of syntax and semantics.
abstracts.009297: This dissertation draws on original fieldwork data from two Mongolic languages – Khalkha Mongolian (henceforth Khalkha) and Kalmyk Oirat (henceforth Kalmyk) – to investigate issues pertaining to clausal nominalisation, syntactic locality, differential argument marking (DAM), and case assignment. The empirical focus is on four embedded clause types in Khalkha, supplemented by comparative data from Kalmyk. These clause types include three types of complement clauses – finite bare CPs, finite nominalised clauses (NCs), and nonfinite NCs – and one type of adjunct clause – converbial adjuncts. Chapter 2 provides a brief introduction to the Mongolic language family, fieldwork context, and the basic morphosyntactic profiles of Khalkha and Kalmyk. Chapter 3 shows that each of the four embedded clause types under consideration in Khalkha can be uniquely characterised along three dimensions: finiteness, nominalisation, and the presence or absence of a DP layer within the nominal superstructure. I argue that converbial adjuncts are small nominalised clauses in that they show evidence of both being nominalised and lacking a DP layer within the nominal superstructure above the clause. I further argue that, assuming some form of parallelism between clausal and nominal domains, NCs projecting a “smaller” nominal structure above a “larger” clausal structure are unattested both in Khalkha and cross-linguistically. I propose a novel explanation that links their absence to more general constraints on structure building formalised via the Williams Cycle. Chapter 4 investigates the distribution of embedded subjects across the four clause types, using diagnostics from long-distance extraction and cross-clausal binding. I argue that accusative subjects occupy the highest phase edge of embedded (nominalised) clauses, genitive subjects occupy Spec,nP within a full DP superstructure, and case-unmarked (“nominative”) subjects occupy Spec,TP of the embedded clause. A key finding is that binding and extraction differ in their locality domains: while extraction appears to obey phase-locality, binding appears to be possible out of nominal domains irrespective of the presence of nominal phases. This suggests that locality domains for extraction and binding may not uniformly align with locality domains imposed by a standard conception of phases. Chapter 5 shows that accusative-based DAM in Khalkha adheres to two similar but ultimately distinct referentiality scales. I propose a movement-based account of DAM that results in accusative objects being located in Spec,vP and accusative subjects being located in the highest phase edge of an embedded (nominalised) clause. Building on previous work, I argue that accusative is best analysed as a dependent case in Khalkha and show how it interacts with the movement-based account of DAM for dependent accusative case assignment on objects and subjects. Next, I discuss novel data from subjects of subject clauses in Khalkha that reveal that containment relations between nominals, in addition to local c-command ones, are relevant for dependent accusative case assignment. That containment relations are relevant for dependent accusative case assignment offers novel support for an Agree-based approach to dependent case over a configurational one. Under the Agree-based approach, accusative arises as the spell out of the features of a previous goal of Agree on another DP. I extend this analysis to account for genitive subjects in Khalkha, and show how it may offer an underlying explanation for the absence of case marking on certain objects and subjects in the language. Taken together, this dissertation demonstrates that a detailed investigation of clausal nominalisation not only contributes to our understanding of Mongolic morphosyntax, but also yields important insights into issues of broader theoretical significance in syntax, such as the interactions between clausal and nominal structure, syntactic locality, and dependent case theory.
abstracts.009298: Participants in this study of language awareness, related to the relationship between speech and writing, provide self-report reflection on the learning of Chinese characters. This topic is the focus of a larger ongoing project focused on second language (L2) learners’ literacy attainment. Interviews with immigrant learners of Mandarin Chinese have suggested lines of research to pursue from a new vantage point, specifically on the question of access to phonological knowledge during the decoding of Chinese characters. How might this processing during reading vary in the case of Modern Standard Chinese Writing (MSCW) between, for example, Mandarin (informants’ target learner language, L2) and Cantonese (first language, L1)? Interviews revealed a consistent perception by learners of a closer “alignment,” for learning purposes, between phonology and script for MSCW and Mandarin Chinese than for the latter, MSCW and Cantonese. On a related note, regarding phonological processing, participants commented on the productive use of Vietnamese pinyin for learning the Chinese characters. These aspects of metalinguistic awareness appear to be related to extensive early experience with bilingual learning, language and literacy, in the home country (Vietnam), a separate but interesting research question. Regarding this question, the overall language acquisition and learning context of participants is relevant to the ongoing debate on the, by hypothesis, influence—via transfer—of prior L1 knowledge on L2 learning (V. 25, I. 3-4, pp. 255-275).
abstracts.009299: Matthias Mahlmann’s Mind and Rights (M&R) argues that the mentalist theory of moral cognition - premised on an approach to the mind most closely associated with generative linguistics - is the appropriate lens through which to understand moral judgment’s roots in the mind. Specifically, he argues that individuals possess an inborn moral faculty responsible for the principled generation of moral intuitions. These moral intuitions, once sufficiently abstracted, generalized, and universalized by individuals, gave rise to the idea of human rights embodied in such conventions as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. I am sympathetic to this argument. I thus take my comments on M&R as an opportunity to preempt topical challenges to the mentalist theory arising in machine learning. Through this challenge, I make clear the foundations of mentalism (generativism). On these foundations, I argue against the use of computational models as theories of human cognition and for limiting their scope as proxies for theories. Counter-arguments are developed, centering on the notion that computational models, like Large Language Models (LLMs), circumvent the leap from non-linguistic to linguistic during (pre-) training. Additionally, LLMs’ learning objectives are constrained by closed-sets of language-specific data over which they operate, circumventing a test of domain-specific vs. domain-general cognitive mechanisms for language acquisition. Focuses of this argument include the format of the input, the constraints on learning, and the means of data collection. These arguments are tied into M&R’s core themes, specifically concerning the necessity of rich descriptive accounts and the theory-dependence of data-interpretation.
abstracts.009300: Theoretical approaches to null subjects standardly focus on the narrow syntactic module. I offer a postsyntactic alternative in terms of PF deletion applying to salvage an unlinearizable derivation. Support for this alternative comes from microvariation in three closely-related West Slavic pro-drop languages spoken primarily in Poland (Kashubian, Polish, and Silesian), in which the distribution of null subjects is sensitive to the postsyntactic realization of [PERS/NUM] agreement. I argue that this microvariation indicates that in these languages at least, the licensing of null subjects takes place at PF, which in turn suggests that PF has a bigger role to play in a general theory of null arguments than has so far been assumed.
abstracts.009301: Dependent cases in Dependent Case Theory (DCT) fall into two directions: during case competition between two nominals, “dependent-down” cases are assigned to the lower nominal (such as accusative), and “dependent-up” cases are assigned to the higher nominal (such as ergative). It is a well-known, not often discussed, issue why accusative case can be assigned to multiple arguments, while ergative case can only ever appear on one argument, and must appear on the highest argument. In this thesis, I argue that this is not accidental but follows from computational considerations: a formal grammar checking whether a given dependent-down case is licensed is less complex (in a formal sense) than a formal grammar checking whether a given dependent-up case is licensed: For a dependent-down case, the possible licensors are the NP’s c-commanders, which is a single sequence, while for a dependent-up case, the possible licensors (the NP’s c-commandees) need to be looked for in every local subtree. Chapter 2 gives an overview over the range of “versions” of DCT in the existing literature, and presents the assumptions made in this thesis. Chapter 3 reviews data from Turkic that illustrate that the same NP can serve as licensor for accusative on multiple lower arguments. Chapter 4 presents the argument that there is a complexity difference between dependent-up and dependent-down cases. Chapters 5 and 6 argue for a novel view on Turkic cases. Chapter 5 argues that in Turkic, dative is never a dependent-up case (against Baker & Vinokurova 2010), but always lexical/inherent: We don’t have evidence that it should be a dependent-up case, and (assuming chapter 4 is on the right track) because there is no Single Dative Generalization in Turkish. Chapter 6 argues that Turkic genitive is the dependent-up case in the nominal domain, assigned by case-competition against the possessum (Baker 2015a): If it were an unmarked case, we should observe GEN getting overwritten by movement into a different case assignment domain (like nominative), and its being an inherent/lexical case would violate Bobaljik’s (2008) Revised Moravcsik Hierarchy for the accessibility of cases for ϕ-agreement.
abstracts.009302: Why do humans alone develop language? Rather than specialized processing modules, I argue that evolution selected for a simple attentional bias, hyperpriors that amplify communicative signals (eye contact, infant-directed prosody, hierarchical rhythm). This precision-weighting ensures linguistic patterns dominate learning without requiring language-specific architecture. Echolocation demonstrates the principle. Blind humans achieve remarkable spatial discrimination through self-generated sounds, a complex capacity that emerges without specialized adaptations. This spandrel falsifies the common inference that complex abilities require direct selection. If echolocation can arise from generic neural systems plus experience, so can language, given appropriate attentional focus. The attention hypothesis explains why language emerges universally while echolocation remains rare (only language has inherited attentional support), why other vocal learners never develop language (they lack the relevant hyperpriors), and why adults struggle with low-salience L2 features (they lack children's automatic orientation to these patterns). Three experiments could test this: cross-species neonatal preference tests, computational models varying only attention parameters, and fNIRS measurement of precision-weighting in newborns. The account reframes language evolution as selection for what we notice, not what we compute.
abstracts.009303: Can machines mean what they say? Generally not, because current AI systems lack the cognitive capacities that allow humans to recover meaning from and infuse meaning into language. However, from a cognitive standpoint, human and machine language are not entirely dissimilar. Specifically, while at present there are hardly circumstances in which machines function as humans typically do vis-à-vis meaningful language use, there is at least a circumstance in which humans appear to function as current generative language AI: during somniloquy or ‘sleep talk’. I first show that somniloquy and machine language unfold in similar restricted cognitive conditions. I then use this observation to suggest that AI’s linguistic output should be given a similar ‘semantic status’ to human somniloquy, and I consider some implications of this idea.
abstracts.009304: This study is concerned with the nature of syntactic silence and how to diagnose it. Syntactic structures may be "silent" in the course of derivation through several pathways: (i) movement (followed by Copy Deletion), (ii) ellipsis, and, less often discussed, (iii) linearization of shared/multidominant nodes. This study offers a novel diagnostic for (iii), namely, focus association of the exclusive particle 'only', which requires c-commanding an overt focus associate. Drawing cross-linguistic data from English and Cantonese (as well as Vietnamese), we demonstrate that focus association with apparent gaps is possible in Right Node Raising. We argue that only Parallel Merge (Wilder 1999, Citko 2005, Gračanin-Yuksek 2007) generates the correct structural relations for the association, whereas movement and ellipsis fail to do so. We further propose that Right Node Raising is structurally ambiguous between multidominance and ellipsis: the former feeds focus association while the latter bleeds it, supporting a non-uniform/"eclectic" approach (Barros & Vicente 2011, Belk et al. 2023). Finally, we show that the diagnostic extends to other constructions such as syntactic amalgams and right dislocation. [For how focus association (and wh -association) pans out in right dislocation, see: https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/009305 ]
abstracts.009305: [Published in Proceedings of GLOW, 47: https://biecoll.ub.uni-bielefeld.de/index.php/glow/article/view/1262 ] This study argues for a multidominant approach to right dislocation (RD), the first of its kind, with data from Cantonese and Mandarin as well as Japanese and Korean. The crucial evidence comes from focus/ wh -association of ‘only’/‘( wh -)the-hell’ expressions in RD, which requires a “leftward” c-command configuration. This challenges current monoclausal movement and biclausal sluicing approaches, but naturally falls out from a multidominant structure formed by Parallel Merge. The findings suggest that focus/ wh -association serves as reliable and moreover novel diagnostics for multidominance, which can be extended beyond RD to Right Node Raising and possibly other constructions. [For how focus association pans out in RNR, see: https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/009304 ]
abstracts.009306: In Spanish, usted ‘you (formal)’ and ustedes ‘you all (formal only in regions of Spain)’ have second-person semantics but appear with third-person, or default, agreement morphology. After exploring the possibility that these expressions are nominal imposters, I determine that they are genuine second-person pronouns on the basis of two phenomena: the ability of ustedes to occur in pronoun-article-noun constructions and the sensitivity of both usted and ustedes to the Person-Case Constraint. The question then becomes how to represent these forms as vocabulary items since a [PART(ICIPANT)] feature alone does not distinguish usted from tú/vos ‘you (informal)’ in all varieties of Spanish or ustedes from vosotros ‘you all (informal)’ in most varieties of Peninsular Spanish. To this end, I argue that usted is generated with an [HON(ORIFIC)] feature as well and extend the same view to ustedes in the relevant varieties of Peninsular Spanish. Next, I attribute the agreement behaviour of usted and ustedes to two postsyntactic rules of impoverishment that delete [PART] from the terminal nodes in which verb endings and pronominal clitics are inserted. The first rule is triggered by the presence of [HON], and the second rule, which only applies in Latin American Spanish, is triggered by the presence of [PL]. Finally, I propose a denotation for [HON] that reflects its contribution to the expressive dimension of meaning. Not only does this account capture the unique properties of usted and ustedes in Spanish, but it also lays the groundwork for the analysis of etymologically related pronouns in other Western Romance languages.
abstracts.009307: This chapter aims to dissociate linguistic intuitions and world knowledge intuitions by re-examining the introspection-based judgments of Japanese modality and evidentiality reported in Hara & Davis (2013); Davis & Hara (2014) and Hara (2017) as well as the results of an electroencephalography (EEG) experiment conducted by Hara, Orita, Ying, Koshizuka & Sakai (2020).
abstracts.009308: This paper discusses a case of exceptional extraction from Russian PPs that only happens in sluicing / fragments. The proposed analysis rests on a version of repair by ellipsis pursued in the Cyclic Linearization literature (Fox, Pesetsky 2005; Davis 2021; Mendes, Kandybowicz 2023): illicit non-successive-cyclic movement is possible when the conflicting linearization statements are deleted via ellipsis. The analysis extends to other cases of exceptional extraction in Russian, when coupled with a Scattered Deletion analysis of LBE (Fanselow & Ćavar 2002, Bondarenko & Davis 2023). Finally, we discuss a number of overgeneration issues for our account.
abstracts.009309: This essay challenges the prevailing metaphor of “learning” used to describe Large Language Model (LLM) training, proposing instead that these systems represent a form of hyper-accelerated, data-driven evolution. Through analysis of Daniel Dennett’s hierarchy of evolutionary competence and examination of the poverty of the stimulus problem, we argue that LLMs are Darwinian creatures evolved at computational speeds in environments of pure text. This framework explains their linguistic capabilities through convergent evolution rather than learning, resolves paradoxes about their competence without understanding, and for our understanding of the relevance for these models for generative grammar. Questions/feedback very welcome!
abstracts.009310: This paper presents three distinct linguistic interpretations of a circular Linear A inscription, derived from comparative methodologies most likely resembling the Linear A writing system: Proto-Hungarian phonetic mapping, Linear B phonetic equivalence, and ancient Egyptian/Coptic semantic analogues. Despite differences in language families and theoretical models, all three interpretations converge thematically on the concepts of light, divine descent, spirit, and celestial origin. This suggests the inscription preserves a ritualistic or poetic message aligned with religious practices in Bronze Age Crete. This study invites archaeologists, epigraphers, and linguists to consider broader frameworks for deciphering Linear A by employing multilingual comparative resonance and modern technological tools.
abstracts.009311: We investigate the status of weak crossover violations (WCO) in Spanish restrictive relative clauses. Claims in the literature lead to the expectation that Spanish does not show sensitivity to WCO in this context; however, ours is the first systematic investigation of the phenomenon in the language. We find that Spanish restrictive relative clauses do exhibit WCO violations: when the relative clause is headed by que, participants rate crossover configurations lower than configurations without crossover; when the relative clause is introduced by a quien, the status of WCO violations is less clear. We consider two explanations for our results in a quien clauses: potential structural differences between que and a quien, and the possibility for an appositive parse for some of our a quien configurations. Our results set the stage for further cross-linguistic investigations of crossover phenomena.
abstracts.009312: This paper challenges the hypothesis that ideophonic sequences are syntactic structures built from lexical roots by the recursive operation Merge through the mediation of a functional head, taken to be either a coordinate (Corver 2015) or a determiner (Corver 2023). Drawing on Generative Grammar theory and new data from Brazilian Portuguese, we argue that the evidence for this hypothesis is weak at best. We first show that these sequences do not behave consistently as constituents. While they can stand alone, be coordinated, and resist intrusion, they fail to undergo movement and ellipsis. Taken together, this suggests that they are most likely linear sequences. They lack the formal features responsible for mediating grammatical interactions with the surrounding syntactic context and on which asymmetric structures are built. Moreover, the evidence on which Corver relies is mostly phonological and as such does not provide strong support for the conclusion that ideophonic sequences are asymmetric structures. Following the general tenets of Minimalism, we conclude that, in the absence of strong and uncontroversial evidence, it is best to assume that sequences formed by canonical ideophones are linear strings or symmetric structures distinct from ordinary syntactic phrases.
abstracts.009313: Anomaly has always attracted the interest of language scholars, either as a possible mechanism for language change or as a window into speakers’ judgments and competence. Here I will discuss the use of errors in neurolinguistics, focusing on Moro’s prolific ideas to disentangle grammar in the brain by presenting selective anomalies to neurotypical individuals as well as clinical groups. This prompts further considerations of the nature of anomaly for the study of language as a whole, from its core structures to its most creative nuances.
abstracts.009314: Northern Vietnam, in particular the regions along the international border, is home to a rich diversity of language communities. Important research opportunities have presented themselves in the Tai-speaking communities in rural districts near Laos with an emphasis on the development and preservation of the Tai languages. One opportunity in particular focuses on the new generation of bilingual school-age children. Preliminary results of the present study regarding the sociolinguistic setting are reported to better understand the language use context of community bilingualism. The method applied for this exploratory survey included different components, each one gathering different kinds of data: interviews with parents of elementary school students and their teachers, in-depth discussions with local language scholars, a study of the previous research on language and literacy in the Tai languages of the region, and assessment of the bilingual ability of the 6-year-old population of a village known for its conservation of the local variant of the language. Findings confirmed that the local community language has been preserved in the child population. At the same time, assessment data point to the rapidly growing influence of the Vietnamese language in every domain of village life, including at home. Overall results of the study place the finding of language preservation in the context of modern-day regional interrelation and historical connection. The concluding discussion of results presents a hypothesis that these tentatively observed favorable conditions might represent a distinctive case.
abstracts.009315: The goal of this paper is to explore negation in Nduindui, drawing out empirical generalisations regarding negation and the implications of such generalisations in terms of analysing the clause structure in the language. Nduindui shares an interesting feature with many of its neighbours: consistently exhibiting discontinuous bipartite negation, where the two negators he and tea encircle verbal material. This paper presents novel data regarding negation in Nduindui and its interaction with other elements in the clause like tense and aspect. Empirical generalisations are formed from the attested patterns of negation, and a comparative discussion is provided with other languages in the region. The paper then explores what might be the best way to capture the generalisations within a generative syntactic framework. One of the most widely accepted theoretical analyses for bipartite negation is based on French (see Pollock, 1989), where the two negators are argued to be the head and the specifier of the same phrase/NegP; this paper discusses how the Nduindui patterns present challenges to such an analysis. The paper then evaluates the consequences of extending three alternative analyses that can capture bipartite negation: (a) the PolP account of Oosthuizen (1998) and also Biberauer (2007, 2008), (b) the Expanded/Articulated NegP of Bell (2004), and (c) an account with two separate NegPs combined with VP/V-movement. The paper demonstrates how the Nduindui patterns remain a challenge to all the existing theoretical approaches, as none of them can explain the patterns without either making wrong predictions or needing additional stipulations.
abstracts.009316: This paper shows that that differential object marking (DOM) is not a unitary phenomenon, and observes that its two subtypes, differential object flagging (DOF) and differential object indexing (DOI), probably have rather different explanations. The cross-linguistic patterns found with both subtypes of DOM can be described by the scales of referential prominence (animacy, specificity, and so on), but DOI is like differential subject indexing (DSI) in that it conforms to the prominent indexing universal, while differential subject flagging (DSF) shows the mirror-image pattern of DOF: Flagging is preferred when the subject is not prominent on one of the prominence scales. The paper provides examples from a wide variety of languages showing that indexing behaves rather differently from flagging. Thus, DOM is not a unified phenomenon, as was already noted by Siewierska (2004) and some earlier authors.
abstracts.009317: The relevance of probabilistically variable patterns has long been controversial in linguistic theory, historically led by two dominant schools. On the first view, which I call Principles Without Probability, variable patterns are outside the purview of formal theories of grammar, composed solely of categorical principles (Newmeyer 2003). The second view, Probability Without Principles, holds that unit and collocation frequencies form the basis of mental representations, and denies the existence of formal categories (Bybee and Hopper 2001). I argue that these approaches should be reconciled in a theory with Principles and Probabilities: Language is mentally represented as a generative system with formal categories and principles, as well as probability distributions over possible structures. I illustrate this approach with an analysis of word order variability in Cherokee that integrates Minimalist derivations with constraint-based optimization (Heck and Müller 2003), specifically the probabilistic computation of optimality of Maximum Entropy Harmonic Grammar (Goldwater and Johnson 2003). This approach expands the predictive and explanatory power of generative Minimalism to a broader range of word order phenomena, while maintaining its insights about the feature-driven nature of movement.
abstracts.009318: Panjabi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken primarily in the Punjab province of Pakistan and the Indian state of Punjab. Long vowels contrast in nasality in the language, but this contrast is neutralized before nasal consonants: [ṼṼN], *[VVN]. This paper presents air pressure data from Pakistani Panjabi showing that predictably nasal vowels before nasal consonants in the language, [ṼṼN], are statistically equivalent in nasality to contrastive nasal vowels, /ṼṼ/ (Exp. 1). However, predictable [ṼṼN] and contrastive nasal /ṼṼ/ vowels behave differently in their interaction with a nasal harmony process, in that only contrastive nasal /ṼṼ/ vowels trigger nasal harmony (Exp. 2). This difference in phonological behavior can be straightforwardly analyzed by assuming (i) that pre-nasal vowels are underlyingly oral, even in morphemes which never show alternations in nasality, and (ii) that only underlyingly nasal vowels trigger harmony. These findings support a view of phonology in which abstract underlying representations (URs) can be completely covert, never surfacing in any allomorph without some kind of symbolic alteration. Surface-oriented approaches to phonology which reject covert URs—including usage-based models relying exclusively on observed exemplars to form lexical representations—have difficulty accounting for these facts.
abstracts.009319: In this paper I put together two ingredients: (i) featurally relativized probes (Béjar 2003 et seq.); (ii) a featural approach to the A/Ā-distinction (van Urk 2015). These two, combined, predict that we should find movement phenomena that are non-local, and yet show no other Ā-type properties (i.e. "non-local A-movement"). I show that this does in fact exist: in Äiwoo, a less local argument can move to spec,TP over a closer one if it has the right features. The existence of this type of movement supports van Urk (2015)'s argument that the locality properties of canonical A/Ā-movement are completely epiphenomenal, and only determined by the features searched for by the movement-triggering probe. Even without appealing to Ā-features of any kind (i.e., without resorting to "mixed A/Ā-movement"), we can still derive this kind of non-strictly-local A-movement as long as there is a featural motivation for it. [Note: this paper is a proceedings-sized, simplified version of what I cover in chapters 3/6 of my dissertation (Roversi 2025, "Locality: a case study from Äiwoo"), also posted on lingbuzz.]
abstracts.009320: This article provides a contrastive analysis of the constructions nem todos (os) in Brazilian Portuguese (BP) and bù dōu (“not all”) in Mandarin, focusing on their formal-semantic properties and implications for the teaching of Portuguese as an Additional Language (PAL). Following Quadros Gomes (2023), we argue that nem functions as a discourse-structuring particle: when combined with todo, it denies the universality of quantification and corrects expectations of totality anchored in the conversational background. In contrast, bù dōu in Mandarin operates as a more general sentential negation, without equivalent positional restrictions. We also compare these constructions with todos não/dōu bù, which express total negation and are frequently lexicalized in BP as ninguém/nenhum (“nobody/none”). After formally examining these interactions between negation and quantification, we propose a task-based pedagogical activity designed to foster the meaningful use of nem todos (os) in the teaching of BP to Mandarin speakers. We conclude that such contrastive analyses not only deepen the formal-semantic description but also provide pedagogical insights for integrating form and meaning in the language classroom.
abstracts.009322: One of the main challenges of language science is to draw inferences about internal computations from external observations–in recent terminology, to deduce what is I-language from E-language. Since grammars, human or otherwise, are presumptively part of brain-internal computational systems, their activity is typically not directly observable, for example, in terms of the sentences or “language” that comprise external behavior. This gap is part of a long history of a tension between reductionist and emergentist approaches in the analysis of complex systems, extensively and explicitly analyzed, perhaps most famously explicated by David Marr in terms of his notion of “three levels of explanation.” More recently, in the context of speech and language, David Poeppel has dubbed this the “mapping problem,” and during the past two decades there have been many explicit attempts by neuroscientists and cognitive/computational linguists to address this issue. Here we examine one specific computational way in which Marr’s levels and Poeppel’s mapping problem might be concretely realized: how “grammars” engaged as language parsers can be obscured from direct observation, even given (hypothetical) direct observation of the human brain’s neural activity at the individual neuronal level in known language areas. This thought experiment suggests that the challenge of how linguistic computations are actually implemented in the brain might be even more difficult than generally has been thought. It amounts to an updating of David Marr’s methodological program that might well also be called “Moro’s Problem,” in light of Andrea Moro’s efforts in a series of research papers over the past several decades that also aim to bridge between direct brain recordings and what we know about human language syntax.
abstracts.009323: The problematic syntactic symmetry which disallows linearization, is mirrored by an equally problematic symmetry in the semantic component. I will explore the conjecture that movement chains can solve the problem in the compositional interpretation as well.
abstracts.009324: Recent literature treats nominals bearing non-structural case either as ordinary DPs or as DPs encapsulated in a structural shell (PP or KP). This paper argues that both representations must be recognized in the grammar, since both co-exist within a single language. Novel observations from ATB movement in Greek reveal that the class of non-structural genitives is syntactically heterogeneous in this language: not all genitives can combine with each other in ATB movement, despite their systematic identity in form. The paper argues that assigning some genitives the status of plain DPs and others the status of PPs correctly accounts for the asymmetries in ATB movement, which is independently subject to a category-matching constraint in Greek. This analysis additionally allows for a unification of the ATB observations with previously noted asymmetries between the three non-structural genitive classes regarding cliticization, clitic doubling, and the availability of a PP alternant. Alongside the crucial categorial difference, this unified account relies on independently motivated thematic differences associated with the distinct genitive classes in Greek.
abstracts.009325: This paper provides evidence favoring one of two hypotheses regarding the structure of measure phrases in pseudopartitives ( three boxes of books ). It compares the ‘Spec’ hypothesis (Schwarzschild, 2006), which places measure phrases ( three books ) in Specifier position of the substance, and the the ‘Comp’ hypothesis (Stickney, 2009), which places substance phrases ( of books ) in Complement position of the measure. Only the latter requires nominal complements to nominals (recursion inside NP, which has been more controversial than clausal recursion – Stowell, 1989; Frank and Kroch, 1994; Frank, 2002; Chomsky, 2008; Kayne, 2008; Citko, 2014). The Spec hypothesis is motivated by semantic considerations relating to ‘Monotonicity’, but Monotonicity appearing in verbal comparatives (Wellwood 2019) undercuts this as an argument for this syntax for pseudopartitives. Syntactic diagnostics (agreement, constituency, movement and ellipsis, and locality) show that the Spec hypothesis cannot be correct.
abstracts.009326: Lewis (2023, 2024) proposes that languages that use the same marking to indicate additive and associative plural must lack free-standing definite articles (e.g. Turkish, Japanese). This property is attributed to these languages instantiating the negative value of the DP parameter. Based on original fieldwork data from Rural Iberian Spanish, we show that this variety of Spanish is a genuine counterexample to Lewis's generalization: plural-marked first names (e.g. lo-s Roman-es) may be understood additively or associatively; crucially, a plural-marked definite determiner is obligatory for the associative understanding. Based on a series of diagnostics, we argue that plural-marked names understood associatively are referential expressions, much like bare unmarked proper names, and as such they require a proprial definite article. From our findings, we can conclude that the presence or absence of dedicated associative morphology is not reducible to different values of the DP parameter. Instead, the presence or absence of dedicated associative morphology will depend on the interplay of two factors: (A) the syntactic representation available to generate plural referential expressions; and (B) the rules of exponence for the relevant terminal nodes in the language.
abstracts.009327: This paper is aimed at accounting for the limited distribution of the wide scope existential (WSE) uses of bare dual NPs in Kazym Khanty. The author argues that the reason for this limitation is pragmatic in nature: while bare duals are existential quantifiers and the ability to get wide scope is always semantically available, some WSE uses are independently blocked by a QUD-based constraint. Namely, in such cases, bare duals are infelicitous because they are forced to address a QUD that targets their not-at-issue content, namely the duality meaning. The case of Kazym Khanty bare duals shows that absence of a WSE reading in a particular sentence does not suggest that the tested NP can not take variable scope and that the QUD parameter should be controlled for to avoid a “false negative” result.
abstracts.009328: The Projection Principle (Beaver et al. 2017) states that semantic content projects iffit is not-at-issue. This paper presentsa counterexample to this claim: the dual number in Kazym Khanty featuringthe duality implication that is not-at-issue content that does not project.
abstracts.009329: This paper investigates how Korean Sign Language marks anaphoric definiteness, focusing on NPLOC and NP-IXTHIS. Two central claims are that in Korean Sign Language, NPLOC is a strong definite comparable to demonstrative anaphoric NPs in spoken Korean, and that NP-IXTHIS, which combines a nominal with simultaneous pointing, encodes anaphoric noteworthiness, paralleling emphatic demonstratives like “this very N” in spoken English. We propose a formal semantic analysis of NPLOC and NP-IXTHIS, adopting Kim’s (2023b) locative-relation based framework, in which indexing and locus are separated from each other. The proposed analysis will be shown to have implications for anaphoric definiteness marking in American Sign Language as well as other (bare noun) languages.
abstracts.009330: The article provides an overview of variability in natural language by looking at the limits of intra-individual, inter-individual, and crosslinguistic variability at all levels of grammar. We review evidence for the hypothesis that variability forms an integral part of natural language and often provides valuable insights into speakers’ linguistic competence. We will discuss in turn (i.) different subtypes of variability; (ii.) the difference between systematic linguistic variability, as driven by grammar or processing-related factors, and random noise including performance errors; (iii.) the phenomenon of hidden variability, where linguistic expressions can differ in their underlying structure in spite of parallel surface strings; (iv.) the extent to which variability is accounted for in existing grammatical theories; (v.) variability in experimental quantitative data as a window into the underlying grammatical systems and processing mechanisms; (vi.) variability in language as an important trigger for diachronic change and language acquisition.
abstracts.009331: We test whether language models (LMs) exhibit sensitivity to fine-grained discourse features that influence referential form choice in human language. Using a controlled paradigm from prior behavioral studies, we evaluate 19 LMs on their ability to distinguish between demonstratives (e.g., that) and definites (e.g., the) when referring back to previously mentioned entities, using expert-created stimuli across four languages (English, German, Turkish, Mandarin). In human data, demonstratives show selective licensing effects based on the presence or absence of contrastive noun phrases and discourse continuity. We find that only larger models replicate these effects reliably, with stronger correspondence to human judgments and higher item-level correlation. These results suggest that pragmatic constraints on reference are increasingly achievable at scale, and they introduce a new cross-linguistic testbed for probing the pragmatic competence of LMs.
abstracts.009332: This paper introduces CV Wave Theory, a unified framework for understanding connected speech simplification. Human speech unfolds as a continuous stream shaped by the principle of articulatory economy. The theory formalizes spoken language as oscillations between consonantal closure (C, valleys) and vocalic openness (V, peaks), conceptualizing entire sentences as “one long word.” By modeling speech as a CV waveform, the model explains why phenomena such as linking, elision, reduction, and assimilation naturally occur: consonant clusters collapse into a single valley (e.g., next day → [neks deɪ]), adjacent vowels trigger linking or intrusion (e.g., law(r) and order), and non-prominent vowels reduce to schwa (e.g., going to → [gənə]). The framework extends beyond English. Cross-linguistic data from French (liaison), Spanish, Mandarin, and Russian show that syllable structures and vowel fusion also exhibit CV-wave dynamics, suggesting that CV Wave Theory may capture a universal principle of spoken fluency. The contribution of this model is threefold: 1. Integration – it unifies multiple connected speech phenomena under a single explanatory framework. 2. Visualization – it provides a waveform-based representation of speech rhythm. 3. Predictive power – it anticipates which sounds are most likely to be weakened, elided, or linked. CV Wave Theory bridges phonetics, phonology, and articulatory physiology, offering both a theoretical and pedagogical tool for analyzing natural speech flow.
abstracts.009333: The Unaccusativity Hypothesis (UH) is supported by unaccusative-unergative distinctions in English resultatives, but is challenged by the apparent lack of such distinctions in Mandarin resultatives. This paper shows that, despite appearances to the contrary, Mandarin transitive resultatives do exhibit unaccusative–unergative distinctions, and proposes a non-uniform analysis of Mandarin resultatives with unaccusative abd unergative matrix verbs, in accordance with UH. The proposal not only sheds new light on the Uniformity of Theta-Assignment Hypothesis, but also advances a general theory of resultative argument structure.
abstracts.009334: Romanian stands apart from its Western Romance counterparts in the evolution of the Latin neuter. While most Romance languages resolved neuter nouns into either masculine or feminine classes—often reanalyzing neuter plurals (‑a) as feminine singulars—Romanian preserved the neuter as a distinct morphological and syntactic class in the singular, but innovated by assigning feminine plural agreement to neuter nouns. This development constitutes a mirror-image reanalysis: instead of eliminating the neuter distinction through full assimilation, Romanian maintains the category by reinterpreting its plural behavior. The result is a system that is both morphologically conservative and syntactically adaptive, retaining a Latin inheritance in uniquely Romanian terms.
abstracts.009335: Since the middle of the 20th century, a fierce battle is being fought between symbolic and distributed approaches to language and cognition. The success of deep learning models, and LLMs in particular, has been alternatively taken as showing that the distributed camp has won, or dismissed as an irrelevant engineering development. In this position paper, I argue that deep learning models for language actually represent a synthesis between the two traditions. This is because 1) deep learning architectures allow for both distributed/continuous/fuzzy and symbolic/discrete/categorical-like representations and processing; 2) models trained on language make use of this flexibility. In particular, I review recent research in interpretability that showcases how a substantial part of morphosyntactic knowledge is encoded in a near-discrete fashion in LLMs. This line of research suggests that different behaviors arise in an emergent fashion, and models flexibly alternate between the two modes (and everything in between) as needed. This is possibly one of the main reasons for their wild success; and it makes them particularly interesting for the study of language. Is it time for peace?
abstracts.009336: The term “Mentawai”, which has been haphazardly applied to the languages indigenous to the Mentawai island chain off the coast of West Sumatra, is not an endogenous identifier for any of the language groups which it covers. However, due in large part to a lack of adequate primary data, these languages have hitherto been treated as exemplifying a singular “Mentawai” language, accompanied by either the (baseless) insistence that the island chain is linguistically unified, or an addendum regretting the inadequacy of presuming a single “Mentawai” language, and stating that the true status of these languages requires further investigation. This paper aims to resolve this undesirable situation by reconstructing the phonology, phonotactics, and part of the lexicon of the shared proto-language of the Mentawai languages. In doing so, it confirms the status of the Mentawai languages as constituting a small subfamily of closely related but nonetheless distinct languages, comparable to the Batak subfamily on the Sumatran mainland. Sound changes and numerous irregular processes are posited to explain the evolution of Proto-Mentawai from Proto-Sumatran and into its various daughter languages. Finally, the status of the Mentawai (sub)family as a primary branch of the recently described Sumatran family is evaluated; evidence for subgrouping with Enggano and Central Barrier Islands is evaluated in turn, with a potential link to Enggano showing promise on account of shared idiosyncracies in pronominal indexing.
abstracts.009340: This paper revisits Saussure’s scalar analysis of phonemes, offering a modern reinterpretation that replaces binary features with phonological dimensions grounded in measurement theory. By redefining Saussure’s [openness] and [backness] as ordered scales and Chomsky and Halle’s “combination and concatenation” as partially ordered scales, the paper introduces a notion of “[phono]logical simultaneity.” This framework renders the variously-defined phoneme and segment redundant, and shifts the focus of distinctiveness to the linguistic sign, the morpheme. It demonstrates how phonological dimensions link continuous articulations and acoustic signals (e.g., F1 and F2) with discrete linguistic signs through calibrated distinctive features. The analysis identifies Saussure’s two dimensions as the only universal phonological dimensions, with all others being optional, providing a novel basis for cross-linguistic classification. By reframing distinctive features as discrete calibrations of phonological dimensions, the paper reconciles high-level morphophonemic processes (e.g., vowel harmony) with phonetic alternations. Furthermore, it proposes an algorithm for discovering phonological dimensions, applicable both to specific languages and linguistic universals, advancing the theoretical scope of phonology. This work positions phonological dimensions as essential for linguistic analysis, bridging phonetics and phonology while situating distinctive features within interlinguistics, socio-linguistics, and historical linguistics, opening avenues for understanding the universality and specificity of language structure and use.
abstracts.009341: Pierre Marie, the arch-enemy of Jules Déjerine and Augusta Klumpke-Déjerine, is apparently enjoying a new wave of popular- ity (Coutinho, Caramelli & Teive 2021, Weiller, Glauche & Rijntjes 2022) . While some of his anatomical work may be justly appreciated, a careful reading of his work on aphasia indicates that his theoretical stance was deeply flawed.
abstracts.009345: Grammatical patterns of intra-sentential code-switching (ICS) provide a testing ground for architectural questions in generative linguistics. ICS shows that bilinguals are able to derive sentences containing material in more than one language. We investigate the nature of a minimal unit for ICS, which must remain unilingual, and propose to derive it from already established properties of grammar, specifically the mapping from syntax to phonology. We report data from three acceptability studies on Hebrew-English bilinguals, investigating ICS patterns at the CP edge, the DP edge, and with pronominal subjects. Our results point to a prosodically-defined minimal unit for ICS, which does not adhere to the boundaries established by Phase theory, contra López et al. (2017)’s theory of “code-switching by Phase”.
abstracts.009346: Famously, English conditional constructions licence the use of past tense verb forms to refer to present or future time and the use of past perfect structures where we would normally expect to see past simple ones. The occurrence of such verb forms in conditionals is here termed “conditional backshift” in line with scholars such as Dancygier (1998). Across linguistics, philosophy, psychology and related fields the standard view is that conditional backshift conveys that the proposition in the antecedent of the conditional is unlikely to occur, is regarded with doubt by the speaker or is counterfactual. The aim of this paper is to overturn the standard view. To this end, two sets of data are presented. The first is a body of theoretical evidence from the language. The second consists of the results from a research survey administered to 1,300 respondents from a UK Russell Group university. The results provide overwhelming evidence that conditional backshift neither entails nor implicates improbability, negative epistemic stance or counterfactuality on the part of speakers.
abstracts.009347: In Cinque 2013 I considered one potential argument for Universal Grammar. One stemming from the limited number of functional notions that are grammatically encoded in the languages of the world. What we find is that only a fraction of our cognitive concepts and distinctions seems to receive a grammatical encoding. Here I focus on the specific domain of emotions.
abstracts.009348: On the strength of novel data from Tamil, which notably lacks hyperraising but optionally allows (classic) raising, this paper argues against two prominent analyses of hyperraising – in terms of the Activity Condition and in terms of CP intervention – which, we will show, overgenerate the possibility of hyperraising in this language. In contrast, we show that proposals that seek to explain the availability of hyperraising in terms of the Williams Cycle (WC, Williams, 2003) acting in conspiracy with the Phase Impenetrability Condition (PIC, Chomsky, 2001, et seq.) accurately predict its absence in Tamil. Further independent empirical support for this line of analysis comes from Spanish, Tiriki and varieties of colloquial English, showing that a hyperraised subject in these languages occupies a higher-than-canonical position that is at least as high as Spec, CP. On the strength of these findings, we propose that hyperraising is possible in some language L if and only if long subject movement can obtain in L without violating the PIC or WC, and the subject A-moves to an athematic position. A language that manifests hyperraising must conjunctively satisfy all and only these input conditions. Since there are many ways to violate these conditions and exactly one way to obey them, our proposal also predicts the crosslinguistic rarity of this phenomenon.
abstracts.009350: This position paper introduces the concept of noun reverse entailment, a bidirectional inference mechanism that formalizes how derived noun forms (e.g., plurals, possessives, nominalizations) entail backward to confirm the base form’s nominal properties. I propose the Reverse Entailment Diagnostic (RED), a tool for proving that lexical and syntactic entities (including phrases and parts of speech) can act as syntactical noun entities in dynamic linguistic contexts. Using examples like “square/quadrilateral,” “to book carefully,” and “her house,” I demonstrate how RED reveals category flexibility, challenging rigid lexicalist frameworks and supporting usage-based models. This framework has implications for syntax, semantics, and cognitive linguistics, emphasizing listener interpretation and holistic sentence processing
abstracts.009351: This paper argues that Roots introduce their own internal arguments (IAs) as complements. Korean non-derived nominals with argument-licensing capacity (Yoon & Park 2008) and their light verb (LV) predicate counterparts must utilize a √(Root)P (Harley 2014), as both verbal and nominal functional alternatives are empirically inadequate. Comparison across different types of LV constructions reveals that low IAs introduced directly by Roots and higher IAs introduced by verbal functional structure can be empirically differentiated by differential object marking, with low IAs necessarily originating in an acategorical constituent (the √P). Consequently, Roots are fully functioning syntactic heads that project phrases and take complements, contrary to the mainstream view of Roots in decompositional morphosyntactic theory, which assumes Roots to be syntactically deficient, unable to introduce complements and unable to exist in a structure without assistance from categorizing heads (e.g., Alexiadou 2014; Borer 2003, 2014; Lohndal 2020; Merchant 2019; Embick & Marantz 2008).
abstracts.009352: This paper investigates restrictions on subject movement within Chomsky's (2024) MC framework, which replaces successive-cyclic movement with an interpretive operation, Access. We decompose Chomsky's Access into two parts, proposing a phase-level operation, Mark, which determines which syntactic objects are available to the interpretive systems. We argue that restrictions on subject movement are derived from the interaction of Mark with theta-domains, assuming that the CP phase delimits the domain of Mark. Based on this idea, we analyze the that-trace effect, subject island constraints, and the movement of subjects in passives, raising predicates, and copular constructions. We further extend the framework to account for island and the that-t effects in multiple wh interrogatives. The analysis suggests that movement restrictions fall into two categories: syntactic constraints on Mark, and constraints that block reconstruction across islands. Comparing our proposal with Chomsky's (2024) and Kitahara's (2024) frameworks, we argue that the accessibility for Access is detemined by whether a syntactic object is located in a theta-domain, thereby offering a novel perspective on the division between predicate and discourse structures in human language.
abstracts.009353: This paper is concerned with a set of diagnostics – agent-oriented adverbs, instruments and passivization – that are commonly used to detect the presence of a thematic Voice head. It analyzes a hitherto undocumented construction in Turkish, involvee causatives (InvCs). While InvCs surface with standard causative morphosyntax, they do not receive a causative interpretation and also fail the above diagnostics. In previous work, this profile has been taken as evidence for an unaccusative syntax. For InvCs, however, a wide range of evidence contradicts an unaccusative analysis. InvCs do contain a thematic Voice layer, but their argument does not receive an agent interpretation, which accounts for the failure of the diagnostics. Overall, this study problematizes the use of only agent-oriented adverbs, instrument phrases and passivization as tests for thematic Voice and advocates for a more nuanced approach to unaccusativity diagnostics.
abstracts.009354: The observation that wh-expressions in many languages can be interpreted either interrogatively or non-interrogatively has led to the widely accepted thesis that wh-expressions originate as variables, with their interpretations determined through being bound by a question operator or other non-interrogative operators (Cheng 1991; Li 1992; Tsai 1994; Cheng & Huang 1996; among others). However, recent studies on a specific non-interrogative wh-construction in Mandarin—wh-conditionals—challenge this variable-binding approach (Liu 2016, 2017; Xiang 2016, 2020; Li 2021). In wh-conditionals, two wh-clauses are connected to express a conditional meaning. These studies advocate for a question-based approach, proposing that the meaning of wh-conditionals stems from interrogative meaning rather than variable binding. As a result, the question-based approach predicts that wh-conditionals should be linguistically closer to wh-questions than to other non-interrogative wh-constructions. This paper confirms the prediction using wh-constructions in Khorchin Mongolian. Despite their distinct theoretical commitments, the two approaches can be reconciled to address challenges pointed out by Cheng & Huang (2020), Tsai (2023), and Pan & Kuang (2023) to the question-based view.
abstracts.009355: This article introduces the Reverse Entailment Diagnostic (RED), a novel bidirectional inference mechanism demonstrating that all parts of speech can be nominalized to occupy nounslot positions (e.g., subject, object) as syntactical noun entities, suggesting a universal noun slot in the linguistic mind. Using examples—“square/quadrilateral,” “to book carefully,” and “her house”— across English, Mandarin, and Tongan, I show how derived forms (e.g., possessives, nominalizations) entail backward to confirm nominal potential. RED challenges lexicalist frameworks like Transformational Generative Grammar, supporting dynamic models such as Distributed Morphology and Construction Grammar. Cross-linguistic evidence and cognitive implications underscore a universal cognitive capacity for nominalization, with applications in syntax, semantics, and natural language processing
abstracts.009356: Children can use distributional information about where words occur to figure out their meanings. But what happens when two very different words not only have most of their distribution in common, but also compose to form indistinguishable sentential meanings in those common cases? As a negative polarity item (NPI), any is selectively licensed by certain linguistic environments, the most common of which is negation. This is the context in which children hear any in around 80% of their input. However, under negation, the meaning of any looks just like a negative quantifier in concord with the higher negation (a negative concord item; NCI). While studies of children’s production indicate that they hardly ever produce any without a licensing negation, suggesting competence with its distribution, we hypothesize that some children may have misanalysed its meaning. To investigate what children think any means, we tested 106 monolingual English-speaking children between 2 and 6 years of age, as well as 20 adults, in two picture-choice comprehension tasks. These tasks assessed their interpretation of any without a preceding negation, both in a licensed (free choice) and an unlicensed context. While most children interpreted any the same way adults did, we also found a group of children who systematically responded to any as if it meant no, consistent with a negative concord (mis)analysis. In addition to illustrating how much children rely on distributional information to learn such abstract words, this finding bears on several debates. It raises the question of whether it is possible to represent the licensing conditions of NPIs prior to knowing their meanings. And it suggests that children may be biased to assume that their language uses negative concord constructions even when it does not.
abstracts.009357: This paper examines the properties of existential constructions in Serbian and Lithuanian. Existential constructions share some interpretive properties with locative constructions, in that both express a proposition about the existence or the presence of someone or something in a context. However, Serbian and Lithuanian existentials display a cluster of properties that set them apart from locatives: unmarked verb-subject order (with pivot following copula), lack of agreement between copula and post-copular pivot, genitive case on the pivot and a dedicated form of the copula. The case properties of the pivot in existentials depend on specific interpretive properties related to agentivity, volitionality and definiteness and there are structural distinctions between existential and locatives, which are captured in syntax with parallel Agree operations: in locatives, the copula agrees with the pivot; in existentials, it agrees with an expletive pro.
abstracts.009358: D-quantification and A-quantification are two basic apparatuses of meaning in natural language. There has, however, been a recent attempt to reduce the former to the latter, especially for exclusive focus particles, where adfocal only is claimed to be a "concord" marker, whereas adverbial only functions as an exclusive operator (A-quantifier) (Quek & Hirsch 2017; Branan & Erlewine 2023, among others). This paper argues that such a view is too strong and cannot be upheld universally. Specifically, I argue that both D- and A-quantification are available in the semantic domain of exclusives. Crucial data are drawn from Vietnamese and Yorùbá, where adverbial and adfocal particles are lexicalized differently ( chỉ and mỗi ; kàn and nìkan , respectively) and may be doubled with the same focus association ("exclusive doubling"). I show that the choice between D- or A-quantification is parameterized: while Vietnamese adverbial chỉ is an exclusive operator, Yorùbá adfocal nìkan is an exclusive (D-)quantifier, with evidence from backward association, multiple association with focus, scopal interaction with negation, and wide scope under ellipsis. Furthermore, I demonstrate a four-way typology of exclusive doubling, in which exclusive semantics may be encoded on (i) adverbial particles (e.g., Vietnamese); (ii) adfocal particles (e.g., Yorùbá); (iii) neither of them but rather a null operator (e.g., Kasem; pace Aremu forthcoming); or (iv) both of them (e.g., Mandarin; pace Sun 2021). Finally, I discuss how this typology parallels variations in negative concord (Biberauer & Zeijlstra 2012).
abstracts.009359: This article examines two operations which are used to encode focus in Czech: word order alternation and stress shift. Based on data from a previous production experiment, we ran a rating study where participants rated the authenticity of utterances with manipulated information structure. The results showed that alternating word order to encode focus is free, supporting the claims about the flexibility of Czech word order. Shifting stress is a more costly operation -- it is possible (in terms of competence), but it is not necessarily easy (in terms of performance). Moreover, applying a word order alternation and stress shift at the same time (in object fronting cases) leads to a significant decrease in rating, which cannot be accounted for by a mere cumulative effect of noncanonical word order and noncanonical stress. We argue instead that the noncanonical structure is blocked by a more economical one, where the same information structure is conveyed with the default structure and prosodic pattern.
abstracts.009361: Version change: Missing bibliography added. We discuss number, and to a lesser extent person, feature value cooccurrence restrictions between a head (Tense here) and a conjoined DP subject. We conclude that these restrictions instantiate semantic agreement, which arises in cases in which the features values on T do not match the features values of this DP. In the case of conjunction, this is because, we conclude, a conjunction of DPs lacks such features as there are no syntactic feature resolution rules. Instead, semantic agreement on T is ad sensum, meaning based, and can trigger presuppositions on the subject's denotation. We also discuss cumulative agreement cases, concluding it is not semantic, at least not in the same sense. [More general cases of semantic agreement are discussed here: https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/009362 ]
abstracts.009362: This latest version is the published version augmented with a few post publication comments (appearing in red in the ms.) We discuss cases in which agreement between a head and a DP seems to drive, or be driven by, interpretive properties of this DP rather than its syntactic properties as for example in: (i) this team are ready; (ii) une moitié de nous six est/sont/ sommes toujours présent(e/s) (one half of us six is/are-3P/are-1P always present). This discussion centers mostly on the case of subject/verb number and person agreement (but its conclusions would extend to other cases of agreement between a head and a DP). In such a configuration, agreement features on T do not seem to match the feature values of its DP subject. We conclude that features on agreeing heads (probes in the Agree sense of Chomsky, 2000) can and sometimes must be semantically interpretable. In such cases, the values of the features on T can target the denotational properties of its DP subject, instead of its syntactic phi-feature (values): they can or must trigger a presupposition about this DP subject’s denotation. We also conclude that person agreement is always semantic (presuppositional). [The specific case of semantic agreement in coordination is discussed here: https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/009361 ]
abstracts.009363: This article introduces the Reverse Entailment Diagnostic (RED), a bidirectional inference mechanism that demonstrates the universal capacity of all parts of speech—nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, interjections, and articles—to be nominalized into syntactical noun entities occupying noun-slot positions (e.g., subject, object). This capacity suggests a universal noun slot in the linguistic mind, a cognitive mechanism enabling flexible categorization. Using examples—“square/quadrilateral,” “to book carefully,” and “her house”—across English, Mandarin, Tongan, Spanish, and Arabic, we illustrate how derived forms (e.g., possessives, nominalizations) entail backward to confirm nominal potential. RED challenges lexicalist frameworks like Transformational Generative Grammar (TGG), aligning with dynamic models such as Distributed Morphology (DM) and Construction Grammar (CG). Supported by cross-linguistic evidence, neurological findings, and novel computational applications in natural language processing (NLP)—including syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling (SRL), and multilingual disambiguation—RED bridges theoretical linguistics, cognitive science, and computational linguistics. A proposed RED-based algorithm enhances NLP pipelines, with implications for parsing complex nominals and low-resource languages
abstracts.009364: This paper reanalyses the morphosyntactic–semantic structure of Japanese nominal adjectives (NAs), also referred to as na-adjectives. The core of NAs lies in NA stems ending in '-ni', as in 'jukai-ni' "pleasant" and 'suki-ni' "like". These NA stems are lexical predicates selecting either one argument or two — a theme in 'jukai-ni' and an experiencer–theme pair in 'suki-ni'. However, outside small clauses serving as complements of cognition or perception verbs, as in 'watasi=wa [sore=o jukai-ni] omot-ta/kanzi-ta' "I found/felt [it pleasant]", they cannot function as predicates in their bare '-ni' form. Consequently, an NA stem forms a nominal-adjective phrase containing PRO, as in [PRO jukai-ni], which constitutes the complement of the adjunctive-conjunction suffix '-te', yielding a ConjP such as [[PRO jukai-ni]-te]. This ConjP is then adjoined to — or, metaphorically, "parasitises on" — the VP headed by the one-argument existential verb 'ar-' within a (topic-marked) tensed construction, as in [soreᵢ=wa tᵢ ar-Ø-Ø] "it exists" ('-Ø-Ø' represents the sequence of the covert allomorph of the non-past suffix '-ru' followed by the phonologically null functional head Topic⁰Ø). Only in this configuration can the NA stem function as one of the two predicates of an independent simple sentence, as in [soreᵢ=wa [PROᵢ jukai-ni-te] tᵢ ar-Ø-Ø] "(lit.) it, being pleasant, exists". This construction surfaces as 'sore=wa jukai-d-a' [soreᵢ=wa [PROᵢ jukai-d] tᵢ a-Ø-Ø], schematically representable as EXIST(it) ⋀ PLEASANT(it) — whose default negation is, as expected, the scope-limited EXIST(it) ⋀ ¬PLEASANT(it), realised as 'sore=wa jukai-de=wa/jukai-dj-a nai' "(lit.) it, not being pleasant, exists", crucially with the scope-limiting '=wa' or its more colloquial allomorph '-a'.
abstracts.009365: Most literature on 'too' has focused on its "regular" uses, where, as a first approximation, 'too' triggers a presupposition that one of the focus alternatives to its prejacent, distinct from the prejacent itself, is true (e.g., 'Axel likes cats.
