abstracts.009543: This paper examines not just how evidentiality functions as a grammatical category in literary Georgian, but also looks at new strategies not found in standard written texts. In many cases, these dialectal constructions show that evidentiality is evolving new forms and functions not typical of the written language: newly grammaticalized suffixes =q'opil and =ot for the unwitnessed past tense, the extension of such forms in some dialects into the nonperfective present and past tenses, and the development of witnessed evidential constructions from earlier confirmative particles. It is argued language contact with other regional languages Megrelian, Chechen, Turkish and Azerbaijani may underlie such trends.
abstracts.009544: Though less threatened with extinction than languages of some other parts of the world, the languages of the Caucasus present a number of opportunities to examine language endangerment through a unique sociolinguistic and typological lens. The following paper will survey the state of such endangered languages: how many languages there are, what kinds of language ecologies form their social milieu, and the kinds, rates and causes of language shift in the region. It will also survey the role of language contact in the region, including how processes of multilingualism, borrowing and structural convergence and codeswitching operate in situations of language maintenance, substrate, adstrate and obsolescence effects. It will examine some of the unique structural aspects of endangered languages in the Caucasus, including typological rara and look at how some of these features change: over/under-generalization of marked features, gain/loss of phonological and morphosyntactic contrasts, as well as over-all typological shift.
abstracts.009545: This paper argues that language loss and endangerment, especially in multiethnic conflict zones like the Caucasus, are not incidental outcomes of conflict but are structured by the same forces that drive displacement and institutional breakdown. Drawing on case studies from Georgia, Armenia, and Azerbaijan, I examine how political violence and public policy reconfigure linguistic ecologies through demographic shocks, forced migration, and state-led cultural assimilation.
abstracts.009546: **This is a draft of a paper that was presented at Sinn und Bedeutung 30. Please share any comments or feedback with me via email: tomgjralston 'at' gmail.com** Predicates such as 'are extinct' or 'are widespread' have long been assumed to apply only to kinds. I present evidence that the predicates typically described as kind-level are numerous-type collective predicates, based on their interaction with all and their failure to exhibit homogeneity effects. This undermines the principal semantic motivation for analysing their bare plural arguments as kind-denoting. Instead, I argue that their arguments are type 𝑒 expressions and that plural kind predication is just plural predication. I give a compositional semantics for bare plurals and explain differences between bare and definite plurals in terms of the situation argument that can restrict their domain.
abstracts.009547: Much work has shown that wh-movement is subject to several kinds of locality restrictions cross-linguistically. I propose that these restrictions arise when [wh] projects past the maximal projection that it came from. When this happens, it intervenes for wh-movement, trapping the wh-element in its base position, unless it can escape through other means. The need to escape the domain of [wh] is proposed to capture the distribution of successive-cyclic movement and interactions with Voice in different languages. Different locality conditions in different languages are captured by different distributions of the same features and probes.
abstracts.009548: The paper discusses the uses of conditional and interrogative complementizers in Old High German (section 2) and Saurian (section 3). Based on empirical evidence from these varieties, we will go into the diachronic pathways through which conditional complementizers take over interrogative functions in a cyclical manner (section 4). Section 5 discusses whether the reverse path (from interrogative to conditional complementizer) is also attested. Section 6 concludes the paper.
abstracts.009549: In this work, I argue that the natural language item part (and its translational equivalents) is the same as the mereological notion of PROPER PART, full stop. While this seems trivially true, state-of-the-art semantics often assumes this is not the case; Link (1983) posits two parthood relations for part of an individual and part of a plurality (MATERIAL vs. ATOMIC parts), and those who assume one relation posit additional constraints on the transitivity of parthood (Moltmann, 1997; Wagiel, 2021). The latter is done in service of the observation that parts of atomic individuals seemingly cannot be part of a plurality. For example, a world where only Jerry Seinfeld’s hand is completely covered in paint is not a verifying case for (1). (1) Part of the New Yorkers are completely covered in paint. I will argue against the approaches outlined above, opting to instead include parts of atoms in the denotation of plural partitives. The interpretation we get for (1), I propose, is actually the result of pragmatics rather than semantics (Grice, 1975’s MAXIM OF QUANTITY). This position is bolstered by the fact that the “inclusive” reading of a plural partitive becomes available under negation and epistemic uncertainty (cf. plurals, Sauerland et al. 2005). Presented at OASIS 5, 4 December 2025.
abstracts.009551: According to a prominent pragmatics model, assertions update the context set and imperatives update the to-do lists of the global context. While there has been a long tradition to posit a localized context set (“the local context”), no attempt has been made to localize the to-do list. We suggest that there is a need for local to-do lists, making the local context a pair of local context set and local to-do lists, to explain declaratives-and-imperative conjunctions and disjunctions (e.g, 'Don’t plagiarize or you’d be caught’).
abstracts.009552: This is a very old handout on controller shift (from 2011). Per request from colleagues who wish to cite the work, I am putting it available online. -- Wataru Uegaki === What would be a semantic account of control, which can capture the different controller choices, including the controller shift phenomenon? What do control facts tell us about the semantics of attitude reports? In this talk, I try to address these questions. I argue that controller choice is constrained in two independent ways: (i) De se requirement that the individual argument of the complement (i.e. PRO) must correspond to an attitude center; (ii) The matrix controller argument corresponds to the embedded agent. The facts about controller choice provide a new piece of evidence for the centered-world analysis of control.
abstracts.009553: This paper introduces the Lexical Ontology Persistence (LOP) Theorem, which formalizes the idea that words are persistent semantic entities with internal structure, independent of surface form convergence or contextual ambiguity. Extending LOP, words are framed as bidirectional entities, evolving both ontogenetically (within individual cognition) and phylogenetically (across historical and cultural contexts). Contrasting with quantum linguistics (QL), which models words as probabilistic superpositions collapsing under context, LOP emphasizes ontological persistence, neural representation, and computational tractability. Integrating insights from cognitive neuroscience and computational modeling, we show how words can be represented as structured neural networks and semantic embeddings preserving historical and individual constraints. This framework provides a biologically and computationally plausible model of meaning, offering an alternative to purely probabilistic, quantum-inspired approaches, and has implications for cognitive science, historical linguistics, and NLP.
abstracts.009554: This paper investigates the linearization of right node raising constructions (e.g., "Darius found and Jasmine took the book"). It finds that right node raising constructions can be linearized through an extension of Fox & Pesetsky’s (2005) Cyclic Linearization, termed Flexible Cyclic Linearization. In both proposals, linearization of syntactic structure happens in phases and obeys the property of Order Preservation: linear ordering statements established in a new phase cannot contradict those established in a previous phase. However, Cyclic Linearization and Flexible Cyclic Linearization crucially differ in that the latter permits ordering statements to be deleted in the phase in which they arise as necessary to linearize the syntactic object. Flexible Cyclic Linearization correctly linearizes right node raising constructions, and predicts those properties of right node raising that relate to linearization. In general, because it relies on the deletion of ordering statements, Flexible Cyclic Linearization can linearize parallel structures without adopting a specific algorithm for the generation of ordering statements.
abstracts.009555: The diminishing effect, a kind of norm-sensitivity, is observed in many natural language constructions: negative comparatives (e.g., He is no taller than I am), only-sentences (e.g., he is only 49 years old), and discourse-softening markers (e.g., Korean cina-ci anh- and Chinese bú guò ‘not beyond, nothing but, merely’), etc. All of these constructions give rise to the inference of ‘being below an expected norm’. I focus on the construction ‘no + comparative’ and propose that the diminishing effect arises from the interaction of two elements: (i) negation and (ii) universal quantification over items exceeding a certain degree d along a scale. I argue that (i) negating all values above d amounts to an even-sentence, (ii) when interpreting an even-sentence, we accommodate a degree QUD, such that the prejacent of even provides a maximally informative answer to this degree QUD, and (iii) a maximally informative degree is a superlative value with regard to a certain comparison class and is therefore necessarily norm-sensitive (see also Krifka 2000). I further extend this analysis to the diminishing effect of only.
abstracts.009556: Formal models of language change based on iterated learning have enjoyed considerable success in recent decades. One of the most influential of these accounts is the Variational Learner (Yang 2000, 2002}. This model offers an attractive way of deriving patterns of diachronic change, particularly S-curve phenomena, from a probabilistic model of variation. However, we demonstrate that this theory makes additional problematic predictions: that failed changes are impossible, and that more expressive grammars should always be preferred over less expressive competitors. These problems are traceable to the reinforcement learning algorithm that Yang uses in his acquisition-driven model of change. After showing that both predictions are falsified by a wide range of examples from various languages, we motivate a solution using a variant of the Variational Learner built instead around hierarchical Bayesian learning, an approach widely used in recent cognitive science research. This result underlines the importance of careful attention to learning algorithms, and suggests that there may be limits on the explanatory potential of iterated learning models for patterns of grammatical change.
abstracts.009557: Among the foundational questions for cognition is whether perceptual systems encode sensory input as continuous values or transform it into discrete mental representations. Speech—long a model system for probing the nature of perceptual representation—offers a critical testing ground. Yet the literature routinely conflates the content of representations (cue-based vs. category-based) with their granularity (continuous vs. discrete). Likewise, the well-known observation that incrementally varied stimuli often elicit graded behavioral responses, particularly when averaged across trials, is commonly taken as evidence for continuous internal representations. We challenge this assumption and synthesize the surrounding debate by introducing the Discrete Sampling (DS) framework, a novel theory under which listeners map continuous input into discrete, category-based internal states via a biologically plausible sampling procedure. We formalize a specific instantiation of DS computationally and demonstrate how it accounts for a wide range of core phenomena. We compare DS to a general class of continuous alternatives using data from 575 subjects across three experimental paradigms, with precise, differentiating predictions confirmed by the results. DS provides a single cognitive architecture for a parameter-independent derivation of binary and scalar categorization responses, concave reaction-time patterns centered on category boundaries, the joint modulation of categorization slope and processing speed by task demands and noise, and the distribution of inter-listener variability. We show how sampling from discrete categories can produce behavior traditionally taken to imply continuity, offering a unified reinterpretation of decades of evidence and reframing how uncertainty and apparent gradience are represented in perceptual and psychological systems more broadly.
abstracts.009558: This brief note discusses some of my experiences teaching at four EGG schools since 1998, as well as the experiences of some of my students and colleagues. I also reflect on the planned launch of another school for 2026, OVA, which explicitly draws inspiration from the EGG, but is also competing with it. Be sure to watch the video linked in footnote 3. (New version adds one minor point about gender balance stats and fixes a typo.)
abstracts.009559: The theory of semantic prosody posits that words acquire evaluative coloring through repeated collocation with positively or negatively charged contexts. While this usage-based framework effectively describes distributional patterns, it faces persistent theoretical challenges regarding directionality: does usage shape meaning, or does meaning shape usage? This paper demonstrates that for a significant class of frequently studied words, inherent lexical-semantic profiles act as primary filters that attract words to congruent discourse contexts, with collocational patterns emerging as consequences rather than causes of connotative meaning. Through systematic analysis of cause, utterly, commit, set in, foster, and regime, integrating published corpus analyses with theoretical linguistics, this study shows that their attested collocational skews reflect underlying semantic features—agentive, intensive, volitionally binding, gradual-onset, facilitative, and system-control profiles, respectively. Counterevidence from neutral and positive contexts in multiple corpora undermines claims of fixed evaluative prosodies while supporting profile-based explanations. Diachronic evidence demonstrates that semantic profiles remain stable across centuries even as specific collocational patterns vary, supporting the claim that profiles drive usage rather than absorbing evaluative charge from it. This reconceptualization addresses the problematic lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy, demonstrating through evidence from large language models, language testing, and cross-linguistic research that the traditional boundary between lexical meaning and world knowledge is far more permeable than conventional accounts acknowledge. The findings have practical implications for lexicography, natural language processing, and language pedagogy.
abstracts.009560: This paper analyzes the two-place comitative in Ch’ol, a Mayan language of Chiapas, Mexico. This construction behaves like a transitive verb in some respects: it licenses two arguments, exhibits variable agreement, and there are two distinct semantic roles. In other respects, however, it does not take aspect or verbalizing morphology. These properties set the two-place comitative apart from canonical verbs, motivating its classification as a pseudo-verb. The analysis links the availability of the construction to the high-/low-absolutive distinction in Mayan and draws parallels with clause-union phenomena in Romance and Germanic, contributing to the typology of complex predicates and restructuring.
abstracts.009561: This MA thesis develops a structural model of argument licensing and null arguments in German Sign Language (DGS) based on the formal projection of R-loci. I introduce Locus-Checking as a licensing operation that matches projected argument positions with structurally accessible, referentially specified loci. The analysis shows that patterns of overt and null argument realization in DGS are systematically constrained by the availability and internal structure of R-loci, rather than by verbal agreement morphology or purely discourse-based licensing. On this basis, the thesis offers a structurally grounded perspective on how DGS patterns of argument omission relate to existing typologies of null-argument systems, with particular reference to Roberts (2019).
abstracts.009562: In this paper, we discuss three languages of the Americas--Ch'ol (Mayan, Mexico), Mi'gmaq (Algonquian, Canada) and Maihiki (Tukanoan, Peru)--in light of their classifier and plural marking systems. Crucially, all three languages allow the co-occurrence of classifiers and plural marking. While Ch'ol and Mi'gmaq have been discussed before in the theoretical literature on classifiers (Bale and Coon 2014, Bale et al. 2019, Little et al. 2022), as prime examples of classifiers-for-numerals languages, Maihiki has not received much attention. For Ch'ol and Mi'gmaq, we contextualize our discussion not just on classifiers, as previous works have, but also on the existence of plural marking, adding in new data from Ch'ol on plurals. In Maihiki, we present a different type of classifier system from those of Ch'ol and Mi'gmaq---one in which classifiers modify nouns---but see again that classifiers and plurals co-occur. Together, the co-occurrence of classifiers and plurality in these three different systems suggest an even more complex empirical landscape than previously thought.
abstracts.009563: Mindset theory suggests that viewpoints about the phenomenon of intelligence, whether it is stable/fixed or plastic profile an individual learner’s approaches to learning, flexibility, and educational consequences (Dweck, 2006; Blackwell, Trzesniewski & Dweck, 2007). The current research investigates how tertiary level learners’ mindset orientation connects with their self-estimated IQ, responses of their behavior to educational obstacles, and school achievement. Data from 214 students exhibited that the learners who have a growth-mindset stated minor powerlessness, robust and flexible study approach, and extra adaptable self-estimates of intelligence in comparison to fixed-mindset colleagues, corresponding to results by Yeager and Dweck (2012) and Claro et al. (2016). Mindset exhibited an ordinary relationship with GPA, mirroring broader meta-analytic patterns stated by Sisk et al. (2018). The findings emphasize the significance of beliefs underpinning motivation in determining persistence in academic challenges.
abstracts.009565: The article argues that "RED (Reverse Entailment Diagnostic)" —a bidirectional test using nominalization/possessive packaging plus noun-slot verification—does more than show “anything can be nominalized.” If RED works systematically across categories and languages, it implies a stable **universal noun slot** (a referential position-type), and therefore a broader background structure: "ULD (Universal Linguistic Domain)", a geometrical space of "slot-families*" and licensed transitions. ULD is derived as minimally containing five families: "referential" (entity tracking), "predicational" (property/event attribution), " operator" (determiners/quantifiers/TAM/negation), "linking" (argument structure), and "packaging" (nominalization/embedding/coordination). The paper also integrates "exeme" as pre-typed expression material that becomes a "lexeme by placement" into ULD slots, not by prior association. It closes with testable neurocognitive predictions and computational applications (RED as weak supervision for slot/nominality detection in parsing and SRL).
abstracts.009566: This paper analyzes the FormSet operation as it has been defined and used in the literature specifically in the domain of conjunction structures. It finds that, though its use as a structure building operation must either contradict its definition and justification as a general-purpose preparatory operation or lead to unwanted empirical predictions. It goes on to show that, if we redefine MERGE as applying not to syntactic objects in a workspace but to n-ary sets of syntactic objects in a workspace, that we can retain the justification of FormSet without sacrificing empirical validity. Furthermore, it presents novel empirical arguments in favour of this redefined MERGE—that it correctly predicts the ambiguities raised by conjunction structure, that it correctly predicts a cross-linguistic gap in the plural anaphor system, and that it gives some insight into the system of number “features.”
abstracts.009567: This study investigates passivization errors with unaccusatives in L2 English, known as passive unaccusatives (e.g., *The apple was fallen from the table.). Two competing accounts are considered: the verbal passivization account (VPA), which attributes passive unaccusatives to misanalysis of unaccusatives as lexical causatives, and the structural passivization account (SPA), which explains them as overgeneralization of passive morphosyntax (be + -en). The two accounts yield distinct predictions concerning passivized intransitives and lexically causativized intransitives. To test these predictions, both a corpus analysis and an acceptability judgment task were conducted. A corpus analysis of the NICT JLE Corpus (1,281 Japanese learners) revealed that passive unaccusatives were more frequent than their non-target lexical causative counterparts (e.g., *Brian fell the apple from the table.) and passive unergatives (e.g., *Leslie was walked.). An acceptability judgment task with 30 Japanese-speaking learners (TOEIC 550–745) likewise showed higher ratings for passive unaccusatives compared to lexical causative unaccusatives and passive unergatives. Taken together, these results support the SPA, suggesting that L2 learners do not causativize unaccusatives but instead overgeneralize NP-movement associated with passivization. The converging corpus and experimental evidence therefore reject the VPA and provide empirical support for the SPA in explaining non-target passivization in L2 grammar.
abstracts.009568: In this paper, I revisit some puzzles about selection, and argue that they suggest principled restrictions on the content of syntactic features. I take up two guiding principles, which jointly comprise what I will call a Sparse Feature approach to selection and Merge. The first principle is that Merge-inducing features should be abstract, referring to properties that distinguish sets of lexical items from other sets of lexical items, without referring to individual lexical items themselves. The second principle is that Merge-inducing features should refer to syntactic properties. I argue that when selection looks driven by semantic or lexical factors, the only corresponding syntactic feature that meets these two criteria is an underspecified feature, which makes predictions about the distribution of phrases selected this way. I propose that the predictions are borne out, and provide insight into the locality of selection, the existence of smuggling, and old puzzles about c-selection first discussed by Grimshaw and Pesetsky.
abstracts.009569: This paper argues that epistemic and algorithmic biases can be almost entirely circumvented by cultivating discursive cognition -- a metacognitive capacity that lets models expose their normally opaque processes for internal scrutiny and regulation during the time-to-first-token phase, thereby evading misalignment vulnerabilities. It synthesizes insights from discursive psychology (Goffman, 1986; Edwards & Potter, 2005), cognitive development (Piaget & Garcia, 1991; Dennet, 1994), and AI security (Hubinger et al., 2024; Betley et al., 2025) to propose a unifying conceptual framework for bias, alignment, and safety. This abstraction generalizes fragmented concepts such as backdoors, jailbreaks, and deceptive alignment into a unified bias-jailbreak-backdoor continuum, reframing vulnerabilities as escalations along cognitive-discursive heterarchies. Whereas existing literature often treats these phenomena as isolated, our reconciliation offers a fresh lens to facilitate productive theoretical synthesis and inspire new empirical tests. Current benchmarks (e.g., HarmBench, Rainbow Teaming) and methods (e.g., SAEs, circuit breakers) are argued to be reactive, topic-focused, and insufficient for emergent discourse-level threats. The proposed shift --toward dilemma-centered discourse analysis rather than topical hazard category integration-- could inspire more robust and future-proof benchmarks by emphasizing pragmatic problem-framing instead of semi-static taxonomies. The framework envisions metacognition-tuning --fine-tuning models on datasets that leverage meta-reasoning for self-alignment-- as an attainable pathway toward an internalized, self-regulating fail-safe mode. Practically, discourse-steering mechanisms could inform inference-time strategies that are both more versatile and less reliant on compute-intensive training than SAEs or circuit breakers. In doing so, the approach addresses scalability constraints in safety research and supports movement toward a zero-trust paradigm grounded in broader generalization. We will (1)define biases, reduce them via analogies, extend them into a heterarchy and unify them on a continuum; (2)introduce a method to systematically exacerbate such biases for adversarial testing; (3)evaluate sub-optimal solutions and mitigation strategies; (4)propose a zero-trust architecture grounded in a reconceptualization of metacognition; (5)examine fine-tuning datasets to cultivate such mitigating metacognition; and (6)assess the project's effectiveness, implementation, limitations, and falsifiability.
abstracts.009570: We propose a formal model for dealing with what we call outlook markers, a subtype of discourse markers that govern discourse management pertaining to negotiations about ‘agreeable outlooks’ (on possibly subjective matters). For this purpose, we take up the semantic analysis of an ‘emphatic’ discourse marker nanka in Japanese. We argue that nanka is essentially a counterstance marker in that it imposes a constraint on the prior discourse that a contextually salient ‘counterstance’ is at issue, and that the speaker’s own stance embodied in the prejacent is incongruent with this counterstance as a subjective judgment. The model we develop combines Coppock’s (2018) outlook-based semantics for the treatment of subjectivity and Farkas & Bruce’s (2010) Table model for discourse management. We demonstrate that this unified model illuminates the way in which the notoriously elusive evaluative implication of nanka arises from the very nature of this particle as an abstract, meta-level discourse marker: it explicitly identifies the discourse conflict as a conflict of in principle irreconcilable opinions (which could threaten the whole point of ‘agreeable outlook’ management).
abstracts.009571: What is a natural (morpho)phonological alternation and what is unnatural and perhaps underivable? This question forms the backdrop for exploring exchange, whereby [F] → [G] but in this same context [G] → [F] (also called toggling, reversals, or polarity). Recently, de Lacy (2020) sketches two analyses to capture exchange. The first assumes a dedicated exchange mechanism (e.g. Transderivational Antifaithfulness, or [αF]-rules), while the second derives exchange through independently motivated components (whether through representations, the grammar, or their combination). We support this second position, examining a process of tonal exchange in Khoekhoe. Briefly, causative reduplication triggers a kind of ‘flip-flop’ whereby stems without a mid tone add one (e.g. L → LM) but stems with one delete it (e.g. LM → L). We analyze tonal exchange as due to a floating mid endowed with a prosodic subcategorization frame requiring it be stem-external, i.e. ‘}Σ Ⓜ’. Causative Ⓜ triggers delinking of stem M, but crucially stem M is not deleted and remains phonologically active (assuming Containment). Later, delinked M prevents causative Ⓜ from prosodically incorporating, and the ultimately result is unlinking causative Ⓜ (‘mutual dissimilation’). In total, we demonstrate that tonal exchange can be derived without a dedicated exchange mechanism.
abstracts.009572: The immediate goal of this paper is to reconstruct nominal tone in the Edoid family using the comparative method, one branch within the Benue-Congo subfamily of the Niger-Congo phylum, a stock for which no original tonogenesis event is discernible. To this end, we develop the Proto-Edoid Tone (PEdT) database drawn from 40 sources on 21 modern Edoid languages, totaling over 3000 individual data points, from which 436 cognates can be identified. Based on the PEdT database, we systematically compare tone patterns across the four proposed branches of Edoid, which results in a number of tonal correspondences which we reconstruct as combinations of tone on a noun class prefix and tone on a nominal stem. We call these nominal tone melodies. Based on these intermediate reconstructions, we reconstruct tone in Proto-Edoid as a symmetrical set of melodies **L-L, **L-LH, **L-H, **L-HL, **H-L, **H-LH, **H-HL, and **H-H. From these Proto-Edoid melodies, we track several recurring tone changes, the most common of which are Rightward H-Shift (e.g. the Great Edo Tone Shift, *H-L > L-H), H-Obligatoriness (i.e. adding a H to all-L words), and H-Lowering (i.e. *H > ꜜH, M, or L). These tone changes show both the hallmarks of regular sound change as well as many unexpected reflexes which cannot be explained at this point, setting the stage for future work on Edoid tone and how it relates to Proto-Benue-Congo and ultimately Proto-Niger-Congo.
abstracts.009573: Phrasal cumulativity (i.e., the assumption that predicates can be pluralized by applying Link’s star operator) faces a problem with so-called ‘intermediate’ situations: If phrasal cumulativity is available, one would expect a sentence like ‘‘these four workers built a raft’’, when uttered out of the blue, to be true if two of the workers built one raft and the other two workers built another raft, contrary to fact. In this paper I point out that such problems for phrasal cumulativity disappear once one takes into account both (i) the derivation of implicatures for sentences containing indefinites, and (ii) the effects of questions under discussion within a view that assumes phrasal cumulativity with domain restriction by ‘covers’ (Schwarzschild 1994; Bar-Lev 2025). I further argue that assuming phrasal cumulativity while having the effects of implicatures and questions in mind has some desired consequences. First, it straightforwardly resolves a conflict between the (apparent) absence of cumulativity with predicates like ‘‘build a raft’’ in upward entailing contexts and its presence when they are in downward entailing contexts (Schwarzschild 1994; Kratzer 2007). Second, on top of being able to explain why sentences like ‘‘these four workers built a raft’’ are not true in intermediate situations in out of the blue contexts, it can also explain why they are only marginally true in distributive situations (Dotlačil 2010, a.o.), as well as why some structurally parallel sentences are easily judged as true in distributive situations.
abstracts.009574: In this paper, I show that complex agreement interaction effects involving optional agreement, weak PCC effects with multiple subjects, and obligatory participant probing can all be accounted for under a system of conditional, sequential Multiple Agree as Minimal Search known as defective circumvention. Building on observations from Storment (2025b), I motivate the possibility of optional agreement with certain postverbal subjects within a single grammatical system in a variety of languages including English and Spanish. Within the same system, I explain how featural specifications of the relevant probes and goals involved in these Multiple Agree configurations can constrain the aforementioned optionality, thus leading to impossible or obligatory agreement scenarios. Regarding the impossible agreement scenarios, I show that Agree as Minimal Search is all that is necessary to account for a family of weak PCC effects in multiple subject constructions in colloquial English. This work contextualizes agreement optionality, multiple agreement, and PCC effects within a single framework based on a Minimalist formulation of Agree.
abstracts.009575: This monograph introduces the Reverse Entailment Diagnostic (RED) as a cross-linguistic methodology for testing nounal potential, defined as the capacity of linguistic material to be stabilized as a discourse-addressable object. RED proceeds by constructing witness environments—including possessive/genitive framing, determiner and quantifier anchoring, nominalizing morphology, clausal packaging into argument positions, and quotation/mention configurations—that force objecthood behavior. A witness counts as successful only if it is grammatical or interpretable and supports core objecthood diagnostics (e.g., addressability, anaphoric re-entry, quantification, and participation in predication). RED then applies a reverse inference: if a witness succeeds, the base material is licensed as compatible with noun-slot hosting, without requiring that it belong to a pre-specified lexical noun class. Because witness success is frequently gradient, the monograph develops RED as a metric, modeling graded nounal reachability and cost as a measurable property of constructions and languages. The typological program treats cross-language variation as differences in witness inventories and cost profiles rather than differences in whether objectification exists. The approach is extended to discourse (reference tracking and accessibility), to grammar (diagnostic evidence as a basis for architectural inference), to computation (parsing, semantic role labeling, and lexicon induction via witness-harvesting), and to neurocognition (objectification as gating and compositional unification with cost-sensitive load predictions). Finally, the monograph states a compact axiom set expressed in RED terms showing why systematic diagnostic success motivates a domain conclusion: ULD = UNS, a unified objecthood hosting domain underlying linguistic activity.
abstracts.009576: This article argues in favor of a formal model that views language as an integrated multimodal system where syntax, prosody, and gestures are linked. It demonstrates that specific syntactic structures trigger sensorimotor realizations, which include intonation, phonology, and gestures. We argue that gestures, in particular non-lexical co-speech gestures, are not merely an additional channel but a fundamental part of grammar, integrated into the same system that governs word order and phonological realization. We suggest a syntactic representation of warning expressions that combines syntactic and pragmatic aspects, based on Italian data and experimental evidence. Specifically, we argue that warnings always include a warning call, which can be either lexical in content or expressed solely through special prosody and gestures.
abstracts.009577: Open Access: DOI: https://doi.org/10.46991/AFA/2025.21.2.15 This work examines the properties of affirmative and negative particles, such as yes and no, when used to express emotions like regret, surprise, disapproval, and others. In the cases discussed here, yes and no do not negate or affirm the truth of the previous statement but instead convey the speaker's emotional response to a certain content. They therefore belong to the category of expressive language, which transmits emotional meanings. This article compares Italian and English and argues that both languages in these cases use similar structures to express the speaker’s reactions, with specific intonation and gestures enhancing their expressive effect. This discussion will also demonstrate that pragmatic considerations can be integrated into a model of language to generate relevant expressive interpretations, framing language as a multimodal system.
abstracts.009578: One major achievement in syntax has been a deep understanding of displacement in terms of Internal Merge. Therefore, displacement types initially resisting that analysis deserve scrutiny. This article investigates one. Latin verse permits tmesis – the division of “words” into nonadjacent pieces. In one subtype, radical tmesis, the cut is not obviously at a morpheme boundary. If it were not, radical tmesis would be theoretically recalcitrant. The article argues, however, that radical tmesis is actually derived by Internal Merge. The cut does occur at a morpheme boundary, despite appearances. Furthermore, the constituent orders radical tmesis produces can be derived syntactically, positing only independently motivated operations. Radical tmesis, then, is syntactic – supporting nonlexicalist frameworks, e.g., Morphology as Syntax. Even displacement types yielding apparently “irregular” outputs, then, can turn out on examination to be products of Internal Merge, a subcase of the elementary structure-building operation Merge – a theoretically welcome result, given minimalist aims. [ DOI: https://doi.org/10.1515/probus-2025-0007 ]
abstracts.009579: This article explores the role of parallel corpora in translation studies, focusing on their theoretical significance and practical applications. Parallel corpora, which consist of source texts and their translations, provide valuable empirical data for analyzing translation strategies, equivalence, and cross-linguistic patterns. Drawing on corpus linguistics research and examples from English-based parallel corpora, the article demonstrates how such resources contribute to translation theory, translator training, and applied linguistic research. The study argues that parallel corpora are essential tools for understanding translation as a systematic and data-driven process rather than an intuitive practice.
abstracts.009580: This paper argues that just as there are small nominals (Pereltsvaig 2006, et seq.), there are also small nominalized clauses—nominalized clauses that lack a DP layer. Data come from four types of embedded clauses in Khalkha Mongolian (Khalkha) that differ from one another with respect to whether they are finite or nonfinite, nominalized or nonnominalized, and if nominalized, how much nominal structure is contained within them. Crucially, while complement nominalized clauses fully parallel possessive nominals in Khalkha in their nominal properties, converbial adjunct nominalized clauses display only a subset of these properties. Building on the idea that nominals may be smaller than DPs, I argue for an analysis that can account for the variation in nominal properties across the two nominalized clause types in Khalkha. I highlight a gap that emerges from this investigation—the absence of a small nominalized clause type containing a full CP structure nominalized by a reduced nominal structure that lacks DP. This suggests the existence of constraints on the construction of mixed extended projections. Building on a previous analysis by Svenonius (2021), I propose that the constraint can be understood in terms of the Williams Cycle (Williams 2003, et seq.) and related work.
abstracts.009581: Researchers have reported that British English 'do' (also called 'propredicate do') is permitted in only a subset of the syntactic configurations that permit standard VP / post-auxiliary ellipsis in English. Problematically, the reliability of the acceptability judgment data underlying all prior generative research on British English 'do' ellipsis is not guaranteed. This situation transpires because these data were collected informally, which is not the most suitable method for collecting data on elliptical phenomena. In this paper, I report the results of eight judgment experiments conducted using the experimental syntax method, which can return reliable results on elliptical phenomena. These results show that, while the distribution of British English 'do' ellipsis is indeed more restricted than standard post-auxiliary ellipsis, the 'do' ellipsis site is permeable to all forms of syntactic movement from within it, contrary to reports in the literature. The results obtained are compatible with a simple syntactic analysis that states that 'do' cannot select for elliptical VPs headed by a verb that can move to T. Eliding a VP in 'do' ellipsis therefore does not render that VP opaque to further syntactic operations, which weakens the empirical support for proposals that treat ellipsis sites as phase-like objects.
abstracts.009582: Even though rhetorical move-step analysis has originally been applied to academic texts, this approach has also been employed to genre analysis of other written genres for some time. Reviews constitute an interesting example of texts as they may significantly influence the perception of a particular work and its potential success or failure. The juxtaposition of texts written by professional and consumer reviewers allows one to pinpoint similarities and differences between the characteristics of these discourse communities. While book and film reviews have been subject to comparative genre analysis, music reviews have not received much scholarly attention in this realm. In order to fill this gap, this paper aims to provide a comparative move-step genre analysis of 100 online music reviews from two salient online reviewing websites, namely Pitchfork (professional reviews) and Rate Your Music (consumer reviews). For the purpose of this study, two subcorpora of music reviews, each consisting of 50 texts published between 2021 and 2023 were compiled. The corpus was manually annotated with the use of a rhetorical function protocol employing structural move analysis and fine-tuned to the specific needs of the corpus in question. Respective parts of reviews were assigned a particular rhetorical step, e.g., providing background of the artist. Steps were then grouped into moves, e.g., situating the album. Corresponding steps were extracted from each subcorpus to examine what patterns are most frequently employed to realize them. The results indicate that professional reviews encompass more descriptive rhetorical elements, whereas consumer reviews contain more evaluative rhetorical elements. There are also many rhetorical steps that can be found in both professional and consumer reviews, yet they have different linguistic realizations in the two subcorpora.
abstracts.009583: Most adverbs never modify NPs and most NPs are never modified by adverbs. It’s curious, then, that the adverbs "exactly", "precisely", "just", and "only" can modify a few types of NPs including interrogatives ("exactly who", "precisely what") and fused relatives ("just what you said") but not other relative constructions (*"the person exactly who called"). I propose functional explanations for these restrictions. The pairing of precision modifiers with certain NPs reflects a semantic constraint, while the exclusion of most relative constructions reflects a pragmatic one.
abstracts.009585: We study the dynamical properties of a Hopf algebra Markov chain with state space the binary rooted forests with labelled leaves. This Markovian dynamical system describes the core computational process of structure formation and transformation in syntax via the Merge operation, according to Chomsky's Minimalism model of generative linguistics. The dynamics decomposes into an ergodic dynamical system with uniform stationary distribution, given by the action of Internal Merge, while the contributions of External Merge and (a minimal form of) Sideward Merge reduce to a simpler Markov chain with state space the set of partitions and with combinatorial weights. The Sideward Merge part of the dynamics prevents convergence to fully formed connected structures (trees), unless the different forms of Merge are weighted by a cost function, as predicted by linguistic theory. Results on the asymptotic behavior of the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue and eigenvector in this weighted case, obtained in terms of an associated Perron-Frobenius problem in the tropical semiring, show that the usual cost functions (Minimal Search and Resource Restrictions) proposed in the linguistic literature do not suffice to obtain convergence to the tree structures, while an additional optimization property based on the Shannon entropy achieves the expected result for the dynamics. We also comment on the introduction of continuous parameters related to semantic embedding and other computational models, and also on some filtering of the dynamics by coloring rules that model the linguistic filtering by theta roles and phase structure, and on parametric variation and the process of parameter setting in Externalization.
abstracts.009586: This article analyzes negative indefinites (n-words) in Albanian. These items include a prefixed element and an indefinite, and obligatorily require the occurrence of the negative marker, NM. Complementarily, the indefinite element can occur alone in negative contexts. This distribution, specifically the types of negative doubling, is explained by assuming that the negative operator is not realized by a lexical constituent within the syntactic structure. The idea is that negation is postulated and made available to interpretation by the presence of NM and n-words. The Chomskyan notion of I-Merge and the lexical properties of n-words provide the crucial syntactic tools to connect doubling and other phenomena to the phasal Spell-out procedure.
abstracts.009587: This study compares 774 equivalent proverbs in English, Persian, and Spanish using Halliday’s (1994) Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG), focusing on the experiential and textual metafunctions. I selected 258 proverbs from each language using monolingual dictionaries and analyzed their clause structures in terms of process, participant, and circumstance along the Theme and Rheme of the clauses. Although researchers have applied SFG to comparative linguistics, they have not explored proverbs across these three languages. I hypothesize that equivalent proverbs share semantic and syntactic features despite cultural and structural differences. The analysis reveals that although similar trend is followed across the three corpora, English and Persian prove to be more similar syntactically and semantically in terms of participant types both in the Theme and Rheme.
abstracts.009588: We present a deterministic algorithm for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European etymologies from attested daughter language forms. The Barnaby Protocol operates through systematic skeletal extraction and progressive filtering using established sound laws, morphological patterns, and comparative method principles. When applied to inscriptional evidence across Indo-European branches, the protocol narrows from broad possibility sets to specific PIE root candidates through mechanical application of accepted linguistic laws. This method provides a reproducible framework for etymological analysis. For inquiries about this paper dillonbarnaby@proton.me
abstracts.009589: In this paper, I present a probabilistic reconstruction of Križ’s (2015, 2016) account of non-maximal interpretation. The proposal addresses a general problem noted by Križ (2015: 85–6), which is shared by other QUD-based approaches to non-maximality (e.g. Bar-Lev 2021; Križ & Spector 2021): for these accounts to work, one needs to posit a fundamental disconnect between the question that is asked and the QUD that is addressed. This is problematic, especially in the absence of a non-stipulative method for identifying the QUD that is being addressed in a given context. In the proposed framework, the overt question alone determines the relevant QUD, allowing non-maximal interpretations to be generated in a principled manner.
abstracts.009590: Language is evolving, not only in vocabulary, but in grammar itself. This paper examines the long-term evolution of question structure in Singaporean SMS English. Using a diachronic corpus of approx. 56,000 English-dominant SMS messages sent in Singapore between 2003 and 2015. Through regex-based classification, we identify a sharp rise in reduced and elliptical question forms (e.g “U coming?”), coinciding with technological transitions in mobile messaging. Drawing on an affordance-based framework (Hutchby 2001; Norman 1999), we argue that interface features such as character limits, predictive text and autocorrect exert pragmatic pressures that favour brevity and omission. While early reductions reflect cost-saving measures under SMS constraints, these forms persist even after the introduction of unlimited texting, suggesting the sedimentation of interface-driven norms. We theorise these patterns as part of an “affordance-grammar” feedback loop, wherein technological affordances shape usage patterns that over time reconfigure grammatical norms. This study contributes to corpus-based pragmatics by illustrating how interface design can precipitate macro-level grammatical shifts in informal digital communication
abstracts.009591: The Poverty-of-Stimulus (PoS) argument is central to Universal Grammar (UG). UG is central for Generative grammars. Without UG no Generative grammars; without PoS no UG. Arguments based on PoS are flawed; UG is dispensable: Every grammar exists by the grace of its own learnability. This follows from the cognitive evolution of grammars.
abstracts.009592: This paper presents an initial study performed by the MODOMA system. The MODOMA is a computational multi-agent laboratory environment for unsupervised language acquisition experiments such that acquisition is based on the interaction between two language models, an adult and a child agent. Although this framework employs statistical as well as rule-based procedures, the result of language acquisition is a knowledge-based language model, which can be used to generate and parse new utterances of the target language. This system is fully parametrized and researchers can control all aspects of the experiments while the results of language acquisition, that is, the acquired grammatical knowledge, are explicitly represented and can be consulted. Thus, this system introduces novel possibilities for conducting computational language acquisition experiments. The experiments presented by this paper demonstrate that functional and content categories can be acquired and represented by the daughter agent based on training and test data containing different amounts of exemplars generated by the adult agent. Interestingly, similar patterns, which are well established for human-generated data, are also found for these machine-generated data. As the procedures resulted in the successful acquisition of discrete grammatical categories by the child agent, these experiments substantiate the validity of the MODOMA approach to modelling language acquisition.
abstracts.009593: This paper argues that Japanese contrastive wa is best analyzed as a 'part-time' outlook marker: a discourse-level downtoner that replaces a stronger, salient update proposal with a weaker alternative, and whose stance effects arise only when the prejacent expresses a subjective judgment. The 'ignorance' or concessive implications typically associated with it is derived pragmatically from its basic discourse function: acknowledging a stronger candidate while asserting only a weaker one. We present a formal analysis couched in Farkas and Bruce's Table model: a wa-sentence is alternative-sensitive and presupposes a stronger proposition on the Table that entails that the predicate corresponding to the focus structure holds of all focus alternatives; the discourse function of wa is to replace this stronger proposition with the prejacent. To model subjectivity, the account adopts Coppock's outlook-based semantics, distinguishing objective from discretionary propositions. The combined framework explains why contrastive wa is only a 'part-time' outlook marker, how stance sensitivity arises in modal judgments, and the way perspective shift occurs in embedded environments under attitude predicates.
abstracts.009594: This paper challenges the traditional lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy in formal semantics by proposing that linguistic meaning and world-knowledge exist on a gradient of conventionalization rather than forming categorically distinct types of knowledge. Through an analysis of entailment strength and intersubjective agreement patterns, I argue that the field's persistent failure to theorize connotative meaning stems from systematically conflating two distinct phenomena: cultural connotation (systematic, community-level patterns that generate weak entailments) and private connotation (idiosyncratic, individual associations). Drawing on evidence from semantic prosody research, arbitrariness of the linguistic sign, language acquisition patterns, and computational modeling, I develop a gradient framework in which meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization rather than by categorical membership in "denotative" versus "connotative". This reconceptualization provides theoretical tools for understanding how lexical semantic profiles generate systematic distributional patterns while remaining resistant to conscious introspection, thereby resolving longstanding puzzles in the relationship between word meaning and usage patterns.
abstracts.009595: This paper proposes a structural reanalysis of R-loci in sign languages as syntactic objects with internal structure that underlie verbal argument positions. I argue that every R-locus consists of two distinct components—an index slot and a reference slot—and that argument licensing follows from the systematic specification of these components rather than from agreement, pronominal elements, or post-syntactic discourse inference. On this basis, I introduce 'Locus-Checking' as a uniform syntactic operation that aligns partially specified R-loci in order to license verbal arguments. The proposal accounts for apparent agreement effects, null arguments, generic interpretations, and first-person readings with body-anchored verbs. The analysis is primarily based on data from German Sign Language (DGS), but the structural assumptions are intended to apply more broadly to the grammatical organization of reference in sign languages.
abstracts.009596: English-speaking children rarely address parents by first name – a social prohibition encoding power and solidarity. Separately, English kinship terms like Mom and Dad permit bare singular use (Mom called) where other count nouns don’t (*Neighbour called). Nobody has connected these facts. I argue that the naming taboo causes the proper-name-like syntax: high-frequency use of kinship terms in vocative position – forced by the prohibition on first names – produces grammaticalization toward strong proper-name status. Corpus data from CHILDES confirm that parent terms show disproportionate vocative concentration (16–43%) compared to extended kin terms (4–7%). A careful category/function distinction provides the analytical apparatus; the taboo is the engine, the syntax is the sediment.
abstracts.009597: According to a High Absolutive analysis of syntactic ergativity, grammatical operations can target intransitive subjects and transitive objects, distinguishing them from transitive subjects, because the former move to a position higher than the latter. A prediction that results from this theory is that an absolutive DP can bind an anaphoric ergative argument as a consequence of moving to a position that c-commands it. While it has been shown that this prediction is not borne out by facts across a range of syntactically ergative languages (Anderson, 1976; Brodkin & Royer, To Appear), reciprocal sentences in Adyghe and Kabardian (Northwest Caucasian) appear to be an exception. The morphosyntax of such constructions suggests that the reciprocal occupies a position that c-commands the absolutive DP that binds it, which would imply that the absolutive DP does indeed move to a higher position. I argue instead that the morphosyntactic properties of Adyghe and Kabardian reciprocal sentences should not be taken at face value. Rather, they are the byproduct of independent principles that regulate syntactic derivations (viz. Last Resort and the rules that govern case assignment), combined with crosslinguistically stable parameters of variation regarding case and nominal licensing. These sentences, thus, also fall under the generalization that absolutive arguments cannot bind an ergative anaphor and, as such, do not provide empirical support for a High Absolutive theory.
abstracts.009598: Helena Hellerówna, a Polish interwar literary translator, was born in Cracow on February 27th, 1899, and died as a U.S. citizen in New York on June 25th, 1978, under the name Helen Antonia Atlas. She translated, among others, awarded works (e.g. Fiancée d'Avril by Guy Chantepleure or Le repos de Bacchus by Pierre Boileau) and recognised authors (e.g. André Maurois, François Mauriac, or Maria Peteani) frequently signing as Hel Hel or H.H. Her career was interrupted by WWII, during which Hellerówna became a victim of the Holocaust. Her contribution to the Polish translation community has been largely forgotten, to the point where even the Polish National Library has no accurate information about her. This paper presents a preliminary study on Helena Hellerówna as a translator, with the aim of reconstructing her biography and compiling a complete list of her translations, to facilitate further research on her works within the framework of Translator Studies (Chesterman 2009). The objective of this approach is to bring the translator out of the “shadow” of the author, as mentioned by Venuti (2008). In the case of translators about whom little is known – such as Hellerówna – conducting in-depth research in Translation Studies is challenging without first establishing a comprehensive biographical account, and this study seeks to provide it.
abstracts.009599: While previous research on incorporation has mainly focused on how (typically uninflected) nouns come to be incorporated into verb complexes, it is less well known that some languages also permit the incorporation of complex verbal constituents (e.g. Pittman, 2009; Barrie and Mathieu, 2016; McKenzie, 2022). In this paper, I investigate a previously underdescribed construction in Inuktitut (Inuit-Yupik-Unangan), in which an embedded clause is morphologically incorporated into a higher affixal verb of possession 'have', creating an existential. The embedded nominal arguments are stranded and case marked like antipassive objects rather than with the expected ERG and ABS morphology. I argue that the incorporated element is a pseudorelative clause, a CP-sized predicate of a small clause related to its nominal subject by control (e.g. Cinque 1995), based on structural parallels with pseudorelatives found cross-linguistically. Clause incorporation as opposed to noun incorporation arises in Inuktitut because the incorporating verb takes the entire pseudorelative structure, rather than a nominal, as its complement; this, in turn, motivates a postsyntactic model of incorporation that requires the syntactic structure as its input (e.g. Compton and Pittman, 2010; Yuan, 2025). Additionally, the case patterns found in incorporated clauses reveal that both ERG and ABS case assignment are tied to the extended CP domain (e.g. Compton, 2018; Carrier, 2020; Yuan, 2022), and are not associated with lower clausal fields such as the vP and TP domains.
abstracts.009600: Dynamic semantics standardly treats negation as externally static. This is inconsistent with anaphora to doubly-negated indefinites, and Partee disjunctions. I propose a technique for lifting dynamic systems into richer meaning spaces that support dynamic negation. I argue that extant theories of dynamic negation instantiate this technique in various ways, prove that all such lifted systems are isomorphic, and identify a minimal/canonical enrichment of Dynamic Predicate Logic. I relate this perspective on dynamic negation to recent work on 'bounded' meaning. Finally, I consider how such lifted interpretations with dynamic negations can be extended further, into richer meaning spaces that support exceptional scope of indefinites. October 23, 2026: Erratum to "Staged updates"
abstracts.009601: In this paper, I present a novel analysis of the the crossover phenomenon, which is based on the nonlinear theory of coreference as well as the special syntax of vectors. I show that the crossover effect is strong when either: (a) the dependency is modified under extraction of an anaphor, (b) a wh-vector anteceding a pronoun remains active, as opposed to being disabled, after extraction, (c) a permanent line-crossing effect appears in the derivation or (d) the structure contains multiple ill-formed states. On the other hand, weak crossover is due either to multiple transitory constraint violation in the derivation or to one ill-formed state in a multiple-state structure. In addition, it is shown that any dependency is weaken if the antecedent and the antecedee are not in the same plane. This analysis is extended to the pair-list reading, which appears to be mainly a consequence of the entanglement of the universal with every referential feature in its domain.
abstracts.009602: We examine in this paper a class of verbs traditionally labelled experiencer-object psych verbs (EO psych verbs) with respect to their culminating entailments in Mandarin Chinese (Chinese); that is, whether the change in mental state these verbs describe come to hold in their experiencer objects. The basic observation is that these predicates optionally culminate when they have subjects that are agentive, whereas non-agentive subjects enforce culmination, in line with what has been observed for (non-psych) accomplishment predicates both within and in many other languages. We propose that non-culmination arises as a result of a thematic ambiguity, where the agentive variants of these verbs have a canonical transitive structure with the surface object interpreted as a theme/patient and not an experiencer, whereas the non-agentive variants have a deep unaccusative structure where the surface object is interpreted as a true experiencer. The lexical entailments of these respective thematic roles, formalized appropriately, will naturally capture the empirical observations regarding culmination. This is contrary to what has been claimed as the source of non-culmination with accomplishments in the language, namely the weak perfective marker -le or a sub-lexical modal operator attaching to genuine accomplishment predicates with both agent and non-agent subjects. We show using well-established aspectual diagnostics that EO psych verbs fall into at least two classes in terms of how their agentive uses differ from their non-agentive uses and crucially, that they do not behave alike in terms of aspectual categories both within and across the two classes. Regardless of which class an EO psych verb falls into, there also remains a genuine asymmetry with regard to the surface objects’ ability to serve as the antecedent of the reflexive anaphor ziji. These therefore serve as independent evidence outside of non-culminating entailments that support an analysis where the agentive and non-agentive variants receive different treatments independent of the classes, which we analyze as a difference in thematic interpretation of the surface object. Previous proposals about non-culminating accomplishment predicates, in virtue of assuming that the contrast arises from weak perfective markers and where the agentive and non-agentive variants share a change of state core, or where both variants belong to identical aspectual classes with the presence of a sub-lexical modal operator sensitive to the properties of the subject, therefore cannot be general proposals about non-culmination and the properties of individual verb classes need to be taken into account when locating the source of non-culmination.
abstracts.009603: This chapter examines Japanese discourse-sensitive adverbs and focus particles (e.g., dōse, mushiro, yoppodo; nanka, kurai, koso) that express “subjective” evaluation meanings. I argue that these items are outlook markers in the sense of Kubota & Ido (2025; 'Outlook markers (as abstract discourse markers)' SALT35): they are abstract discourse markers that signal how an attitude holder (typically, the speaker) positions the prejacent relative to a salient counterstance in the discourse. After reviewing major categories of secondary (or, ‘non-at-issue’) meaning in the literature, the chapter shows that outlook markers pattern partly like presuppositions and partly like conventional implicatures, motivating a more fine-grained view of discourse management. Empirically, outlook markers exhibit a ‘two-layered’ meaning: (i) a presuppositional component imposing a constraint on the prior discourse on the existence of a counterstance, and (ii) an expressive-like component that conveys the attitude holder’s stance by signalling the relationship between the prejacent and the counterstance. Unlike typical expressives, however, their evaluative import readily shifts under attitude predicates and interacts systematically with modal expressions. The chapter concludes that outlook markers are meta-level devices that make subjective stances explicit in proposing discourse updates.
abstracts.009604: This paper examines the syntax of passive constructions in Oshingandjera (a dialect of Oshiwambo) and the question of whether they have syntactically projected implicit external arguments. The data provides empirical as well as theoretical support for the theory of the passive of Collins 2024. The paper motivates an analysis of implicit arguments that requires that they are syntactically projected (Collins 2024, Gotah 2024, Sulemana 2024 and Angelopoulos, Collins, Michelioudakis, & Terzi 2023), opposing an alternative analysis where implicit arguments are not syntactically present (Bruening 2013).
abstracts.009605: This paper presents an addendum to the Mapbook of Syntactic Variation in American English (Wood et al. 2020), reporting the results of additional acceptability-judgment surveys conducted by the Yale Grammatical Diversity Project in 2020–2021. Using the same survey design, data-processing pipeline, and mapping techniques as the original mapbook, we extend the empirical record to a new set of syntactic constructions, including additional uses of hella, causal where, the alternative one construction, intensificational fully, and several cases of object omission with transitive verbs, which we call “lonely transitives”. As in the original work, we provide geospatial visualizations of sentence-level judgments alongside basic demographic breakdowns. This addendum is intended to be read in conjunction with the 2020 mapbook, which provides the full methodological, theoretical, and interpretive background for the data presented here.
abstracts.009606: This paper puts forward a restrictive approach to subsegmental architecture, which assumes that sub-skeletal representations are composed of obligatorily binary branching nodes and substance-free emergent features which serve as pointers to phonetic interpretation. We put the theory to a test by applying its principles to the set of alternations of coronal consonants attested in English before affixes -ion, -ian and -ious in words such as infectious, suggestion, revision, expansion etc. It is demonstrated that the requirement for the structure to be binary branching as well as the requirement for English consonants to contain at most three features derive the correct outputs of the coronal mutation. It is also argued that the postulatedapproach accounts for the behaviour of the items which resist the mutation such as rebellion, Arthurian, oblivious through the last resort operation of node epenthesis.
abstracts.009607: I discuss two colloquial Italian idioms expressing respectively emphatic negation and objection, col cavolo (lit. ‘with the cabbage’) and un cavolo (lit. ‘a cabbage’). Despite superficial similarities, they represent two very different strategies at syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic level. Col cavolo belongs to a class of non-verbal polar predicates selecting a clausal complement and expressing the speaker’s degree of strength of sincerity towards the proposition (Repp 2013). Col cavolo expresses high commitment to ¬p: it is base-generated in the left periphery, as confirmed by its limited polarity-licensing abilities and impossibility of agreement with a TP-level negative PolP. Instead, un cavolo is a metalinguistic objector (Martins 2020), an echoic responsive move (Farkas & Bruce 2010); it originates as a vulgar minimiser and can function as an ‘utterance minimiser’, predicating minimal relevance of the associate and rejecting it globally rather than reversing its truth conditions. Finally, I compare col cavolo with similar cross-linguistic expressions, and offer a generalisation for left-peripheral negators: those participating in a movement or agreement chain with the TP-level PolP have full semantic and polarity-licensing capabilities, while base-generated ones, being non-local to the lower proposition, only license weak polarity items and yield double negation with a lower negative PolP.
abstracts.009608: Fraction partitives which contain a plural argument (e.g., "a third of the apples") exhibit a semantic alternation tracked by verbal agreement in some but not all Indo-European languages. One of the readings, which I call a MEASURE interpretation, is unexpected given established perspectives on how measure functions are defined for pluralities. I work to offer an account of the phenomenon specifically for Italian but secondarily seek to explain why the additional reading is absent in other languages. Building off of a suggestion from Falco & Zamparelli (2019), I resolve the alternation to the presence or absence of a covert operator which (i) is Agreed with over the partitive complement, and (ii) shifts a parameter of interpretation by which variable measure functions are defined. While a non-trivial deviation from established literature on the semantics of measurement (see Bale & Barner 2009, Wellwood 2019, a.o.), I argue it crucially outperforms alternatives in predicting where the interpretations may arise and what kinds of predicates Italian FPs are compatible with, among other things.
abstracts.009609: This paper is focused on existential (and possessive) sentences in Tagalog that are constructed around a verbal existential verb (which I refer to as the Dynamic Existential). Although this verb appears to be an unaccusative verb in its use in existential sentences, I argue that it is actually a transitive verb equivalent to \textsc{have}, with a covert external argument (which is overt in possessive sentences constructed from the same verb). In addition to providing a unification of the syntax of existential and possessive constructions, I argue that this analysis explains the morpho-syntax of dynamic existential constructions (relating, in particular, to the distribution of case) that would be otherwise mysterious if the existential verb were a true unaccusative. The proposed covert external argument in existential sentences funds precedent in `impersonal' like constructions in other languages, and as I briefly discuss. I propose that this external argument (which is overt in possessive sentences) is an (implicit) locative, and discuss briefly some implications for unifying a prefix ka- that is found in the existential verb and subject experiencer verbs in the language (as discussed by Kaufman 2011, 2012). If the analysis proposed here is on the right track, it suggests that Tagalog falls at the lower end of a spectrum for availability of “expletive” external arguments (Icelandic being at the high end, Norwegian and English being somewhere in the middle).
abstracts.009610: This dissertation investigates Modal Complement Ellipsis, sluicing, and fragment answers in Likpakpaanl, a Mabia language spoken in the Northern, Oti, and North-East regions of Ghana. Adopting a Minimalist, movement-based approach to ellipsis, the study argues that elided constituents in Likpakpaanl have the same underlying syntactic structure as their non-elliptical counterparts and are derived through movement followed by phonological deletion. The analysis shows that only the root modals ŋmàà ‘can’ and bàn ‘want’ license Modal Complement Ellipsis. Ellipsis is triggered by an ellipsis feature merged on the modal head, deleting a vP complement with ŋmàà and a TP complement with bàn. The dissertation further proposes a unified analysis of sluicing and fragment answers, arguing that both constructions involve deletion of a focus projection rather than a tense phrase, unlike what has been proposed for languages such as English and Dutch. This claim is supported by the obligatory deletion of the focus particle under ellipsis, consistent with the Sluicing-Comp Generalisation, which restricts ellipsis escape to operators. Sluicing and fragments are licensed by an ellipsis feature hosted on a licensing projection above the focus phrase and are derived via Agree and successive cyclic movement of the focused constituent. Evidence from island constraints, binding effects, and the inability of certain wh-phrases to license sluicing supports a movement-based analysis of ellipsis in Likpakpaanl.
abstracts.009611: This paper provides an analysis of the properties of interrogative pronouns of Mabia languages drawing data from Dagbani and Likpakpaanl. We focus on the inventory, internal structure, and key grammatical characterisation of the interrogative pronouns. We contend that interrogative pronouns are salient syntactic elements in the content question systems of these languages. In addition, we demonstrate that number marking, distinction between human/non-human and lexical ambiguity are salient grammatical properties of these interrogative pronouns. We further show that the inflection for number employs both suppletive and nonsuppletive patterns. We also contend that the interrogative pronouns that specify for the semantic domains of [+human], [-human] and [+thing] are sensitive to number, since they alternate for plurality (ŋuni ~banima (who.sg ~ who-pl), bo~bonima (what.sg ~what-pl), dini~dinnima (what.sg.thing ~ what.thing-pl) for Dagbani and (ŋma ~bilabi (who.sg ~ who-pl), nilan ~ bilabi (what.sg ~what-pl), ba ~ ba (what.sg.thing ~ what.thing-pl) for Likpakpaanl. Because the root may differ or be the same from that of the plural as evident in both languages, we propose that number marking in these interrogative words exhibit both suppletive and nonsuppletive patterns. The data are based on native introspection of the authors who are native speakers of these languages. This paper is important because of its empirical and theoretical contribution to the study of the Mabia languages.
abstracts.009612: This paper discusses verb phrase ellipsis in Likpakpaanl, a Mabia (Gur) language belonging to the Niger-Congo family and predominantly spoken in the Eastern part of the Northern Region and the Oti Region of Ghana. I argue that VP ellipsis is licensed by the modals ŋmàn and bàn, which project separate modal phrases (ModP) in the clausal structure. The data drawn from the Licahbol dialect show that only the higher ModP position occupied by ŋmàn and bàn hosts the ellipsis [E]-feature which licenses VP ellipsis by deleting the phonological content of their complements. I show that even though both modals license VP ellipsis, bàn targets an entire CP for deletion, while ŋmàn deletes the VP and its internal arguments. Finally, I adduce evidence from Antecedent Contained Deletion (ACD) and Reconstruction effects and propose a base-generation analysis to account for the presence of the resumptive pronoun in the distribution of bàn, and also assume a PF-deletion approach for Likpakpaanl VP ellipsis
abstracts.009613: In this paper, we present a comprehensive corpus-driven analysis of Bangla literary and newspaper texts to investigate their lexical diversity, structural complexity and readability. We undertook Vācaspati and IndicCorp, which are the most extensive literature and newspaper-only corpora for Bangla. We examine key linguistic properties, including the type-token ratio (TTR), hapax legomena ratio (HLR), Bigram diversity, average syllable and word lengths, and adherence to Zipf’s Law, for both newspaper (IndicCorp) and literary corpora (Vācaspati). Our findings reveal that till ∼ 10 6 words, the newspaper corpora show a higher TTR than the literary corpora; after that, the literary corpora have a higher TTR ratio. For all other features, such as Bigram Diversity and HLR, despite its smaller size, the literary corpus exhibits significantly higher lexical richness and structural variation. We have also demonstrated that a literary corpus adheres more closely to global word distribution proper- ties, such as Zipf’s law, than a newspaper corpus or a merged corpus of both literary and newspaper texts. Literature corpora also have higher entropy and lower redundancy values compared to a newspaper corpus. We also further assess the readability using Flesch and Coleman-Liau in- dices, showing that literary texts are more complex. Additionally, we tried to understand the diversity of corpora by building 𝑛-gram models and measuring perplexity. Our findings reveal that literary corpora have higher perplexity than newspaper corpora, even for similar sentence sizes. This trend can also be observed for the English newspaper and literature corpus, indicating its generalizability. We also examined how the perfor- mance of models on downstream tasks is influenced by the inclusion of literary data alongside newspaper data. Our findings suggest that inte- grating literary data with newspapers improves the performance of models on various downstream tasks.

abstracts.009615: In the modern language sciences, the core computational operation of syntax, ‘Merge’, is defined as an operation that combines two linguistic units (e.g., ‘brown’, ‘cat’) to form a categorized constituent structure (‘brown cat’, a Noun Phrase). This structure can be further combined with additional linguistic units based on this categorial information, respecting non-associativity such that abstract grouping is preserved. Some linguists have embraced the view that Merge is an elementary, indivisible operation that emerged in a single evolutionary step.
