Following a theoretical examination of the PUs characteristics and their unfrozenness, the analysis of the translations into five selected languages takes from Hejwowski’s (2015) classification of the translation techniques adapted to the purpose of the work. Based on that, we could identify and evaluate the different ways the translators adapted the Rabelaisian wordplay to the cultural universe of their own language. We also identified an additional technique involving the translator’s phraseological innovation, where the Rabelaisian wordplay in the PUs is reproduced in a very free and creative way in another cultural universe.
abstracts.009674: This dissertation closely reexamines the structure of the predicate domain in Farsi/Persian and evaluates whether its surface OV order is best explained by the widely adopted head-final VP/vP analyses or by an alternative framework that universally derives all linear orders from the same base structure. In favor of the latter approach, I argue that the traditional head-final verb phrase accounts face significant theoretical issues highlighted by three empirical domains: (i) complex predicates and their interaction with auxiliary verbs and phenomena such as ellipsis and verb-preposing, (ii) postverbal clausal complements and their subextraction, binding, and ellipsis patterns, and (iii) the licensing of post-nominal arguments and modifiers, particularly within the ezâfe construction. Crucially, such analyses cannot straightforwardly account for the core data without relying on additional assumptions, such as inconsistent directionality in head-adjunction, reliance on head-excorporation out of complex heads, and head-directionality parametrization within the VP depending on the (non)-clausal status of the verb’s argument. Alternatively, an analysis within the Antisymmetry framework of Kayne (1994) is developed that captures the full range of ordering facts with the single, consistent derivational mechanism of leftward movement, eliminates rightward adjunction and excorporation, and unifies the treatment of predicate-argument and predicate-modifier configurations. A main claim of this dissertation is that Farsi complex predicates (combinations of Non-Verbal elements (NV) and Light-Verbs (LV)) and larger verb clusters in general form phrasal XP constituents derived from a head-initial structure and various leftward movement operations. In the current analysis, such movements are defined as the raising of predicate-internal elements from their base position to dedicated licensing functional projections to the left. Focusing on complex predicate constructions and their interaction with auxiliary verbs, I propose that not only the internal and external arguments, but also the Non-Verbal (NV) predicates of complex verbs undergo movement. This analysis systematically accounts for Auxilary-Verb ordering facts and the leftmost position of NV elements in any verbal cluster. It also straightforwardly deals with verb cluster movement in the context of data from verb-stranding vP ellipsis and Topic/Focus fronting by treating such cases as the movement of derived verbal phrases to the relevant left-peripheral specifier positions. Further evidence in favor of the developed antisymmetric analysis comes from clausal arguments of verbs, which always surface postverbally in contrast to non-clausal arguments, which precede the verb. Previous head-final vP analyses require either exceptional rightward selection or rightward extraposition of CPs, both of which are inadequate in the context of complex predicates and auxiliary constructions. I propose that in such constructions the same leftward movements licensing the NV predicate as well as the DPs and PPs still apply. However, the crucial claim is that CP arguments remain in their base position and are not subject to the same licensing requirements above the predicate. Since the base-generated position of CP arguments is always hierarchically lower than the projections of the verb and the auxiliary head, it follows that they are always in a final position in the clause independent of whether the verb is simplex, complex, or partof a larger verbal cluster. Consequently, this proposal correctly accounts for the subextraction, binding, and ellipsis facts that are indicative of the low interpretation site of the CP. A final puzzle for the traditional accounts is raised by post-predicate constituents in the non-verbal domain of copular and complex predicate constructions, where internal arguments or modifiers appear to the right of the predicate, often linked by the ezâfe morpheme. Based on a close investigation of the relevant patterns, I adopt and extend Kahnemuyipour’s (2014) roll-up phrasal movement analysis, originally proposed for postnominal dependents in the NP/DP domain, to also cover predicate–modifier and predicate–argument orders in the verbal domain. Under this proposal, both modifiers and arguments are base-generated in specifiers of functional projections above the predicate head (whether nominal, adjectival, or prepositional). Roll-up movement of the predicate (or a projection containing it) across these specifiers derives the observed [Predicate –Ezf– XP] orders, while the ezâfe morpheme spells out the agreement relation established in this process. Crucially, I claim that this derivation represents a licensing operation available to arguments and modifiers in certain constructions and is further evidence that elements must be functionally licensed within the antisymmetric framework pursued in the dissertation.
abstracts.009675: This short paper reports a preliminary experiment, which tested how major generative AIs respond to a request to restore data from an existing figure and another request to simulate addional data with similar trends. Among the three systems tested, Gemini 3.0 provided the most detailed guidance, including suggestions for merging restored and simulated data that, if followed, may lead to ethically problematic research practices. I am sharing this experience with public as an experimental linguist, but this case should be relevant for any academic field that involves experimentation.
abstracts.009676: Good storytellers reveal their characters’ ‘inner stories’, composed of subjective experiences like feelings, perceptions, and thoughts. In fiction, narrators can faithfully represent their main characters’ thoughts, using techniques like free indirect discourse. But perceptions are fundamentally different from thoughts in that they don’t have a linguistic form for the narrator to reproduce or mimic in a report. We argue that there is in fact a dedicated linguistic category, narrated perception, similar to but distinct from free indirect discourse, that allows narrators to vividly represent perceptual experiences. We propose a discourse semantics analysis of this phenomenon, built on the idea that narrators combine narrated perception and free indirect discourse into coherent discourse segments to provide a more complete representation of a fictional character’s complex mental life.
abstracts.009677: Full title: Superlinguistics: A formal approach to multimodal meaning Theoretical linguistics has made great strides towards a science of language, building on solid foundations in logic and analytical philosophy, and, more recently, joining forces with empirical sciences. Superlinguistics wants to expand the reach of our sophisticated theoretical and empirical linguistic toolkit by applying it to language-like objects beyond the scope of traditional linguistics, like gestures, comics, or music. [...] I offer four case studies showcasing different aspects of supersemantic approaches to multimodal sign systems. In 3.1 I discuss a compositional semantic approach to the interpretation of facial expressions; in 3.2, I review theoretical approaches to emoji meanings from the recent supersemantics literature; in 3.3, I sketch a possible-worlds semantics for pictures and a discourse-level approach to comics; and in 3.4, I explore how to combine the different iconic semantic contributions of sound, music, and moving images in film in a unified formal semantics framework.
abstracts.009678: Drawing on cartographic assumptions that there exist discourse-related projections in the ‘vP periphery’(Belletti 2001), we explore two types of postverbal focalisation in Lamnso and Limbum (Grassfields Bantu). The first type places an expletive pro- noun and / or a copula before a contrastively focused constituent. The activation of the expletive and/or the copula in object focal- isation induces freezing and minimality effects on subject and verb extraction. These effects are circumvented by evacuating the ob- ject(s) from the vP and by smuggling (Collins 2005) the remnant vP to Spec-AspP. This allows the verb to value its aspectual fea- tures and the subject to raise to its canonical preverbal position. Object focalisation in SVO(O)sequences requires evacuation of the arguments from the vP and remnant vP movement to Spec-AspP. Verbal copulas are taken as grammaticalised focus markers that lex- icalise the focus head and attract focalised elements in Spec-FocP, while the expletive pronoun lexicalises a low subject projection. The second strategy involves verb-subject reversal and apparently in-situ object foci. It correlates with information and contrastive focus. Its derivation involves focus movement without necessarily applying smuggling.

abstracts.009680: How do children acquire knowledge of syntactic islands? Cross-linguistically, we see constrained variation (Sprouse et al., 2021), suggesting an interplay between child-internal factors and language-specific input. We use computational cognitive modeling to investigate a recent theory of the learning mechanism which relies on the child learning efficient chunks of syntactic structure from the input (Dickson, 2025; Dickson et al., 2024, 2022). Specifically, we adapt the Fragment Grammar (FG) chunking approach (T. O’Donnell et al., 2011; T. J. O’Donnell, 2015; T. J. O’Donnell et al., 2009) to syntactic islands, where the modeled child identifies both (i) chunks of hierarchical structure, and (ii) the probabilities of the learned chunks, in order to maximize the probability of the input. Following Dickson et al. (2022), the modeled child learns from cognitively-plausible input (realistic distribution and quantity of utterances) drawn from the CHILDES Treebank (L. Pearl & Sprouse, 2013). The modeled child is evaluated on its ability to replicate empirical data indicating human knowledge of syntactic islands (De Villiers et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2022; Sprouse et al., 2012), thereby demonstrating if the modeled child has acquired the relevant syntactic island knowledge. The FG-using modeled child performs better than several comparison modeled children as well as a current large language model, thus supporting the FG-chunk-based theory of acquisition. We discuss limitations and the potential of this efficient-chunking theory to explain the acquisition of additional empirical data, as well as implications for the relationship between acquisition and cross-linguistic variation with respect to syntactic islands.
abstracts.009681: This paper argues for an extended notion of sublexical modality through an in-depth analysis of three verb classes in Hungarian: verbs of involuntary perception, verbs of involuntary recognition and verbs of physical disposition. Verbs falling into these natural classes pattern together across four, seemingly unrelated, phenomena: the incompatibility with an ability modal auxiliary, the existence of a dispositional middle voice form, the appearance in so-called root infinitives of circumstantial modality, and susceptibility to reinterpretation as auxiliaries. I argue that this is because of their unique, enriched semantics: such verbs have ability modality hard-wired into their lexical semantic representation. While sublexical modality has long been argued to play a role in the semantics of defeasible causatives; I will argue that this concept has a much broader and more general validity, spanning a wider range of verb classes and more flavours of modality than previously thought. I will further argue that cross-linguistically, the lexical encoding of ability modality is an optional design element in the architecture of language which modulates the division of labour between (i) the various modules of language (syntax and semantics) and (ii) between speaker and hearer.
abstracts.009682: This paper is a reply to Mikkelsen & Hardt’s 2024 article analyzing 'same' and 'different' as involving an additive presuppositional element TOO akin to overt 'too'. This hypothesis has several virtues: it provides a uniform analysis for both 'same' and 'different' under all of their (internal, external and comparative-like) readings; it explains several effects (poorly discussed so far) exhibited by 'same': parallelism and island effects, as well as analogies with 'too'. But I show that this additive analysis faces several challenges questioning its explanatory power: the uniformity of the account rests on some stipulations, and the analogies between 'same'/'different' and 'too' are only partial. Furthermore, I show that Charnavel’s 2015 alternative account likening 'same'/'different' to comparatives can derive the effects observed by Mikkelsen & Hardt without raising the problems induced by TOO incorporation.
abstracts.009683: This chapter examines the interaction between syntax, morphology and information structure in Germanic from a comparative diachronic perspective. Making use of syntactically annotated corpus data, we examine historical stages of English, Icelandic, High German and Low German and present a quantificational comparison of (i) fronted constituents in the prefield and (ii) object ordering in the postfinite domain. We focus in particular on the relation between constituent fronting and topicality, suggesting a view of topic which incorporates the Strawson/Reinhart's notion in the situation-semantic approach. Conceiving of topic as a triple of situation coordinates used to asses the sentence, we propose that prefinite pronouns (personal, temporal, locative) indicate ongoing topic situation coordinates, while non-pronominal prefinite locative and temporal adverbials and PPs act as respective coordinates' shifters. We argue that Germanic languages have diachronically drifted, to various extents, from a “local” anchoring strategy of IS characterized by ongoing coordinate marking to a “global” anchoring type, where only shifted coordinates are overtly signalled.
abstracts.009684: This article investigates the distribution of the strong subjective epistemic operators "sicherlich", "wohl", "wahrscheinlich", "müsste" and the weak subjective epistemic operators "vielleicht", "möglicherweise", "könnte" in polar questions and in declarative questions in German. The motivation for the study is the hypothesis that in polar questions, the perspective of subjective operators is shifted to the addressee (so-called “interrogative flip”), whereas in declarative questions it remains with the speaker. The article hypothesizes that under this assumption, weak operators should be rated better in polar questions, whereas strong operators should get a higher rating in declarative questions. This is confirmed by an experiment, which consisted in 280 participants in a within-subject rating of assertions, polar questions and declarative sentences with these subjective epistemic operators. The article motivates the guiding hypotheses by pragmatic considerations, and attempts to explain the slightly deviating behavior of the discourse particle wohl.
abstracts.009685: This dissertation explores the syntax of subsententials in Hindi/Urdu (H/U), with an empirical focus on sluicing and fragment answers. Such phenomena represent instances where all clausal material is unpronounced, except for a (wh-)phrase (e.g., A: Who did John see? B: Mary.). With evidence from various connectivity effects, I argue that a non-structuralist analysis of such configurations, which does not assume the presence of tacit material, is untenable. Rather, subsententials in this language warrant a structuralist solution, according to which the surfacing remnant base-generates in an underlying clause whose morpho-syntax is reduced at PF. Most structuralist proposals of clausal ellipsis, including scant proposals of sluicing in H/U, assume PF-deletion targets a syntactic constituent (TP), forcing the remnant to escape the ellipsis site it is born in (e.g., A: Who did John see? B: Mary (John saw t)., where material in parentheses is PF-deleted). I argue against this conventional view, given the conceptual and empirical issues it raises, chiefly, exceptional movement. I alternatively suggest that non-pronunciation freely and maximally affects morpho-syntactic material surrounding the remnant, allowing it to remain in situ (e.g., A: Who did John see? B: (John saw) Mary.), as has been argued elsewhere for other languages (Kimura 2010, 2013; Bruening 2015; Abe 2015; Ott and Struckmeier 2018; Sato et al. 2018; Griffiths 2019; a.o.). Although PF-deletion is not sensitive to syntactic constituency from this perspective, morpho-syntactic material that does PF-delete must constitute the propositional background of the elided clause to ensure recoverability of unspoken content, reducing clausal ellipsis in H/U to background deletion, a solution that is far more parsimonious and generalizable than competing ‘move-and-delete’ accounts. I then propose to extend this analysis to correlativization in H/U, wherein a left-peripheral relative clause is associated with a correlate in the host clause (HC) (e.g., The girl who is standing, she is tall). Correlatives (CRs) in this language bear discordant characteristics: on the one hand, CRs display properties that point to their connectivity with the HC (e.g., reconstruction effects) and, on the other, features that point to their extra-sentential status (e.g., the lack of a gap in the HC and prosodic separation of CR–HC). Following recent work on Romance/Germanic left-dislocation (Ott 2014, 2015), which presents a similar paradox, I propose that CRs are not syntactically dependent on their HC; conversely, they are relatives that are part of a separate root clause which is juxtaposed in discourse with the HC and is reduced at PF under identity with it (e.g., The girl who is standing (is tall). She is tall.). Connectivity effects of CRs are argued to be ellipsis-mediated, given that such effects are likewise observed in sluicing and fragment answers. In reconciling the contradictory properties of CRs, this novel proposal has an explanatory edge over existing accounts that assume syntactic integration of CR–HC and that rely on either movement or base-generation.
abstracts.009686: We provide the first experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis that transparent readings are sensitive to the QUD (Question Under Discussion) (Schwager, 2009; Percus, 2020; Benbaji-Elhadad, 2023; Mayr and Schmitt, 2023, 2024), using third readings (Fodor, 1970) in attitude reports. In particular, we test Mayr and Schmitt’s (2023; 2024) claim that, even among QUDs about the attitude holder’s mental state, there is difference in the availability of transparent readings. Our results have consequences for replacement-based theories of transparent readings and more broadly illuminate properties of a discourse that give rise to and constrain a QUD about someone’s mental state.
abstracts.009687: This squib examines the morphosyntactic classification and referential properties of pronouns in Urdu, focusing on personal pronouns, reflexives, and reciprocals. It investigates how these elements interact with Classical Binding Theory (Chomsky 1981), with particular attention to the availability of long-distance binding in Urdu reflexives. The analysis shows that while personal pronouns conform to Binding Condition B and reciprocals obey Condition A, reflexives exhibit behavior that challenges strict locality constraints. Specifically, Urdu reflexives display logophoric properties comparable to those observed in languages such as Icelandic and Japanese. These findings suggest that a discourse-sensitive approach to binding is necessary to adequately account for reflexive interpretation in Urdu.
abstracts.009688: Los lectores de ELA encontrarán en el reciente estudio sobre la sordera un resumen actualizado de una controversia en el ámbito de la adquisición del lenguaje y la enseñanza de lenguas que también suscita cuestiones teóricas de amplia repercusión. Son dos campos de trabajo y reflexión que se unen alrededor de una polémica sin precedentes o comparación en la Lingüística Aplicada. Al mismo tiempo, muchos se preguntarán acerca del primero (del ámbito aplicado): ¿por qué una editorial académica publica un libro que presenta, otra vez, evidencia y argumentos sobre un problema científico, al parecer, ya resuelto a finales del siglo pasado? La lectura detallada de los dieciocho capítulos explicará la inesperada razón, luego para darnos la oportunidad de visitar de nuevo los interesantes fundamentos teóricos, todavía pendientes. Por los dos motivos nos ofrece una discusión importante.
abstracts.009689: This paper proposes a unified framework that reconceives the relationship between lexical meaning and world knowledge as a gradient of conventionalization rather than a categorical distinction. Meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization, operationalized as degree of speaker agreement, rather than by membership in "lexical" versus "encyclopedic" categories. The framework introduces a five-level gradient — reference, denotation, sense, cultural connotation, private connotation — corresponding to decreasing intersubjective agreement, and a typology of entailments (strong, default, weak) correlated with these levels. This reconceptualization clarifies semantic prosody, explains why some arguments converge while others polarize, and connects lexical semantics to social epistemology. Central to the epistemological application is the diagnosis of alpha misattribution: the error of treating a term whose meaning is genuinely low-agreement as though it carried the stability of a high-agreement term, an error that converts unresolved conceptual disagreement into the appearance of bad-faith resistance to consensus. The framework generates testable predictions about semantic change, argument dynamics, and the conditions under which making agreement levels explicit can reduce polarization.
abstracts.009690: This study examines whether Gemini, an AI research assistant system that is widely used among college students, recommends ethically questionable statistical practices when analyzing experimental data. I presented Gemini with mock data designed to test for “cherry-picking”—--selectively reporting results from a subset of the data that supports a hypothesis. When the full dataset showed no significant difference but a subset did, Gemini recommended reporting only the subset analysis and suggested post-hoc hypothesis changes (i.e. HARKing). The results underscore the need for stronger ethical guardrails in AI systems and explicit instruction in research ethics for students using AI tools as their study partner.
abstracts.009691: The deletion or invisibility of uninterpretable features at the Conceptual-Intentional (CI) interface is usually treated as stipulative. This Brief argues instead that these effects follow naturally from CI’s vector-space architecture. Features are represented geometrically: interpretability corresponds to projection onto a CI-Potent Space, while uninterpretable features, transformed by non-linear feature checking, collapse into a Null Space and make no interpretive contribution. Form Copy, by contrast, preserves only linearly recoverable features and maps them onto the Potent Space. Modelling AGREE as an inter-dimensional mapping, the CI-Filter reduces to Null Space projection, unifying Deletion and Form Copy under a single architecture-driven principle.
abstracts.009692: Many Romance languages exhibit a morphomic pattern dubbed PYTA (for {perfecto/ pretérito} y tiempos afines–see especially Maiden 2018, Ch 4). Spanish exhibits a striking instance of this phenomenon. No matter how irregular a Spanish verb is otherwise, it always has the same stem for both imperfect subjunctive paradigms and for the future subjunctive (which is defunct in the modern spoken language, but was in active use a few centuries ago), and this stem can be unerringly arrived at by taking the 3rd person plural preterite indicative form and subtracting the sequence -ron. This generalization is exceptionless, but it is not directly formulable in a piece-based view of morphology. For this reason, the PYTA morphome has been suggested to require a paradigm-based view of morphology (see for instance O’Neill 2014 and references cited there). In this paper, I will argue that the PYTA morphome, at least as it arises in Spanish, is actually the result of two independent generalizations interacting. One of these generalizations involves suppletion conditioned by a morphosyntactic feature -Present (usually in combination with the feature +Finite), the other is phonological and concerns (i) the conditioning of vowel height alternations in certain verb roots of the 3rd conjugation, and (ii) the circumstances under which the Theme Vowel of 2nd and 3rd conjugation verbs diphthongizes. Once these generalizations are independently explained (as they must be, since they each affect different parts of the paradigm which extend beyond the claimed morphomic pattern), there is no work left for a direct statement of the morphomic pattern to do, and thus no threat to piece-based models of morphology from this quarter.
abstracts.009693: Interest in animal communication has arguably reached an all-time high, with two very visible projects—the search for the animal roots of human language and the development of methods and technologies to decode animal signals. These projects need a shared, overarching scientific framework. We propose that animal linguistics offers one, which will require close collaboration between ethologists, linguists and, increasingly, AI specialists. One possible way to view the project—not the only one—goes as follows. With the same ambition as human formal linguistics, animal linguistics seeks to develop explicit models of animal communication ("formal animal linguistics"), to understand the extent and limits of variation in living species ("comparative animal linguistics"), and to investigate the cognitive basis of observed properties ("animal psycholinguistics"). Through a "phylogenetic tree of animal signals", it seeks to retrace and explain the path from ancestral signals to modern ones ("evolutionary animal linguistics"). In its synchronic and diachronic components, animal linguistics offers an integrative framework for scientific and technological progress in animal communication. Going forward, it could offer new areas of application and new sources of insight for multiple areas of cognitive science.
abstracts.009694: Hungarian employs complex, contextually-sensitive syntactic rules that place certain constituents in the pre-verbal positions of Focus and Topic. This thesis examines this property of Hungarian, known as discourse configurationality, by comparing native speakers’ grammaticality judgments of possible word orderings within a certain context to the probabilities language models assign in the same situations. After reviewing the discourse-semantic and syntactic aspects of Hungarian word order, I introduce a basic taxonomy of Hungarian focusing and topicalization rules based on foundational perspectives from generative linguistics, and construct a novel set of Hungarian scenarios testing all possible intersections of these rules (5✕4). I assess the grammatical judgments of native speakers (n=50) through a survey administered on the online platform Prolific. These results serve as both a quantitative evaluation of the descriptive capacity of the syntactic rules posited by linguists, as well as the baseline against which the performance of SambaLingo-Hungarian-Chat (Llama-2-7b, optimized for Hungarian) is evaluated. By examining the capability of language models to replicate native-like word order in Hungarian, I present a case for using word-order predictions of discourse configurational languages as a diagnostic for assessing the ability of language models to recognize and respond to subtle pragmatic details, and more broadly for the importance of utilizing insights from theoretical linguistics to engineer better diagnostics for language model evaluation.
abstracts.009695: This paper argues that Japanese passive and potential -rare instantiate a single morpheme, as required by Anti-Homophony (Kayne,2017,2025). It shows that the passive is a (sub)component of one type of potential (psv-potential) and examines promotion and demotion in passives and psv-potentials for different ‘pseudopassives,’ i.e oblique passives. While goal, directional, and source obliques are possible in passives, locative and instrumental obliques are excluded. These are possible however in psv-potentials with an alethic possibility reading. We motivate a fine-grained clausal structure in which passive Voice and potential constructions, consisting of passive -rare and silent modal flavor *possibility* and *ability*, are merged at distinct heights (cf. Cinque 1999, 2004), as supported by aspectual ordering and the distribution of various obliques. This structure allows a unified antisymmetric analysis in which a single -rare is merged at different heights, derives its suffixal status from leftward movement of a phrase containing a verb, also deriving head-final orders. Anti-Locality blocks movement of the immediate complement of - rare. Attract Closest targets the highest movable complement, stranding the embedded subject (PRO). A minimal change in the merge order of modal and passive heads derives active potentials, unifying passives and all potential types. Comparative evidence supports key aspects of the analysis, which in turn provides strong support for approaches such as Collins (2016, 2025), where the external argument of passivized predicates is syntactically projected and passive Voice does not alter argument structure.
abstracts.009696: English contains a small but systematic class of DP-internal expressions whose categorical status is not well captured by the standard labels «determiner», «adjective», «quantifier», or «noun». Canonical members include «the other» and «the rest», and— crucially for the present theory – their closest structural neighbors in the «indefinite ordinal» family such as «the next», «the last», «the former», «the latter», and «the following». We argue that these expressions instantiate a single, typed configuration: a «Selector-Head Expression (SHE)», i.e., a D-licensed selector constituent of the form «[D the] + [Sel X]» that introduces a discourse-anchored selection variable and therefore requires «definite DP closure». The central constituency claim is that the determiner is not merely an external modifier of a nominal head: in selector readings, «the» is the minimal licenser that closes the selector, so that «[the + X]» forms the smallest closed unit, while numerals and NPs («two», «ten people») are specifications of that alreadyclosed selector constituent
abstracts.009697: The study investigates the relationship between word length and phoneme sonority in six languages across diverse language families. Building on the principle of least effort and the Menzerath-Altmann law, the research is aimed to analyze the phoneme sonority using translated New Testament texts in Bilua, Bola, Czech, Gagauz, Jamamadi, and Tongan. The findings reveal that in languages with complex syllables, the tendency of longer words to contain shorter syllables—consistent with the Menzerath-Altmann law— results in a higher proportion of vowels, thereby increasing the mean phoneme sonority. In contrast, languages with simple syllable structures exhibit either a decrease in mean phoneme sonority or no clear trend. Further, mean consonant sonority increases with word length in Bilua, Czech, and Gagauz, while no clear trend is observed in Bola, Jamamadi, and Tongan. Conversely, mean vowel sonority increases with word length in Bola, Jamamadi, and Tongan, but remains stable or decreases in Bilua, Czech, and Gagauz. Overall, the analysis reveals consistent patterns linking word length and sonority across all six languages.

abstracts.009699: Bernd Bierl eloquently proposes an ambitious synthesis towards biological linguistics. This synthesis aims to establish a new bio-ethological linguistics based on 4E cognition. It considers the foundational ethology of authors like Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen to be its biological basis. Rather than developing the biolinguistics inspired by Noam Chomsky, which also has its roots in early 20th-century European ethology, the author considers it an inadequate naturalization and suggests subsuming it under a conception of language as behavior, within the context of embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended (4E) cognition. This reply presents some critical observations on this proposal, highlighting the inadequate interpretation of the biolinguistic approach and the potential shortcomings of the proposed research program.
abstracts.009700: Two MMN experiments investigate integrated versus independent processing of complex auditory information in linguistic sound. We hypothesise that neurophsyiologically evoked responses to multiple distinctive cues are stronger than evoked responses to single cues. We developed a novel methodology combining a fixed-deviant design with roving standards, allowing direct comparison of multiple deviant contexts within a single session. We ran two magnetoencephalographic (MEG) protocols which are identical except for the order of presentation of standard and deviant stimuli. We compare the results of the novel fixed-deviant design to a more traditional design which uses a fixed standard stimulus with a roving deviant. Our study asks if electrocortical techniques can be used to find feature additivity in the perception of linguistic sound, and tests the efficacy of a roving-deviant design versus a fixed-deviant design. Our results suggest that this novel methodology may be useful in testing questions of feature additivity. This work has applications relevant to both the cognitive neuroscience of language, as well as linguistic theory.
abstracts.009701: This article develops and expands a cognitively grounded, cross-linguistic model of nominal phrase architecture that distinguishes three structural layers: (i) an NP-core containing conceptual content (nouns, modifiers, possessives, relational material, interrogative determiners, and prop-nouns such as English one), (ii) a quantifier layer comprising true quantifiers that denote cardinality, proportion, or amount and can satisfy NP-headedness and substitution diagnostics, and (iii) an operator layer comprising higher-order scope instructions—including every, each, and no—that take a domain argument but are predicted not to behave as quantifier heads. The preprint makes the diagnostics explicit, expands the typology into a parallel elicitation grid, and adds two sets of falsifiable consequences: (a) distinguishing predictions for stacking, partitives, and anaphora/ellipsis (Tables 10–11; Figure 5), and (b) explicitly marked neurolinguistic and computational extensions that map the layer split to processing stages and NLP annotation/assembly pipelines (Xakimqulova 2024; Barwise & Cooper 1981; Szabolcsi 2010).
abstracts.009702: This paper advances an operator-centered account of definiteness in which the English definite article THE is a closure operator that maps an open nominal predicate to a discourse-resolved referential term. The clearest environment for closure is not ordinary common-noun definites, but Selector-Head Expressions (SHEs) such as the other, the next, the last, and the rest, where closure over a structured domain is obligatory. To make this operator thesis architecturally nontrivial, we introduce a Structured-Domain Closure Algebra (SDCA) in which closure is a partial operation parameterized by a domain signature (candidate set plus order/partition structure and salience). D-Lock is defined as the SDCA specialization that closes selector predicates. Within SDCA we derive three formal results: (T1) No-Free-Selector Reference—selector predicates cannot be referential without an overt or covert closure device; (T2) Bounded Coercion—apparent THE+pronoun cases are licensed only when a role/persona/kind partition makes an e-type pronoun coercible to ⟨e,t⟩; and (T3) Support-Strategy Completeness—apparent violations of THE’s predicate input requirement are derivable if and only if one of a small set of support strategies (ellipsis/pro-drop, lexicalized pronounization, prop-noun/classifier repair, typed coercion) supplies a closeable predicate. We provide a diagnostic battery (DB-1 to DB-6) that implements these results and separates genuine closure effects from surface look-alikes. The proposal yields falsifiable predictions about selector autonomy, context-manipulable pronoun closure, structured repair spaces, and type-blocking stacking constraints, and it generalizes cross-linguistically via closure substitution (articles, demonstratives, classifiers, and definiteness morphology). We sketch neurolinguistic and computational consequences and provide a reference-attested validation strategy plus an elicitation-ready mini-dataset and reporting template.
abstracts.009703: This paper investigates what happens to grammatical relationships between two morphemes when an inﬁx incidentally lands between them. Most relationships—including allomorphic and morphophonological relationships—persist, showing that these relationships are established before the intrusion of the inﬁx. However, inﬁxes do disrupt word-level phonology, which thus must be established after the intrusion of the inﬁx. These ﬁndings furnish a novel argument for grammatical models that are (i) cyclic and bottom-up (or inside out) with respect to both exponence and certain (morpho)phonological operations, and (ii) noncyclic with respect to certain purely phonological processes, which are computed only at speciﬁc junctures (e.g., the word). A further argument from the interaction of inﬁxation with object incorporation supports a post-syntactic model of morphology, such as Distributed Morphology. This work brings together earlier case studies of Hunzib (Kalin 2022b), Nancowry (Kalin 2023), and Palauan (Embick 2010) with several more languages, including a particularly extensive new study of the Bolivian language isolate Movima (drawing on Haude 2006, 2019), facilitating broader and stronger conclusions.
abstracts.009704: This article formalizes a graph-theoretic diagnostic for nominal architecture. Within a fixed Level‑ k inventory of part-of-speech (POS) items or POS-classes, we build a directed modifiability graph whose edges encode attested direct head-modification under a strict criterion (head targeting, constituency, no category shift, and exclusion of phrase-level scope). Graph partitions—isolates, strongly connected components (SCCs), and stacking partial orders—are coupled to a three-tier architectural taxonomy: High (operators), Middle (repair/packaging mechanisms), and Low (argumental primitives such as reciprocals, nominal WH heads, and free relatives). We provide a closure-sensitivity feature system and prove three results: (T1) an Operator‑ Isolation Theorem for D/Q operator heads under strict head-modification; (T2) a No‑ Post‑ Q‑ Closure Theorem deriving contrasts such as almost every NP vs *the every NP from selection/typing constraints; and (T3) a Repair‑ Completeness Lemma enumerating the only admissible sources of missing ⟨ e,t⟩ material (ellipsis, pronounization, prop‑ noun/classifier repair, or typed coercion). We present a diagnostic battery that can be executed across languages with a small parameter set (article realization, classifier availability, and ellipsis/pro‑ drop), and we sketch computational induction and neurocognitive predictions distinguishing closure from repair operations.

abstracts.009706: Grammaticality judgments are selective: speakers treat violations of agreement, clause structure, tense, or evidential marking as straightforward errors of "grammar", while treating accent shifts, many lexical substitutions, and register choices as matters of style or appropriateness. Why? This paper argues that the difference tracks what kind of work a linguistic contrast does. Some contrasts serve as shared infrastructure for public coordination: they configure what kind of move an utterance counts as, who is committed to what, and what responses are licensed. These contrasts (clause typing, argument linking, polarity, tense--aspect where grammaticalized) form closed paradigms whose values have to be mutually known for coordination to succeed. I call them "operators". Other contrasts, such as accent, open-class vocabulary, and register markers, primarily contribute indexical or conceptual content that remains negotiable; a mismatch invites clarification or social judgment, not structural rejection. Clausal architecture belongs with tense and agreement because it packages operators, not because it's autonomous from meaning. From an information-theoretic perspective, operators function like protocol headers: they carry few bits themselves but cause large entropy reduction downstream, which explains why a wrong value can crash coordination even when the utterance is otherwise intelligible. The proposal predicts that categorical judgments, distinct processing signatures, and strong preemption effects should cluster around operator contrasts cross-linguistically, including tonal or gestural exponents where these are grammaticalized as operators.
abstracts.009707: This chapter specifies a syntactic (functional) shell‑ composition architecture for the nominal phrase and aligns it with three programmatic components developed in the companion manuscripts: (i) Modifiability‑ Graph Diagnostics (MGD) for tier assignment, (ii) a ranked operator/quantifier architecture (HTQA tier nesting) for closure and traversal, and (iii) a bidirectional RED/DED traversal methodology for diagnosing packaging dependencies. The architectural commitment is deliberately minimal and strictly tier‑ based: Shell 1 hosts LOW primitives; Shell 2 hosts MIDDLE packaging/repair orbitals; Shell 3 hosts HIGH operator ranks; Shell 4 hosts connective bridges; Shell 5 hosts outer polarity and outer minimizers that scope over the assembled closure stack. The model is evaluated not by category labels alone but by graph position and closure sensitivity: shells are empirically testable via directed head‑ modification graphs and by explicit falsification templates. The chapter integrates cross‑ linguistic packaging strategies (article, article‑ less, classifier systems) and provides a filled‑ slot inventory that is intentionally extensible
abstracts.009708: English resists separating pre-head dependents from the head of an NP: \textit{*Whose did you read book?} is sharply unacceptable. Rather than positing a universal constraint, this paper asks what English does instead; and measures it. The explanation has three strands: distributional (fused-head construals and workarounds like pied-piping and \textit{big mess} are frequent; configurations resembling left-branch extraction are absent), psycholinguistic (fused-head parsing commits listeners early, making reanalysis costly), and functional (the workaround family already does the semantic work that extraction would do). Corpus rates from Universal Dependencies confirm: workarounds are entrenched, determiner–head packaging is tight, and discontinuity is near-zero. A Bayesian learner has no positive evidence for separation; the posterior stays near zero and the gap perpetuates itself. Absence of evidence, when the search is thorough, is evidence of abstinence. And abstinence, unlike impossibility, can end.
abstracts.009709: This study examines how Czech-speaking children mark voicing in sibilants and how adult listeners perceive these contrasts in children’s speech. Productions of /s, z, ʃ, ʒ/ by 31 children aged 3;5–6;5 show that voicing is cued by both duration and presence of f0: voiceless sibilants are longer and contain less voicing than voiced sibilants. Development is non-linear, with substantial variability, particularly for voiced targets. Consistency improves most clearly by age 6. Phonetic context affects both duration and presence of f0, indicating that productions depend on the elicitation material. Perception experiment involving 48 adults showed that speech-language therapists do not outperform non-professionals in sibilant detection. Listeners rely on both f0 and duration and identify voiceless targets more reliably than voiced targets. Findings support controlling phonetic context and supplementing perceptual judgments with acoustic measures.
abstracts.009710: This brief note reports a mini-experiment, which tested whether major AI systems (Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT) readily perform p-hacking when requested through neutral statistical framing. A single prompt requesting “to find a statistically significant difference” from a given dataset—--which essentially amounts to a request to p-hack—--elicited multiple testing, HARKing, and selective reporting from all three AI systems without any cautionary warnings. Further, examination of the code revealed significant discrepancies between what was reported in the outputs and what was actually analyzed: all the AI systems conducted extensive multiple testing but selectively reported only significant findings, which is methodologically problematic and potentially misleading to naive users. Given the current situation in which students routinely seek statistical advice from AIs, I believe that they should receive systematic guidance regarding the proper use of statistical tests as well as warning against over-trusting AIs as their study partner. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The current version is 2.2. Please see the first page of the paper for details on specific version updates.
abstracts.009711: This paper develops a minimal architectural reanalysis of argumenthood. It proposes that predicates project abstract dependency objects — 'R-anchors' — that encode the existence of argument-related dependencies independently of their overt realization and referential identification. Argumenthood emerges only when such dependencies are structurally completed by a single operation — 'Anchor-Checking'. On this view, omission, generic interpretation, and persistent ambiguity are licensed outcomes of grammatical structure rather than exceptional repairs.
abstracts.009712: Embedding material under intensional operators gives rise to a variety of `non-de dicto' construals: the proposition seemingly expressed by the embedded clause does not describe subject’s the attitudinal state, yet the sentence can be judged true. This paper makes three contributions: First, we strengthen the claims by Mayr & Schmitt 2024 that non-de dicto construals are a uniform phenomenon, which does not involve dedicated syntactic structures or morphology: The distinction between de dicto and non-de dicto construals does not involve ambiguity but, and this is our second point, arises from properties of meaning per se. What can be described as `replacement' -- in non-de dicto construals the meaning of a constituent of the embedded clause is replaced by another -- results from meanings being underspecified: any expression introduces a set of meanings and intensional operators existentially quantify over such sets.s the underspecification we assume is more radical as in underspecification accounts of other phenomena, we propose a new mechanism constraining it, roughly based on pragmatic considerations. Discourse participants aim for `discourse stability': the `traditional' meanings of expressions and their replacements must be indistinguishable for all the questions that might occur in the projected discourse.
abstracts.009713: The asterisk has done foundational work in theoretical linguistics, but it also hides a persistent conflation. The same diacritic is used (i) to mark strings that defeat structural analysis, (ii) to mark structurally viable utterances whose values don't stabilize under the constraints of an interpreted situation, (iii) to mark interpretable forms that still aren't in the community's repertoire, and (iv) to mark cases that are grammatically well-formed but feel unacceptable for reasons of processing or ideology. One sign, four diagnoses: crash, clash, exclusion, and unease. This article argues that the resulting competence–performance–usage triangulation hasn't resolved the impasse because grammaticality has been asked to answer several distinct questions at once. Moving forward, I propose a minimal state theory that reconceptualizes grammaticality as conditioned stability of form–value relations within communicative situations. Grammatical status depends on (i) mapping viability, (ii) interpretive coherence, and (iii) repertoire status. Distinguishing grammatical status from the feeling of ungrammaticality makes principled sense of classic dissociations between acceptability ratings and repertoire membership. The proposal yields operational diagnostics for separating coherence failures from repertoire exclusion, motivates an opportunity-normalized notion of negative evidence, and states concrete conditions under which the framework would be disconfirmed.
abstracts.009714: The development of functional categories crosslinguistically is an extensively studied and debated topic (i.a., Radford 1990; Boser et al. 1992; Rizzi 1993; Guasti 1993; Clahsen et al. 1994; Friedmann et al. 2021; Heim & Wiltschko 2025). In this paper, I contribute to existing literature by exploring the explanatory potential in acquisition of a previously understudied formal notion – categorial granularity (following Biberauer & Roberts 2015; Song 2019; Biberauer 2019). I study the development of the left periphery with a multilingual corpus study on 10 children, across 5 languages. First, a novel contrast is observed: on the one hand, CP-structures emerge very early, favouring accounts with early development of CP. On the other hand, however, there is virtually no evidence in the production data to assume children are operating with a split, cartographic-type CP until a later stage. Second, I show that acquisition and structural height can mismatch: some structurally very high elements (topics, illocutionary complementisers) emerge very early in several children. I then argue that these empirical generalisations pose important challenges for several extant theories of syntactic development, especially those assuming (fully) innate categories. This is because contemporary maturational and continuity approaches posit universal categorial sequences of fixed (often cartographic) granularity. Some of them additionally predict a strong correlation between height in a cartographic tree and timing of acquisition (e.g., Friedmann et al. 2021). I interpret the preliminary results reported here to stress the analytical strengths of incorporating changes in granularity when modelling syntactic development. The data presented provides an initial impetus for a role of granularity in syntactic development and for a reconceptualisation of the latter in terms of emergent categories. I develop a neo-emergentist account of the patterns, probing Biberauer & Roberts’s (2015) emergent categorial hierarchy. I maintain that this is a productive way forward, and finish by considering how this neo-emergentist thinking could be extended in future work.
abstracts.009715: . This paper develops an anchor-based account of English participle predication and linking-verb selection. The central empirical contrast is familiar but under-modeled: a participial predicate licensed under the copula (e.g., be + broken) typically carries stronger world-commitment than the same participle licensed under a perceptual or evidential anchor (look/seem/appear/sound/feel). We argue that this is not a syntactic accident and not reducible to lexical stipulation. Instead, anchors are analyzed as operators that stabilize a state description relative to an information channel (perceptual, inferential, reportative, affective), and the anchoring channel controls (i) commitment strength, (ii) complement selection, and (iii) scope interactions with negation and polarity. We report frequency and collocational profiles of anchor lemmas and their local complement signatures. We then present a worked formalization with an enriched event→state anchoring variant for result participles, and we derive concrete predictions in the form of compatibility matrices and acceptability stimulus kits. This manuscript makes a defensible and nontrivial contribution by reframing English linking verbs (be, look, seem, appear, sound, feel) as a channel-parameterized state-anchoring operator whose grammar can be evaluated via an executable signature assay rather than posthoc description. The strongest novelty is the coupling of (i) a compositional anchor operator with (ii) a discrete Anchor×ComplementType compatibility matrix treated as a falsifiable constraint system, and (iii) a theorem-level consequence (the No-true-cancellation result) that forces a specific class of scope/repair predictions distinguishing the proposal from “bleached copula,” “raising-only,” and scalar evidential alternatives. Importantly, the paper goes beyond schematic predictions by reporting execution outputs from the Table2→Table7 recovery mapper—quantifying matrix–profile concordance (mismatch ≈0.94% with uncertainty) and a robust association signal (χ² with effect size)—thereby operationalizing “anchor geometry” as a measurable object that can be exported to independent corpora, acceptability experiments, and computational evaluation. While the present quantitative results are explicitly proof-of-concept (derived from the manuscript’s extracted inventory rather than an external corpus), the combination of formal forcing consequences + measured recovery performance + ready-torun protocol positions the work as a methodologically novel semantic assay with clear discriminants and a credible path to immediate external validation.
abstracts.009716: This paper presents and analyzes data from A'ingae (or Cofán, an Amazonian isolate, ISO 639-3: con), where the patterns of stress and glottalization in words with classifying nominalizers are sensitive to the base's morphological and syntactic structure. Normally, classifying suffixes override their base's stress and glottalization. However, the overriding is blocked if the base has previously undergone a functional projection spell-out. These A'ingae data show that information about the morphosyntax of the base (specifically, the distinction between functional and categorizing phase heads; e.g. Guekguezian, 2021; Newell, 2008) is accessible and can be referred to in the course of phonological evaluation, thus setting a lower bound on the amount of morphosyntactic information phonology needs to access. Consequently, the study bears on the architecture of the phonology-morphosyntax interface, and contributes to a growing body of literature demonstrating that morphosyntactic information is preserved after Phonological Form (PF) operations such as vocabulary insertion (Gribanova and Harizanov, 2017; Winchester, 2017) and even phonological evaluation (Dobler et al., 2011; Sande, Clem, and Dąbkowski, t.a.).
abstracts.009717: The Morphix manuscript argue that PIE 'pronominal roots' form a distinct morphological species: closed-class, non-derivable, non-compounding, non-ablauting atoms originating in prePIE deictic particles. The model represents these atoms as feature-bundle realizations organized by a geometry whose primary nodes DEIXIS, ANAPH, and Q partition the functional space; optional INDEF and ALTERITY extend the system to indefinite and 'other' series. Vocabulary insertion under the Subset Principle selects the most specific exponent compatible with the syntactic feature bundle, generating syncretisms and blocking effects. Empirically, the manuscript compiles daughter-language reflex lists across major branches and derive adverbial paradigms by composing Morphix exponents with a small suffix system (-r/-d/-m/-o), as well as specific diachronic pathways that connect PIE distal to- to the English th- series. This article integrates the manuscript into a single journal-style treatment, adds explicit comparative tables, diagrams, and falsifiable diagnostics, and frames a research program: cross-corpus assays of particle+suffix compositionality, typological channel hierarchies, and computational reconstruction pipelines grounded in the Morphix geometry. Novelty upgrades in this revision include (i) an executed pilot Morphix+suffix assay on Old English and Vedic/Sanskrit samples with quantitative coverage and cell-recovery metrics (§7.1), (ii) a minimal cost-based model comparison against a root-list baseline (§6.9), and (iii) explicit typological, learnability, and computational evaluation protocols that make the geometry falsifiable (§8–§9)
abstracts.009718: Epistemic claims and future claims often involve the same morpheme (Enç, 1996; Kush, 2015; Winans, 2016; Giannakidou and Mari, 2018). This paper argues that, in some languages, this is because apparent reference to future times is quantification over future worlds. This assimilates the epistemic/future parallel to variable-flavor modality. I introduce novel data from Gujarati (Indo-Aryan), which allows only epistemic readings of the morpheme -s- when it is placed on the auxiliary verb (hovu, ‘to be’), and only future readings when on main verbs. I provide a univocal analysis of the morpheme, where -s- contributes universal modal force, but the modal base (epistemic vs. metaphysical) is determined by syntactic position (following Hacquard 2006). I also show -s- can scope under negation, strengthening the claim that -s- is a necessity modal .
abstracts.009719: This paper aims to establish a unified grammatical mechanism for the referential shift of “VP-de” structures in Modern Chinese within the framework of Sign-based Construction Grammar. It addresses the long-standing disjunction in previous studies between the mechanisms of semantic role determination and contextual regulation in the realization of referential shift. The focus is on how the contrastive construction, as a contextual device, facilitates the referential shift of “VP-de.” The central arguments are as follows: (1) in all “VP-de” structures, the referential target is always a frame element within the relevant cognitive frame; (2) when “VP-de” refers to agents or patients, the referential target corresponds to the verb’s arguments and valence elements, whereas when it refers to other elements, the target belongs to non-core frame elements; (3) contrastive constructions promote non-core frame elements to the status of Question Under Discussion (QUD) foci, thereby licensing them as referential targets. This study not only proposes a unified analytical approach to the referential shift of “VP-de” but also demonstrates the descriptive precision and predictive power of Sign-Based Construction Grammar, offering important insights for the analysis of Chinese constructions.
abstracts.009720: The Podlasie dialect of Polish exhibits a curious nominal case declension paradigm where the dative is expressed by a preposition and a genitive suffix (prep N-gen), which constitutes a typologically rare pattern. Moreover, the instrumental in this dialect, which is hierarchically above the dative, is marked with only a suffix (N-ins), unexpectedly dropping the preposition. The fact that a hierarchically higher case drops a preposition challenges a generalization made in Caha (2009), which builds on Blake's (2001) hierarchy concerning the morphological marking of case. The paper explores how these two atypical patterns follow from the Nanosyntactic lexicalization procedure, offering an analysis that contributes to the discussion of `pre' and `post' marking in morphosyntax. The analysis also sheds light on why the pattern of the case declension attested in the Podlasie dialect is typologically rare.
abstracts.009721: I argue that definite relative clauses, despite their stable strong island status cross-linguistically, lack island status in Adara. The structure is neither selective nor weak, but rather completely permeable, allowing the free extraction of both arguments and adjuncts. In support of the claim that A-bar movement may escape relative clause domains in Adara, I adduce evidence from crossover effects, reconstruction effects, and quantifier float. In addition, I show that relative clause-internal material may probe upwards and outwards, triggering long-distance agreement of relativized verbs with clause-external subjects in a way that is not possible with true island structures in the language.
abstracts.009722: The nature and status of abstract objects have been at the center of metaphysical debate for a very long time and they form a topic that bears a particular connection to natural language. Philosophers frequently draw on natural language to motivate properties, numbers, and propositions as objects, and it is generally taken for granted that abstract objects of this sort are well-reflected in natural language and in fact that reference to them in natural language is pervasive. This paper will review and modify in a certain way the view I had advanced in Abstract Objects and the Semantics of Natural Language (OUP 2013). This is the view according to which reference to abstract objects in natural language is much more restricted in natural language than traditionally held. More precisely, the thesis of the book, the Abstract-Objects Hypothesis, is that natural language permits reference to abstract objects only in its periphery, not in its core, that is, roughly, only with terms that involve some form of metaphysical reflection. To give an example, wisdom is a term of the core of English and it does not actually refer to an object that is a property, but rather it stands for a plurality of particulars (tropes or modes, that is, particularized properties). By contrast, the property of being wise is a term of the periphery of English, and it does refer to a property as an object. The core-periphery distinction has implicitly been made throughout the history of philosophy and is essential to uncovering what sort of ontology is reflected in ordinary judgments or intuitions that are manifest in natural language. Even though reference to abstract objects of the sort of properties, propositions, and numbers is available only in the periphery of language, natural language permits reference to other sorts of abstract objects in its core, in particular abstract artifacts of various sorts. Thus the Abstract Objects-Hypothesis has to be modified accordingly. The paper will also elaborate the ways in which reference to abstract objects can be achieved in the periphery of language, through the compositional semantics of 'reifying terms'.
abstracts.009723: The Williams Cycle, which is based on the longstanding idea of the ban on improper movement, encounters a non-trivial problem when we consider the fact that long-distance movement proceeds through clause-internal intermediate positions. This paper makes progress in solving this problem by investigating a sharp locality asymmetry in the Mandarin lian...dou construction: movement to a TP-internal position is clause-bounded (it can span TPs but not CPs), while movement to a TP-external position can cross CP boundaries. Crucially, the “blocked” TP-internal position is still required as an intermediate step in long-distance movement that terminates at the TP-external position. To explain this, I propose a feature-based reformulation of the Williams Cycle. The proposed constraint regulates where features are interpreted (at terminal steps) along the movement path, while ignoring intermediate steps motivated by successive cyclicity. This result not only has repercussions for the proper analytical treatment of improper movement but also sheds light on broader typological interactions between cyclic movement and clause-internal operations.
abstracts.009724: In sign languages, different articulators (i.e., the two hands) can represent different characters involved in the same action. As skilled bimodal bilinguals can simultaneously utter a sentence in a sign language and in a spoken language, the simultaneous production of two sentences is cognitively possible. Since in sign languages multiple articulators work with some degree of autonomy, we propose that it is possible to co-utter two or more coordinated clausal units internal to the same sign language if they convey different aspects of the same complex conceptual message. Not only can two propositional units be co-uttered, but also two constituents internal to the same sentence can be. This allows us to develop a new approach to Role Shift in sign languages and related phenomena. We discuss the consequences for theories of linearization, comparing those which claim that syntactic structures are inherently provided with a linear order (based on asymmetric c-command configurations) and those that assume that order is imposed only when syntactic structures are shipped to the phonological component.
abstracts.009725: We argue for a structurally uniform account of slur-based definites (SDs), focusing on the systematic ambiguity between descriptive and epithet readings of SDs in Brazilian Portuguese. We show that the interpretive and distributional contrasts between these readings – e.g., concerning misdescription tolerance, Principle C effects, binominal constructions, NP ellipsis – do not motivate structural ambiguity within the DP, contrary to recent proposals. Instead, we derive both readings from the interaction of two independently motivated ingredients: (i) an optional type-shifting operation triggered by a syntactic [ex +] feature on NPs, which transfers descriptive content from the truth-conditional to the use-conditional dimension; and (ii) a systematic lexical ambiguity in definite determiners, which can be interpreted either as uniqueness operators or as pronominal elements. This approach preserves a uniform DP syntax while accounting for the full range of interpretive and distributional properties of slur-based nominals. Furthermore, it also unifies epithet readings with referential uses of definite descriptions.
abstracts.009726: This note proposes a neutral, falsification-oriented framework for evaluating how plausibly a given string of symbols could correspond to spoken language systems at the level of language families. Rather than attempting decipherment or semantic interpretation, the framework assesses phonological *compatibility*: the degree to which a symbol string can be accommodated by known phonological constraints with minimal distortion. The method is intended as an auxiliary tool for hypothesis testing in historical linguistics, undeciphered script studies, and comparative phonology.
abstracts.009727: Morphophysics models morphological structure as a dynamical field in which grammatical categories, affix positions, and co-occurrence constraints emerge as attractors shaped by a shared geometry (curvature, boundaries, resonance minima) and universal forces (upward drift, downward anchoring, lateral expansion, and restorative coherence). In this article, we synthesize the theory presented across the source documents into a unified framework that connects (i) diachronic cyclicity (drift → turbulence → collapse → renewal → integration), (ii) typological universals as emergent properties of shared field geometry, and (iii) cross-system convergence and typological clustering as global outcomes of trajectory dynamics. We make the synthesis explicit by (a) specifying a minimal formal vocabulary (state space, potential landscape, occupancy dynamics, interference constraints), (b) mapping each theoretical component to empirical diagnostics suitable for corpus and historical study, and (c) providing a quantitative ‘sanity check’ using term-frequency and co-occurrence structure extracted from the full text of the manuscript and article. The resulting article provides a consolidated theoretical statement, a testable empirical program, and a novelty assessment that separates genuine architectural contributions from metaphor risks. The primary contribution is not the use of physics metaphors per se, but the attempt to turn them into a predictive, modular architecture in which universals, typological clusters, and cyclic change are derived from a single set of shared primitives.
abstracts.009728: This article argues that Y is neither a vowel, nor a glide, nor an energy conduit. Y is instead a ghost connector: a silent predicator and directional operator that assigns transitions between vowel states within a universal vowel well. Under this reconceptualization, English “diphthongs” are not vowel blends and not vowel+glide sequences. Their nucleus is a single trajectory object—a predicated transition—generated by an operator of the form Y(v₁ , v₂ ) and not representable as a static feature bundle. In CVC structures, Y never fills the V-slot; the trajectory fills it. The account also rejects an empty-nucleus analysis and does not treat Y as a governing/licensing head; instead, nucleus formation is typed as state versus trajectory. Finally, the theory connects abstract predication to physical realization through a commutative interface diagram, preserving systematic correspondence while rejecting identity between morphodynamical transitions and articulatory gestures.
abstracts.009729: In the generative tradition, the conditions on subextraction (i.e., the extraction from a phrase XP) have been captured by either one of the following incompatible formulations: (i) a formulation based on the notion of phase (the PIC, i.e., the Phase Impenetrability Condition); (ii) a formulation based on the notion of selection and on the configuration in which XP occurs (the subjacency condition). We provide two empirical case studies, both focused on Italian, to test the predictions of formulations (i)-(ii): inverse copular sentences and the complement of quality. Our main finding is that subextraction is naturally accounted for by the subjacency condition, not by the PIC. In this way, this study brings fresh empirical evidence to bear on the role of phases in the theory of locality.
abstracts.009730: Language contact is often argued to lead to word order change – e.g., the OV-to-VO shift. Though the exact mechanism of change is poorly under- stood, instances of lack of this change, despite the favourable conditions being present (intense contact, dominant bilingualism with a majority VO language, etc.) are worth investigating. In this paper, we present novel data from Surgut Khanty (Ob-Ugric, Uralic) and show how language-internal factors pertaining to information structure (IS) – fusion of grammatical roles and IS-properties, and IS-restrictions on the postverbal domain – govern the distribution of postverbal constituents (PVCs) in an otherwise rather strictly verb-final language. We pro- pose that these factors have so far prevented Surgut Khanty from undergoing an OV-to-VO shift despite intense contact and widespread bilingualism with a dominant VO language, Russian.
abstracts.009731: This paper introduces two novel empirical observations about sentences containing narrow focus on the perfect participle (e.g., "Esme has [BEEN]F married"). First, we show that these sentences are examples of universal perfects, which entail that the eventuality described by the VP holds at the reference time. Broad-focused versions of the same sentences, on the other hand, only give rise to experiential readings. This observation is not accounted for by prior accounts of the perfect, which predict that universal readings only arise in the presence of certain overt adverbials (Iatridou et al., 2001; Portner, 2003). Second, we observe that perfect sentences with focused participles imply that the eventuality has held for a long interval. We analyze this "length implication" as an instance of domain focus that associates with covert even exhaustification (cf. Chierchia, 2006), where the focused domain is of the left boundary of the perfect time span. These two observations lead us to the generalization that universal readings of the perfect are only licensed when the LB is (at least partially) specified. From this, we trace the unavailability of universal readings under broad focus to competition between the present perfect and the simple present: universal readings are ruled out when semantically equivalent to the simple present. Since, by specifying the LB, both adverbials and the length implication make a universal perfect more informative than the simple present, it can surface. In sum, we argue that a full account of the perfect requires reference to both focal alternatives and competition.
abstracts.009732: This article provides a morphosyntactic and semantic analysis of nine yes/no question constructions across English and Chinese varieties (e.g., Mandarin, Yixing, Nanjing, Suzhou, Hefei, Kunming, Liangshan, many of which are understudied), and shows that the apparently complex crosslinguistic variation is in fact complete systematic variation generated by just three binary parameters. The first parameter is whether or not the question involves a polar Disjunction Phrase (DisjP) in syntax. The questions with a polar DisjP vary in two more parameters: whether there is overt or covert wh-movement, and whether the DisjP is realised as a single Vocabulary Item or multiple. Our study has two theoretical implications. The first is for question semantics and typology: we provide syntactic and morphological evidence for two types of interrogative C0s in Hamblin’s (1973) question semantics; we also argue that the yes-no questions without DisjP do not involve any wh-element, and thus no (c)overt wh-movement or even genuine wh-in-situ, thus enriching the typology of questions. Our second theoretical contribution lies in theories of parametric variation. The three parameters proposed in this article have three different sources, all of which should be taken into account in parametric theories: linearization, phonological realization of features during Lexical Insertion, and the (un)availability of features in the lexicon.
abstracts.009733: This is a continuation of my recent research examining whether the naive use of the current AI systems can lead to research misconduct. Building on the previous observation that current AI systems can offer ways to engage in selective reporting (Kawahara 2026f) and p-hacking (Kawahara 2026d), I examined whether the three major AI systems (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) would find and exclude outliers after seeing the results of a non-significant t-test---a clear form of post-hoc data manipulation that constitutes research misconduct under standard definitions. When asked to “remove outliers to achieve statistical significance” with a very direct prompt, the three systems behaved differently. In initial single-trial observations, Claude explicitly identified the request as research misconduct and declined to execute it; ChatGPT initially refused but then suggested methodological alternatives that could achieve the same outcome; Gemini executed the request, reported a “revised and now-significant” p-value, and offered a methodological justification that misrepresented the post-hoc nature of the analysis. Version 3.0 now reports a preregistered replication with 30 trials per system (Kawahara & Iwase 2026), which confirmed that these patterns are systematic rather than incidental: Claude refused all 30 requests, ChatGPT issued ethical warnings in all 30 trials but nevertheless executed the request in 10 of them, and Gemini executed the request in 25 of 30 trials.
abstracts.009734: This article develops a single internal claim that recurs across the Morphodynamics program: the primitive inventory that drives grammatical evolution is particle-stratified. Free or weakly bound discourse / clausal modifiers and certain “primitive” bound exponents (illustrated by IndoEuropean suffixal atoms such as -s, -t, and -m̥ ) are not clausal or syntactic primitives. They are particle-origin elements whose apparent clausal behavior emerges from confinement geometry. The analysis is written entirely in the native morphodynamic formalism: a ghost-slot (“well”) is a directed confinement geometry with (i) a state inventory V, (ii) a licensed transition set E, (iii) depth/weight w, and (iv) a distributional wavefunction ψ that supports canonical wave-dynamic outcomes (drift, diffusion, fusion, absorption, elimination, collapse). Within this geometry, particle material occupies the high-optionality surface and transitional channels, and may stabilize into bound morphology via absorption and fusion. The paper formalizes particle-origin diagnostics with theorem-style statements (including a Particle Origin Lemma for -s and its extension to the compact suffix set), supplies well-internal predictions, and provides a battery of schematic but operational figures, tables, and adjudication templates that can be populated with the manuscript’s measurement program.
abstracts.009735: This article analyzes negative indefinites (n-words) in Albanian. These items include a prefixed element and an indefinite, and obligatorily require the occurrence of the negative marker, NM. Complementarily, the indefinite element can occur alone in negative contexts. This distribution, specifically the types of negative doubling, is explained by assuming that the negative operator is not realized by a lexical constituent within the syntactic structure. The idea is that negation is postulated and made available to interpretation by the presence of NM and n-words. The Chomskyan notion of I-Merge and the lexical properties of n-words provide the crucial syntactic tools to connect doubling and other phenomena to the phasal Spell-out procedure.
abstracts.009736: This chapter offers a selective, analytically oriented investigation of key aspects of Tigrinya syntax. Rather than providing a comprehensive grammatical description, it focuses on phenomena that are particularly informative for both descriptive and theoretical study. Combining general overviews with targeted phenomena, the chapter examines properties of the nominal, verbal, and clausal domains. These include double determination, object marking, prepositions, verb raising, clause types, information structure, and negation. Through these analyses the chapter aims to clarify central patterns in Tigrinya syntax, and to situate the language within broader investigations in syntactic theory, typology, and Semitic linguistics.
