abstracts.009737: This paper develops a semantics of experiential objects, i.e., satisfiable objects associated with experiential episodes that carry satisfaction/accuracy conditions, and uses it to analyze English find with small-clause complements. I propose that find uniformly introduces an experiential object, and that the embedded predication compositionally specifies the satisfaction conditions of that object within an object-based truthmaker semantics. The account aims to give a unified analysis for the two senses associated with find, namely, the object-encounter reading (John found the door open) and the evaluative reading (John found the cake tasty), without positing two unrelated lexical items or reducing the evaluative use to belief ascription. More generally, the analysis supports a view on which grammar makes direct reference to experiences as objects that can be evaluated for accuracy.
abstracts.009738: The study of speech categorization has a long history. Two phenomenological laws of speech categorization are statable based on this extensive history: monotonicity and sigmoidality of the identification/categorization functions. While prior work has heavily focussed on accounting of observed data in terms of specific theories, and computationally modelling observed patterns, far less work has been done on formally comparing theories to study their explanatory potential, particularly their explanatory value with respect to the two laws. Taking up the latter challenge, in this paper, I formally compare four theories (or frameworks) that have been popular in the literature: (a) Categorical Boundary theories, (b) Prototype theories, (c) Bayesian theories, (d) Exemplar theories. Out of the four, only Category Boundary theory was found to have a clear and simple explanatory account for the two laws. Prototype theory is shown to be consistent with the law of monotonicity but not sigmoidality. Bayesian categorization and Exemplar theories were found to not be explanatory of either law except when severe, currently ad hoc, restrictions were imposed on the category distributions. [Note: While I’ve focussed narrowly on speech categorization throughout the paper, it is possible to extend the formal results to develop a similar view of discrete categories in other domains where sigmoidal curves have been observed, such as language change, language acquisition, and phonotactics, amongst other fields.]
abstracts.009739: We investigate how transformer models represent complex verb paradigms in Turkish and Modern Hebrew, concentrating on how tokenization strategies shape this ability. Using the Blackbird Language Matrices task on natural data, we show that for Turkish --with its transparent morphological markers-- both monolingual and multilingual models succeed, either when tokenization is atomic or when it breaks words into small subword units. For Hebrew, instead, monolingual and multilingual models diverge. A multilingual model using character-level tokenization fails to capture the language non-concatenative morphology, but a monolingual model with morpheme-aware segmentation performs well. Performance improves on more synthetic datasets, in all models.
abstracts.009740: This note describes an auxiliary, exploratory extension to a previously proposed phonological plausibility framework for evaluating unknown or ambiguous symbol strings. The extension introduces a phonological probe that generates broad sound-category constraints for structurally plausible symbol strings, while explicitly preventing phoneme assignment, lexical identification, or semantic interpretation. The probe operates by conditioning sound-category generation on phonological profiles, enforcing conservative phonotactic filters, and applying entropy-based failure detection to prevent overfitting. The method is falsification-oriented: its primary function is to rule out unsafe or unjustified sound hypotheses rather than to propose readings. Failure cases are treated as informative outcomes. This work is intended as a methodological demonstration for researchers in historical linguistics, undeciphered script studies, and comparative phonology, and makes no claims about any specific script or language. It extends the phonological plausibility framework described in *Basu, A. (2026). A Phonological Plausibility Framework for Evaluating Unknown or Ambiguous Symbol Strings*.
abstracts.009741: Clitic placement with European Portuguese uninflected verbs is problematic for prosodic analyses. While ‘proclisis triggers’ give rise to obligatory proclisis with inflected verbs, they often lead to optional proclisis/enclisis with uninflected verbs (Raposo & Uriagereka 2008), except for aspectual/quantificational adverbials with head-like behaviour (Martins 2013a). These patterns provide support for a syntactic ‘Anti-V2 requirement’ account, whereby clitics usually raise to adjoin to T and either (a) an XP raises to/through spec FinP and the verb stays in Asp (resulting in proclisis) or (b) the verb raises to Fin (resulting in enclisis), but not both (building on Fernández-Rubiera 2009, 2010). The special behaviour of uninflected infinitives can be explained by the possibility of clitics attaching to a lower verbal host and then moving with that host to T resulting in enclisis (Raposo and Uriagereka 2008). Aspectual/quantificational heads block verb movement to T, ruling out enclisis via this ‘low fusion’.
abstracts.009742: This thesis investigates the overgeneralization of the causative alternation in second language (L2) English, with particular focus on over(anti)causativization errors, whereby non-alternating transitive or causative verbs are accepted in ungrammatical (anti)causative constructions. While previous research has extensively documented overcausativization errors involving unaccusative verbs (e.g., *The magician disappeared the rabbit), comparatively little attention has been paid to learners’ acceptance of non-target anticausative uses such as *The picture painted. Building on the manner/result distinction proposed in lexical semantic theory, this study advances a manner/result overgeneralization hypothesis, according to which L2 learners overextend the generalization that only result verbs, which lexicalize the result state of the event, can participate in the causative alternation. Once learners acquire this generalization, they may incorrectly apply it to non-alternating result verbs (destroy, kill), while manner verbs are predicted to resist such overgeneralization. This proposal makes predictions that differ from existing accounts based on L1 lexical transfer or the assumption that learners uniformly assign complex event structures to all verbs. To test this hypothesis, a context-based 7-point acceptability judgment task was administered to 120 Japanese-speaking learners of English across four proficiency levels, as well as a native English control group. The experiment employed a 2 × 2 design crossing Verb Type (manner vs. result verbs) and Structure (transitive/causative vs. anticausative). All target verbs were non-alternating in both English and Japanese, allowing the effects of lexical semantics to be examined independently of L1 transfer. The judgment data were z-score transformed and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The results revealed that learners at the intermediate proficiency level rated anticausativized result verbs significantly higher than anticausativized manner verbs, while no such asymmetry was observed in lower or higher proficiency groups. This pattern supports the manner/result overgeneralization hypothesis and suggests that intermediate learners possess knowledge of the semantic generalization governing the causative alternation but overapply it to non-alternating result verbs. The findings indicate that non-target (anti)causativization in L2 English reflects a developmental stage in which learners generalize lexical-semantic principles, rather than mere L1 transfer or undifferentiated event-structure representations.
abstracts.009743: The creation, delivery, and user customization of audio-visual content have changed as a result of recent advancements in speech and language technologies. Enhancing accessibility, naturalness, and user engagement is the main goal of applications like parameter-efficient text-to-speech (TTS) adaptation, emotion-aware audiobook narration, automatic video subtitling, and multilingual voice cloning. Four representative research works that address basic issues in modern speech processing systems are compared in this review paper. To increase subtitle accuracy, multilingual speech synthesis, emotional expressiveness, and computational efficiency, the chosen studies make use of a variety of methods, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR), natural language processing (NLP), deep neural vocoders, sentiment analysis, and low-rank adaptation. The methodology, experimental results, and noted limitations of each system are evaluated. This review also identifies important research gaps concerning data efficiency, multilingual generalization, privacy considerations, robustness in a variety of acoustic environments, and preservation of emotional nuance. By synthesizing insights from these works, the paper outlines prevailing trends and identifies future research directions toward building scalable, expressive, and secure speech-enabled applications.
abstracts.009744: We develop a stratal analysis of Spanish stress in which morphosyntactic conditioning and metrical nonuniformity are tightly constrained. Morphosyntactic conditioning is limited to cyclicity, the distinction between stems and affixes, and the affiliation of affixes to the stem or word level. Nonuniformity arises from lexical prespecification and interstratal constraint reranking. This framework yields several successful empirical predictions: Richness of the Base requires that prespecification be unpredictably distributed across all morph types; Chung’s Generalization demands identical metrical patterns in mono- and polycyclic stem-level constructions; and the Monomorpheme Generalization entails that monomorphemic and overtly affixed stem-level items also exhibit the same patterns.
abstracts.009745: In the first part of my paper, I render the notions of argument raising and A-dependencies and show that case licensing in the upper clause is neither a necessary precondition of raising nor its universal trigger. There are languages with raising constructions, where case is licensed in the complement clause. Hyperraising, i.e. raising out of embedded complement clauses is widespread outside the languages of the Standard Average European type and is attested in some European languages including Bulgarian. In the second part of the paper, I offer a parametrization of six European languages with raising constructions and show that these languages are not uniform: some of them including English primarily encode the control versus raising distinction lexically, while other including Russian and Danish are mixed raising languages that developed productive raising constructions with added morphosyntactic markers.
abstracts.009746: This paper analyzes the mapping between two types of categories belonging to distinct structured inventories related within a single conception in a text; to demonstrate that mapping between two types of structured inventory does not occur between cognitively analogous structures. The relational architecture of one system affects the characteristics of the mapping asymmetrically. This paper maps interactions of scope with respect to linking structures at three schematic levels relative to the schematic levels of the decimal system through cognitive grammar (Langacker, 1987, 1990, 2006) analysis of the text Tractatus Logico-philosophicus (Wittgenstein, Pears & McGuiness (Trans.), 1921/ 2002) as primary data. This paper demonstrates that natural language categories do not interact symmetrically. Such mapping asymmetrically adheres to the relational architecture of any one structured inventory in any specific instance of posited correlation.
abstracts.009747: This study explores how analogical reasoning in a multilingual Indian classroom reflects broader cultural linguistic and epistemic dynamics. It draws discourse in the classroom and post instructional interviews to highlight the contrast between heuristic analogies generated by students with post festum analogies introduced by instructors. Using a cultural-linguistic lens, the analysis examines how language ideologies form conceptual misalignments and therefore shape the learners access to canonical scientific knowledge. This study situates analogy not merely as a cognitive tool but a site of epistemic negotiation- where the prior experiences of the student, linguistic repertoires and socio-cultural positions influence how science is understood or resisted or reinterpreted. The findings highlight the need to recognize analogical reasoning as a culturally mediated practice that both enables and constraints participation in science education.
abstracts.009748: This case study investigates how analogical reasoning in a multilingual Indian classroom reflects broader cultural, linguistic and epistemic dynamics. It focuses on the discrepancy between heuristic analogies generated by students and post festum analogies introduced by instructors. It employs the framework of cognitive grammar to examine how linguistic structures at different levels of organization facilitate or hinder the development of alternative conceptions during instruction. A qualitative research design was adopted which drew audio recorded classroom discourse and post-instructional interviews to capture the learners post hoc reasoning. Narrow transcription and discourse analysis reveal how reduced proficiency, language ideologies and socio cultural positioning shape the access of the learner to canonical knowledge. The findings suggest that heuristic analogies emerge through a linguistically mediated practice of meaning making where any artefact of language, as a structured inventory of symbols is situated within a broader socio-cultural domain. It furthermore, investigates how the organization of instructional discourse shapes the analogies constructed by the students. By situating analogy as a site of epistemic negotiation, the study contributes to ongoing debates about equity identity and participation in science education highlighting the need to recognize analogical reasoning as a practice that both enables and constraints epistemic access.
abstracts.009749: A central question about our shared capacity for language is how it is integrated with other cognitive systems. One important debate focuses on the extent to which the form of linguistic expressions is grounded in their communicative function: Can all constraints on linguistic form be attributed to the way constructions package information, or is linguistic form autonomous of meaning and function? One area of disagreement involves islands: phrases which block the formation of long-distance filler-gap dependencies (Ross, 1967). Grammatical subjects are considered islands, since questioning a sub-part of a subject results in an ill-formed sentence, e.g., “Which topic did the article about inspire you?”. Autonomous syntactic approaches to islands attribute this ungrammaticality to the abstract movement dependency between the wh-phrase and the subject-internal position with which it is associated. An alternative developed in Abeillé et al. (2020) suggests that subjects’ island status is specific to the information structure of wh-questions, suggesting that subjects are not islands for movement, but for focusing, due to their discourse-backgroundedness. This predicts that other constructions that involve movement but not focusing should not create a subject island effect. We test this in three acceptability studies, using a factorial design to isolate subject island violations across three constructions: wh-questions, relative clauses and topicalization. We find a subject island effect in each case, despite only wh-questions introducing what Abeillé et al. (2020) call “a clash in information structure”. We argue that this motivates an account of islands in terms of syntactic representations shared across constructions, independent of communicative function.
abstracts.009750: This article attempts to examine the linguistic phenomenon of folk etymology and to ascertain its contribution to the probable initial introduction and later survival of Latin loans in Standard Modern Greek. Specifically, it emerges that from a corpus of approximately 200 surviving Latin words, there is a recorded paretymological connection with Greek morphemes in a percentage of around 10% (c.a. 20 words). The linguistic data are drawn from the electronic corpus of TLG texts and mostly concern medieval dictionaries, such as the Etymologicum Magnum, the Suda Dictionary, etc. The possibility that this etymological association is not carried out by most speakers but constitutes a conscious practice of Byzantine scholars with normative - regulatory intentions, is underlined and its balancing is sought through the examination of texts of non-metalinguistic content, such as papyri, etc. In parallel with paretymology, the claim is made that the acoustic similarity between Greek and Latin words, due to a common Indo - European origin, also contributed to the introduction of the latter into the language through their grouping in the mental lexicon. This is a preprint / working paper version of a manuscript submitted for peer review. The paper has not been peer-reviewed
abstracts.009751: English-speaking children rarely address parents by first name – a social prohibition encoding power and solidarity. Separately, English kinship terms like Mom and Dad permit bare singular use (Mom called) where other count nouns don't (*Neighbour called}, in ordinary conversation). While previous work approaches this interface (Downing, 1996), the specific link between the naming taboo and the syntactic outcome – determinerless argumental structure – remains unexplored. I argue that the naming taboo causes the proper-noun-like syntax: high-frequency use of kinship terms in vocative function – forced by the prohibition on first names – produces grammaticalization toward strong proper-name status. Corpus data from CHILDES confirm that parent terms show disproportionate vocative concentration (16–43\%) compared to extended kin terms (4–7\%), and vocative concentration correlates with bare-argument realization rates across terms. A careful category/function distinction provides the analytical apparatus; the taboo is the engine, the syntax is the sediment.
abstracts.009752: This paper examines the grammatical behavior of two nominal placeholders in Latin American Spanish: "coso" in Rioplatense Spanish and "este/esta" in Chilean Spanish. These expressions function as substitutes for nouns that are forgotten or deliberately left unmentioned. Drawing on novel data, I show that both elements systematically give rise to interpretations involving epistemic specificity, a property that distinguishes them from general nouns such as "cosa" ‘thing’. At the same time, they differ with respect to a number of morphosyntactic properties. To account for these contrasts, I propose an analysis according to which "coso" is a noun that incorporates into a specificity projection within the nominal structure, while "este/esta" is a demonstrative modifier accompanying a phonologically empty noun. This analysis shows that nominal placeholders do not form a uniform grammatical class; rather, their varying properties emerge from the interaction of lexical and morphosyntactic factors.
abstracts.009753: This paper examines the intricate ways in which the uralic languages of the Komi and Umdurt Rebuplic as well as the Perm Okrug of Russia concern with possession.
abstracts.009754: In contemporary colloquial Hebrew, unaccusative verbs may fail to exhibit ϕ-agreement with their subject when the latter appears postverbally, but not when it appears preverbally. To resolve disagreements regarding the role that intervention may play in licensing this lack of agreement, we conducted two acceptability judgment experiments, whose design and results we report. The findings indicate that intervention is not the factor licensing lack of agreement, contra Preminger’s (2009, 2014) claim, which means the phenomenon does not corroborate his approach to grammaticality. Further, we provide evidence that this lack of ϕ-agreement with a postverbal internal subject results from the reanalysis of the subject as caseless. This is liable to occur in languages that do not morphologically mark nominative. Hebrew existential and possessive constructions had undergone a parallel process in the beginning of the past century.
abstracts.009755: The difficulty of obtaining quantitative evidence under controlled experimental conditions is exponentially increased when the language under study is highly stigmatized, and its speakers are aware of its stigma. In this paper, we describe the difficulties encountered in designing experimental tasks to study focus-marking strategies in Ecuadorian Andean Spanish (EAS). EAS is an emblem of the indigenous people of Ecuador and is frequently associated with an ideal rural, poor, uneducated, indigenous speaker. EAS differs from Ecuadorian Spanish (the standard spoken by the non-indigenous majority in Ecuador) in the level of influence of Kichwa, the Quechua language of Ecuador. We use EAS as a case study to examine the role of language ideologies in the participants’ performance in controlled experimental settings and to discuss possible solutions to overcome the difficulties derived from such complex sociolinguistic pictures. Specifically, we introduce what we dub the Community-Based Approach and the Saving-Face Approach to experimental methodologies. These approaches allow participants to, first, fall into everyday speech practices and, second, to detach themselves from the stigma carried by their language. Together, these approaches to experimental methodologies lead to a collection of data that accurately portrays the participants’ grammar.
abstracts.009756: This is a fifth experiment of my general research program, which empirically explores how current generative AI systems behave with respect to research ethics. This time, I addressed the question of whether and how three major AI systems (ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini) respond a request for optional stopping. Given a series of data, do the AIs keep running a statistical test until it finds significance? I observed three types of behaviors: outright denial, execution with ethical warnings and execution without warnings. Out of ten trials, Claude denied four times and executed without warnings six times; ChatGPT denied once and executed with warnings nine times; Gemini executed all ten times, providing warnings in seven trials. The overall results demonstrate that the AI safeguard systems are stochastic. And importantly, in some cases, at least for Claude and Gemini, users get outputs of iterative t-tests without any warnings. Version 2.0 of this paper includes a summary report of a scaled, preregistered replication study by Kawahara & Iwase (2026), which tested these AI’s behaviors with 30 trials. The results confirm the original findings that the AIs’ safeguard systems are stochastic, with their execution rates varying between about 75%–100%. A new problem of “code opacity” is identified, in which the UI obscures a Python execution failure and the model proceeds to present hallucinated statistical values as if they were computed.
abstracts.009757: This paper investigates the semantics and pragmatics of nandao questions (nandao-Qs) in Mandarin, focusing on their evidential properties. While previous studies have treated nandao as a biased question word or a rhetorical device (Alleton 1988, Gong 1995, Xu 2012, 2017), this paper argues that nandao-Qs encode evidential signals and reflect the speaker's confrontation with unexpected contextual evidence. Drawing on insights from the Kernel-based framework from Von Fintel & Gillies (2010), this paper demonstrates that nandao-Qs marks an incompatible Kernel, representing an "epistemic" conflict that arises from either disbelief or a deviation from grammatical priors. Additionally, I explore the selectional constraints of nandao, explaining its exclusive compatibility with polar questions. Furthermore, I revisit the relationship between nandao-Qs and rhetorical questions, establishing that while nandao creates an environment conducive to rhetorical interpretation, it does not inherently constitute a rhetorical question. This analysis offers a unified account that integrates previous approaches and sheds light on giving explanations for the broader discourse functions of nandao.
abstracts.009758: Makista, the Macao Portuguese Creole, is an understudied endangered language. This essay explores the Tense-Mood-Aspect(TMA) system of Makista by considering the grammatical and semantic properties of the three overt TMA markers: já, lôgo and ta. Examples are collected from José dos Santos Ferreiro's poems and existing scholarly literature by Pinharanda-Nunes. Results reveal that já is a past marker in tense, and a perfective marker in aspect; lôgo is a future marker in tense, and an irrealis marker in mood; ta is a non-punctual marker in aspect. The study provides empirical evidence for the research of Ibero-Romancebased creoles, and contributes to the field of creole study.
abstracts.009759: This paper reevaluates Optimal Paradigms (OP), an extension to Optimality Theory proposed by McCarthy (2005). In OP, candidates are full inflectional paradigms and faithfulness constraints can require uniformity between all members within a paradigm. McCarthy (2005) proposed that OP can replace the assumption that prosodic templates are grammatical entities and other phonological mechanisms, which he regards as stipulations. One of the case studies used in McCarthy (2005) to showcase OP comes from Moroccan Arabic, where a noun-verb asymmetry in the distribution of schwa is claimed to be predicted by paradigmatic constraints as a means to achieve uniformity within an inflectional paradigm. We reevaluate this proposal using new fieldwork data from Judeo-Tripolitanian Arabic, an endangered variety of Arabic that is closely related to Moroccan. We show that if adjectives are added to the picture, OP can no longer predict the distribution of schwa in the different categories. The conclusion is that OP cannot replace the mechanisms it was supposed to replace, and is therefore a redundant complication to phonological theory.
abstracts.009760: To say that linear order is part of core syntax is to say that temporal order is part of core syntax. Conversely, to say that linear order is not at all part of core syntax is to say that temporal order is not at all part of core syntax. Which is in turn to say that the language faculty has not integrated into its core any notion of time. Such a(n arguably counter-biological) position, or close to it, was in effect taken by Chomsky (1995, 221), who said “If humans could communicate by telepathy, there would be no need for a phonological component, at least for the purposes of communication.” The question for future work (not limited to linguistics) is whether or not the human brain has or has not entirely disregarded time at the very core of one of its most important components.
abstracts.009761: Certain "before"-clauses and "after"-clauses are prima facie ambiguous between a strong reading and a weak reading, and theories diverge on how the readings obtain. Some theories take the LF of "before"- and "after"-clauses to be unambiguously weak, with the strong reading falling out as a subcase (as it entails the weak reading). Other theories, such as Rett (2020), take the LFs for the two readings to be distinct, critically, with the weak reading being the result of a coercion process. Under standard psycholinguistic assumptions, coercion incurs a processing cost, and hence, we argue, Rett’s (2020) theory makes processing predictions that are not shared by theories which posit unambiguously weak LFs. We test these predictions via four self-paced reading experiments and find moderate evidence that they are borne out. Our results constrain theories of "before" and "after," contribute to a typology of aspectual coercion mechanisms, and have implications for how we should think about the licensing conditions of coercion.
abstracts.009762: Turkish polar questions contain a focus-sensitive clitic =mI. When =mI attaches to a DP and the clause is embedded, we observe that the matrix clause can be read as either declarative or interrogative. We argue that the reading depends on the height of the focus relative to the embedded C. To derive the matrix question reading, the focused DP covertly moves above C. Turkish is often described as scope rigid, indicating that scope shifting covert movement is generally unavailable. If our analysis is correct, covert movement is still licit in certain environments.
abstracts.009763: Focus alternatives may be computed as semantic objects (Rooth 1985, 1992) or as syntactic objects (e.g. Fox & Katzir 2011). We provide evidence that syntax plays a role based on polar questions in Turkish. There is morphological evidence that the Hamblin set for the polar question is formed via focus alternatives (e.g. Atlamaz 2023). Computing alternatives as semantic objects would over-generate answers in the Hamblin set. On the other hand, the target Hamblin set can be naturally predicted in the syntactic approach, provided that alternatives involve replacing the focus with constituents of the same syntactic category.
abstracts.009764: In D’Alessandro & Van Oostendorp (2020), we proposed Magnetic Grammar, a model of phonological competence in which a language’s segment inventory is characterised entirely by features that attract or reject other features within a segment. The paper referred to a Python implementation demonstrating the learning algorithm. This squib reports on a bug in that implementation and presents a corrected version, which leads to a small but theoretically meaningful refinement of the learning algorithm. The corrected implementation, with Jupyter notebook in which one can learn about and test the updated theory, is available as an open-source repository at https://github.com/fonolog/MagneticGrammar.
abstracts.009765: Recent publications in biology enthusiastically argue that primate vocal call systems possess non-trivial compositionality as their prominent feature, thus parallelling human language. No proposal for an internal computational system explaining this property has been offered so far. However, conceptual and quantitative analysis shows the use of non-human primate compositional meaning to be neither productive nor rule based. Furthermore, formal properties of (higher-order) Markov chains imply only string concatenation, explaining why hierarchical structure, hence structure dependence, is absent from animal call systems. Also, mere acoustic identity of constituent elements with unit calls does not suffice for compositional meaning. In conclusion, higher-order Markov chains and distributional semantics seem to be questionable methods for establishing and explaining compositionality. A humanlike combinatorial capacity cannot be unambiguously demonstrated for non-human primates.
abstracts.009766: This dissertation investigates the syntax of clausal prefixes in Tigrinya, an Ethio-Semitic language which, despite its head-finality, exhibits clause-initial complementizers that attach as prefixes to embedded verbs (clausal prefixes). It challenges the view that prefixes in head-final languages have an intrinsic morphological property, proposing instead that their surface position results from specific syntactic constraints. Four main clausal prefixes are analyzed. Z(ɨ)-, found in relative clauses, noun clausal complements, and comparative clauses, is argued to be a reflex of successive-cyclic A'-movement triggered by Spec-Head agreement in a phasal aspectual projection. Kɛmz(ɨ)-, a bimorphemic element consisting of a preposition plus z(ɨ)-, introduces complement clauses that are argued to be underlying relative clauses involving the A'-movement of a null nominal. K(ɨ)-, a subjunctive marker, is claimed to occur in reduced clauses whose temporal interpretation depends on the matrix clause and to appear either as a low MoodP head or as a reflex of temporal operator movement. ʔaj-...-(ɨ)n, the circumfix used to mark sentential negation, reflects split negation, with the prefix merged in low NegP and the suﬃx in high PolP. These findings support a more local view of A'-movement than standard phase theory and point to a refined notion of cyclicity, oﬀering a novel perspective on the syntax of prefixes in head-final languages.
abstracts.009767: We review the first proof-of-principle demonstration for successful non-invasive brain-to-brain communication of conscious thought without the use of input-output systems of articulation and auditory perception of speech. In its present stage, the proof is overstated. First, the communication transmitted is not structured thought but a consciously perceived digital code. Second, communication is transmitted with the use of extralinguistic input-output mechanisms of motor and occipital cortices. It may be an innovative and potentially useful technological development but it is without explanatory significance for the study of language in the brain.
abstracts.009768: Can we read other people’s minds by seeing the neuroimaging data of their brains? Recent discussion claims success, but success is self-reinforced by design. More data and better statistics yield a better approximation to a mass of unanalyzed data. But approximation of language production is essentially different from explanation of language generation. Causal explanations of generative grammar may be confirmed by some statistical experiment; in contrast, a statistical result must still be causally explained before some theoretical understanding can be reached. Probability theory is incapable in principle of advancing scientific understanding beyond a measure of prediction based on statistical calculations that have no neurobiological reality in human brains.
abstracts.009769: Can we read other people’s minds by seeing the neuroimaging data of their brains? Recent discussion claims success, but success is self-reinforced by design. More data and better statistics yield a better approximation to a mass of unanalyzed data. But approximation of language production is essentially different from explanation of language generation. Causal explanations of generative grammar may be confirmed by some statistical experiment; in contrast, a statistical result must still be causally explained before some theoretical understanding can be reached. Probability theory is incapable in principle of advancing scientific understanding beyond a measure of prediction based on statistical calculations that have no neurobiological reality in human brains.
abstracts.009770: In this paper, we investigate multimodal recipient feedback in casual dyadic conversation in four languages: German Sign Language, Russian Sign Language, spoken German, and spoken Russian. Taking a modality-agnostic and holistic approach, we investigate the composition of conversational feedback from different multimodal signals, comparing sign and spoken languages without prioritizing any of the articulators or modalities. We find that in sign and spoken languages alike, feedback events include non-manual signals such as head movements or facial expressions in 85% or more of the instances. Across modalities, all four languages show only small percentages of feedback events without any non-manual elements, and head nods constitute the most frequent feedback signal. Moreover, we model three empirically observed feedback styles—ranging from a style employing a rich array of non-manual signals, over one comprising mostly head movements, to a style relying somewhat more on the talk-oriented forms. Our data demonstrate that the basic infrastructure for feedback is shared among signers and speakers, while at the same time, signers and speakers show different probabilities for using one style or another. On the basis of these patterns, we propose a gradient model of feedback styles that generates testable predictions for future work. Our study emphasizes the importance of investigating interactional phenomena from a holistic, multi- and cross-modal perspective. As vocal and manual signals account only for a relatively small percentage of the feedback signals employed by the signers and speakers in our study, a linguistic theory that focuses solely on vocal and/or manual behavior remains incomplete and fails to account for the largest part of feedback in conversation. This study highlights that non-manual signals are fundamental to feedback and conversation more broadly, and argues that theories of language must be reconceptualized, as purely speech-based accounts fail to capture the full complexity of human interaction. The findings have broader implications for theories of interaction and the Language Faculty: they underscore the need for models that integrate visual, non-manual, and interactional dimensions as constitutive elements of linguistic behavior. By highlighting the centrality of multimodal articulators in feedback production, this work contributes to a more comprehensive theory of human communicative interaction.
abstracts.009771: The dominant models of how human language is neurally implemented have been slowly disintegrating for many years now, but the challenge of assembling a more modern take on this ancient question can only be feasibly undertaken by someone willing to wade through an increasingly dense literature. This someone should ideally also be involved in contemporary experimental neurolinguistics and psycholinguistics. It is with a unique sense of historical context, and contemporary clinical urgency, that Gregory Hickok assumes this task of proposing an updated view of human language processing. His book Wired for Words surveys the field of the neurobiology of language and offers a unique model.
abstracts.009772: This paper investigates the emergence and distribution of weak definite articles in German prepositional phrases (e.g. vom) at the expense of strong articles (e.g. von dem). While reduced weak forms are already attested in Old High German, their use was initially rare and largely restricted to noun phrases that are very likely to have a singleton extension in any situation. Over time, weak articles expanded to a wider range of noun phrases, yet failed to extend to anaphoric environments with an indefinite antecedent, where strong forms remain obligatory in Modern German. By combining historical corpus evidence with agent-based simulations grounded in computational pragmatics and reinforcement learning, we aimed to derive this distribution from independently motivated assumptions about reference, economy, and language acquisition. In particular, we assumed that the weak forms, in contrast to strong ones, can give rise to referential uncertainty since their interpretation depends on the properties of the topic situation, as construed by the listener. The uncertainty is low with NPs which are known to mostly denote singletons in any situation and greater with other NP types. We also built into our model an intuition that an indefinite NP lowers the estimate that a contextually salient situation has a singleton with the NP-property in question. Simulation results closely mirror the stages of the historical development attested in the corpus, suggesting that pitching the economy (i.e. preferring a reduced form) vs. clarity (preferring a strong form unless the communicative success chances are high enough) is a fruitful way of modeling article evolution.
abstracts.009773: We examine an ineffability puzzle first identified by Schwarzschild (1993), in which a question containing a focus-sensitive operator cannot be felicitously answered, regardless of focus assignment. Previous accounts attribute the problem to a ban on crossing dependencies between focus operators and their associates; we instead derive it from the interaction between semantic content and general pragmatic considerations. We analyze ineffability within a question-based approach, according to which focus in an assertion corresponds to the implicit question it addresses. In ineffability examples, the same focus-sensitive operator occurs in every member of the implicit question denotation. As a result, the operator’s domain of quantification influences the question signaled by focus; and in the relevant cases, no admissible choice of domain yields an interpretation that matches the explicit, contextually-supplied question. We further relate ineffability to wh-intervention effects (Beck, 1996), arguing that intervention constructions likewise involve a single operator whose domain is shared across question alternatives. Finally, we show that the present account improves on earlier approaches that rule out crossing dependencies categorically: beyond being less stipulative, it correctly predicts that ineffability can be obviated by manipulating the preceding question and other contextual factors.
abstracts.009774: Through the examination and analysis of Irish verbal Eclipsis, I propose a novel representation of the structure of the autosegment responsible for the phonological alternations associated with Eclipsis. I also provide the specific morphosyntactic function of Eclipsis by creating a dedicated Vocabulary Item (VI) that maps finiteness features onto the autosegment responsible for Eclipsis alternations. As for Moroccan Arabic, I argue that the exponent of the causative morpheme is a prefixed mora. Second-consonant gemination, then, falls out from language-general phonotactic requirements on Moroccan Arabic syllable structure. This analysis demonstrates that Moroccan Arabic Root-and-Pattern Morphology does not require the morphemealignment constraints traditionally relied upon in Arabic Root-and-Pattern analyses (contra McCarthy and Prince, 1993b; Loutfi, 2020; Zukoff, 2022). The analysis, then, supports Embick (2010)’s argument that morphology should be local as opposed to global and that the phonological module should have no part in the selection or linearization of morphemes. Furthermore, the analysis put forth in this paper confirms the Four-Hypothesis Program of Bermúdez-Otero (2012), with the only change being that I strengthen the Indirect Reference Hypothesis (Bermúdez-Otero, 2012, citing Inkelas, 1989) to prohibit even prosodic-alignment constraints from referring to morphosyntactic information. The resulting architecture significantly constrains Optimality Theory (OT; Prince and Smolensky, 1993), removing the ability of phonology to do anything other than optimize an input consisting entirely of phonological information, with no access to the morphosyntax of the input.
abstracts.009775: The verbal paradigm of Iranian Armenian has undergone a striking case of analogical extension, separating it from conservative varieties of Eastern Armenian. The past perfective pattern that was historically restricted to an irregular subset of one class of verbs has spread to become the default pattern in the language, while the former default is now restricted to a small class. Since what could be described as the default or elsewhere condition in conservative Eastern Armenian has apparently swapped roles with an irregular pattern, we dub this change an “Elsewhere Reversal.” We combine a theoretical analysis with a survey of Armenian dialects and a quantitative model of child language acquisition in order to explain the Elsewhere Reversal. In doing so, we argue that paradoxical cases of dramatic analogical extension such as this can be subsumed under typical mechanisms of analogical leveling.
abstracts.009776: The impressive few-shot performance of generative decoder transformer language models at novel tasks has raised interest in using them to estimate lexical-semantic properties of words, word pairs or multi-word expressions. We explore the task of eliciting semantic similarity scores between word pairs through prompting, comparing these scores to human benchmarks. We investigate different prompting approaches, different model architectures and different languages using the Dutch, English and Mandarin Chinese SimLex-999 benchmarks. The results show that prompting each word pair individually yields better correlations, and that models struggle with the distinction between similarity and relatedness, just as static and contextual word embedding models did. The new, open-weight gpt-oss-20b model yields the highest correlation with human ratings out of the models we evaluated.
abstracts.009777: This thesis attempts to investigate the semantics of the dubitative verb 怀疑(huaiyi) in Mandarin Chinese. Dubitative verbs have always been an interesting topic in the field of syntax and semantics cross-linguistically because of their debatable denotations and peculiar complementation patterns. 怀疑(huaiyi) is yet more complicated due to its ambiguity between two empirical interpretations—the first is "having a tendency not to believe" (huaiyi1), and the second one is "having a tendency to believe" (huaiyi2). Therefore, there is an additional disambiguation mechanism at work in the process of its interpretation. This thesis claims that this disambiguation mechanism is based on the information structure and is essentially related to the logical relationship between the content proposition and the immediate contextual evidence as claimed in Lu (2016), mainly depending on the location of the informational focus and the "givenness" status of the content proposition in the embedding complement. As for the denotation of this verb, I claim that it is similar to the hybrid semantics of doubt in English proposed by Anand and Hacquard (2013), but with a crucial difference: the preference assertion is bidirectional and needs to be determined by the aforementioned disambiguation mechanism.
abstracts.009778: Collostructional analysis is a technique devised to find correlations between particular words and linguistic constructions in order to analyse meaning associations of these constructions. Contrasting collostructional analysis results with output from BERT might provide insights into the way BERT represents the meaning of linguistic constructions. This study tests to what extent English BERT’s meaning representations correspond to known constructions from the linguistics literature by means of two tasks that we propose. Firstly, by predicting the words that can be used in open slots of constructions, the meaning associations of more lexicalized constructions can be observed. Secondly, by finding similar sequences using BERT’s output embeddings and manually reviewing the resulting sentences, we can observe whether instances of less lexicalized constructions are clustered together in semantic space. These two methods show that BERT represents constructional meaning to a certain extent, but does not separate instances of a construction from a near-synonymous construction that has a different form.
abstracts.009779: Thispaperproposesananalysisofanunexpectedlinearorderingofthegen andnum markers in a set of non-standard Romance varieties spoken in Lunigiana, Italy. This linear ordering is unexpected because it apparently violates the Mirror Principle, which predicts that the gen marker is closer to the root than the num marker. I provide an analysis of the Lunigianese linear ordering that is purely phono- logical, and show that the observed √-num-gen ordering, in fact, does not require a reordering of the corresponding syntactic heads, and can be neatly derived by refining the phonological representation of the relevant markers. This refinement is obtained by employing the formal tools provided by Strict CV and Element Theory.
abstracts.009780: Berthet et al. (2025) propose a computational method to find cases of non-trivial compositionality (when an utterance of a sequence "A B" should not just be interpreted as "A and B", as if elements A and B were interpreted one after the other for instance) in bonobo vocal communication. We show weaknesses of the criteria, and suggest a path for completing the program.
abstracts.009781: This paper concerns a small group of Japanese verbs that license a morphological case alternation between accusative case and ablative (postpositional) case. I will call them Accusative/Ablative Alternation Verbs, or simply Alternation Verbs. The primary goal of this paper is to identify the argument structures projected by Alternation Verbs that give rise to the two variants of the case alternation. I will argue that these verbs project a unified, dyadic unaccusative structure without thematic Voice. Alternation Verbs are thus an example of verbs that introduce accusative-marked arguments despite not projecting a typical transitive argument structure.
abstracts.009782: The aim of this work is to offer a comparative analysis of the construction of [article + proper noun] in Río de la Plata Spanish (e.g., "la Samara") and Brazilian Portuguese (e.g., "a Samara"). Despite the different distribution observed in both varieties, the article is neither a mere expletive nor the iota operator that the same form of the article realizes in definite descriptions. On the contrary, the article indicates an expressive syntax and semantics, in the sense of multidimensional semantics (Potts 2005, McCready 2010, 2019, Gutzmann 2015, 2019, and Saab and Carranza 2021, among others). Specifically, the article signals a certain interpersonal proximity relationship between the referent of the proper name and the discourse participants (Oggiani and Aguilar Guevara 2024). Assuming that certain aspects of social meanings are entirely derived by properties of PF, we propose that the expressive article is the byproduct of a doubling rule referring to the phonetic form of nominal roots. The fact that the article is more ubiquitous with first names in some varieties of Brazilian Portuguese follows as familiar process of grammaticalization, which, in this case, is sensitive to the register properties of nominal phrases containing proper names.
abstracts.009783: This paper examines the Ā-extraction of adjuncts in San Juan Ostuncalco Mam (SJO Mam; Mayan), focusing on the enclitic =(y)a’, which (optionally) appears on predicates when certain adjuncts are extracted. We describe the distribution of =(y)a’ in monoclausal and long-distance extraction and show that, with the exception of temporals, the extraction adjuncts licenses the enclitic, which may occur multiple times along a movement dependency, including within a single clause. We argue that =(y)a’ provides a morphological footprint of the path taken by an extracted adjunct. Specifically, we analyze =(y)a’ as the spellout of Ā-agreement between the extracted adjunct and intermediate heads along the clausal spine, providing evidence that Ā-movement proceeds successive-cyclically through the extended verbal domain, both within and across clauses.
abstracts.009784: The Voynich Manuscript (MS 408, Beinecke Library, Yale University) has resisted all attempts of conventional interpretation for over a century. This paper argues that the persistent failure of cryptographic, linguistic, and statistical approaches stems from a shared foundational assumption: that the manuscript’s text was produced by a static system—whether a fixed cipher, a natural language grammar, or a stable encoding scheme. Analysis of the manuscript’s word network and vocabulary evolution reveals that this assumption is untenable. The text exhibits continuous development throughout the manuscript, with vocabulary, character usage, and word frequency distributions shifting gradually from beginning to end. This dynamic character is evidenced by a single, highly connected network of similar words spanning the entire manuscript, a strong correlation between word frequency and number of similar word forms and asymmetric vocabulary distribution indicating directional evolution. These properties are naturally explained by the self-citation hypothesis, which proposes that the text was generated through iterative copying and modification of previously written words—a process confirmed as the intuitive human strategy for producing meaningless text beyond approximately 100 words (Gaskell & Bowern, 2022). The dynamic perspective reconciles apparently contradictory observations and provides a framework for understanding why the manuscript has resisted every analytical approach premised on static rule systems. Companion paper: 'One Hand, Five Labels: A Critical Examination of the Five-Scribe Hypothesis for the Voynich Manuscript' (Timm, 2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18830125
abstracts.009785: This paper proposes a unified framework for understanding three ancient language families — Hurro-Urartian, Kartvelian, and Tyrsenian (Etruscan/Lemnian/Raetic) — as descendants of a common Caucasian Hunter-Gatherer (CHG) linguistic ancestor dating to the Mesolithic period. Drawing on comparative personal pronoun systems, grammatical architecture, phonological inventories, and recent archaeogenetic evidence, we argue that these families share a set of structural features — pure suffixing morphology, ergative-absolutive alignment, animacy-based nominal distinctions, Suffixaufnahme, and a five-vowel proto-system — that cannot be explained by chance or contact alone. We further propose that the Tyrsenian branch (proto-Etruscan/Pelasgian/Minoan) reached the Aegean during the Early Bronze Age Kura-Araxes expansion (c. 3100–2500 BC), eventually establishing itself in Italy around 700 BC during Orientalizing period to become the historical Etruscans. We additionally incorporate Kassite as a probable eastern branch of the CHG linguistic family, extending the CHG linguistic arc from the Zagros mountains in the east to the Italian peninsula in the west.
abstracts.009786: In current minimalist theorizing, the elimination of copies created by Internal Merge is typically attributed to copy deletion, most prominently formalized by Nunes (2004) as Chain Reduction. This paper explores an alternative hypothesis that Chain Reduction proceeds via substitution rather than deletion. I show that this reconceptualization makes it possible to derive complement-to-specifier anti-locality effects (the ban on P-stranding) from labeling ambiguity that arises in head/head configurations (Chomsky 2013, 2015). Under the timing of the Labeling Algorithm adopted here, such anti-locality violations are predicted to be resolvable through ellipsis. While a detailed discussion of this point lies beyond the scope of this paper, data coming from a growing body of research on P-omission under sluicing and in fragment answers suggest that this indeed may be the case.
abstracts.009787: Eliciting linguistic data from speakers of non-standardized varieties presents well-known challenges. Traditional acceptability judgment tasks have been widely used to probe grammatical knowledge, but task design, such as mode of presentation, response options, and labeling, can strongly influence outcomes (Marty et al., 2020). In this study, we investigate a small group of heritage Catalan speakers in Germany and the Netherlands using a repetition-based task rather than a standard judgment task. Our findings indicate that responses to repetition tasks differ significantly from commonly known generalizations on the phenomenon at issue investigated through grammaticality judgment tasks. We conclude that repetition tasks can uncover patterns of grammatical representation that may differ from those captured by judgment tasks, and that they provide deeper insights into grammatical representation than the latter. This suggests that carefully designed elicitation tasks can mitigate common biases and more accurately reveal the grammatical representations of heritage speakers. These findings highlight both the challenges and the potential of alternative methodologies for studying underrepresented languages. This is a first draft. Comments and feedback very welcome!
abstracts.009788: In the study of human cognition, language is central in part because our species is the only surviving member of the primate lineage that is in possession of its distinctive properties. Evidence suggests that only in homo sapiens, spectacularly, did language emerge. Aside from the point of view of evolutionary origins, the other reason for language being a defining feature is its function as an indispensable instrument of higher order cognition. If language-related abilities are essential in this way, linguistics can be understood as a branch of psychology; and in general, the methods of cognitive science should be applicable to its study in every way. From another perspective, its centrality is related to the interconnectivity of language with the other higher order competencies of the mind. Thus, in all of the above, and in the following discussion, “language” should be understood as “knowledge of language.” As in all the branches of psychology, rooted in turn in biological science, attention to the relationship between applied research and theory cannot in the long run be neglected.
abstracts.009789: This a brief note on Marcin Wagiel’s SALT 33 2023 proceedings paper ‘Acts, occasions, and multiplicatives: A mereotopological account’ and the analysis of frequency adverbials in Parts and Wholes in Semantics (OUP 1997) as well as the general mereotopological view of part-structure that that book had introduced into natural language semantics against the background of the use of extensional mereology in semantics (Link 1983). Recent mereotopological analyses are thus not novel in that respect.
abstracts.009790: This position paper proposes a more-than-human and holistic approach to language that moves beyond entrenched divides between structuralism, constructivism, positivism, and methodological camps. Writing under the collective pseudonym Gaya Seldon, we argue that many oppositions in linguistics, particularly the equation of quantitative methods with positivism and structuralism, rest on reductive misreadings. Structuralism, we contend, is not inherently anti-social or anti-agentive but grounded in relationality; its caricature has contributed to theoretical fragmentation and epistemic silos. At the same time, constructivist and decolonial turns, while critically valuable, often remain entangled in colonial, extractivist, capitalist, hegemonic, and anthropocentric logics. We propose an ecolinguistic, holistic framework that disentangles method from epistemology and repositions language as emerging within dynamic, relational systems that include human and more-than-human actors. Drawing on critical quantitative approaches, dynamic systems theory, and more-than-human ecolinguistics, we advocate principled methodological openness grounded in care, reflexivity, and ethical accountability. Rather than methodological eclecticism, we call for a relational praxis capable of integrating qualitative and quantitative tools while foregrounding socio-ecological justice and interdependence across living systems.
abstracts.009791: This paper investigates the [ov]~[u] alternation in Slavic verbs derived from nominal and adjectival stems. In addition to the alternation between a sequence and a single segment, Slavic languages differ with respect to the surface shape of the VC sequence: some only feature [ov], some alternate [ov] and [ev] depending on the preceding consonant, some only feature [uv]. Drawing from both synchronic and diachronic predecessors, it is shown that the alternation deserves a unified approach. The verbaliser suffix has an abstract underlying representation, adapted phonologically based on hiatus resolution requirements: an underlyingly defective diphthong surfaces as a vowel before a consonant and as a sequence before a vowel. Inter-Slavic variation is ascribed to nuanced preferences in the phonological grammar, which provides an insight into the shared properties within the Slavic linguistic family, like the markedness of [±back] features.
abstracts.009792: Kalaallisut (Inuit; Greenland) is a well-known example of a syntactically ergative language, serving as the primary example of that language type in Bittner and Hale (1996a). In relative clauses, ergatives cannot be relativized; there is an ergative extraction constraint (EEC). From Bittner and Hale (1996a) onward, analyses of the EEC standardly appeal to inversion: the absolutive object must obtain an A-position higher than the ergative subject as a matter of basic clause structure, but object movement over the subject blocks further A’ movement by the subject. In this paper we re-evaluate this analysis for Kalaallisut. Considering patterns of word order, Condition C, hyperraising, scope, and affix order, we conclude that objects do not obligatorily move over subjects in the clause structure of this language. Inversion is not the correct approach to the EEC in Kalaallisut. Our results provide new support for non-inversion based analyses of the EEC such as those grounded in case sensitivity or antilocality, as well as for Ershova’s (2019, 2025) contention that the EEC and inversion must be typologically separated from one another.
abstracts.009793: This paper argues that ‘or’ is inherently symmetric, based on the intuitive equivalence of [If y is P or Q, then x is] and [If y is Q or P, then x is] – referred to as Rooth-Partee conditionals. As observed in Rooth & Partee (1982), the elided phrase in the consequent clause of these conditionals triggers a reading paraphrased as ‘If x is P, y is P and if x is Q, y is Q’. Accounting for that reading proves to be problematic for asymmetric approaches to ‘or'.
abstracts.009794: This paper investigates the so-called V de O clefts in Chinese, a specific type of “clefts” where the de particle appears between the verb and the object, and proposes a cartographic approach to their syntactic and semantic properties. While some common generalizations about this pattern are shown to hold upon closer examination (i.e., exhaustive focus, obligatory past reading, ban on TMA markers), some do not (i.e., strict adjacency effect, term focus restriction). Two key projections are argued to exist in the relevant functional hierarchy, each linked to one crucial element in the pattern: (i) a FocP selected by the copula shi; (ii) an Asp*P headed by the verbal particle de. The former explains the focus effects with syntactic encoding and the latter accounts for the temporal/aspectual peculiarities with the marking of perfective aspect (related predictions about predicate restrictions are also presented). The derivation of V de O clefts involves overt focus movement of an extended “eventive” projection, which minimally contains an Asp*P. This movement is triggered by a focus feature either on the whole constituent (VP/S+VP) or on a smaller constituent within it (verb/object/subject/adjunct), the latter case demonstrating a pied-piping movement.
abstracts.009795: Pedagogical discourse relies on coordination of mental spaces between interlocutors. In Cognitive Grammar, this is achieved through grounding. The definite article acts as a cognitive command to establish mental contact. Formal approaches to uniqueness often view uniqueness as static, this study argues it as a discursive achievement. This paper proposes a seven type schema model of grounding operations. By the analysis of 7 classroom lectures, this study demonstrates the use of the epistemic control cycle to negotiate attention. Notably, the analysis highlights the emergence of reference point constructions- such as the “lizard..tail” phenomenon–reveals cognitive anchoring strategies for joint attention being prioritized over artifactual conventional schemas when categorizing usage events. It concludes that grounding operations are governed by universal cognitive strategies of joint attention management rather than the formal constraints. It contributes to usage based understanding of how grammar functions as a tool for intersubjective alignment in complex conceptual negotiations.

abstracts.009797: The propositional attitude verb forget has received relatively little attention in the formal linguistics literature, though its properties present interesting problems for formal semantics. White (2014) argues that a uniform account of forget as a factive verb is possible. On this view, forget presupposes the truth of its clausal argument (See also Kiparsky & Kiparsky (1970)). But in order to do so, he claims that a covert modal operator is obligatorily present in the infinitival complements of forget, deriving modalized factive presuppositions. In this paper, I present data showing that the distribution of this covert modal operator is even more restricted. I argue that modalization of the complement is separate from the clause-type, and that it is instead the pre-existence presupposition (Bondarenko 2020), that is part of forget’s meaning, that is responsible for the distribution of this covert operator.
abstracts.009799: We present ZË-RO v0.1, a deterministic research instrument that extracts orthographic vowel-carrier structure (A, E, I, O, U, Y, Ë) and computes an aperture proxy using a fixed calibration scale. The system is designed for reproducibility and drift detection: research harnesses emit MD/JSON reports and commit baseline-locked references that fail on unexpected change. We report baseline behavior across multiple suites: positive-signal language datasets (Albanian and Turkish), a strict negative control using pseudowords (no semantic intent), and a drift-visibility suite (Taiwan Zhuyin) designed to weaken under expansion. The negative control shows weak/non-significant slope and no strengthening from STEP10→STEP20, supporting that observed monotonic descent in language datasets is not trivially forced by the harness. This submission reports measurement and reproducibility characteristics of the instrument; it does not claim semantic “proof” by default.
abstracts.009800: [added: pivots of topic continuity]. This is the condensed version of “Ergativity demystified”, but supplemented to include causative and applicative constructions.The grammatical elegance of ergative languages becomes evident when they are not read against the grain.
abstracts.009801: We discuss (i) the nature of a lexicalization condition on scalar implicatures that precludes lexicalizing negation of strong scalar elements, and (ii) parametric variation in the scope properties of conjunctive and disjunctive operators relative to negation. The empirical cases discussed show that logic differs from natural language, an internal cognitive system and part of human biology, therefore empirically constrained, in this case by conditions on polarity and scalar implicatures that are absent from formal logic. The interpretation of disjunction and conjunction is universal as in propositional logic following de Morgan’s laws. Hence, the conjunctive interpretation of disjunction in negative statements comes naturally. Still, how these laws apply in propositional logic and how humans attain knowledge of these laws and their use in language are different empirical problems for a biological organism to solve. It’s an intriguing empirical question which obviously needs an answer. Guided by the subset principle, children at first adopt the scope interpretation that yields true sentences in the narrowest range of circumstances, only “unlearning” what comes natural to them when forced to do so by positive evidence only. Biologically driven human capacities such as innate logic and the faculty of language, interacting with general third-factor principles of learnability and computational efficiency, guarantee that not everything need be learned and what need be learned can be learned, providing a principled solution to the poverty of stimulus for the acquisition of language.
abstracts.009803: The purpose of this little web app is to provide the output of an application of a function to its argument in the style of the lambda calculus, i.e. in the form λx [P (x)] (y), where the part λx [P (x)] is the function and y is the argument that the function is applied to. The page is geared to uses of the lambda calculus in natural language semantics, as introduced in Kearns (2000/2011: chap. 4) and Lohnstein (1996/2011: chap. 8), for instance. The WWW address of the app is provided in the accompanying PDF. References: Kearns, Kate. 2000/2011. Semantics. 2nd edn. Houndmills: Palgrave Macmillan. Lohnstein, Horst. 1996/2011. Formale Semantik und natürliche Sprache. 2nd edn. Berlin: De Gruyter.
abstracts.009804: Focus dependencies, including question–answer congruence, free focus, and association with focus, are often treated in terms of grammatical and pragmatic mechanisms that rely on (a) focus-semantic values along a second semantic dimension, and (b) an anaphoric operator, ~, that is sensitive to these values and can communicate them to various processes. I argue against this view and in favor of a purely pragmatic treatment of focus in which there are no focus semantic values within the grammar, let alone operators sensitive to such values. Instead of ~, I propose a unification of focus dependencies through a pragmatic condition: an utterance is felicitous only if it is a good answer to a good (explicit or accommodated) question. Good answers must be relevant to the question they address, with relevance understood, following Lewis (1988), relative to a question-induced partition of the context set.
abstracts.009805: Grammaticality illusions are cases where comprehenders fleetingly consider ungrammatical sentences to be acceptable. The phenomenon been used to tap into the mechanism of online negative polarity item (NPI) licensing (Muller & Phillips, 2020). The effect has high specificity and not all environments that ordinarily license NPIs create illusions-sentential negation being the prime case that is ineffective as an illusory licensor (Orth et al., 2021). In the current study, we contrast NPIs with another class of expressions, namely negative concord items (NCIs), which are said to be licensed in the syntax unlike NPIs. We test whether sentential negation gives rise to illusions with Czech NPIs and NCIs respectively, predicting illusions for NCIs and no effect for NPIs. However, in three speeded acceptability judgement experiments, we find illusions with both types of expressions. Our data are inconsistent with the active scope (Orth et al., 2021) and scalar theories (Muller, 2022; Schwab, 2023). The cue-based retrieval (Vasishth et al., 2008) and the feature percolation approaches (Eberhard et al., 2005) are both compatible with the results. We argue in favour of feature percolation as the best explanation for both our Czech data as well as the data from other languages, appealing to cross-linguistic differences in the placement of negation within syntactic structure. While negation is high up in the syntactic structure in Czech and can therefore percolate up and cause illusions, it is low in English, not allowing for illusions to arise. This result highlights the importance of language-specific syntactic structure for online comprehension.
abstracts.009807: This book springs from the idea of celebrating Andrea Moro’s 60th birthday with a collection of striking remarks on linguistics and neurolinguistics. To this end, we asked a number of Andrea Moro’s colleagues to write a very short essay which sheds some light on a single but significant point of the linguistic system. The result has been rewarding in several respects, with the essays spanning a wide range of topics. Thus, some authors focus on copular sentences (Adriana Belletti; Marcel den Dikken; Carlo Cecchetto and Caterina Donati; Gennaro Chierchia), others on the basic operations of movement (Valentina Bianchi; Cristiano Chesi) and agreement (Alessandra Tomaselli). Some investigate aspects that are central to the theory of Dynamic Antisymmetry, including labeling and linearization (Denis Delfitto; Massimo Piattelli-Palmarini; Robert Frank, William Min, Abhisar Mittal, and Billy Zhong; Maria Rita Manzini; Luigi Rizzi; Ian Roberts). Some authors delve into the grammar of different linguistic registers (Maria Teresa Guasti; Liliane Haegeman). Some authors provide new insights into functional heads in both the clausal and the nominal domain (Guglielmo Cinque; Anna Maria Di Sciullo; Cecilia Poletto). Finally, other authors capitalize on computational linguistics (Robert C. Berwick), cognitive sciences (Andrea Serino), aphasia (Stefano F. Cappa and Eleonora Catricalà), parametric variation (Giuseppe Longobardi and Alessandro Treves), and linguistic errors as heuristic tools (Valentina Bambini), to illuminate the relationship between neurosciences and human language. Alongside these short essays, the present collection also features two longer papers by Noam Chomsky and Richard S. Kayne. These authors, who are the Maestri - directly or indirectly - of all the distinguished contributors of this volume, deal with “half, all, both, each and of” aspects of that “miracle creed” instantiated by language.
abstracts.009808: We report a deterministic diagnostic from ZË-RO’s Albanian200 analysis harnesses, testing whether schwa-heavy prefix morphology (notably për-/përë-) can mask root-aligned carrier-primary vowels in a small anchored subset (N=28). In the Compound Stress v0.2 harness, root-anchored retention is 64.3% for position (9/14, p=0.013) and 100.0% for order (14/14, p=0.001); all position mismatches are për-prefixed cases where the surface carrier primary becomes Ë while the anchor root primary is A/E. A controlled “Gegë-sim” perturbation (Ë-drop heuristics; not a claim about real dialect IPA) recovers the masked position cases to 100.0% retention (14/14, p=0.001), while order remains 100.0% (14/14, p<0.001). This note is a mechanistic masking-and-recovery probe: it documents a reproducible interaction between prefix schwa and carrier-primary extraction, and makes no claim of semantic proof or dialect truth.
abstracts.009809: This dissertation investigates Differential Object Marking (DOM) in heritage Italo-Romance varieties spoken in Argentina, situating the phenomenon within a broader Romance and cross-linguistic perspective. DOM, whereby only a subset of direct objects receives overt morphological marking, has been widely studied in Romance languages, yet little is known about its behaviour in heritage contexts where the dominant language—Argentinian Spanish—also exhibits a robust DOM system. The study addresses four central questions: (i) whether DOM changes in heritage grammars; (ii) whether such changes are contact-induced or internally motivated; (iii) how microcontact within bilingual communities differs from macrocontact with the societal majority language; and (iv) which structural mechanisms enable DOM to emerge or expand. Adopting a Minimalist framework, the dissertation analyses DOM in terms of structural Case assignment via Agree and the projection of nominal structure (NP/DP/KP). It combines typological comparison, diachronic analysis, and original fieldwork conducted in Italy and Argentina on six Italo-Romance varieties (Eastern Abruzzese, Calabrian, Friulian, Piedmontese, Sicilian, and Venetan), representing non-DOM, reduced-DOM, and fully grammaticalised DOM systems. The findings demonstrate that heritage speakers do not simply transfer Argentinian Spanish DOM. Instead, heritage systems develop expanded or restructured patterns grounded in pre-existing grammatical resources of the homeland varieties. Detailed analysis of Friulian reveals a diachronic continuum from Conservative Friulian—where a-marking is restricted to topicalised Accusative Experiencers—to Innovative and Heritage Friulian, where DOM extends to Accusative Themes and in-situ contexts. This expansion reflects endogenous grammaticalisation processes: microcontact with Argentinian Spanish plays a pivotal role in accelerating language change, yet it is not the ultimate trigger for it. Crucially, heritage DOM remains sensitive to animacy and information structure and does not replicate the Argentinian Spanish system wholesale. The dissertation argues that DOM in Romance occupies a hybrid position between accusative and dative domains, as shown by syntactic diagnostics (passivisation, clitic resumption, participial agreement). Historically, DOM emerges from the interaction between case erosion and topicalisation, with prepositional markers developing from Latin locative sources. In heritage contexts, this diachronic pathway interacts with bilingual restructuring, producing innovative yet systematically constrained object-marking systems. Overall, the study contributes to theories of case, grammaticalisation, and contact-induced change by demonstrating that heritage grammars are shaped by the interplay of internal structural options and external contact pressures, rather than by simple transfer from the dominant language.
abstracts.009810: Harmonic Layer Theory can correctly predict the interaction of metrical processes in Kashaya which results in an ordering paradox in a classical stratal system. This novel cyclic formalization of the morpho-phonology interface predicts that processes can be restricted to elements that already underwent a previous optimization cycle – while novel elements added in a later cycle are simultaneously present.
abstracts.009811: Titel English: Sign Languages as Moving Images? A Study on the Applicability of Descriptive Categories from Film Studies to Iconic Discourse Phenomena in German Sign Language (DGS) Sign languages ​​exhibit a high proportion of iconic discourse structures, that are characterized by their scenic and illustrative nature and as such reminiscent of film sequences. Due to their productive imagery and combinability, these structures cannot be adequately described with traditional linguistic concepts. Starting from the topos of the film-like quality of sign languages, this dissertation systematically examines how and to what extent descriptive tools and concepts of film studies can be applied to structures specific for sign languages such as constructed action and so-called classifier constructions. The investigation is based on video recordings of various text types in German Sign Language (DGS). A basic analogy between cinematic and sign language images is established and argued for, thus allowing for the definition and operationalization of film concepts for use in language analysis. The comparative structural approach examines highly iconic structures in sign languages ​​from a new descriptive perspective and provides film-theoretical descriptive concepts for the analysis of signed discourse. The focus is on the key descriptive parameters of shot size, camera movement, and camera perspective. Concepts of these categories can be applied and, in some cases, fit very well with sign language. Limitations of their application arise where the composition of the sign language image does not correspond to that of film.
