As a result, this conceptually organized comparison elucidates the sign language specifics of its iconic structures.
abstracts.009812: Both film and signed languages are media that make use of iconicity and employ motion images for communicative and narrative purposes. This paper focuses on simultaneously presented images that occur in film for example as double exposures and in signed languages as simultaneous constructions. While film and signed languages differ in many ways with respect to iconicity, they can be compared with respect to the way simultaneously presented motion images relate to each other. Superimpositions are defined as a simultaneous view on two or more scenes or as giving two different simultaneous representations of one scene. They serve as a means of dense information packaging. While superimpositions strongly differ in their appearance in film and signed discourse, they exhibit some similarities of structure and functions. They exploit the iconicity of spatial relations emerging in the graphic spatial dimension. Their function is to express a spatial, intentional or temporal connection between two scenes or aspects of one scene, for example the intentional relation between a cognitive activity as seen in the face of a person and the object or content of that cognitive activity.
abstracts.009813: Sign Languages are known for their iconic devices of depiction, such as constructed action and classifier constructions. These depicting constructions are used to show scenes, actions and situations in their temporal unfolding, and they are said to show many spatial perspectives of an event. But what does this look like in a stretch of discourse? How many perspectives are there and how can these different spatial vantage points be identified and labelled for further analysis? How are these perspectives organized to give an oriented view on events and scene? To answer these questions, the poster proposes using a cinematic approach to analyzing depicting constructions in signed language discourse, thus profiting from a discipline that has developed elaborate descriptive tools for film motion images. Depicting constructions are grounded in visual imagery and can be regarded as ‚signed motion images‘, analogous to the concept of a film motion image. Assuming a virtual camera and the signer and his immediate surrounding as screen, signed motion images can be analyzed with respect to their spatiotemporal features of depiction, for example perspective. The analysis of perspective includes viewpoint, orientation of object and distance to object and can be presented in a floor plan. The analysis demonstrated on the poster starts with a broken-down car on the side lane of an express way. The floor plan displays the scene and its development in top view, with all camera locations and movements as well as locations, actions and movements of the character and the props. Further research questions the poster addresses concern the textual organization of perspectives. How are they indicated, are there specific patterns or editing strategies that help meaning construction?
abstracts.009814: This paper makes two contributions to the study of the interpretation of nominals across Germanic and Romance languages. First, it shows that plural kind terms, such as English bare plurals (e.g., lions) and Italian definite plurals (e.g., i leoni), have definite, non-generic uses in sentences expressing generalizations that were traditionally thought to uniformly involve generic quantification. These non-generic uses explain why the distribution of kind-denoting plurals in sentences expressing generalizations is wider than that of singular indefinites, which can only appear in generalizations with a genuinely generic Logical Form (Sects. 3–5). Second, the paper draws on a contrast between English and Italian (and, to a minor extent, French) plural forms, both bare and definite (Sect. 5). This yields a new approach to the mapping between the form and the interpretation of nominals that combines elements from Chierchia’s (Natural Language Semantics 6:339–405, 1998) and Longobardi’s (Natural Language Semantics 9:335–369, 2001) frameworks. On the approach I present, English bare plurals can be mapped either to kinds or to properties; Italian definite plurals, when not referential, can only be mapped to kinds; and Italian bare plurals only to properties. This explains the behavior of these expressions in a wide number of contexts, most importantly in episodic sentences, which raise puzzles for extant accounts. [This paper supersedes the earlier LingBuzz version (LingBuzz/008172), which circulated under the slightly different title "Revisiting kind predication".]
abstracts.009815: Languages routinely generate structurally valid variants, yet derivation alone does not guarantee their survival in use. This essay develops an account of how linguistic forms survive, spread, or are reshaped in use by examining a set of concrete cases, primarily from Telugu plural morphology but extending across registers, dialect contact, and cross-linguistic borrowing. Through a series of illustrations, I show that grammatically possible alternatives are not neutral once enacted in use. Instead, they diverge systematically according to how readily they integrate into ongoing articulatory and structural coordination. Building on this observation, I propose internal evaluation as a context-sensitive process of differentiation operating during speech enactment. By identifying this locus of differentiation, this study reframes variation, regional restriction, and linguistic change as outcomes of coordination-based differentiation during use, rather than as effects of frequency or conscious selection alone. In doing so, it clarifies a persistent explanatory gap in linguistic theory.
abstracts.009816: This paper addresses the possessive structures in Southern Italian dialects, focusing on Northern Calabrian dialects. Generally, in Southern Italian dialects possessives follow the analysis of noun and in predicative contexts are introduced by the article. Besides, Northern Calabrian systems attest another structure in which possessives are introduced by the article preceded by the preposition di in copular predicative contexts and, variably, inside DPs. This arrangement recalls the structures where a linker precedes adjectives or genitives in many languages, among which some Balkan languages such as Albanian and Aromanian varieties. The comparison with the linker structures of these languages provides elements to analyse Calabrian possessives, placing them within a wider typological framework. Our hypothesis is that the sequence di-article can be treated as a sort of linker, introducing an independent lexicalization of the possessive relation and the referential properties identifying the possessum.
abstracts.009817: Force is one of the two major dimensions of meaning along which modals in natural language vary, the other being flavor. In this chapter, we provide an overview of formal approaches to modal force, with a focus on cross-linguistic data and typological evidence. In formal semantics, a common assumption is that necessity and possibility modals express (respectively) universal and existential quantification over possible worlds. However, there are some modals that do not fall into this binary in an obvious way. In this chapter, we explore two such cases: weak necessity modals, which are universal-like, but weaker than strong necessity modals, and variable force modals, which can take on universal-like or existential-like meanings depending on features of their linguistic context. We also briefly discuss other constructions which arguably involve covert variable force modal operators, namely imperatives, generics, and bare conditionals. We focus on the analysis of modal force in formal semantics and pragmatics. For a broader perspective on types of modal meanings across languages, see 1.5. EMPIRICAL FOUNDATIONS OF MODALITY of this handbook. Some other categories of modal meaning lie outside the possibility-necessity binary, but are discussed in other sections of this handbook. Gradable modality can also be categorized as a third type of modal force that falls outside of the usual possibility-necessity dichotomy, but that is the topic of 3.2. MODALITY, GRADABILITY, AND PROBABILITY, so we do not discuss it here. Ability modals exhibit a more complicated force profile modal, and a detailed discussion can be found in 2.3. CIRCUMSTANTIAL AND ABILITY MODALS. Each section in this chapter introduces a particular empirical modal force phenomenon and its associated analyses. In Section 1, we introduce the distinction between possibility and (strong) necessity. In Section 2, we discuss weak necessity modals. In Section 3, we give an overview of variable force modal items. In Section 4, we discuss force in other modal constructions.
abstracts.009818: Quantitative motion-tracking methods are widely used in computational linguistics, psychology, and the cognitive sciences to measure fine-grained behavioral dynamics. By contrast, theoretical linguistics—in particular emerging work on gesture and multimodal meaning—has only recently begun to exploit their methodological potential. This paper argues that such tools are particularly well suited to addressing theoretical questions that turn on non-categorical, scalar variation in linguistic expression, where relevant distinctions are encoded in continuous properties of form, as is the case with gesture. As a case study, the paper investigates intensified head nods as gestural response elements in multimodal assertion. When used as standalone responses, head nods can function analogously to affirmative particles such as 'yes', yet their realization varies continuously in kinematic features such as amplitude, velocity, and number of repetitions. The central hypothesis is that this gradient modulation functions as a visual analogue to intensified response particles in speech (e.g., 'absolutely') by strengthening perceived speaker commitment. To test this hypothesis, nod intensity is operationalized through computational kinematic measurement and evaluated in a controlled perception experiment. The results show that increased kinematic intensification systematically correlates with stronger commitment attribution. This paper illustrates how computational approaches can support multimodal measurement in addressing theoretical semantic questions and advancing the empirical study of gesture.
abstracts.009819: This study investigates gesture-prosody coordination in naturalistic Twi-English code-switching speech, focusing on gesture type distribution, temporal alignment between gesture strokes and prosodic prominence, and gestural activity at code-switching boundaries. A corpus of 11 video clips totalling 65.1 minutes was annotated using ELAN 7.0, yielding 837 gesture strokes classified according to McNeill's typology. Fundamental frequency was extracted using Praat's autocorrelation algorithm, and code-switching points were identified through a computational language inference pipeline built on FFmpeg speech detection. Results show that beat gestures dominated the corpus at 68.0%, consistent with the prosodic-structuring demands of the speech genres studied. Gesture stroke onsets clustered near local pitch peaks, with a mean signed time difference of -36.8ms and a median of -14.0ms. 51.6% of strokes fell within 50ms of a pitch peak and 70.8% within 100ms, with broadly similar patterns across gesture types. Gesture density was 2.30 times higher within ±500ms of code-switching points than in surrounding speech, a difference confirmed as statistically significant at t(10) = 6.51, p < .001. These findings demonstrate that code-switching in Twi-English bilingual discourse is a multimodal event in which gesture and prosody jointly mark language transitions. The study contributes an empirical account of bilingual multimodal communication in an understudied African language contact setting and presents a fully reproducible computational analysis pipeline for multimodal bilingual corpus research.
abstracts.009820: This paper describes the morphology and morphosyntax of verbs and clauses in A'ingae (or Cofán, ISO 639-3: con, an Amazonian isolate). A'ingae is characterized by rich, predominantly head-marking morphology, robust pro-drop, relatively free (often verb-final) word order, and nominative-accusative morphosyntactic alignment. Themes emphasized in the description include the functions of A'ingae suffixes and clitics, their morphosyntactic restrictions, and the types of clauses they can appear in.
abstracts.009821: In his recent (2024) book “The Language Puzzle,” Steven Mithen argues, among other things, that universal grammar has been altogether debunked, and that the question of the origin of natural-language syntax and compositionality has largely been answered by the work of computational evolutionary linguists Simon Kirby and collaborators, thus: “syntax spontaneously emerges from the generation-to-generation language-learning process itself.” I show that Kirby and collaborators’ work in fact presupposes the entirety of syntax in an innate language of thought, and that it subscribes to a notion of universal grammar no weaker than the mainstream one from generative linguistics in the twenty-first century. I point out that Mithen’s negative outlook on generative linguistics is quite pervasive among the general scientific community, even if generative linguistics still dominates many linguistics departments. I submit that such widespread misconception about the status of key research programs in linguistics has very pernicious consequences for science. I point to the generalist scientific journals’ failure to perform their central function, and to old rifts among linguists of different traditions as noteworthy sources of this problem. I propose that it is high time, after the linguistics wars, for a linguistics détente.
abstracts.009822: In a binary feature system that allows underspecification, which of these sets of segments constitute natural classes, where /D/ is a coronal stop unspecified for Voice?: {t, d}, {t}, {d}, {t, D, d}, {D}, {t, D}, {D, d} The answers and their implications fall out from basic logic, perhaps best understood as “third factor” (Chomsky 2005) effects. Some recurring misconceptions in natural class logic are examined, along with the relationship between natural classes and the notion of “possible rule”. We introduce the three basic operators of Logical Phonology and apply them in rules that obey natural class logic to account in purely phonological terms for the behavior of “exceptionally” non-deleting segments in certain Catalan morphemes. The underspecified nature of non-deleting segments is counterintuitive, but follows logically from our assumptions. [April 2026 version fixes typos and other minor issues.]
abstracts.009823: This dissertation takes as its starting point the assumption that word formation is syntactic (and piece-based, with Distributed Morphology and related frameworks), and focuses on a point of tension that is inherent to this assumption: If word formation is syntactic and `words’ are really just smaller syntactic structures, then why do they appear to behave differently from larger syntactic structures for purposes of interpretation at the interfaces? Why are they so selective in determining which pieces may become a part of the structure? Why do they show so many idiosyncratic and unpredictable forms and meanings? These questions are investigated in the empirical domain of German derivational morphology, with a focus on phenomena involving prefixation and category change. In a syntactic theory of word formation, morphologically complex structures are syntactically complex, involving Roots, categorizers, and preverbal elements all as syntactically distinct components of the structure. These small but complex structures are the testing ground for hypotheses in response to the questions posed above.
abstracts.009824: This study investigates the evaluation of verb phrase ellipsis (VPE) and sluicing by English-dominant Spanish heritage speakers (HSs). Spanish permits VPE only with modal remnants (ModVPE), while English allows both ModVPE and auxiliary-stranding VPE (AuxVPE). Sluicing, in contrast, behaves similarly in both languages inasmuch as it is constrained by voice-matching requirements stemming from the universal identity condition on ellipsis. We thus test whether HSs’ difficulties with silent elements (“the Silent Problem”) are observed across structures, or whether they are particularly notable when transfer from the dominant language is available (i.e., AuxVPE in English transferring into Spanish). In a written/aural acceptability judgment task, HSs (n = 39) and Spanish-dominant controls (n = 33) rated expected grammatical (ModVPE and Voice Match Sluicing) and ungrammatical (AuxVPE and Voice Mismatch Sluicing) sentences. Both groups rejected voice-mismatched sluicing equally. However, HSs penalized AuxVPE less than the baseline group, suggesting English transfer. The results support the view that HSs exhibit reduced inhibition of the dominant language which may lead to the [E]-feature that licenses ellipsis in English AuxVPE to ‘seep’ into Spanish. We suggest that constraints on silence that are universally observed are maintained more robustly in HSs’ grammars whereas aspects that we expect to vary a priori are susceptible to divergence in such grammars.
abstracts.009825: In this paper, I investigate the properties of an elliptical construction in the Nakh-Daghestanian language Muira Dargwa, in which only part of a complex predicate goes missing. I show that this process has a number of common features with Verb Phrase Ellipsis in English and related phenomena in other languages. Under an analysis of complex predicates where the light verb is the realization of the v head, the deleted constituent can be associated with the complement of v. Thus, the process diverges from similar phenomena in that the size of the ellipsis is smaller, allowing for a larger number of mismatches between antecedent and elliptical clauses.
abstracts.009826: The article deals with anaphoric phenomena that involve concepts, kinds, specimens, parts, and totalities. It sketches a theory that explains the use of singular vs. plural kind anaphors that assumes different morphosyntactic features for mass vs. count nouns. It discusses the phenomenon that concept antecedents are not restricted by anaphoric islands, and proposes that this is because they are name-like. It proposes an implementation within DRT and in compositional dynamic interpretation.
abstracts.009827: We consider a subclass of result verbs in Rappaport Hovav & Levin’s (2010) sense built on roots that entail change (Beavers & Koontz-Garboden, 2020), e.g., break, melt, explode, and tear. We argue that this class of roots possesses different grammatical properties between English and Spanish with respect to resultative constructions: these roots productively appear in both strong and weak resultatives in English but form only weak resultatives in Spanish (Washio, 1997). We propose an account of this asymmetry between the two languages rooted in differences in the semantic properties of the root class and independent differences in the inventory of prepositional heads available in each language: English possesses eventive change of state roots and eventive prepositions that express change of location/state, while their Spanish equivalents are stative, with the roots entailing change of state. This suggests that translational equivalents of roots across languages may differ in their grammatical properties and, therefore, possess different distributions in other constructions despite contributing the same conceptual content.
abstracts.009828: We introduce a new class of linguistic inferences, "parasuppositions", triggered by diverse constructions, notably appositive participles (e.g. 'Ann drinks, taking enormous risks'); post-speech gestures—e.g. 'Ann drinks – DRINK', where DRINK is a gestural representation of drinking; and parenthetical conjuncts q of the form p (and q)—e.g. 'Ann drinks (and takes enormous risks)'. With special reference to French, we show that parasuppositions give rise to projection patterns reminiscent of presuppositions: 'Ann might smoke, taking enormous risks' yields the inference that if Ann smokes, she takes enormous risks. These projection patterns suggest that parasuppositions must be locally trivial (= entailed by their local context). But parasuppositions differ from presuppositions in two key respects: they are informative, and they are typically deviant under not and none-type quantifiers. While some appositive relative clauses (ARCs) might well trigger parasuppositions, our target constructions differ from ARCs in being preferentially interpreted in situ, and thus they do not display the "wide scope behavior" of ARCs. To explain the target behavior, we propose that parasupposition triggers must be entailed by their speaker's local context, computed on the basis of their linguistic environment combined with the speaker's beliefs (rather than with the common ground). We explain their deviance under not and none by the fact that in such environments they make a trivial contribution: 'Nobody smokes, taking enormous risks' triggers two inferences, namely Nobody smokes, and Everyone who smokes takes enormous risks. But the second component is trivially true because of the first component, and the sentence has a simpler equivalent alternative, namely 'Nobody smokes'. Long-term, our analysis raises questions about the typology of presupposition-like phenomena in language, and of their derivation.
abstracts.009829: This study investigates the acoustic phenomenon where the Japanese name for the tiger beetle, Ooenma Hanmyou (オオエンマハンミョウ, Cicindela japonica), sounds perceptually identical when played in reverse. Originating from an investigation on the Japanese television program "Tantei! Night Scoop," this finding challenges conventional understandings of palindromes. Unlike orthographic palindromes (e.g., "tomato"), which are visually symmetric but acoustically asymmetric due to stop consonant bursts, the word Ooenma Hanmyou represents a rare class of "acoustic palindromes." Through International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) analysis, this paper demonstrates that true acoustic reversibility requires two conditions: (1) a palindromic phoneme sequence in IPA (accounting for phonetic realizations such as moraic nasal assimilation), and (2) an all-sonorant consonant inventory. The analysis reveals that under a specific phonological interpretation where the palatal glide /j/ is treated as acoustically equivalent to the front vowel /e/, the word forms a perfect phonetic palindrome. Furthermore, the exclusive presence of sonorant consonants (/m/, /h/, /j/) ensures the acoustic symmetry necessary for reversibility. These findings have significant implications for phonological theory, highlighting the distinction between symbolic representation and acoustic reality in speech perception.
abstracts.009830: Kalomoiros and Schwarz (2024) report symmetric presupposition projection across disjunction, a key datum for theories of projection. This study further asks whether projection across disjunctions is affected by exclusive interpretations. We observe that many fully semantic implementations of exclusivity and presupposition projection converge on the same, previously untested prediction: exclusive disjunction yields uniform projection (i.e., no filtering for either disjunct), so increasing exclusivity should reduce filtering. Mayr & Romoli (2016a) derive this prediction for Strong Kleene semantics when exclusivity is computed via bivalent exhaustification, and we show that it also follows, under the same assumption, for George’s (2008) algorithm, and for dynamic semantics (Rothschild, 2011). We also derive this prediction for strong-negation variants of trivalent exhaustification (Spector & Sudo, 2017). We then test this prediction in a Mandarin acceptability-judgment experiment adapted from Kalomoiros and Schwarz (2024), manipulating the rate of exclusive readings via environmental monotonicity. In fact, we find no evidence that increasing exclusivity affects filtering. If this null effect proves robust, it puts pressure on most of the above semantic implementations and appears compatible with only a weak-negation version of trivalent exhaustification that has been argued to be undesirable for independent reasons (Spector & Sudo, 2017), so we discuss possible future paths.
abstracts.009831: This paper presents a phonemic analysis of the West-Central variety of Haryanvi spoken in parts of Bhiwani and the Hansi region of Hisar district in Haryana, India. Based on minimal pair evidence and native speaker data, the study identifies an inventory of thirty-two consonant phonemes, nine vowel phonemes, and three diphthongs. The study also examines syllable structure and the phonotactic distribution of segments. The findings contribute to the phonological description of Haryanvi, which remains relatively under-documented in linguistic literature.
abstracts.009832: Geoffrey K. Pullum has repeatedly made severe accusations that the linguist Daniel L. Everett suffered mistreatment in Brazil because his research on the Pirahã people and their language threatened Chomskyan theory. The present article presents a large trove of previously unavailable evidence (official Brazilian government documents, citizen information requests, interviews, etc.) that are directly relevant for assessing the claims that Everett was slandered and unjustly blocked from field research. The evidence disproves these claims, which have circulated widely in what I am designating as the Persecution Hoax. The evolution of Everett’s problems with Brazil’s National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (FUNAI) is traced and found to be due to his own behavior and not to the action of Noam Chomsky or his affiliated linguists, nor to envious linguists in Brazil. Some variants of the Persecution Hoax myth, which are incompatible with the evidence and with each other, are described, along with comments. This myth is unfavorable for the development of indigenous linguistics in Brazil, as are Pullum’s suggestions for fieldwork. This is discussed briefly and alternative suggestions are offered.
abstracts.009833: Recent theoretical work in music semantics has proposed a formal framework to model how music can convey information about the extra-musical world. At the same time, a large body of empirical research on cross-modal correspondences has evidenced systematic mappings between perceptual dimensions across sensory domains. In this paper, we present several experimental audiovisual paradigms designed to show that the two efforts should be integrated, and argue that music semantics must be grounded in cross-modal correspondences while allowing for more expressive forms of meaning. We first demonstrate that pitch and loudness can be interpreted as the level of energy of a visual object, or as its distance from a viewpoint (experiment 1). Second, we provide evidence that pitch and dynamics can be used to pick specific objects as referents (experiment 2). Third, by evidencing preferences for persistent timbre/object associations, we show that timbre can be associated with objects on the fly in the absence of any salient cross-modal correspondence, a prediction that cross-modal correspondences alone cannot make without a richer music semantic model (experiment 3). Finally, we show that these associations persist and can be reused to infer the behavior of a specific object, even in the absence of visual cues (experiment 4). Taken together, a parsimonious interpretation of these results is that music can refer to objects of the extra-musical world and simultaneously convey some properties of these objects.
abstracts.009834: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a high degree of stylistic adaptability, yet they frequently produce unstable responses in terms of discursive register, enunciative position, and pragmatic coherence across extended interactions. A common practice among users is persona prompting, in which the model is instructed to assume a specific discursive role. Although widely used in practice, this technique has been treated primarily as a prompt engineering strategy, with limited analysis from the perspective of linguistics and discourse pragmatics. This paper proposes interpreting persona prompting as a mechanism of discursive framing (persona framing) in human–LLM interaction. It argues that persona instructions function as pragmatic devices that establish discursive registers, delimit enunciative positions, and constrain the stylistic space of generated responses. At the same time, the concept of persona framing is proposed not only as a linguistic interpretation of an existing technique, but also as a useful conceptual lens for the design of structured interactions with language models. As an exploratory study, we analyze structured interactions with a system of discursive personas called Nemosine, in which different linguistic roles have defined discursive vocations and are maintained throughout dialogue. Based on this analysis, we propose a preliminary typology of framing levels in human–LLM interaction: (1) ephemeral persona framing, in which the persona appears only in a single isolated turn; (2) persistent persona framing, in which the persona remains active across multiple turns; (3) environment framing, in which interaction takes place within a symbolic space of interpretation that allows the invocation of different personas; and (4) system-level persona framing, in which the architecture of the interaction system is organized around multiple personas with specific discursive functions. The qualitative analysis suggests that persona-based framing contributes to greater consistency of register, greater stylistic stability, and greater pragmatic predictability in the model’s responses. The results indicate that persona framing may be understood as an emerging linguistic interface for interacting with LLMs, connecting prompt engineering practices with classical theories of discursive framing, polyphony, and pragmatic organization of discourse.
abstracts.009835: This paper examines the vowel tenseness indicator θ₁ in the English vowel /ɑː/ and compares the results with previously reported findings in Ishizaki (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025a, 2025b) in order to provide a more comprehensive discussion. An investigation of the English vowels /ɑː/, /æ/, and /ʌ/, which may cause confusion for Japanese speakers, shows that /ɑː/ and /ʌ/ display similar θ₁ patterns, whereas /æ/ behaves differently. If vowel tenseness is assumed to be defined in the same way for both close and open vowels, comparison with the θ₁ behavior of the close vowels /iː/, /ɪ/, /uː/, and /ʊ/ may provide further insight into the tenseness of /ɑː/, /æ/, and /ʌ/. Ishizaki (2025a) proposed the parameter “force of tenseness,” and further consideration of this parameter based on the present study may help clarify what vowel tenseness represents. The findings should be regarded as preliminary, as they are based on a limited dataset.
abstracts.009836: This proposal introduces a new principle, the Perceptual Compression Hypothesis (PCH), which postulates that subsyllabic elements—onset, nucleus, and coda—represent segmental temporal units in phonetics capable of hosting multiple phonetic segments, thereby giving rise to complex segments. Following the tenets of Strict CV theory, which proposes that CV is the only syllable structure existing in phonology, this framework argues that the onset position admits only complex segments, while the arrangement of complex segments within rhyme elements depends on grammatical patterns exclusive to each language. The hypothesis distinguishes between two types of complex segments: primary complex segments, which obtain their linear order from a subsegmental algorithm following Wagner Oviedo (2026), and derived complex segments, which occur during derivation through the fusion of linear elements into a single segmental temporal position. To identify these structures, three diagnostics are proposed: predictability, separability, and distributional identification. The proposal further argues that, at a specific point in the derivation, primary and derived complex segments neutralize, exhibiting identical effects in phonological processes. Finally, this model is applied to three languages showing distinct arrangements: Spanish, characterized by more derived than primary complex segments; Sanskrit, with a similar distribution of both; and Huautla Mazatec, which features a predominance of primary complex segments.
abstracts.009837: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance across various sentence-based linguistic phenomena, yet their ability to capture cross-sentence paradigmatic patterns, such as verb alternations, remains underexplored. In this work, we present curated paradigm-based datasets for four languages, designed to probe systematic cross-sentence knowledge of verb alternations (change-of-state and object-drop constructions in English, German and Italian, and Hebrew binyanim). The datasets comprise thousands of the Blackbird Language Matrices (BLMs) problems. The BLM task– an RPM/ARC-like task devised specifically for language– is a controlled linguistic puzzle where models must select the sentence that completes a pattern according to syntactic and semantic rules. We introduce three types of templates varying in complexity and apply linguistically-informed data augmentation strategies across synthetic and natural data. We provide simple baseline performance results across English, Italian, German, and Hebrew, that demonstrate the diagnostic usefulness of the datasets.
abstracts.009838: Syntactic complexity varies not only between languages but also across textual genres, reflecting structural, stylistic, and communicative factors. This study explores the interplay of these two dimensions by analyzing six syntactic complexity metrics (SCMs) across 17 languages and four genres in a large multilingual corpus. We examine how SCMs correlate across languages and genres and assess which metrics best predict language versus genre. Correlation analysis reveals two robust metric clusters – clausal and phrasal. Inter-metric correlations are high in legal texts and movie subtitles, but substantially lower in parliamentary proceedings and fiction, likely due to greater internal variation in syntactic complexity within these genres. Using random forest classification, we show that SCMs strongly predict genre, with noun phrase metrics ranking highest. In contrast, mean dependency distance (mdd) and its standard deviation are most predictive of language. Misclassification tendencies confirm the affinity of English with Romance languages, previously observed in lexical studies. By emphasizing not only central tendencies (mean values) but also the dispersion of metrics within texts, this study adds methodological nuance to the measurement of syntactic complexity. It also confirms the need to account for both language and genre in crosslinguistic syntactic complexity research.
abstracts.009839: This squib analyzes matrix clauses with no overt aspect morpheme in Mam, a Mayan language of Guatemala and Mexico. These clauses involve systematic failure of absolutive (Set B) agreement with intransitive subjects and transitive objects; if either is pronominal, must be expressed overtly in argument position (i.e. not pro-dropped). I argue that these clauses involve a phonologically null completive aspect morpheme (Ø, glossed 'NCOM'), which realizes a T/Infl head that idiosyncratically lacks a phi-probe. Evidence is presented that this agreement failure is not reducible to the phonological status of either the aspect morpheme itself or the Set B morphemes (cf. Woolford 2011). I propose that Set B agreement in Mayan must therefore be disentangled from both argument licensing and object-over-subject inversion, the latter of which is independently required in high-absolutive Mayan languages like Mam (Ranero 2021, Scott 2023).
abstracts.009840: Across the world’s languages, one of the most common clausal complementation strategies involves a form of the verb “say.” Most research in this area assumes “say” to be equivalent to the English complementizer “that.” The present paper argues that an element in Lubukusu (Bantu, Kenya) that was formerly treated as an agreeing complementizer is actually a stative verb meaning “say.” This “say” predicate is the head of a clausal adjunct that merges at the VP level of the matrix clause, reasonably mimicking a complementizer. However, we demonstrate a number of reasons to think it is a verb. As a consequence of this analysis, an otherwise complex agreement system is reduced to run-of-the-mill subject-verb agreement both within the matrix clause and within a clausal adjunct. A central part of the argument is claiming that the verb “say” introduces two arguments, a source argument and a communicated content argument; this argument structure explains a broad range of properties of “say” cross- linguistically and correctly predicts a range of otherwise unexpected patterns in Lubukusu. If correct, this proposal advances our understanding of complementation structures and solves a standing agreement puzzle. We introduce a broad range of new Lubukusu patterns relevant to the argument structure of this verbal element, with implications for complementation, multiple-verb constructions, and agreement. In the course of the argument, we also address common objections to this kind of approach by showing that “say” in English has a number of previously under- appreciated properties that parallel the Lubukusu facts. We conclude with some brief comments on the implications for a theory of selection.
abstracts.009841: This paper presents the first systematic description of headless relative clauses in Tigrinya (Semitic; Eritrea and Ethiopia; SOV). Drawing on novel fieldwork data, it examines three types of headless relatives, namely light-headed, super-free, and free-choice relatives. The data show that, unlike many other languages, Tigrinya forms both headed and headless relative clauses using the same morphosyntactic strategy, which involves the relativizer z(ɨ)- without overt wh-elements. Headless relatives in Tigrinya do not rely on interrogative wh-structures, in contrast to languages such as English. Notably, free relatives are not attested. Instead, all headless relative clauses share a structural core with headed relatives, differing only in the presence or absence of nominal and determiner layers. By documenting this pattern, the paper identifies a previously underdescribed strategy in Afro-Asiatic. These findings refine the typology of relativization, provide empirical evidence for cross-linguistic variation in relative clause formation, and establish a foundation for formal analyses of Tigrinya and related languages.
abstracts.009842: This paper is devoted to what I will call the ‘non-endorsement puzzle’: a distinguished feature of hearsay evidentials such that they allow the speaker to disavow the prejacent. Ever since it was ﬁrst brought to the forefront of formal semantic research by Martina Faller (2002), the puzzle has been the subject of lively debates in the literature. My goals in this paper are fourfold: (i) to delineate the desiderata for a theory of non-endorsement by placing evidentials in a larger context of speech and attitude reports; (ii) to disentangle the modelling of the core semantics of evidentials from the modelling of the discourse effects of utterances that contain them; (iii) to propose theory-neutral diagnostics of evidential intensionality, thus vindicating a modal analysis for at least some hearsay evidentials; (iv) to argue, building on (Korotkova 2020), that the evidential signal is not conventionally marked as not-at-issue content and that it is at-issue in discourses whose QUD structure allows it (cf. Hunter 2016; Koev 2022 on parenthetical constructions). The existing literature focuses on the modeling question: how to best formulate the denotation of hearsay evidentials to make non-endorsement non-contradictory. At the same time, there is an overlooked dimension to the puzzle: the overall discourse function of hearsay utterances with overt non-endorsement. As I will argue, the view that evidentials aren’t conventionally not-at-issue allows us to make signiﬁcant headway in understanding this latter question.
abstracts.009843: It is a common view that the wide range of readings of the possessor construction and of 'have' are due to polysemy. The talk presents semantic data that require a unified have-relation even in the absence of HAVE in syntax. It will pursue a unified relation along the lines of a 'reference-point relation' in the sense of Langacker (1993).
abstracts.009844: This paper examines so-called active participles in three languages with different morphological systems (Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, English, and Hebrew). Based on a range of morphological, syntactic, and interpretational diagnostics, I argue that these elements are uniformly deverbal adjectives. This result challenges a substantial body of work claiming that active participles show an adjectival/verbal ambiguity, but it is in line with Bešlin 2023 which analyzes passive participles as deverbal adjectives. Importantly, deverbal adjectives may denote predicates of properties or predicates of eventualities (events or states), depending on the characteristics of the verbal structure they embed. If these conclusions generalize to other languages, then there is no need to assume that (verbal) participles constitute a separate grammatical category, which is a desirable theoretical outcome. The results presented in this paper argue for an architecture of the grammar in which there is no one-to-one mapping between an item’s syntactic category and its meaning.
abstracts.009845: Research in Distributed Morphology (DM) has found that many patterns of allomorphy can be explained if allomorph selection is done cyclically. Several ancillary mechanisms have been argued to further delimit allomorphy; they include (i) linear adjacency (Embick 2010, a.o.); (ii) structural adjacency (Adger, Béjar, and Harbour 2001, 2003, a.o.); and (iii) accessibility domains, a claim that roots are visible up to the first node above the first categorizer (Moskal 2015). In this paper, I show that there are violations of (i)-(iii) in Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian (BCS) allomorphy. In section 2, I show that n(ominalizer)s in BCS complex nominals show allomorphic conditioning by a linearly non-adjacent morpheme. In section 3, I show that the root and comparative affix are visible to each other in BCS negative comparative adjectives despite the structural intervention of the a(djectivizer) and negation. Hence, the root and the comparative morpheme are visible to each other in a configuration that does not involve structural adjacency, and where the comparative morpheme is outside of the root’s hypothesized accessibility domain. Finally, in section 4 I discuss the implications of the evidence reported here and in the existing literature for the timing of Vocabulary Insertion (VI) and linearization.
abstracts.009846: This paper documents three independent lines of evidence that liquid-context jers in OCS were not real reduced vowels. First, a categorical distributional split: strong-position jers in non-liquid envi- ronments vocalize to full vowels in 100% of cases across Czech (n = 23), Serbian (n = 22), and Slovak (n = 23)—68 out of 68 words—while strong-position jers adjacent to liquids vocalize in 0% of cases (n = 27). The seven Modern Czech words with /e/ near liquids (červ, černý, blecha, pleť’) are secondary epenthesis of the 13th–15th centuries, documented in Old Czech as syllabic consonant forms (črv, črný, blcha, plt), and post-date the jer fall by centuries. Second, a quality test: when Czech hard syllabic /l/ resolved, it yielded /u/ (žlutý, dlouhý), not /e/—the vowel that 100% of non-liquid jers produce. The quality tracks the liquid, not the jer. Third, a quality diagnostic from Russian and Bulgarian: in both branches, the same front jer ь in strong position produces different vowels depending on the adjacent liquid. In Russian, ь yields /e/ before /r/ (верх, зерно, смерть) but /o/ before dark /l/ (волк, полный, жёлтый). In Bulgarian, ь yields /e/ in non-liquid contexts (ден, пес) but /ɤ/ (the back-jer reflex) before either liquid, in 12 of 12 etymologically eligible cases. If Havlík’s law were operating, the conditioning would be the jer (front →/e/ regardless of environment). Instead, the conditioning is the liquid—the signature of liquid-conditioned epenthesis, the same mechanism that backs /e/ to /o/ before dark /l/ in East Slavic polnoglasie (melko →молоко). We argue that liquid-context jers were notational conventions for already-syllabic consonants, and that Havlík’s law applies only to genuine reduced vowels from PIE *i/*u. The apparent liquid exception disappears: there was never a vowel to vocalize.
abstracts.009847: This paper demonstrates that in Gitksan, measure phrases (MPs) occurring with relative gradable adjectives (GAs) like ’wii ’nakw ‘tall’ receive differential interpretations even in the absence of an overt comparative operator or an overt standard phrase, a pattern which has been only reported in Japanese (e.g., Snyder et al. 1995) and Korean (Oda 2008; contra Sawada and Grano 2011). In contrast, MPs occurring with minimum-standard GAs like ḵ’aḵ ‘open’ receive absolute interpretations, as in many languages including Japanese (Sawada and Grano 2011). However, Gitksan differs from Japanese in two crucial ways. First, the distinction between relative and minimum-standard GAs is observed even without MPs: relative GAs can easily receive comparative interpretations on their own, while minimum-standard GAs cannot. Second, Gitksan has a morphologically free, overt morpheme k’aa, which can give rise to comparative readings with any GA and hence makes the possibility of a covert comparative operator less plausible. On a closer investigation, the comparative readings of relative GAs without k’aa show mixed behaviours of what have traditionally been called ‘explicit’ and ‘implicit’ comparatives (Kennedy 2007). I propose that these comparative readings arise from inherently context-sensitive denotations of relative GAs, building on Oda’s (2008) analysis of Japanese. The latter half of the paper examines the semantics of k’aa and analyzes it as a superlative morpheme, and highlights the role of consideration of alternatives to the subject in comparative readings observed without k’aa.
abstracts.009848: The Old Church Slavonic letter yat (Ѣ, ѣ) represents Proto-Slavic *ě, a vowel unique among Slavic phonemes for producing four distinct modern reflexes: Ekavian /e/, Ikavian /i/, Ijekavian /ije/, and Bulgarian /ja/. We demonstrate that this four-way divergence is not a Slavic-internal accident but a continuation of a deeper pattern: yat systematically marks Proto-Indo-European (PIE) phonological positions where the vowel nucleus was complex—either a laryngeal sequence (*eh1) or a diphthong (*ey, *oy, *ay). We construct a 74-word corpus of yat-bearing OCS words with established PIE etymologies and quantify cross-IE vowel divergence at each yat position using a formal Lability Score (LS). Of 67 testable entries, 91% show at least moderate cross-IE vowel lability (mean LS = 3.4), compared with 2.64 for a control set of 53 non-yat *e words (p<0.001). An independent loanword test examining 45 early borrowings into Proto-Slavic confirms that *ai diphthongs and long *ē in donor languages were mapped to yat with 98% accuracy, while other vowel types were never assigned yat (Fisher’s exact test, p<0.0001). A test for correlation between PIE source group and dialect-internal yat reflex exceptions yields a negative result, indicating that the two PIE sources had fully merged before intra-Slavic divergence began. We argue that yat functions as a graphemic marker of inherited PIE vowel instability—a “written laryngeal” that captures the phonological class where IE branches systematically disagree on vowel quality.
abstracts.009849: Displaced reference — the use of a signal for what is not in the perceptual field — is a defining feature of human language (Hockett 1960) and, as Bickerton (2009) argued, the central problem for any account of its origin. The standard scenario derives it from the need to recruit others to distant food; but where pointing, leading and pantomime would serve, an offline representational system is not obviously worth its cost. This paper proposes a different first case. In the cooperative-breeding arrangement reconstructed for early Homo (Hrdy 2009; Burkart et al. 2025), a mother handed her infant to an allomother and left to forage, so that mother and infant were repeatedly placed in perceptual situations that no longer specified one another. What is at issue is not distance but a partition between situations: how to go on holding one specific, non-fungible individual when one's own situation supplies no index of it. A perceptually grounded gesture has nothing to work on there; an individualized vocalization does. The first displaced signal, on this account, was a proper name rather than a food call. The semiotic core is the broken index. An index signifies through a connection that holds at the moment of signifying; when the referent goes, that connection lapses and cannot be restored by producing the signal again. What takes over its office is a sign of another type: a vocal form tied to one individual, which keeps the singularity of pointing while working without perceptual contiguity. Four stages that "proper name" otherwise runs together are separated — an infant-associated form, its displaced use by the mother alone, a mapping organized by the referent rather than by any caller, and a public name — with Kripkean rigid designation characterizing the last rather than the first. The token is relational at the outset, which makes the portable name the product of a first decomposition rather than an atom. On this reading the proper name is not a defective case within a system whose norm is the common noun, but the paradigm from which the principle of arbitrariness was tacitly generalized (Zimmerling 2025); and the relational handle the decomposition leaves behind is what seeds recombination. Evidence is drawn from cooperative breeding and life history, vocal-respiratory control, development, comparative vocal individuation in dolphins, chimpanzees and marmosets, and neural work on cross-modal identity representation. Three levels of decoupling are distinguished — from arousal, from here, and from now — and the mechanism is placed at the third, which the published comparative record does not document. The account is offered as a reconstruction, not a demonstration. This is version 4, revising version 3. The hypothesis is unchanged: §1.2 now states the mechanism in one pass, the four stages are separated, and the evidential status of each claim is marked. A companion Supplementary Materials document, not hosted here, develops the intellectual genealogy of the displacement problem, the pre-cooperative-breeding ecology, the modal philosophy of the sign, the synchronic windows on the genitive contour, and the cultural elaborations of the mechanism: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20488658.
abstracts.009850: Russian verb-stranding constructions, in which a finite verb appears without its internal argument, have been analyzed as instances of either Verb-stranding VP Ellipsis (VVPE) or Argument Ellipsis (AE). Recent work has established that AE is restricted to arguments of semantic type e, providing a diagnostic: if verb-stranding shows degraded acceptability with non-e-type arguments, AE rather than VVPE is the operative mechanism. This study extends prior experimental evidence for AE in Russian (Kasenov & Rudnev, to appear) by decomposing the non-e-type category into four subtypes: naming complement, predicative nominal, predicative adjectival, and argumental adverbial. In a pre-registered acceptability judgment experiment (N = 260), the e-type baseline (dp object) was rated significantly higher than three of the four non-e-type conditions, with medium-to-large effect sizes (d = 0.57–0.83). The contrast between dp object and predicative nominal did not reach significance (d = 0.25, p = .133); however, the post-hoc analysis indicates that the study was underpowered to detect effects of this magnitude, leaving open whether predicative nominals pattern with e-type or non-e-type arguments. The results of the study provide further support for AE as the primary analysis for Russian verb-stranding and raise the question of whether predicative nominals admit an individual-denoting reading that renders them compatible with argument ellipsis.
abstracts.009851: The elicitation of naturalistic linguistic data depends on the cultural and ecological suitability of the stimuli employed to prompt speaker responses. Standardized visual tools in language documentation are typically based on Western contexts, creating a mismatch in linguistically diverse settings such as India. This mismatch results in cognitive load and can affect elicited data due to increased code-mixing, reduced deictic accuracy, and interrupted speech. This paper puts forth a methodological proposal in the form of a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) workflow for generating culturally grounded elicitation stimuli using generative AI. The approach formalizes iterative prompt engineering, ethnographic constraint specification, and pre-field validation to produce stimuli aligned with specific linguistic targets. Rather than treating generative models as autonomous systems, the framework positions the linguist as an active agent who constrains and evaluates outputs. The paper does not present an empirical evaluation; instead, it demonstrates the operational logic of the HITL methodology and documents the prompt design process in supplementary materials. The contribution is a replicable and transparent workflow for integrating generative AI into linguistic fieldwork.
abstracts.009852: English interjections have been denied category status (Jespersen 1924), dismissed as uninteresting (Huddleston & Pullum 2005), or acknowledged as "marginal and anomalous" (Quirk et al. 1985). This paper argues that interjections are a thin-but-genuine homeostatic property cluster (HPC): a set of co-occurring properties (prosodic isolation, non-inflection, syntactic non-integration, non-referentiality, emotive force) maintained by identifiable stabilisers. At least three diachronic pathways — grammaticalization via semantic bleaching (historically demonstrated), pragmaticalization via syntactic deactivation, and nonce coinage via onomatopoeia (both proposed with clear examples) — converge on the same synchronic cluster, extending Gehweiler's (2008) analysis of gee! to a general theoretical claim. A perturbation probe suggests that removing a stabiliser produces predictable, asymmetric category shifts. The paper's distinctive contribution is that interjection projectibility is primarily pragmatic rather than truth-conditional: the most frequent interjections are interactional tools (continuers, repair initiators, change-of-state tokens), and categorizing a novel form as an interjection licenses inferences about prosodic behaviour, interactional distribution, and stance expression. A field-relative decomposition shows that syntacticians, semanticists, and interactional linguists each track distinct HPCs with overlapping but non-identical extensions. The category that embarrassed classical theory is a natural fit for HPC — and its pragmatic projectibility extends the framework to a new domain of inference.
abstracts.009853: The core of the Dutch diphtong system are three diphthongs, one at each of the major places that Dutch also reserves for monophtongs: front unrounded /ɛi/, front rounded /ʏy/ and back rounded /ɑu/. In this chapter we first discuss these three core diphtongs, their historical origin and their place in the current system. We also compare these to two other sets. The first are the so-called ‘false dipthongs’ /uj, aj, oj, iw, ew/. These differ from the ‘real’ diphthongs in that the consist of vowel parts that are at different places of articulation (whereas real diphtongs are all in one place, differing only in height), and in their syllabification properties (true dipthongs allow non-coronal consonants in the coda, but false dipthongs do not). The second set to which true diphthongs need to be compared are the mid vowels which in (Netherlands) Dutch tend to be diphtongized at least phonetically: /ej, øj/øw and ow/. Again the syllabification properties are different and in spite of their phonetics they phonologically still seem to fit completely in the set of monophthongs.
abstracts.009854: This paper focuses in particular on Peirce's Foundational Habit (Semeiosis) vs. Chomsky's Basic Operation (Merge). The concept of instinct has long played a central but controversial role in explanations of human cognition and behavior. In biology, psychology, and cognitive science, instinct is often invoked to explain capacities that appear early in development, recur widely across individuals, and emerge without explicit instruction. Yet critics have frequently argued that the concept is theoretically ambiguous and risks functioning as a placeholder explanation when underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This chapter reexamines the role of instinct in contemporary debates about language and cognition by contrasting two influential conceptions: Charles Sanders Peirce’s pragmatist account of instinct as a form of abductive inference and Noam Chomsky’s rationalist interpretation of instinct as innate cognitive structure underlying language. It is argued that Peirce's abductive inference sets the logical framework for current research in AI/LLMs. After tracing the historical development of the instinct concept and reviewing major definitions used in modern research, the chapter surveys arguments both for and against instinctive explanations of cognition. Evidence from comparative biology, infant cognition, and evolutionary theory supports the existence of biologically grounded predispositions, while critiques from developmental systems theory, anthropology, and philosophy of biology emphasize the importance of environmental interaction and cultural transmission in shaping cognitive development. The central comparison focuses on Peirce’s theory of instinctive abduction and Chomsky’s theory of Universal Grammar. Whereas Chomsky interprets instinct as structured cognitive architecture that constrains the acquisition of grammar, Peirce understands instinct primarily as an evolutionary tendency that guides hypothesis formation in inquiry. The chapter argues that Peirce’s account provides a more flexible framework for integrating biological predispositions with learning and cultural evolution. It concludes by proposing that instinct is best interpreted as probabilistic cognitive bias rather than fixed innate structure, thereby offering a synthesis that accommodates insights from linguistics, philosophy, and cognitive science.
abstracts.009855: The Continental West Germanic languages provide a fertile ground for studying the structure of the clausal peripheries and the syntactic relations (movement or otherwise) between elements in the clausal peripheries and positions in the remainder of the clause. The left periphery is marked by the verb-second effect, positioning the finite verb to the immediate right of the first constituent. There is some evidence for distinguishing separate positions for topics and wh-elements in the left periphery, but very little evidence for the full range of left-peripheral positions proposed in the literature. In addition, there appears to be a position for even more peripheral elements that do not trigger the verb-second effect, i.e., left-dislocation. The right periphery likewise shows a distinction between more and less canonical peripheral regions, involved in extraposition and right-dislocation (backgrounding or afterthought), respectively. Neither the structure of the right periphery nor the processes by which elements come to occupy these positions are fully understood, suggesting that the traditional tool kit for describing them (including rightward movement) may need to be replaced or enriched by others, involving conjunction and ellipsis.
abstracts.009856: [This paper supersedes a previous ms. found at https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/008258] [[Oct '26: Updated version contains additional data analysis that supports Benbaji-Elhadad and Pesetsky's (2025) claim that ellipsis of predicate nominals does *not* result in degraded acceptability of verb-stranding constructions]] Russian verb-stranding constructions are argued to exemplify either verb-stranding VP ellipsis (Gribanova 2013b) or argument ellipsis (Bailyn 2017; Landau 2020b). As recent work shows, the debate between verb-stranding VP ellipsis and argument ellipsis is murky due to various confounds in the employed diagnostics (Simpson 2023; Landau 2023b). This paper reports on an acceptability judgment study focused on whether the semantic type of verbal arguments influences acceptability of verb-stranding constructions (as has been observed for Hebrew by Landau 2018). Our results support Landau's finding only partially: only ellipsis of adverbial arguments was found to lead to a decline in acceptability, while no effect of ellipsis of predicate nominals was found. However, if a VP ellipsis derivation were available, all sentences would have an acceptable parse. The reported study thus supports the view that argument ellipsis is the only available structure for Russian verb-stranding constructions with overt subjects. We contrast the findings with Russian verb-stranding constructions that involve polarity focus and conclude that the scope of our claim is limited to verb-stranding constructions that do not involve syntactic head movement (assuming a distinction between types of head movement proposed by Harizanov & Gribanova 2019).
abstracts.009857: This dissertation investigates the what for-construction (WFC), an adnominal wh- construction attested in a limited set of European languages, including Germanic, Slavic, and Baltic varieties. The WFC combines an interrogative pronoun with a preposition-like element (for, für, za, par) and a nominal complement, and it displays a cluster of properties that distinguish it from ordinary wh-determiner phrases, including wh-split, atypical case behavior, and variation between KIND and TOKEN interpretations. The dissertation pursues three main goals. First, it provides a detailed descriptive overview of the WFC across languages, based on grammatical descriptions, existing theoretical work, and new corpus data. Second, it traces the diachronic development of the German WFC from Old High German to Early New High German. The corpus evidence shows that the construction emerged from an earlier wh + NPgen pattern and that the loss of robust genitive marking played a crucial role in triggering structural reanalysis. The introduction of für coincides with broader changes in the German case and agreement system and cannot be reduced to borrowing or language contact alone. Third, the dissertation develops a unified syntactic analysis of the WFC. Building on earlier insights that attribute a predicational structure to the WFC, the analysis argues that elements such as for, für, za, and voor function as predicators rather than as ordinary prepositions. The construction is analyzed as a Predication Phrase (PredP), which establishes a predicational relation between the wh-item and a nominal (often silent) KIND operator. This analysis accounts in a unified way for the case and agreement properties and the systematic distinction between KIND and TOKEN interpretations. The proposed analysis is compatible with the diachronic development of the construction in German and aligns with broader theories of unidirectional syntactic change and grammaticalization.
abstracts.009858: This paper investigates non-arbitrary phonological patterns in the Mandarin Chinese lexicon, focusing on basic color terms and common adjectival antonyms. An analysis of the six primary basic color terms reveals systematic onset correspondences. Specifically, the terms for non-colors (*bái* ‘white’, *hēi* ‘black’) exhibit maximal contrast in place and manner of articulation. In contrast, warm colors (*huáng* ‘yellow’, *hóng* ‘red’) and cold colors (*lán* ‘blue’, *lǜ* ‘green’) consistently share the onsets /h/ and /l/, respectively. Computational simulations resampling the Mandarin syllable inventory demonstrate that the simultaneous occurrence of these phonological distributions by chance is highly unlikely to be by chance (p < 0.0001). An exploratory assessment of common adjectival antonym pairs further indicates a restricted use of places of articulation, predominantly drawing from alveolar, alveolo-palatal, and retroflex consonants while systematically excluding front and back sounds. These findings provide quantitative evidence for an abstract form of ideophony in Mandarin, where phonological form systematically reflects semantic class membership and sensory contrasts.
abstracts.009859: Logical reasoning is one of humanity's most powerful abilities. A widespread assumption across psychology, linguistics, and philosophy holds that reasoning operates over concepts that refer to objects and properties in the world, yet this has rarely been tested empirically. We introduce a novel paradigm that exploits lexical ambiguity to differentiate candidate representations for human inference: word-forms, reference-fixing concepts, or more abstract "underspecified representations" that constrain meaning without fully determining it. Across three experiments (N=158), participants evaluated deductive arguments equivocating over polysemous or homonymous terms. Although these arguments are logically equivalent under standard analyses, participants reliably accepted non-truth-preserving polysemous arguments while rejecting homonymous ones. This asymmetry -- the Uncommon Sense Effect -- points to underspecified representations as the default basis of logical inference. This challenges a foundational assumption about meaning, and opens new empirical avenues for studying the link between what we think and why we think it.
abstracts.009860: This paper examines a previously unnoticed ‘split’ construction in Greek, where a possessor that originates in a PP occurs together with the P separated from the possessum. I show a correlation between the availability of this split and the interpretation of a PP. This finding poses a challenge to PF-based accounts of splitting, particularly those that assume distributed deletion (e.g., Fanselow and Ćavar 2002; Fanselow and Féry 2006, Bondarenko and Davis 2023, Murphy and Wilson 2025 i.a.). Such accounts require additional mechanisms beyond those independently required by a syntactic account and fail to predict the distribution of split constructions. Instead, I propose a purely syntactic analysis that accounts for splits in Greek based on a correlation between the interpretation of a PP and its merge height (e.g., Alexiadou and Anagnostopoulou 2007, Cinque 1999, Schweikert 2005). These findings together with additional theoretical considerations will be shown to provide strong support for the elimination of distributed deletion as a mechanism in natural language.
abstracts.009861: With initial native speaker judgements suggesting an exclusive plural morpheme in downward entailing contexts in Akan, as reported by Ahenkorah (2022), this research seeks to test these claims through experimental means and to provide a more comprehensive picture of Akan’s plural semantics. The current literature on exclusive and inclusive plurals focuses mainly on English, with some investigation of Western Armenian, Turkish, and Korean (Bale & Khanjian 2008; Renans et al. 2017; Kang 1994: a.o.). These languages have drawn intrigue due to their unmarked form behaving number neutrally, while English’s unmarked form is specified for atomicity. Akan, which marks both singulars and plurals morphologically makes for an interesting addition to this discussion. Ahenkorah (2022) claims that the plural circumfix, used to mark kinship terms, is inclusive, similarly to English, but that the prefix, which is used for most nominals, is exclusive. The present experiments test these two plural morphemes in multiple downward entailing contexts to obtain the full picture of their meanings. The results of the two experiments show that both the plural prefix and plural circumfix have an inclusive reading in downward entailing contexts. Furthermore, this provides evidence that the plural circumfix is not a circumfix at all, but is two separate morphemes: a plural prefix and kinship suffix.
abstracts.009862: Approaches to negativity tags, like English 'neither'-tags, 'not even'-tags, and 'why not', differ in whether they treat the antecedent as a clause with clausal negation (e.g., Klima 1964; Kramer and Rawlins 2009; Brasoveanu et al. 2013) or, more broadly, one introducing a salient counterfactual proposition into the discourse (Hofmann 2022, 2023a). This paper presents experimental evidence for the latter view, showing that negativity tags are rated as natural (compared to an affirmative baseline) when their antecedent is introduced without clausal negation, but in an anti-veridical embedding (e.g., 'It's a lie'), under neg-raising (e.g., 'I don't get the feeling'), or with lexical indicators of irony (Horn 2016, e.g., 'as if'). The naturalness ratings also show fine-grained differences across possible licensors, suggesting additional pragmatic constraints and raising questions about the salience of the antecedent propositions.
abstracts.009863: Matrix questions in Sm’algyax (Tsimshianic; British Columbia, Alaska) are doubly marked. Wh-questions involve the fronting of a wh-expression to the clause-initial position, together with the interrogative clitic =u; polar questions are introduced by the complementizer ał—diachronically derived from negation—and additionally bear the clitic =ii. By contrast, embedded questions only exhibit a single component: wh-fronting for wh-questions and a complementizer element for polar questions. I argue that this asymmetry reflects a two-layer interrogative syntax. The polar complementizer and the null trigger for wh-movement instantiate an interrogative C[+Q] within CP, while the clitics =u and =ii instantiate an illocutionary operator SAASK within a higher Speech Act Phrase (SAP). Because SAP is restricted to main clauses, embedded questions necessarily lack interrogative clitics. This paper contributes novel empirical evidence from an underdescribed language to ongoing debates about the embeddability of speech acts. Sm’algyax shows clear evidence for an unembeddable SAP layer in the formation of canonical, information-seeking questions, supporting the view that SAP is a genuinely root-only projection (in line with Dayal 2023, pace Krifka 2014, 2023, Woods 2016).
abstracts.009864: This study compares the impact of natural and synthetic data on training and evaluating large language models (LLMs), using the case of passive verb alternation in French and Italian. We use Blackbird Language Matrices (BLMs), structured datasets designed to probe linguistic knowledge of underlying patterns across sentence sets. We compare structured templates instantiated with natural sentences extracted from Universal Dependencies to structured templates of synthetic sentences. Experiments show that while models achieve ceiling performance when trained and tested on synthetic datasets, they do not reliably generalize to natural sentences. In contrast, models trained on natural data exhibit robust performance across both natural and synthetic test suites, demonstrating their superior ability to capture abstract linguistic patterns. These results corroborate the value of natural data and of structured set ups in linguistic evaluation for probing LLMs’ syntactic and semantic knowledge.
abstracts.009865: A ‘Trojan’ vowel in a vowel harmony system is a vowel that spreads an underlyingly specified value of the spreading feature even though the Trojan vowel itself redundantly surfaces with the opposite value. We propose an analysis of Trojan vowels with Boolean Monadic Recursive Schemes (BMRS; Chandlee & Jardine 2021), a computational formalism describing phonological maps using conditional IF…THEN…ELSE… terms. We show how a BMRS analysis of Trojan vowel behavior in Hungarian follows straightforwardly when coupled with freely-specified input strings. Our analysis also accounts for the fact that redundantly-specified Trojan vowels in Hungarian are transparent in other contexts, and we briefly contrast this with the situation in Yoruba where Trojan vowels are otherwise opaque.
abstracts.009866: English uncountable plurals are plurals whose parts cannot be counted directly, such as (*five) oats/grasslands/news/measles/tweezers. These form a heterogeneous group in terms of semantic field and various morphosyntactic tests. Nevertheless, this paper shows that a unified analysis can account for the fact that their parts cannot be counted directly. In particular, it argues that uncountable plurals denote maximal clusters in a mereotopological sense. The maximality of these clusters causes a conceptualisation as wholes, which prevents access to the parts. We provide a descriptive typology of English uncountable plurals to illustrate their analysis as clusters connected through either overlap (Strong Connectedness), adjacency (External Connectedness), or Common Linkage, a connectedness relation first introduced here.
abstracts.009867: We propose a principled account of deixis as a structural property of grammar that is independently required for the constitution of propositional meaning and whose systematic encoding becomes indispensable under the constraints imposed by externalization. Building on an Un-Cartesian model, we assume that grammar operates over intensional representations derived from world-indexed states. Once such representations are externalized into a temporally unfolding signal, encoding under constrained resources does not preserve all aspects of the original representation, yielding irreversibility in the sense of Shannon’s information theory. As a consequence, linguistic signals underdetermine their interpretation, giving rise to a recovery problem. We argue that this problem specifically concerns the anchoring of content to a context of use, and that, since this is precisely the dimension lost in encoding, recovery requires reintroducing these parameters, which grammar encodes through deictic features such as person, time, and location. On this view, deixis is not a peripheral class of expressions but a fundamental component of grammar that both enables propositional content and ensures its recoverability under externalization.
abstracts.009868: Iterated learning experiments demonstrate that languages evolve structure under transmission pressure. The dominant metric for quantifying this process, normalised Levenshtein distance, measures transmission error: how much a signal changes as it passes between learners. We argue that transmission error and transmission fidelity are formally distinct quantities, and that Levenshtein distance is blind to the difference. We reanalyse the full published dataset from Kirby, Cornish & Smith (2008), covering 8 chains, 10 generations, and 27 meanings across both experiments, using normalised mutual information between input and output signal distributions at each generational step. Both experiments converge to low transmission error by generation 10. Normalised mutual information reveals that they do so by different strategies: Experiment 1 (underspecification) reduces error by discarding information, producing a lossy channel; Experiment 2 (compositionality) reduces error while maintaining high channel fidelity, preserving information through structural reorganisation. The fidelity gap is positive in 8 of 10 generations with a mean of 0.162 NMI units (late-generation NMI: Exp 1 = 0.746, Exp 2 = 0.830). This distinction, invisible to Levenshtein distance, formally operationalises the difference between cultural degradation and cultural reorganisation, and identifies compositionality as the information-theoretically efficient solution to the transmission bottleneck rather than merely one solution among equals. We extend this analysis to the four experimental conditions in Kirby, Tamariz, Cornish & Smith (2015), which vary the presence of an expressivity filter and communicative interaction. NMI reveals a systematic fidelity hierarchy across all four conditions: communication combined with a filter (Exp IV) maintains the highest fidelity throughout, underspecification without filter (Exp I) the lowest, with the remaining conditions ordered by their structural constraints. This hierarchy, invisible to Levenshtein distance, confirms that NMI captures a theoretically meaningful dimension of iterated language learning that error metrics cannot.
abstracts.009869: In Czech, the conditional (used in X-marking) is based on the past tense. The containment between the past and the conditional is not unique to Czech. The literature (including Von Fintel and Iatridou 2023, Majdić 2025) found that such a pattern is also attested in other languages. However, there is a difference between Czech and other languages: while Czech appears to have the order VERB-PAST COND (čet-l by), other languages manifest the order VERB-COND-PAST. This chapter proposes a nanosyntactic account of this (apparent) paradox.
abstracts.009870: Using the Hindi-Urdu discourse particle 'lo' as a case study, the present paper models mirativity within the Table model framework (Farkas & Roelofsen, 2017). This comes with an enrichment of the Table model; we propose the discourse structure to encode, in addition to discourse commitments, the time these commitments are publicized. We also incorporate a component that contains the public record of private beliefs. With these two additions, we seek to capture mirativity in the Table model, emphasizing recency as a condition for surprise and underlining the need and the conceptual difficulty of incorporating private beliefs in a public scoreboard of conversation. We show that the difficulty can be overcome to fulfill the modeling need.
abstracts.009871: In a range of cases, cartographic (and other syntactic) work will want to be on the lookout for additional syntactic structure, with more silent elements, and more intricate derivations than might have met the eye, at first glance.
abstracts.009872: What distinguishes register from dialect from discourse community? This paper argues that they differ not in what they are but in what participant expectation is conditioned on: SITUATION, ASCRIPTION, or IDENTIFICATION. These aren't just descriptive dimensions.
