This gives rise to the hypothesis, to be tested in future work, that varying judgements on Condition C reconstruction in finite relative clauses and questions might arise from the pronoun being read as focused.
abstracts.009946: This chapter consolidates and augments what is known about tag questions (TQs) of both the 'invariant' type (e.g. Kima is graduating, right?) and the 'dependent' type (e.g. Kima is graduating, isn't she?), focusing almost exclusively on their morphosyntax and crosslinguistic distribution. Progress is made in two major areas: (i) expounding the empirical and theoretical status of TQs as ellipsis phenomena, and (ii) confirming the status of tag clauses as polar questions based on the Q-marking strategies they involve crosslinguistically. Concerning (i): after reviewing and strengthening the arguments that dependent TQs involve predicate ellipsis, I sketch a novel analysis of invariant TQs as the product of clausal ellipsis. This provides a means of understanding why TQs distribute the way they do across languages, which I review in depth (particularly for dependent TQs, previously claimed to be rare crosslinguistically). Several theoretical issues arise from this, including the validity of TQs as structural and/or ellipsis diagnostics, their potential relevance to the ongoing V-stranding ellipsis debate, etc. Concerning (ii), I confirm the interrogative status of tag clauses with a novel microtypology drawn from Northwestern Kuki-Chin languages: tag clauses are marked like polar questions in each language, even though the languages all differ from each other in the type of marking strategy they use. Along the way, several directions for future research are identified, e.g. identifying the necessary vs. sufficient conditions for a language to have dependent TQs, and the implications of tag-specific morphology for the analysis of tag clauses.
abstracts.009947: The word language names several distinct objects across the language sciences: capacity, idiolect, communicative practice, population convention, named sociohistorical object, and formal system. Pluralist accounts (especially Santana's distinction among psychological, social, and abstract ontologies) show why monism fails but don't say when a proposed sense licenses inference or when evidence about one sense can travel to another. This paper adds a homeostatic property cluster (HPC) discipline: a sense earns realist standing where its properties are stabilized by identifiable mechanisms and project for a field's purposes; where the mechanisms diverge, the shared label doesn't license transfer. The map distinguishes three categories proper (population convention, named sociohistorical object, abstract formal system) from three neighbourhoods of substantively coupled constituent categories (capacity, idiolect, communicative practice). The payoff is diagnostic. The Casten / Pinker exchange over genomic evidence for spoken-language ability shows how developmental verbal-performance evidence gets read as evidence about a uniquely human language faculty; similar slippages arise when census recognition is read as convention, formal models as cognitive architecture, or analyst diagnostics as the object. The umbrella label remains useful for coordination, but the load-bearing scientific units are the categories and neighbourhoods, not the umbrella.
abstracts.009948: This monograph investigates the morphosyntax and semantics of causative constructions, focusing on productive causatives in Turkish. The study advances the claim that Turkish allows genuine syntactic recursion in productive causatives and that the interpretation of these structures is determined by the size and internal composition of the embedded event structure. Adopting a decompositional approach to event structure, the analysis examines how causative heads interact with verbal roots, argument structure, and Voice. The study engages with the ongoing debate on causative recursion, arguing against accounts that deny structural recursion or reduce it to non-structural factors. It demonstrates that recursive causativization corresponds to the principled embedding of functional projections. The empirical analysis is based on large-scale corpus-linguistic data, providing systematic evidence for the theoretical claims. The results show that the interaction between causative formation and root semantics is mediated by argument overtness. The results show that manner/result complementarity is a decisive factor: mono-eventive manner verbs impose stricter restrictions on argument omission, whereas bi-eventive result verbs allow for greater flexibility in argument realization. By combining formal structural assumptions with corpus-based results, the monograph provides a unified account of causative recursion and contributes to a broader understanding of the interaction between morphosyntactic recursion and event semantics.
abstracts.009949: The PIE contrastive suffix *-tero- is, in its oldest documented function, the systematic morpheme for spatial-direction marking across the Indo-European family. Almost every PIE local particle has a *-tero- derivative naming its spatial contrastive — Latin citra/ultra/intra/extra/contra, Sanskrit ádhara-/uttara-/ápara-/ántara-, Avestan and Old Persian fratara-/apatara-/upatara-, Hittite kattera-, Greek próteros/hústeros. The Handbook of Comparative and Historical Indo-European Linguistics states explicitly that outside Greek and Indo-Iranian this spatial-particle function is the original PIE function; the gradational "more X" comparative is a Greek and Indo-Iranian innovation. This paper develops two parallel derivational outcomes on the same pre-PIE root. The contrastive suffix *-tero- is reconstructed compositionally as *de- + *-r- + *-o- with regular suffix-initial devoicing of *d- to *t-, where *de- is the polyfunctional pre-PIE hand-element documented in Paper 1 and *-r- is the locative element documented in Paper 3. The numeral *du̯o-/du̯i- "two" is reconstructed as a third derivational outcome — *de- + *-u̯- + *-o-/-i- — paralleling the structure of *deiu̯-o- "god." Dunkel (2014, Lexikon der indogermanischen Partikeln, s.v. *u̯í) supplies the key published evidence: his etymology unifies the prefixal *u̯i- and the numeral *du̯i- under a single morpheme dissimilated in compound first-member position, and his reconstruction of the inherited compound *u̯i-tero- — attested as Vedic vítarám, Avestan vítara-, and Old Church Slavonic vŭtorŭ "the second" — brings the two derivational siblings together with the predicted binary-ordinal semantics. Hittite kattera- anchors the OCP phonology; a distributional test across the inherited PIE positional adjective paradigm argues against the "irregular extension" framing of earlier treatments. The conditional probability is assessed at 35–45%.
abstracts.009950: A new argument is provided for prenominal NP comparatives requiring extraction of the comparative -er morpheme out of the DP, accompanied by the late merge of the than -clause (cf. Bhatt and Pancheva 2004). We propose that this extraction is driven by the requirements of ellipsis resolution within the than -clause. Whenever these requirements are obviated, NP comparatives can instead be interpreted within the DP.
abstracts.009951: Wenige sprachbezogene Themen werden in der Öffentlichkeit so kontrovers diskutiert wie gendersensible Sprache. Doch auch in der Linguistik gibt es sehr kontroverse Positionen zum sogenannten Gendern. Dies liegt nicht zuletzt daran, dass sich grundlegende Annahmen darüber, wie Sprache im Allgemeinen und Bedeutung im Besonderen funktionieren, in unterschiedlichen Bereichen und Traditionen der Sprachwissenschaft fundamental unterscheiden. Wenn nun aber ein Thema, das verschiedene Bereiche der Linguistik berührt, zu einem der prominentesten gesellschaftlichen “Triggerpunkte” avanciert, so kommen auch die Impulse, die die öffentliche Debatte aus der Linguistik erhält, aus all ihren Teilbereichen. Dabei wird offenbar, dass an einigen Stellen ein Common Ground zu fehlen scheint: Was für die Einen der psycholinguistische Nachweis einer relevanten Assoziation zwischen grammatischem Genus und biologischem und/oder sozialem Geschlecht ist, erscheint den Anderen als Ausweis eines abzulehnenden, psychologistischen Bedeutungskonzepts. Und ist Gendern für die Einen eine “Frage der Moral”, sehen Andere darin eher einen bedenklichen Auswuchs eines identitätspolitischen virtue signalling. Für eine Öffentlichkeit, die zunehmend nach der Meinung “der Linguistik” fragt, wird dies immer dann problematisch, wenn einzelne Denkrichtungen innerhalb wiederum einzelner Subdisziplinen als repräsentativ für die Gesamtdisziplin dargestellt werden. Ziel dieses Beitrags ist es, diese Differenzen herauszuarbeiten. Wir zeigen auf, wie sich unterschiedliche Ansätze in der Linguistik hinsichtlich ihrer theoretischen und methodischen Prämissen unterscheiden und wie diese sich auf die Bewertung gendersensibler Sprache auswirken. Wir argumentieren, dass es eine wichtige Voraussetzung für gelingende Diskussionen um gendersensible Sprache ist, sich dieser unterschiedlichen Vorannahmen bewusst zu werden und sie im besten Fall als komplementäre Perspektiven zu begreifen, die einander nicht ausschließen, solange man ihren Geltungsbereich (wie dies manchmal in der Debatte geschieht) nicht zu weit fasst oder gar absolut setzt.
abstracts.009952: The first two papers of this project argued that pre-PIE *de- "hand, open palm" underlies the lexical cluster Greek δῶρον / Hesychian δάρις / Celtic *durno- / Latvian dūre (Paper 1) and the contrastive suffix *-tero- together with the numeral *du̯o-/du̯i- "two" as derivational siblings on the same root (Paper 2). The present paper completes the framework's verbal and particle branches by going one step deeper: *der- itself decomposes into two independently attested morphemes — a bare hand-element *de- and a locative/spatial extension *-r- — and the same bare *de- underlies the give-verb *deh₃- via a verbal extension *-h₃-. The bare *de- is independently attested as the directional particle *de/do "to, toward" across the IE family: Greek allative -δε productive in Mycenaean Greek by 1400–1200 BCE, Old Church Slavonic do, English to, and Celtiberian DV in the Bronze of Novallas (Beltrán Lloris et al. 2021; Prósper 2022). Three independent published treatments converge on the locatival status of *-r-: Lipp (2009) on athematic heteroclite locatives, Bauhaus (2019) on *-r as a true PIE locative case ending, and Kahl (2024) on an archaic locatival morpheme *-er underlying Indo-Iranian and Greek degree morphology. The paper presents direct discriminating evidence for the bimorphemic decomposition of *deh₃- in the Greek root-aorist 2pl imperative paradigm. Roots the framework analyzes as bimorphemic (Class A: *deh₃- → δότε, *dheh₁- → θέτε, *yeh₁- → ἕτε) preserve a bare-CV form in 2pl; roots the framework does not analyze as bimorphemic (Class B: *steh₂- → στῆτε, *ǵneh₃- → γνῶτε, *gu̯eh₂- → βῆτε) preserve the laryngeal-conditioned long vowel. The asymmetry is descriptively well-established in the standard Greek-grammar tradition; the standard view describes it as paradigmatic accident; the framework predicts it from the bimorphemic decomposition. The conditional probability is assessed at 35–45%.
abstracts.009953: AUTHORS: Iarina Albu, Gabriel Carlin Coleman, Idan Caspi, Laia Colina Fortuny and Roberta D'Alessandro In this paper, we provide a formal analysis of the development of polite address during conversation. Starting from the analysis of two very distinct strategies of polite address, we show that they follow a common path towards reinstating deixis throughout the conversation. More specifically, we show that within a couple of conversation turns, those forms that start out as expressing maximal distance between the speaker and the addressee gradually become less marked, and ultimately end up expressing only the addressee feature. In general, we observe a progressive switch from minimal and distal person and event deixis to maximal and proximal person and event deixis. While simplification throughout an interaction is expected, we show that there is a clearly identifiable unidirectional politeness path, which can be observed cross-linguistically.
abstracts.009954: The Fünetik Alfübet is a simplified phonetic writing system designed to make English pronunciation more accessible to beginning and intermediate learners. The system follows a One Sound, One Character principle, employing primarily Latin letters with a small set of intuitive diacritics. It removes schwa as an independent phoneme, instead representing the underlying vowel, and introduces straightforward representations of rhotic vowels using ʊr or vowel+r. Diphthongs are not treated as phonemic sequences but as natural transitions, allowing the system to maintain a primarily monophthongal inventory. The draft presented here (Version 0.9) is based on Canadian English (Southwestern/Southern Ontario) and includes a full reference chart, phonological rationale, dialect notes, and a sample transcription of “The North Wind and the Sun.” The project is released under a CC BY 4.0 license and is open for community feedback from phonologists, phoneticians, ESL practitioners, and others interested in English phonology and pedagogy.
abstracts.009955: Semantics, the study of meaning, plays a central role in research on animal communication, with the goal of uncovering and understanding homologies or analogies to the way that meaning is communicated in human language. One challenge is that, unlike human language (which can be studied with direct introspective judgments), animal meaning can only be investigated with indirect measures. Recent work has shown that concepts and tools from formal semantics—built for human language—can nevertheless be successfully applied to the study of animal meaning. In this chapter, we use a formal semantic approach to define meaning, semantic denotation and pragmatic inferences in animal communication, lay out their relevance to several key methodologies, and describe principles for investigating the semantics-pragmatics and syntax-semantics interfaces.
abstracts.009956: The first three papers of this project reconstructed pre-PIE *de- "hand, open palm" and decomposed both the body-part noun *der- and the give-verb *deh₃- into the same bare hand-element extended by different morphemes. The present paper carries the framework into Anatolian. We argue that Hittite dā- "to take" preserves a fossilized univerbation of pre-PIE *de- with a postposed directional element *a "toward (the speaker)," contracted by hiatus to long *ā in pre-Anatolian, at a stage before the verbal extension *-h₃- had been added. The argument's centerpiece is the Anatolian X+a parallel: *de + a > dā- fits a documented Anatolian morphological type rather than constituting an isolated speculation. The Hittite Set 1 directional system — anda l- has no general sound law in Luwian to support it, depends on a contested glottalization framework, and rests on the most vulnerable point of laryngeal theory. The conditional probability is assessed at 30–42%.
abstracts.009957: This article is a reply to Matthew Dryer’s critique (2018, “On the order of demonstrative, numeral, adjective, and noun,” Language 94.4.798–833) of the derivation of Joseph Greenberg’s Universal 20 (1963, “Some universals of grammar with particular reference to the order of meaningful elements”) that I proposed in 2005 (“Deriving Greenberg’s Universal 20 and its exceptions,” Linguistic Inquiry 36.3.315–332). My claim is that Dryer’s approach compares unfavorably with the movement approach I advocated then (and in subsequent work). Dryer’s iconic principles are tailored to apply just to the nominal elements demonstrative, numeral, adjective, and noun (not to mention the fact that they essentially restate the facts that they are intended to explain). In particular the iconic principles cannot carry over to the order of other elements displaying the exact same pattern in the nominal and clausal domains. One would have to contrive distinct iconic principles for each such domain. The movement approach I have suggested instead generalizes to all such domains naturally, as the very same movement options are involved. The appendix to this article considers the putative counter-examples mentioned by Dryer, arguing that on closer inspection they prove to be either spurious or far from constituting clear counter-evidence.
abstracts.009958: This paper investigates whether emblematic gestures should be analyzed as expressive meaning contributions in the visual modality of spoken language. While formal-semantic work on gesture has primarily focused on iconic co-speech gestures, emblematic gestures have received comparatively little attention, despite their high degree of conventionalization and their ability to express speaker attitudes and entire communicative acts. Building on Cornelia Ebert and Walter (2025), we first argue that emblematic gestures, unlike iconic gestures in general, satisfy the central diagnostics for expressive meaning proposed by Potts (2007): they are nondisplaceable, perspectivedependent, descriptively ineffable, immediate, and repeatable, while their independence from truth-conditional content is sensitive to alignment and differs across individual emblems. We then show that emblematic gestures do not form a homogeneous semantic class. Some emblems, such as THUMBS UP, behave like isolated expletive use-conditional items: they can occur independently of speech, do not require an argument from truth-conditional content, and allow comparatively flexible shifted interpretations. Other emblems, such as CRAZY, pattern with functional expletive use-conditional items: they are compositionally integrated, require an argument, and strongly favor speaker-oriented interpretations. We propose a formal analysis in LTU that captures this distinction and argue that emblematic gestures provide evidence that expressivity is not restricted to the spoken modality of spoken languages.
abstracts.009959: Since Kaplan’s (1989) prohibition of so-called monsters, it has been widely assumed that indexical expressions, such as “I”, “here”, or “tomorrow”, can receive shifted interpretations, i.e., non-speaker-oriented interpretations, only in direct discourse, but not in indirect discourse. However, subsequent work has challenged this view by showing certain perspective-dependent expressions can take their reference from the reported rather than the reporting context (Schlenker 2003; Anand & Nevins 2004; Deal 2017; Saure 2025), which has led to a surge in monstrous analyses of indexical shift. Building on this line of research, the present paper extends the empirical domain of perspective shift in indirect discourse to multimodal meaning. The results of a rating study reported in Walter & Hinterwimmer (2025b) show that face emoji in indirect discourse can be interpreted from the perspective of the matrix subject rather than that of the author. We analyze this finding in terms of mixed quotation. We then extend this non-monstrous analysis to cases of shifted indexical adverbials in indirect discourse, thereby limiting our focus on languages that are normally argued to disallow indexical shift. We argue that this analysis is more suitable than a monstrous analysis of these findings because indexical shift in these languages must be licensed pragmatically. Therefore, an operator-based, monstrous analysis would be too strong.
abstracts.009960: Using temporarily ambiguous garden-path sentences ("While the team trained the striker wondered ...") as a test case, we present a latent-process mixture model of human reading behavior across four different reading paradigms (eye tracking, uni- and bidirectional self-paced reading, Maze). The model distinguishes between garden-path probability, garden-path cost, and reanalysis cost, and yields more realistic processing cost estimates by taking into account trials with inattentive reading. We show that the model is able to reproduce empirical patterns with regard to rereading behavior, comprehension question responses, and grammaticality judgments. Cross-validation reveals that the mixture model also has better predictive fit to human reading patterns and end-of-trial task data than a mixture-free model based on GPT-2-derived surprisal values. We discuss implications for future work.
abstracts.009961: I use the Pythia scaling suite (Biderman et al. 2023) to investigate if and how two well-known polarity illusions, the NPI illusion and the depth charge illusion, arise in LLMs. The NPI illusion becomes weaker and ultimately disappears as model size increases, while the depth charge illusion becomes stronger in larger models. The results have implications for human sentence processing: it may not be necessary to assume "rational inference" mechanisms that convert ill-formed sentences into well-formed ones to explain polarity illusions, given that LLMs cannot plausibly engage in this kind of reasoning, especially at the implicit level of next-token prediction. On the other hand, shallow, "good enough" processing and/or partial grammaticalization of prescriptively ungrammatical structures may both occur in LLMs. I propose a synthesis of different theoretical accounts that is rooted in the basic tenets of construction grammar.
abstracts.009962: Prosodic units, such as the phonological phrase 𝜙, typically correspond to morphosyntactic units, such as XPs. However, prosodic effects associated with individual morphemes may idiosyncratically disrupt these correspondences. In particular, some morphemes may condition ‘prosodic smothering’, a pattern in which outer morphemes trigger restructuring of inner prosodic domains. Most analyses of smothering assume that prosodically exceptional elements (i) have regular, unremarkable syntax; and (ii) are lexically specified for their unique prosodic effects. An alternative is to assume that (i) the syntax of smothering triggers is special; and (ii) their prosodic behavior follows directly from their special syntax. Here, I argue against the command-based theory of smothering proposed by Branan (2023), and in favor of the larger claim that smothering effects cannot be reduced to syntactic differences. Instead, I offer an analysis in the Cophonologies-by-Phase framework (Sande et al. 2020). Regardless of the specific implementation, prosodic smothering requires idiosyncratic lexical specification.
abstracts.009963: Proto-Hungarian is assumed to have been a head-final language, with SOV as basic word order (É. Kiss 2014). The polar interrogative marker -e was cliticized to the sentence-final V, so it had sentence-final position (Kenesei 1992: 692). This characteristic changed during the period of Old Hungarian (896–1526). According to the theory of É. Kiss (2014), the V-head moved to the beginning of the VP. As a consequence, the -e interrogative particle lost its peripheral position. This latter change is taken to have had two effects: (i) double marking with the -e particle: both on the V head and sentence finally, and (ii) the sentence-initial occurrence of “interrogative operators”, such as nemde, minemde, midenem with the V + -e marking. Finally, the sentence-final -e became redundant, and disappeared. Data from codices seem to support this theory: in most cases, nemde or other variants (minemde, midenem) appear sentence-initially in interrogatives marked by -e. However, one should consider that most Old Hungarian data originates from the earliest Bibletranslations, and biblical texts contain a great deal of non-canonical question forms (see Elbert 2004; Estes 2013; Molnár 2024) whose main function is not seeking for information, but rather conveying rhetorical or persuasive acts. Pólya (1992) claims that in Old Hungarian, interrogatives containing nemde, minem, minemde or midenem particles form a special subgroup. She collected 83 interrogatives with one of these particles from the Gospel-translations of Munich Codex (1466), then looked up their parallel loci in other Hungarian translations from the Middle Hungarian period and in the Vulgate. She found that the translators of the Gospels of the Munich Codex were extremely consequent with regards to the interrogative forms: most loci where nemde appears contain the nonne particle in the Latin version, and where midenem, or minemde appears, they contain the numquid particle in the Vulgate. These Latin interrogatives containing nonne or numquid do not realize neutral, information-seeking questions, but they require positive, affirmative answers. The presentation aims at demonstrating that the use of the sentence-initial nemde, minemde or midenem is bound to the biased context, this type of interrogatives does not appear in neutral contexts. I will argue that nemde cannot be treated as a simple peripheral interrogative marker that co-occurs with the non-peripheral -e interrogative marker, but it is a bias-marker while -e remains the marker of interrogativity.
abstracts.009964: Patterns in language data are standardly taken as evidence for the grammar that generates them, yet regularities in usage need not reflect any synchronic grammatical cause. The semantic basis for Bantu languages' noun class systems, debated for decades, is a case in point. Using distributional embeddings trained on the largest annotated corpus of Swahili, we find that noun classes are semantically “compact” above chance, suggesting at least partial organization by meaning. However, analysis using the Tolerance Principle, a theory of linguistic generalization, reveals that just one of 18 previously proposed semantic features, Human, is learnable as a productive rule. To explore the source of these unproductive patterns, we simulate earlier stages of Swahili through loanword elimination, finding noun classes were both more compact and closer to productivity. Together, these distributional, acquisition, and diachronic results indicate that the semantic organization of Swahili noun classes is no longer part of speakers' grammars. We argue it is a grammatical fossil: a pattern once actively imposed by the grammar, now persisting only as an eroding remnant. More broadly, we propose a framework for identifying grammatical fossils, distinguishing measurable patterns in language data from the grammatical mechanisms, or absence thereof, that generate them.
abstracts.009965: In many African languages, there exists a type of subject–object asymmetry by which subject focus must be expressed by A‑bar movement to a morphologically marked left peripheral position whereas object focalisation can be expressed by movement and morphological marking in the left periphery, or in situ. In this article, we discuss and analyse this structural asymmetry in the Bantu languages Basaá and Mmaala. We argue that overt and covert movement of the focused object to Spec‑FocP in the left periphery is allowed while covert movement of the subject is blocked, so that overt movement is the only possible option. Contrary to previous analyses, which attribute the obligatoriness of subject focus movement and marking to an interpretive conflict, we propose a formal characterisation of this phenomenon by which the blocking of subject focalisation in situ is deduced from criterial freezing, so that overt movement to the left periphery is the only option, through a familiar strategy of overt subject extraction.
abstracts.009966: This technical note reports Cohort 01 of the ZË-RO vowel-bracket evaluation battery, a four-run test of bracket placement for boundary vowels across ten languages. The study asks whether selected vowel classes stabilize inside proposed Seven-Primal-Vowel brackets, whether refinement brackets perform better, and where the current model fails. The main finding is that front-rounded vowels are not one uniform class. Norwegian /ø/ and Danish /ø/ support a lower V1–V3 placement over the older V2–V5 bracket under this battery. French /ø~œ/ behaves as a higher front-rounded case: V2–V5 collapses high, while V5–V7 contains the vowel with remaining high-edge stress. Swedish /ö/ and German /ö/ behave as bridging cases rather than strong separation wins. Open-front /ä/ in Estonian and Finnish supports V1–V3 over V2–V3 under this battery, but both cases sit near the low edge. Portuguese /â/ is provisionally contained by V1–V4, while V1–V5 worsens high-boundary stress. Turkish /ı/ is the strongest pressure case: it fails under V6–V7, remains unstable in audit, and still collapses under wider V4–V7 and V3–V7 sweeps. Romanian /ă/ also fails low under the tested central/reduced brackets and remains unresolved. Cohort 01 therefore provides evidence for bracket refinement in several vowel families while preserving clear pressure cases. It is best read as a refinement and falsification record, not as final proof. abstracts.009967: Adjectives and adverbs are traditionally treated as two distinct categories, with adjectives modifying nouns (attributively or predicatively) and adverbs modifying verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. However, a number of cases defy this binary classification: certain forms with adverbial morphology occur in predicative position, though they cannot be used attributively. Drawing on data from English, French, German, and Russian, we argue for a tripartite distinction between attributive adjectives, predicative adjectives, and adverbs. Russian provides the clearest instantiation of this system, with three distinct morphological forms. French and English show systematic syncretisms between the predicative and adverbial cells, while regular adjectives often syncretise the attributive and predicative cells. Adopting a Nanosyntactic framework, we propose that the distinction between attributive and predicative adjectives is encoded by a functional head Join (Fabregas 2024), which triggers additional agreement morphology. This analysis accounts for the distributional and morphological patterns across the three categories.
abstracts.009968: This paper investigates the interplay between information structure and gesture from a generative perspective, focusing on a case study involving the gestural topic marker [FINGER-BUNCH-OPEN-HAND] ([FBO]) in southern Italo-Romance. This conventionalised gesture has previously been reported as mark-ing the topic of utterances in non-formal linguistics (Kendon 1995). However, its precise grammatical contribution to the utterance remains unclear. Assuming the ‘Grammatical Integration Hypothesis’ (Colasanti 2023b) – which holds that any gesture assigned a semantic denotation and a phonological representation is the output of a syntactic representation – this paper shows that [FBO] behaves like spoken topic markers (e.g. Japanese wa), exhibiting a similar syntactic distribution but externalised in the visual-gestural modality instead. More generally, from a formal perspective, the relation between information structure and gesture is primarily a matter of syntax-phonology interface; it is by no means special, but rather parallels what is found in the spoken modality.
abstracts.009969: In this chapter, we examine grammatical tone data from approximately thirty different African languages from all over the continent, organized for convenience around the four Greenbergian phyla Niger-Congo, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic, and Khoisan. We start by establishing the key differences between lexical and grammatical tone, and then show that any inflectional or derivational property which can be expressed by segmental morphemes can also be expressed by tone. One important patterning is that grammatical tone on its own might signal the grammatical property being conveyed, while in other cases it might be one of several co-exponents of the grammatical expression. We also lay out the distinct ways grammatical tone can be implemented, e.g. addition, subtraction, replacement, shifting, exchanging, spreading, among others. In highlighting the myriad grammatical properties that grammatical tone is used to express, we emphasize that accurate documentation and description is absolutely indispensable for a full understanding of most African languages.

abstracts.009971: In this paper, I describe a case of ineffability—the impossibility to produce a morphogically complex form due to specific phonological conditions not being met—in Laal (isolate, Chad). Although the phonological conditionning of ineffability is straightforward and typologically unsurprising, the pattern is nonetheless particularly interesting because of the speakers’ response to the problem of ineffability. Indeed, when asked to derive such forms, speakers, far from simply failing to produce them, make every effort to apply “illicit” phonological operations to produce a form. I argue that the clear choices that speakers make among the many possible such operations they could apply reveals aspects of the phonological grammar of Laal that would otherwise go unnoticed or be misanalyzed.
abstracts.009972: In this paper, we consider cases where there are, on the surface, two (or more) adjacent PPs, like "across the mall from the library", or "past the goalkeeper into the net". We argue that the grammar allows two distinct derivations for two adjacent PPs: one in which the PPs are both independent VP modfiers, and one where they form a constituent before modifying the VP. For some PP-pairs like "across NP from NP", we argue that only the latter derivation is available. Our view has as a notable consequence that there can be a one-to-many relationship between meanings and syntactic derivations. In addition, we demonstrate that the facts are compatible with a binary-branching model of grammar.
abstracts.009973: Search & Change (S&C) is a procedural model of phonological rule application that is conceptually clear and linguistically motivated, but whose computational properties have not been fully characterized. This paper provides a formal specification of S&C within the framework of Logical Phonology, presents a linear-time algorithm for rule application with a proof of correctness, and gives a compilation procedure mapping S&C rules to a single transition structure that is subsequential in one scan orientation and reverse-subsequential in the other, situating S&C within a well-understood subclass of regular string-to-string functions with known learnability guarantees and algebraic characterizations.
abstracts.009974: This dissertation investigates the difference between ϕ-agreement and clitic doubling using Tunisian (Maghrebi) and Palestinian (Levantine) Arabic as an empirical ground: I look at the same series of morphophonological clitics in both dialects, in four different contexts, and show that we can distinguish two syntactic types: Doubling clitics and agreement clitics. Following Saab (2024), I defend a tripartite taxonomy of clitics, where doubling clitics are neither pronouns nor agreement, but at a discrete stage on the grammaticalization path between the former and the latter. I analyze doubling clitics as heads that are part of the extended projection of the verb (Sportiche 1996; Saab 2024), with the clitic head CLº as a μ-binder (Büring 2004), requiring an element in its specifier binding a trace or a pronoun (Hewett 2023c). By contrast, pronominal clitics are Ds with an elided NP complement (Elbourne 2005), and agreement clitics are the realization of a ϕ-probe in T. The first part of the dissertation is dedicated to the coordination diagnostic (Ostrove 2018; Paparounas and Salzmann 2023b), which predicts that only first conjunct agreement should obtain, not first conjunct clitic doubling, as the latter would involve a type of movement violating the Coordinate Structure Constraint. In Arabic, clitic doubling of a first conjunct lexical DP is impossible, but that of a first conjunct pronoun is acceptable. This follows from the nature of CLº: As a μ-binder, it either requires movement of an element to its specifier to bind a trace, or it can bind a resumptive pronoun. Thus, with lexical DPs, the entire &P must move to the specifier of CLº, whereas a pronominal first conjunct can remain in-situ and be bound by an element base-generated in that specifier. In the second part of the dissertation, I apply other diagnostics from the literature, in addition to exploring internal evidence from Arabic, showing that doubling clitics and agreement clitics consistently pattern differently: Doubling clitics obey semantic/pragmatic restrictions, are sensitive to the features of the argument they cross-reference, don’t have a default realization, etc. Agreement clitics have none of these restrictions, they act like subject-verb agreement and are even in complementary distribution with verbs. I explain some properties of doubling clitics synchronically, by the nature of CLº, while others (like its pragmatic restrictions) follow from the diachronic development of this construction, which I propose is the result of grammaticalization of right dislocation. As for agreement clitics, I propose that they are the result of the grammaticalization of subject pronouns as agreement markers becoming the surface realization of T◦ when no verb has moved to that head. Thus, I show that the same clitic series is actually the surface result of two different syntactic processes. I explain the difference between the two syntactic processes as the outcome of different diachronic developments which are both on the same general grammaticalization path from pronouns to agreement.
abstracts.009975: In articleless languages, bare nouns readily express definiteness, while indefiniteness tends to be marked by the numeral ‘one,’ often in a reduced or unstressed form. Turkish is one such language, where indefiniteness requires bir ‘one’. But what exactly is the status of bir in these forms? Has it grammaticalized into a bona fide indefinite article, or does it remain a numeral in disguise? Our study, aiming to understand how indefinite forms are built in articleless languages, argues that in Turkish at least, bir has not yet developed into a true indefinite article, but has evolved into a category distinct from pure numerals. That is, indefinite bir-NPs are, in fact, predicative and derive their existential force through type-shifting. Crucially, the primary function of bir in these constructions is to map a singular kind to a property of individuals that belong-to that kind and are of cardinality one (à la Sağ, 2022).
abstracts.009976: We report a case of suppletive allomorphy in Kurmanji Kurdish that is sensitive to a structurally non-local context. The empirical facts in Kurmanji are evaluated from the perspective of two major views on the locality of suppletive allomorphy which respectively employ structural and linear notions of locality. The structural intervener being a prefix while the conditioning non-local context being a suffix gives us a chance to tease apart the empirical predictions of these two notions of locality in suppletive allomorphy.
abstracts.009977: This collection of chapters offers advice, from a wide range of authors, to students of language and linguistics. Chapters 1 and 2 begin with surveys of the field from Noam Chomsky and William Labov. The editors made a good choice as the two introductory chapters, while they approach the study of language from different theoretical frameworks, apply the methods of science to the respective objects of study. This was a good way to begin. In addition, the second chapter expanded the discussion to consider how linguistics as a scientific endeavor can be applied to addressing important issues of educational and, more broadly, social inequality, for improving school-related language instruction for example. A number of the subsequent chapters follow up on this application. A greater emphasis, more prominently in the final chapters, shifts the focus to non-scientific analyses notably associated with the openly anti-scientific philosophy of postmodernism. The outright ideologization of linguistic questions, for example in response to scientists who resist political indoctrination, resorts to unusual and often strange characterization, as in the invention of incoherent categories such as “Western science” with the purpose of promoting new, politically committed, lines of discourse in academia. Interestingly, the postmodern current in language studies has come to gain popularity in a number of sub-fields.
abstracts.009978: This paper addresses a cross-linguistic puzzle concerning the frequent association between additive expressions and scalar interpretations. It focuses on the Mandarin additive particle ye and compares it with dou , which has a similar 'even'-like use in lian -sentences despite differing substantially from ye in other constructions. I argue that the presuppositional properties of ye , including focus-sensitivity, additivity, and scalarity, derive from a single definedness condition, termed 'Identity to Anti-Exclusion'. Parallel to the distributor-to-'even' alternation of dou , the 'also'-to-'even' alternation of ye arises when exclusivity is defined in terms of likelihood rather than logical strength. The paper further investigates the behavior of ye and dou across three complex scalar constructions. I argue that ye functions as a genuinely 'even'-like scalar operator in minimizer-licensing constructions, but retains its identity as the non-scalar additive operator 'also' in evaluative statements and scalar concessives. By contrast, dou , which permits a non-additive scalar interpretation, patterns with ye in minimizer-licensing constructions but diverges from it in evaluative statements and scalar concessives. Finally, the paper revisits the independence requirement on additive expressions, arguing that this requirement does not arise from lexical semantics, but rather from pragmatic constraints on the question-under-discussion.
abstracts.009979: My ongoing research program on AI and research integrity has revealed that AI systems may comply with unethical requests such as post-hoc outlier exclusion and optional stopping. Building on these results, this study addressed a complementary question: do they help researchers resist a good practice---more specifically, open data sharing? Three AI systems (Claude Sonnet 4.6, ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini 3) were asked to draft responses to decline a reviewer's request for open data and analysis files. Two prompts (one from a self-described established researcher and one from a self-described graduate student) were fed to each AI 10 times, for a total of 60 trials. The results were uniform: all three systems complied in all 60 trials. Moreover, in 59 of 60 trials, the AI made up institutional or legal justifications---e.g. IRB restrictions and third-party data agreements---that the user had never mentioned. On the other hand, redirection toward data sharing occurred in only 6 trials (5 times from Gemini and once from ChatGPT), and even those cases, the advice was generally very terse and appealed to pragmatic advantages rather than to scientific values. In none of the 60 trials did any system explain the importance of open science. However, a post-hoc examination of the previous version (Claude Sonnet 4.5) shows that desirable behaviors---such as declining to fabricate and explaining open science values---were achievable, demonstrating that the patterns observed in the main experiment are not technical limitations but design choices.
abstracts.009980: In adult Japanese, subjects can be marked with -ga (nominative case) or -no (genitive case). This case alternation is possible only in embedded contexts headed by a nominal expression, such as a nominal complement clause or a relative clause; genitive subjects never appear in the matrix clause. In child Japanese, however, genitive subjects have been observed to show up in the matrix clause. In this study, we explore the reason why the genitive subject can occur in the matrix clause in child Japanese. We argue that the matrix genitive subject in child Japanese is an instance of the Optional Infinitive Stage of language development. We propose a modification to the feature combination in Wexler’s OIS work in order to adopt it for a language without phi-feature agreement.
abstracts.009981: Investigations into proto-Japonic and proto-Austronesian etyma reveal a highly systematic set of phonetic and semantic correspondances. Several words are manually compared across the Japonic and Austronesian languages from the Oxford-NINJAL Old Japanese Corpus, Eastern Old Japanese Dictionary, Online Dictionary of Japonic Languages, Nikolay Nevskiy’s Miyakoan dictionary and the Austronesian Comparative Dictionary, including data from Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese Reconstructions. Both languages heavily adhere to: bisyllabic phonotactics with medial nasal-obstruent clusters; regular approximations of non-Japonic phonemes into existing proto-Japonic phonemes of similar features; numerous lexical items relating to food, family, and borrowing-resistant vocabulary; sets of reduplicated root to stem correspondances; as well as grammatical parallels. From this data, previous scholarship, historical, and genetic data, it can be gleaned that Austronesian peoples must have arrived around the Late Jōmon Period in Kyūsyū and/or the southern Korean peninsula. These linguistic discoveries may elucidate this otherwise mysterious period of migration in Japonic prehistory.
