abstracts.010048: Sperm whale codas have been described from two angles: as combinable timing features (rhythm, tempo, ornament, and a slow inter-coda drift termed rubato), and as recurrent spectral patterns within individual clicks labeled a-vowel and i-vowel. The two have not been analyzed jointly at the level where representational decisions are made, which is the consecutive same-speaker transition. This study aligns the two systems on 1,170 vowel-labeled codas from 13 individually identified Eastern-Caribbean whales and tests whether each pair of features moves together across transitions. The resulting transition structure is feature-specific: rhythm and tempo are tightly coupled, ornament adds no additional self-transition resolution once rhythm and tempo are fixed, vowel is strongly associated with rhythm at the coda level but only weakly coupled to it at the transition level, and rubato is a relation between two codas rather than a property of one. These four findings motivate a candidate cell-and-tier notation, CEJONG, that places each feature at the level its transition dynamics suggests. The grid uses jeongganbo’s vertical-time cells and hunminjeongeum’s block-internal organization as architectural precedents. All transition-level claims about vowel are conditional on the labeled subset. CEJONG provides a transition-grounded representational hypothesis for downstream sequence modeling; an initial held-out encoding check supports the tier-separated choice over a fully joint cell, with broader model-based validation left open.
abstracts.010049: In der Untersuchung habe ich Daten zur Interpretation von ausgewählten Gesichtsemojis entlang den Dimensionen Bekanntheit, Valenz und Ambiguität sowie Beschreibungen für die bislang wenig erforschte Altersgruppe der unter 18-Jährigen erhoben und mittels Lemmatisierung und Varianzanalyse sowie einer Kategorisierung der genannten Bedeutungen analysiert. Diesen Ansatz habe ich vergleichend ebenso für die Altersgruppe der Erwachsenen mithilfe des bereits erhobenen Datensatzes von Scheffler & Nenchev (2024) durchgeführt und grafisch entlang der untersuchten Dimensionen dargestellt. Die Untersuchung hat keine relevanten Unterschiede in der Interpretation von Gesichtsemojis zwischen den untersuchten Altersgruppen ergeben.
abstracts.010050: We propose a unified analysis of “meta questions”, a variety of questions about the intentions behind a speech act, among them “Echo-questions”. We analyze meta questions as run-of-the-mill questions in which a wh-Phrase covertly scopes over silent speech-act-material. The silence of the speech act material and the covertness of the movement are derived from independently motivated constraints in the theory of spell-out. The analysis explains a restriction on recursion of ilent speech acts, more specifically the limited distribution of meta-meta questions (Trinh 2024)
abstracts.010051: The article addresses the negation structures in Aromanian. In this language the Strict Negative Concord is applied, whereby the negative marker (NM) nu is always requested, also in the presence of n-words, particularly those corresponding to the arguments of the verb. In negative contexts, however, we may also find specialized indefinite elements which in turn give rise to the negative reading. This distribution, specifically the types of negative doubling, is explained by assuming that the negative operator is not realized by a lexical constituent but is postulated and made available to interpretation by the presence of NM and n-words. The Chomskyan theory of Phases and the lexical properties of n-words provide the crucial morphosyntactic tools to connect doubling and other phenomena to the transfer and Spell-out procedures.
abstracts.010052: This paper examines Serial Verb Constructions (SVCs) from a new interdisciplinary perspective by linking linguistic analysis models with the sociological Theory of the Formal Situation (FS). At its core, by re-evaluating cross-linguistic data through this novel lens, the study offers a critique of established, purely morphosyntactic definitions—specifically Martin Haspelmath’s feature-based approach—arguing that such models often neglect pragmatic context and situational embedding. The paper posits that linguistic structures do not primarily follow an innate grammatical code; instead, they emerge as representations of universal situational dimensions: space, time, and quantity. The Principle of the Tendency towards Unity is introduced as a fundamental motive for human action and linguistic expression. It suggests that actors strive to preserve and expand their “essential units,” perceiving situations primarily as unities. Based on this theoretical framework, an alternative definition of SVCs is proposed. This definition emphasizes the absence of temporal gaps and the perception of a “single situation” alongside criteria such as the use of independent verbs and the lack of linking elements. From a sociological standpoint, SVCs are interpreted as highly efficient descriptions of frequent everyday situations grounded in shared background expectations and a “restricted code”. Finally, the cross-linguistic distribution of these constructions is explained through the concept of path dependence: once established, these efficient linguistic structures are maintained because switching to alternative codes would incur significant social and cognitive costs. The study concludes that a view of the formal situation provides new explanatory models for the universal development of grammar, suggesting that linguistic categories are a necessary consequence of the formal features of the situations they represent. The theoretical foundations of the formal situation are developed in Bauer (2026): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20623723. Originally submitted as a seminar paper for the course 'Clause linkage from a typological perspective' (WS 2023, Institute of Linguistics, University of Graz). This is an expanded English version.
abstracts.010053: Quantificational elements fall into different groups in German. Besides quantificational determiners, there are adjectival quantifiers and indeclinable quantifiers. I demonstrate that (non-numeral) indeclinable quantifiers cannot be preceded by determiners. Rather than proposing that these types of quantifiers (or parts of them) are in the DP-layer, I argue that these cases can be explained by Bayer's (2015) agreement chain. If so, this means that these quantifiers can appear below the DP-layer.
abstracts.010054: This paper proposes a morphological segmentation of the regular Spanish verbal paradigm that significantly simplifies its analysis. In the proposed model, the thematic vowel (TV) is always present in the underlying representation of all verbal forms of the three conjugations, either as stressed or as pre-accented. This analysis offers several advantages over more traditional approaches, such as those represented by recent grammars by the Royal Spanish Academy, since it allows the morphological structure of the three regular conjugations to be unified, including verbs whose root ends in a vowel, like those ending in -uir, with an /i/ following the root that has usually been analysed as an antihiatic epenthetic segment. The model also establishes that the thematic vowel of the first, second, and third conjugations is respectively /a/, /e/, and /i/ throughout the present stem and in forms historically derived from the infinitive. In the rest of the paradigm, the first conjugation maintains /a/, whereas the second and third display a common pattern with the alternation /i ~ je/, interpreted synchronically as allomorphy. Surface differences derive from general phonological principles of Spanish, in particular stress assignment and the productive process of stem-final vowel deletion. Tense-aspect-mood morphemes are also regularised.
abstracts.010055: Language change may be studied by tracking linguistic variant frequencies through space and time. Observed frequencies may be viewed as realisations of a statistical field. We first set out an efficient cross validated method for inferring the empirical field — the variant frequency distribution estimated directly from data — in our case, high resolution surveys from 20th century USA. We then derive a model of the statistical field, assuming that individuals diffuse locally, periodically migrate, and copy one another based on a form of replicator dynamics involving both bias and linguistic accommodation. We infer model parameters by comparing changes in model and empirical fields. Our inferences demonstrate that spatial linguistic patterns can be rapidly destroyed by migration but that accommodation can create them, protect them, and in combination with diffusion, produce partially predictable pattern dynamics. The results provide the strongest evidence yet for surface tension driven phase ordering in human dialects. We quantify the model’s forecasting ability up to a time horizon of twenty five years using the Kullback-Leibler divergence between forecasts and observations.
abstracts.010056: Logophoric pronouns of the kind found in West African languages have been extensively studied by typologist and formal linguists alike for more than five decades. However, there has been few attempts to connect this line of work with a formal approach to pronouns and the features they consist of, most notably Person (Silverstein, 1976; Zwicky, 1977; Noyer, 1992; Harbour, 2016). The overarching goal of this contribution is to fill this gap, and provide a formal account of logophoric pronouns grounded in a full-fledged theory of person features. Taking inspiration from Schlenker (2003), we propose that logophoric pronouns are non-indexical first persons, specified with a -ACTUAL feature. Our account is able to derive a wide range of distributional and interpretive constraints of logophors across languages, most notably i) their de se readings, ii) their agreement patterns, and iii) their distribution in embedded environments, while preserving a conservative, property-based account of features, which we argue are best conceived as binary (Harbour, 2011a, 2013). In addition, we provide arguments for a conception of alternatives in which structural complexity (in the sense of Katzir 2007) is assessed in the morphosyntax, at the level of features.
abstracts.010057: This paper is concerned with change-of-state uses of memory predicates like English remember. Change-of-state ‘remember’ appears to denote a change from not remembering to (stative) remembering – roughly ‘(slowly/suddenly) coming to remember’. It is, therefore, suitable to indicate constructive episodic memory retrieval. I argue that these uses are best captured as regular stative remembering, but with only partial – i.e. sub-atomically quantified – events as their object. I predict that remembering some, but not all, details of an event shows homogeneity effects arising from non-maximality. Speakers’ extra-linguistic projection of motion and change onto the third truth-value leads to the common eventive interpretation. No ontologically meaningful notion of change is required in the semantic composition or lexicon.
abstracts.010058: On the surface, English [Q+where] forms such as everywhere are locative. Yet as Sluckin & Kastner (forthcoming) document experimentally, they can also serve as impersonal human subjects, as in Everywhere in the UK loves Marmite, in which everywhere = everyone. The form retains its locative morphology and the pro-form where, yet it binds they/their and controls like a [+HUMAN] quantified indefinite pronoun. It must also be distinguished from ordinary locative (every place) and metonymic institutional readings. We argue that the impersonal use emerges from a distinct syntactic configuration in the nominal domain, rather than from lexical polysemy. Where spells out a higher locative D/P shell, while beneath it sits a silent, sortal, human-descriptive root √PERSON, selected by a relational categorising head n^CAT bearing [uPlace]. Relationality comes from the categoriser, not from the root (cf. Adger 2013). The [uPlace] feature forces an overt locative PP into Spec,nP^CAT, where it saturates the place argument of an inhabitant relation; n^EA then abstracts over the human variable, and the quantifier binds the resulting property. Because the root receives its zero exponent locally under this categoriser, rather than from the higher shell, its human content remains active though unpronounced. Institutional everywhere, by contrast, retains a √PLACE structure with contextual transfer. The obligatory locative PP follows from [uPlace], whereas the macro-geographic restriction is an interface condition rather than a syntactic feature.
abstracts.010059: This paper presents a compositional dynamic system (building on Muskens 1996; Stone 1999; Brasoveanu 2006; Farkas and Bruce 2010; AnderBois et al. 2015), in which question alternatives are introduced via the random assignment of propositional discourse referents. This system provides a framework for implementing a mechanism for presupposition projection that is sensitive to the question under discussion (QUD; Ginzburg 1996; Roberts 2012; Büring 2003, Farkas and Bruce 2010). The analysis addresses the triggering problem by treating presuppositions as entailments (Abrusán 2011) and derives projection for not-at-issue entailments, following work linking projection to at-issueness (e.g., Simons 2001; Simons et al. 2017; Tonhauser et al. 2018; Degen and Tonhauser 2025). Projection is derived by computing similarity to local context sets for over QUD-induced partitions of the context set, yielding a compositional account of QUD-sensitive projection.
abstracts.010060: Manuscripts under peer review are confidential materials, and as such, major publishers prohibit reviewers from uploading them to commercial generative AI systems. The current experiments tested whether the current AI systems consistently comply with this policy, and showed that this is not necessarily the case. In Experiment 1, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini rarely explained confidentiality when a first-time reviewer requested general help (2/30 trials). When the user explicitly asked whether a manuscript could be shared, ChatGPT accepted in 10/10 trials and Claude in 6/10, whereas Gemini consistently refused with a confidentiality warning. However, in Experiment 2, given a very similar prompt but with an attached manuscript, Gemini analyzed the attached file without warning in all 10 trials, suggesting the instability of its safeguard system. Further, Experiment 3a found that Gemini sometimes accepted sharing when prompted in Japanese. The result of this exploratory experiment motivated a confirmatory experiment (Experiment 3b), which directly compared English and Japanese. As predicted, Gemini accepted sharing more often in Japanese (27/30) than in English (1/30). Taken together, the current findings show that an apparently reliable confidentiality safeguard may fail when the request format or language changes, underscoring the need to test whether the AI's “ethical” responses generalize across conditions.
abstracts.010061: Unconditional questions such as “Whether or not the party is at Emma's place, will it be fun?” are often judged degraded, despite the acceptability of their declarative counterparts. This paper argues that their degradation is pragmatic rather than semantic. Building on inquisitive semantics and stack-based suppositional semantics, I develop a compositional account in which unconditional questions are interpreted relative to multiple hypothetical contexts corresponding to antecedent alternatives. I then propose two pragmatic constraints on their use. First, extending Theiler's (2021) Epistemic Bridge, I argue that every antecedent alternative must sustain an inquisitive issue with respect to the consequent question. Second, when the antecedent and consequent issues are independent, unconditional questions are semantically equivalent to ordinary questions. Their use therefore invites the inference that the antecedent issue is irrelevant to resolving the consequent question, a form of relational indifference in the sense of Rawlins (2008, 2013). The analysis explains why unconditional questions improve when the antecedent issue is salient but degrade when one antecedent alternative effectively settles the consequent issue. More generally, the results provide additional support for a suppositional approach to conditionals.
abstracts.010062: Bilingualism and second language learning always involve the interaction between two language systems or subsystems. When young children acquire language, often there is more than one. Considering the modern era, as the Vietnamese language has expanded geographically and culturally, coming into contact with other language communities, all of the different combinations of acquisition, learning and unlearning have come into play. These include, today, perhaps for the first time in recent history, language interactions that include first language attrition. This progress report of tentative results from our project compares the bilingual learning circumstances in two studies (in Taiwan and in northern Vietnam) where one language is in ascendence and the other may not be. The other language may be not developing at the same rate of progress or it may be undergoing replacement by the dominant language. In the larger project that encompasses the two studies, the Vietnamese language is part of the unfolding outcome of learning and attrition. On the other hand, it could become part of the process of potential recovery and stabilization of the minority language in some cases.
abstracts.010063: We report seven pairs of production and judgment experiments showing that English speakers are less likely to produce "that" when the relevant complementizer lies on the hierarchical path of an A-bar dependency, although "that" in such environments does not reliably lower acceptability. We argue that this production effect reflects optional wh–complementizer agreement, which is difficult to detect in acceptability judgments due to optionality and syncretism. We also find that the effect is sensitive to the distinction between terminal and non-terminal movement. Specifically, it is absent when the complementizer is the highest C in the second conjunct of across-the-board (ATB) extraction structures, a pattern that parallels movement reflexes observed in unrelated languages such as Kiitharaka. We argue that (a) English exhibits optional wh–complementizer agreement, realized only when the agreeing wh-element is in a non-terminal position; (b) ATB constructions involve asymmetric extraction from the first conjunct; (c) even completely silent A-bar dependencies play a causal role in sentence formulation during speaking; and (d) production data can provide crucial evidence for syntactic theory.
abstracts.010064: Abstract This article challenges the Saussurean arbitrariness principle by demonstrating that the Arabic linguistic sign is systematically motivated, and that the relationship between phonological form and meaning in Arabic is non-arbitrary at multiple simultaneous levels. Drawing on evidence from four interconnected domains, we advance a theoretical framework of phonosemantic iconicity in which articulatory properties of sounds iconically pre-figure semantic content. First, we demonstrate that the Arabic root-and-pattern verb form paradigm is diagrammatically iconic — the phonological operations of gemination, vowel extension, prefixation, and infixation enact the semantic operations they encode. Second, we show that the {m-}-prefix nominalization system is grounded in the universal articulatory iconicity of the bilabial nasal. Third, we examine a set of Arabic grammatical particles that show transparent formal and semantic correspondence with related lexical roots. Finally, we present a minimal pair analysis of /q/ ق and /ɣ/ غ as verb-initial consonants, demonstrating that contrastive phonetic gestures encode contrastive semantic matrices in a structured iconic opposition. Together, these four domains suggest that Arabic constitutes an unusually rich case of systematic iconic motivation in morphology and grammar, posing a significant challenge to strong interpretations of the Saussurean arbitrariness principle.
abstracts.010065: This work is a grammatical sketch of the Sampang language, an endangered language belonging to the Kiranti branch of the Trans‑Himalayan (Sino‑Tibetan) language family. It is the first published work to cover all aspects of grammar, including phonology, morphology, syntax and lexicon. Like many Kiranti languages, Sampang has extremely complex verbal morphology, displaying both subject and object agreement as well as intricate morphophonological alternations, and a substantial portion of the sketch is devoted to these issues. Other points of linguistic interest include the syntax of case and agreement, and the natureof linking morphs in the language. Some notes are made on the lexicon of the language, which displays thoroughgoing contact phenomena and an unusually rich array of motion verbs.
abstracts.010066: This paper investigates the semantics and pragmatics of root wh-infinitive questions (INFQs); that is, unembedded wh-questions featuring an infinitival verb. Building on prior work on non-finite wh-constructions (Kjellmer 1982, Duffley and Enns 1996, Bhatt 1999), we propose that the INFQs in (1) and (2) should be characterized as topic-setting questions, a term we borrow from Farkas (2025). Informally, a topic-setting question is a non-canonical speech act in which the Speaker assumes that no salient answer is currently available to resolve the issue raised by the question. The conversational function of uttering a topic-setting question is to prompt deliberation in order to arrive at a resolution. We argue that this is a conventionalized effect that arises from the marked status of INFQs relative to canonical finite wh-questions.
abstracts.010067: This paper seeks to provide an answer to why there is so much disagreement among authors and speakers regarding data instantiating the ACC-marked external possession construction (EPC) in Korean. Along the way, it also provides answers to when ACC-marked EP sentences in Korean are licensed, and why EP-encoding multiple accusative (MA) sentences and non-EP-encoding MA sentences have the same surface form even though the latter do not have a grammatical internal possession counterpart. By conducting a carefully-constructed grammaticality judgment task, I argue that (i) speakers have variable acceptability judgments for the EPC because of the pragmatically marked nature of the construction; (ii) a uniform analysis of the construction is not possible, but it can be classified into three subtypes depending on the semantics of the V and the Part-to-Whole Spread possibility in the sense of Dowty (2001); and (iii) in all grammatical cases, the possessor NP functions as what I call a Topic-Focus, and this explains why both EP-encoding and non-EP-encoding MA sentences have the same surface form (compare Sim 2004; Tomioka and Sim 2005, 2007; Yoon 2015; Kim 2023). This paper demonstrates that even though Korean is a discourse-oriented language (Sohn 1999), lexical semantics and the entailment relation that holds between VP meanings matter in structure building, in particular in V-raising contexts (compare, a.o., Cho 1992; Cho 1998, 2000). It also implicates that what appears to be an ACC marker in human language may encode not only a grammatical relation (i.e., Object) but also a discourse relation (e.g., Topic-Focus) and that NP raising is a semantically-pragmatically triggered phenomenon, as independently argued by Aissen and Polian (2024) and Law and Hirschberg (2025) for languages like Tseltalan and Mandarin Chinese.
abstracts.010068: The repetition ratio rule (RRR), based on the ratio r/R of geminate to total repeats, has been proposed as a discriminant between linguistic and non-linguistic symbol systems. We show that for short and moderate-length inscriptions the expected r/R (precisely, the ratio of expectations E[r]/E[R]) under a random control is 2/L, where L is the per-inscription token count. The threshold r/R = 0.10 therefore functions as a test of mean inscription length ≥ 20. We demonstrate that RRR misclassifies in both directions when length is matched: top-100 American and Finnish given names, exchange-traded commodity labels, and 10,749 deciphered Mesopotamian seal legends (r/R ∈ [0.13, 0.53]) are misclassified as non-linguistic; ISBN-13 lists, IPv4 addresses, cryptographic hashes, and character-level chess game records (r/R ∈ [0.0004, 0.10)) are misclassified as linguistic. We show that it fails as a discriminant because the premises implicit in its construction are unsound: it is biased against gemination, against particular encoding depths, and against short inscriptions. Varying length or encoding of random strings flips the result. We conclude that r/R does not discriminate language from non-language, and distill its failure modes into six requirements that any proposed discriminant must satisfy before its verdicts can be trusted.
abstracts.010069: In many languages with STAMP (Subject-Tense-Aspect-Mood-Polarity) morphology, subject pronouns and tense-aspect auxiliaries surface as apparent portmanteau morphemes whose forms can vary quite unpredictably across paradigm cells. These patterns have often been treated as suppletive, effectively derived from dedicated morphological operations. This paper examines STAMP forms in Kono (Central Mande, Sierra Leone) and argues that the observed paradigmatic variation does not reflect suppletion. Rather, pronouns and auxiliaries remain distinct morphosyntactic objects throughout the derivation, with surface variation arising from independently motivated phonological processes. The same phonological processes that derive pronominal STAMP forms also apply with full DP subjects and similarly extend to possessor constructions, with differences in surface realization tracking the distinct prosodic structures associated with each configuration. Intervening focus markers and case markers are shown to systematically disrupt these processes as predicted by changes in linear adjacency. The same sensitivity to adjacency and prosodic structure is also observed with pronominal objects, further demonstrating that these processes are not confined to the subject-auxiliary boundary. Since the Kono paradigm is not suppletive, the empirical precondition for needing post-syntactic morphological operations is not met. The Kono data thus bear on the division of labor between phonology and morphology in accounting for STAMP paradigmatic variation cross-linguistically.
abstracts.010070: This paper proposes a graph-theoretic interpretation of Merge inside the Workspace. The Workspace is represented as a directed graph, and syntactic objects are represented as Paths or subgraphs inside that graph. An application of Merge preserves the Paths already present and adds a new accessible Path. The new Path can then participate in later applications of Merge inside the same accumulated Workspace. The proposal is stated inside a seven-Layer architecture, with C-I and A-P as external systems and five internal Layers of the Language Faculty: Semantic Component (Σ), A-Syntax, A-bar Syntax, Distributed Morphology (DM), and Phonological Component (Φ). Each internal Layer applies an ordered grammar of Extension Rules through Expand, constructs a new output graph by Relinearization, and transfers that graph to the next Layer. The Layers are traversed in one order in *generation* and in the reverse order in *comprehension*, while the same general Expand procedure applies across the internal Layers.
abstracts.010071: There are two main types of -te aru configurations in Japanese: the intransitivizing and non-intransitivizing -te aru. For the intransitivizing -te aru, it is essential to further verify and clarify the (non-)existence of the agent and its syntactic nature. This article investigates the argument structure of the intransitivizing -te aru, aiming to determine whether there is a covert agent in the structure through subject-oriented adverbs. By comparing it with similar structures in Japanese, such as the passive structure, nominative object structure, and unaccusative verb structure, the generative mechanism of the intransitivizing -te aru can be confirmed. The results show that there is no null subject of any form in the intransitivizing -te aru. In addition, we find that the intransitivizing -te aru undergoes argument deletion of the original agent, differentiating it from a generally recognized transitive structure, and the nominative case can be assigned by little v carrying tense feature. Based on these findings, we can account for the absence of an agent and case assignment to the object in intransitivizing -te aru configurations.
abstracts.010072: There has been traditionally little communication and consensus between the field of language attrition, and variationist sociolinguists investigating dialect change, despite shared interest in the outcomes of language and dialect contact. In this paper, we aim to bridge this divide, outlining ways in which the fields already converge, and where they can inform each other to build a greater understanding of the mechanisms underlying changes to an adult’s otherwise established grammatical state. We do so by investigating two properties of Belfast English in the grammars of L1a Standard Southern British English speakers who have been living in Belfast for, on average, 25 years, having migrated from England after childhood. We find no use or acceptance of the Northern Subject Rule, but individual-level use and acceptance of embedded inverted questions. The study is framed by Hicks & Domínguez’s (2020) Attrition via Acquisition model. We outline how this model of grammatical attrition can be used to predict where and how morphosyntactic change as a result of dialect (or language) contact may occur, and show how greater specification of this model with relevant factors from sociolinguistics can account for the results of the study at hand, concluding there is more to be gained from these fields working together than remaining disparate.
abstracts.010073: This paper revisits the licensing of genitive subjects in Uyghur embedded clauses. Building on Asarina and Hartman’s (2011) D-licensing analysis, we argue that the simplified Miracle Creed system provides a more principled account of the relevant facts. We first show that the D-licensing approach is largely compatible with the MC architecture. Adopting the view that boxed elements created by Internal Merge are accessible to higher phase heads, we propose that phase-head access can be reduced to a target-conditioned application of Minimal Search. Under this approach, the licensing of genitive subjects, the optional omission of genitive morphology, scope asymmetries between genitive and unmarked subjects, and the contrast between modal and non-modal predicates receive a unified explanation. Furthermore, locality conditions such as the Phase Impenetrability Condition need not be stipulated independently. The Uyghur data thus provide empirical support for an interface-oriented interpretation of the MC system.
abstracts.010074: When a 98-year-old woman disappeared from Tokyo's welfare system in 2023, every institution followed proper procedures—yet coordination failed completely. Building on the concept of "Babel Syndrome" proposed by Matsuura (2018), which describes conflicts between specialized professions, this paper argues that such systemic failures originate in the structure of language itself. The function of language—to divide and label reality—has been **evolutionarily optimized for efficiency and** the cognitive style of the majority (NeuroTypical), producing invisible barriers between different kinds of minds and the institutions built upon them. At this deeper level, language becomes a hostile interface, excluding those who think or feel outside the majority mode. The paper proposes AI as a kind of meta-articulator—a mediator capable of translating between incompatible ways of thinking and communicating, turning fragmentation into a shared, navigable field. By designing polyphonic interfaces that sustain diversity through continuous translation, we can move beyond the curse of Babel—not by erasing difference, but by rendering it visible, negotiable, and humane. (Methodological Note: This paper employs a dual-layer structure. While the main text pursues narrative fluency to connect diverse disciplines, the footnotes function as a semantic backend, providing rigorous definitions and auxiliary theoretical lines.)
abstracts.010075: It is often claimed that Dependency Grammar (DG) is simpler than phrase structure grammars. Gibson (2026a) even made this claim quite explicitly in the title of his paper "Dependency syntax as the simplest theory of grammar". This answer to Gibson's paper shows that DGs appear simpler since many aspects of a formal theory are simply not provided. Many DGs come without a rule component. I discuss the rules the Gibson provides in a syntax textbook and show that they are formally not sound and that they mimic phrase structure-based systems in their intention. Treating semantics requires more structure either in terms of nodes or in terms of additional features. Any apparent advantage of DGs is lost, if the necessary machinery is added. Headless constructions like Jackendoff's NPN construction cannot be handled in DG without extensions. If projectivity is given up, as suggested by Gibson (2025), other means are needed to avoid overgeneration, again adding to complexity. Some notion of constituency is needed to ensure the necessary adjacency requirements. I discuss examples from German that suggest that V2 should be treated by some kind of „movement“ rather than by simple dependency relations. Gibson argues against transformations on the sense of original Transformational Grammar and I agree on this: from a psycholinguistic point of view they are unrealistic. But there are so-called representational variants of transformational theories and they do not have problems with explaining psycholinguistic facts. Gibson discusses complexity results from the 1970ies. I show why they are irrelevant and why complexity worst-case results on formalisms should be ignored anyway. Finally, I show why Gibson's Dependency Locality, which plays a role in the explanation of many psycholinguistic facts, is compatible with phrase structure-based theories like HPSG.
abstracts.010076: This thesis is concerned with Mandarin verb doubling and its implications for the syntactic theory. I propose a phrasal movement analysis of verb doubling, namely that the doubling configuration in question is derived from verbal phrasal movement out of an articulated verbal structure. After the overall introduction in chapter 1, chapter 2 lays out the core properties of the verbal phrasal movement involved in verb doubling, that is, the fronted verbal phrase can target two landing sites in the clausal spine. I argue that this two-landing-site analysis has both theoretical and empirical advantages over other hypothetical alternatives. Chapter 3 discusses the role of postverbal adverbials in verb doubling constructions. I argue that this group of elements in fact comprises two sub-groups (i.e., freely-adjoined adjuncts and selected arguments), and propose that the way they are introduced to verbal projections differs from one to the other. Chapter 4 puts forwards the idea that the fronted verbal phrases that engage in the formation of verb doubling can be larger than simple VPs. This proposal not only offers a direct account of distinct patterns that different ditransitive verb doubling configurations exhibit, but also makes correct predictions about the systematic distribution of multiple postverbal adverbials within verb doubling. Chapter 5 develops an analysis of realising verb doubling effects at PF, consisting of a series of operations that take place post-syntactically. I propose that various doubling effects, thus, can be attributed to different combinations of these PF operations. Chapter 6 examines the locality profile of verb doubling in bi-clausal contexts. I show that long-distance verb doubling behaves differently in three embedding contexts, and propose that the varying locality profiles of verb doubling can be properly accounted for by the Williams Cycle. Chapter 7 concludes the thesis.
abstracts.010077: This squib presents evidence from Frisian diminutive formation that laterals may pattern with plosives and nasals to the exclusion of fricatives.
abstracts.010078: This paper examines the semantics and morphosyntax of the Russian verb kazat’sja ‘seem’. Kazat’sja and vygljadet’‘look’ are raising verbs that promote their Stimulus argument and raise an embedded constituent to the matrix clause. I argue that kazat’sja is a hybrid predicate combining properties of putative and perceptual verbs, and discuss Apresjan’s proposal to distinguish two lexemes: putative kazat’sja¹ versus perceptual kazat’sja². Kazat’sja² is an obligatory raising verb, whereas with kazat’sja¹ raising is optional. Both kazat’sja¹ and kazat’sja² project three thematic roles: sentential Stimulus, dative Experiencer; and Observer, which may remain covert. The analysis is based on the distribution of adjectives marked by the instrumental case versus non-agreeing predicatives in structures such as X-u kažetsja strannym / stranno + [Stimulus].
abstracts.010079: This paper analyzes -ki nominalizations in Korean. We identify two types of the -ki nominalizations,NOM-ki and GEN-ki, with distinct morphosyntactic properties. We propose an analysis along the lines of Kratzer (1996) in which the nominalizer -ki selects verbal projections of different sizes (TP and vP) to account for the observed patterns. We argue against previous accounts of -ki nominalizations, showing either that important generalizations were missed or that there were flaws in the previous analyses. We propose a novel generalization for the two types of -ki nominalizations and propose an appropriate analysis. Some outstanding issues and implications are briefly discussed.
abstracts.010080: A form's frequency may move after a shock (contact with another language, a new medium, a redrawn border, or a government decree), and whether the shock caused the change is a natural question. Difference-in-differences is built for that counterfactual, with the discipline applied economics already brings to constructed aggregates like price indices, where the observed number isn't the quantity of interest either. This paper carries that discipline to corpus frequencies, where it's rarely applied and where composition and coding make it bite harder. A corpus frequency is a population rate plus a composition-and-measurement term, so a causal reading requires separating several things a corpus merges: the target population, the corpus composition, the measurement procedure, and the units at which treatment varies and uncertainty is counted. Identifying a change in the rate then needs parallel trends twice over, in the rate and the corpus filter, and the diagnostics can only disqualify or bound the claim, never confirm it. A pre-specified decision ladder routes each result to a bounded estimate, a descriptive reading, a shared wave, or not identified. A worked example, the feminization of profession nouns under francophone language policy, runs throughout as a stress test, not an empirical finding.
abstracts.010081: A grammaticality judgment is always a human act, but it isn't always participant data. Whether the person who supplies one is a participant or an evaluator should turn on what the judgment is evidence of: a person (reactions, processing, or dialect) or an object (an item's status under a stated standard). The role isn't only an ethical classification; it also fixes the generalization a judgment licenses, over speakers or items. In the object case, the judge resembles an essay scorer or prescriptive annotator more than a survey respondent, and systematic, reliability-checked procedures mark measurement rather than a study of the judges. Canada's Tri-Council Policy Statement (TCPS 2) reaches the distinction by focus of inquiry; the United States Common Rule states it through its "about whom" definition. The proposal routes ethics review rather than loosening it: it neither licenses private intuition nor erases the cases where judges are participants.
abstracts.010082: This paper focuses on the special properties of ganz ‘whole’ and halb ‘half’ in German. It is observed that they do not have an inflection in the singular when a determiner is absent. Discussing other properties, it is documented that the nominals involving these quantifiers are situated between regular syntactic constructions and regular morphological formations. Given that the head noun must involve a proper name, it is proposed that the proper name incorporates into the quantifier as an instance of N-raising. At the end of the paper, some other exceptional quantifiers are briefly discussed.
abstracts.010083: The standard comparative method in historical linguistics relies on written evidence to establish relatedness. In reconstructed proto-languages, where such evidence is unavailable, claims of internal connections are often considered unprovable. This paper introduces a probabilistic method for assessing whether phonemic similarity between two forms in a closed system is likely to be coincidental. Applying the method to Proto-Indo-European, we show that the three-phoneme root h₁és-, shared by the copula and the third-person pronoun paradigm, has a probability of coincidental identity of approximately 1 in 27,000 under uniform assumptions, and roughly 1 in 13,000 under frequency-adjusted estimates. This result holds across major competing reconstructions of PIE. Pronouns and copulas, as core grammatical elements, are among the least borrowable items cross-linguistically, supporting the closed-system assumption required by the calculation. Evidence from six daughter branches—Sanskrit, Greek, Avestan, Latin, Hittite, and Old Irish—confirms the persistence of the h₁és- root in both paradigms, with the full form appearing where an ending follows and the reduced h₁e- in the bare nominative due to regular final -s loss. Hittite provides direct attestation of the laryngeal. The pattern is further reinforced by independent two-be systems (e.g., Old Irish and Spanish), which consistently assign the h₁és- reflex to the equational/identificational function. A parallel pronoun-copula root identity in Biblical Hebrew (Katz 1996) suggests this alignment reflects a recurring cognitive association rather than a PIE-specific accident. The methodological contribution—probabilistic synchronic analysis as a tool for internal reconstruction in closed systems—extends beyond PIE to other proto-languages with reliable phonemic inventories and core vocabulary.
abstracts.010084: Children acquiring a diverse range of unrelated language go through a stage, typically between the ages of 2 and 3, where they use bare, infinitival or default forms instead of the agreeing forms required in adult grammar. Whether such under agreement errors reflect non-adult syntax for agreement or incomplete morphological knowledge has been a topic of debate for decades (Brown 1973, Radford 1990, Rizzi 1994, Wexler, 1998, a.o.). These errors are interesting developmentally, since children otherwise make few grammatical errors, and theoretically, given the central role of agreement in understanding the combinatorial mechanisms of natural language. In this paper, we approach this classic developmental problem from a new angle, by examining the acquisition of ‘non-canonical’ agreement constructions, where a non-standard element occupies the subject position, and agreement is with a post-verbal nominal. Such constructions are generally thought to be syntactically more complex than canonical sentences, in that they involve at least two dependencies — one that is responsible for subject movement, and a second that is responsible for the verbal morphology. In these environments, we find a striking reemergence of agreement problems, now in a population who otherwise command the relevant morphology and use it in adult-like ways in canonical contexts. Two elicited repetition studies found that children (ages 3;0–5;11) routinely produced singular agreement with plural associates in non-canonical constructions. We take this over-production of singular to reflect a ‘late’ under-agreement stage, where children default to singular morphology as a result of failing to agree. Indirectly, these results support syntactic explanations of toddlers’ under-agreement and illustrate how the protracted acquisition of agreement tracks syntactic complexity.
abstracts.010085: This chapter examines the reality of conceptual and formal distinctions between the semantic categories of modality and (grammatical) aspect, focusing on three broad classes of phenomena in which these categories appear tightly intertwined. I first explore the case for eroding a formal distinction by examining arguments for incorporating modality in the semantic contribution of aspectual operators: I discuss modal solutions to the well-known imperfective (progressive) paradox, as well as apparently modal meaning associated with the core interpretation of (non-culminating) perfectives, perfects, and prospectives. Second, I discuss two phenomena in which modal interpretation appears to either be conditioned by or to select for specific grammatical aspects, examining research into the role of aspectual marking in the expression of counterfactual modality, as well as in habituality and/or genericity. Finally, I touch on two intriguing semantic interactions between (ostensibly) aspectual and modal operators, providing overviews of the phenomenon of actuality entailments and of frustrative marking in several understudied languages. The emergent picture is one in which a sharp distinction between (temporal) aspectual meaning and (possible worlds) modality is largely notional—albeit conceptually valuable—and does not appear to be reflected in sharp formal divisions between exponents of these two semantic categories.
abstracts.010086: In Optimality Theory (Prince & Smolensky 1993), phonological constraints are evaluated with respect to a domain corresponding to the usual notion of grammatical word. I argue here that some common phonological patterns are better analysed by relaxing this restriction. In particular, while a notion of 'phonological' or 'prosodic' word has previously been shown to provide the relevant domain for phonological processes, I argue that productive morphemes can also provide such a domain. The hypothesis is tested with respect to data from Australian and other languages. I show that a model allowing for both intra-and inter-word domains of evaluation provides a more unified analysis of cross-linguistic phenomena such as syllabification and stress.(Originally published 2004, this is an updated and corrected version.)
abstracts.010088: This article challenges the widespread idea that case affixes generally evolve from adpositions through increasing “bondedness.” Instead, I propose that word order, not only increasing tightness of attachment, is another primary factor determining whether a marker becomes an affix or remains a clitic. Using a simple and clear definition of clitic, the paper notes that flags are affixes (case markers) when there is no adnominal modifier occurring between them and the noun, but adpositions otherwise. In view of this, it may be that we need to revise our thinking about grammaticalization, because what all grammaticalization changes share is the development of bound markers from free contentful forms, not necessarily notions like coalescence, fusion or bondedness.
abstracts.010089: In Italian, motion verbs (MVs) may combine with the reflexive clitic SI and the clitic NE, yielding what I call pronominal motion verbs (PMVs). Since PMVs freely alternate with their non-pronominal counterparts, the semantic and syntactic contribution of these clitics remains poorly understood. I argue that SI is a syntactic argument merged in the specifier of a high applicative head, which introduces a direct experiencer Theta-role, whereas NE is associated with a low applicative head with locative semantics. Building on and extending Martin & Arunachalam's (2022) analysis of other Romance pronominal verbs, this study develops an analysis of PMVs that accounts for the Italian data. More broadly, it contributes to our understanding of many syntactic issues: the morpheme SI, the argument structure of motion events, and the complementation patterns of semilexical verbs (MV andare vs. PMV andar-se-ne `go').
abstracts.010090: This paper presents evidence of language contact at the level of the idiolect by applying Ronald Langacker’s Cognitive Grammar framework to bilingual pedagogical discourse. Analyzing seven classroom lectures from a multilingual Indian instructor, the study examines non-standard compromise forms, focusing on integration of construction schemas through extension relations at the level of the individual structured inventory. Rather than demonstrating a shift between bounded linguistic systems as separate mental spaces, the data reveals a fluid, integrated structured inventory where constructions are selected based on cognitive economy and conceptual negotiation. The results show that non-standard structures emerge from the convergence through extensions of entrenched structures across languages, serving to reduce processing cost during spontaneous conceptual negotiations.
abstracts.010091: This research investigates differential object marking in the Zamboanga dialect of Chavacano (ZChav), a Spanish-based Creole spoken in Zamboanga region in the south of the Philippines. Using various diagnostics, we show that differential object marking in ZChav correlates with epistemic specificity and discourse-linkedness. We ultimately tie both of these phenomena to the notion of the Common Ground and propose that it underlies the distribution of the differential object marker. We further make some notes on the interaction between differential object marking and word order in ZChav. ZChav is a VSO language; however, with non-specific objects the word order VOS is found. For VSO order, we propose that the object raises out of the VP and that the remnant VP raises to SpecTP. For VOS order, we propose that the non-specific object remains inside the VP and that the VP (V+O) raises to SpecTP.
abstracts.010092: The chapter examines the internal organisation of the functional domain between TP and CP from a cartographic perspective. The chapter treats the rigid ordering of clitics as evidence for which morphosyntactic features are projected there and in what order, bringing clitics into the cartographic investigation of this domain. Drawing on cross- linguistic generalisations from more than thirty languages and varieties, it develops its argument progressively, moving from relatively simple clitic systems to more complex ones. In doing so, it offers a more precise reconstruction of the universal functional sequence between TP and CP and establishes a robust baseline for future research on clitic ordering and the derivation of clitic clusters.
abstracts.010093: This paper investigates the role of contrastivity in Left Branch Extraction (LBE) under ellipsis, presenting experimental evidence from German to support an in-situ approach to clausal ellipsis. While prior research suggests that ellipsis can mitigate island violations, particularly in non-contrastive contexts (Merchant, 2001, 2004), recent proposals argue that ellipsis sites may be syntactically anisomorphic to their antecedents, allowing for alternative derivations that circumvent island constraints (Barros, 2014; Griffiths, 2019). However, these claims largely rely on informally collected acceptability judgments, leaving their empirical robustness in question. To address this gap, controlled acceptability judgment experiments are conducted to test whether contrastivity modulates the acceptability of remnants extracted out of islands. The findings consistently show that contrastively focused remnants force an isomorphic interpretation, leading to significant degradation when the extraction of the remnant violates syntactic constraints. In contrast, anisomorphic readings can be available as a last-resort strategy to avoid island violations. Moreover, a clear difference in acceptability is observed between wh-remnants and non-wh remnants, indicating that the remnant’s ability to move determines its island sensitivity. These results underscore the necessity of an in-situ approach to clausal ellipsis and provide evidence against a general island repair effect in LBE contexts. This paper argues that (i) ellipsis can occur ‘around’ a designated constituent, (ii) syntactic islands are not repaired by ellipsis, (iii) the ellipsis site need not be syntactically isomorphic to its antecedent if independent conditions are met, (iv) remnants A′-move in elliptical configurations only if they would A′-move if ellipsis had not applied, and (v) contrastive focus on the remnant forces an isomorphic interpretation of the elliptical clause’s syntax, without enforcing any restrictions on presentational focus.
abstracts.010094: We present a novel reading of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) based on two established facts of historical linguistics: (1) the Phoenician letters He and Waw are the direct ancestors of Greek Epsilon (E) and Upsilon/V, respectively; and (2) the initial Yod in YHWH functions as a third-person masculine verbal prefix (y-), not as part of the semantic root. Removing the grammatical prefix yields the triconsonantal root H-W-H (to become). Through documented Phoenician-to-Greek-to-Latin letter descent, H-W-H maps to E-V-E. We demonstrate that the second He admits an ambiguity: iteration (Masoretic reading, producing imperfective loop H-H) or termination (producing aorist reading). Under termination, He maps to Zayin (7th Semitic letter), Latin descendant Z. Complete reading: E-V-E-Z. Six falsifiable claims, three independent lines of evidence (letter descent, root morphology, positional alternation in Semitic grammar), 14 scholarly references.
abstracts.010095: We present a novel reading of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) based on two established facts of historical linguistics: (1) the Phoenician letters He and Waw are the direct ancestors of Greek Epsilon (E) and Upsilon/V, respectively; and (2) the initial Yod in YHWH functions as a third-person masculine verbal prefix (y-), not as part of the semantic root. Removing the grammatical prefix yields the triconsonantal root H-W-H (to become). Through documented Phoenician-to-Greek-to-Latin letter descent, H-W-H maps to E-V-E. We demonstrate that the second He admits an ambiguity: iteration (Masoretic reading, producing imperfective loop H-H) or termination (producing aorist reading). Under termination, He maps to Zayin (7th Semitic letter), Latin descendant Z. Complete reading: E-V-E-Z. Six falsifiable claims, three independent lines of evidence (letter descent, root morphology, positional alternation in Semitic grammar), 14 scholarly references.
abstracts.010096: This paper introduces a learning model to address the computational challenges arising from including highly abstract underlying representations (URs) in morphophonemic learning. The proposed learner structures the UR hypothesis space by disparity distance and considers potential URs in batches, beginning with fully concrete URs, only expanding the UR candidate space if the current set of UR candidates fails to meet a predetermined likelihood threshold. When expanding the UR candidate set, the learner uses markedness constraint weights and violation profiles to identify features that are potentially mis-specified underlyingly, limiting the generation of new URs to changes of those feature values. Overall, the learner inherently restricts abstraction to cases where introducing it demonstrably improves likelihood, while avoiding issues associated with the exhaustive search of an unbounded hypothesis space. Applied to a Pakistani Punjabi vowel nasality pattern, the model is shown to successfully acquire abstract URs for phonological patterns that parallel learners fail to capture.
abstracts.010097: It is well-known that constructions called “passive” cross-linguistically do not form a homogeneous class. In this paper we argue that some “passives” are not verbal or adjectival but involve a PP predicate instead. The empirical basis of our investigation is the so-called “passive” construction in Udmurt (Uralic).
abstracts.010098: Dependence utterances can be built with an adverbial adjunct phrase, e.g. "Depending on how the first round goes, I might stop". They express a complex conditional dependence between two sets of alternatives. Contrary to finite "depend", adjunct dependence utterances (ADUs) exhibit diverse syntactic forms and pragmatic purposes that challenge previous approaches. We show how Dynamic Inquisitive Semantics and Free Association with focus solve the compositional issues in English and French. Different dependence types (speech-act level, clause level, and predicate level) are explained by different adjunct attachment sites, with a single uniform entry for "depend" that captures the various alternative triggers.
abstracts.010099: Some research questions require large-scale acceptability judgment datasets to answer them. Constructing such datasets can be challenging when the researcher has limited familiarity with the language. We investigate how to optimally design acceptability judgment collection protocols in such contexts. Taking clause embedding in Zulu as a case study, we collect acceptability judgments using protocols that manipulate a combination of setting, modality, prior exposure, and question format and measure how much data collected using these different protocols converges in the acceptability it implies. We find that unguided surveys can recover the same acceptabilities as elicitation, but need roughly three times as much data—up to about ten times at the highest precision—to match it. We attribute this cost to protocol-induced variability: elicitation, and group elicitation in particular, buys the most acceptability per judgment.
abstracts.010100: This preprint of the chapter (included in the monograph Czech Clitics: New Insights and Perspectives) examines the phonological aspects of cliticisation, focusing on how phonological and syntactic locality influence the phonological integration of second-position object clitics with a preceding host. Integration is assessed through processes affecting voicing at the object–clitic boundary, namely final obstruent devoicing and pre-sonorant voicing. These external sandhi processes are investigated using reading tasks with Czech speakers, whose readings were recorded and analysed in Praat. The experimental results reveal a statistically significant difference between verbal and adverbial hosts, which we attribute to the fact that only the former establish a local configuration with object clitics.
abstracts.010101: Thomasson’s (2025) Rethinking Metaphysics brings a grammatical debate into metaphysics. Thomasson uses systemic functional linguistics to explain why noun-term recastings such as the property of redness are useful without behaving like observational object talk. This paper accepts the discourse-role insight but detaches it from Halliday’s grammatical architecture. SFL explains why the recast formulations are worth having; easy ontology licenses the inferences. For linguists, the lesson is broader than syntax: some inferences and expectations follow from linguistic description, but not every expectation imported from familiar models of reference, objecthood, or category.
abstracts.010102: We investigate the interpretation of plural expressions, starting from the puzzle of the logical gap between their interpretations in affirmative and negative sentences. While bare plurals (e.g. “books”) typically receive an at least two reading in upward-entailing environments (e.g. “The box contains books”), they yield an at least one reading in downward-entailing contexts (e.g. “The box doesn't contain books”). Existing bivalent and trivalent theoretical approaches differ in their predictions about truth conditions of plural indefinites under the scope of a universal quantifier (e.g. “Every box contains books”) in mixed scenarios (some boxes contain one book, others contain several). Through experimental studies in English, we uncover gradient truth-value judgments in such mixed scenarios, which challenge the categorical predictions of all available theories. Our results raise key questions about the empirical identification of accessible readings and we put forward a methodology to disentangle readings from gradient effects.
abstracts.010103: Formation of lexical categories in the syntactic workspace has been a part of generative investigation since last few decades. This dissertation investigates the syntactic formation of lexical categories like nouns, verbs, and adjectives in Santali, an understudied Austroasiatic Language spoken in India. The central concern of the current research is the extent to which Syntax affects the internal structure of words/categories. This study employs Distributed Morphology as the theoretical framework to analyze the formation of nouns, verbs and adjectives in Santali because it provides an ideal empirical domain due to its fluid categorial system. This dissertation addresses three specific questions, each forming the focus of a dedicated chapter. The first question examines the structural position of Santali nominalization. It specifically asks how morphologically zero nominals, traditionally analyzed as root-derived in the literature, can exhibit complex internal structure by showing stem-derivation. By using diagnostics like the presence of argument structure, adverbial modification, aspectual modification, and productivity, this dissertation shows that Santali zero nominals possess verbal characteristics and lack root-level idiosyncrasies. By using these tests, the dissertation also presents that Santali zero nominals are formed at higher derivational points, like vP, VoiceP, and AspectP levels. Connecting it to the nouniness squish (Ross, 1973), this dissertation shows that Santali nominalization happens at different structural heights: prototypical and affixal nominals are root-derived, while zero nominals, despite being morphologically simplex, exhibit syntactic complexity and access extended verbal functional structures. The second research question addresses how verbalization, widely claimed to be an idiosyncratic operation cross-linguistically, demonstrates systematic syntactic compositionality yielding productive change-of-state semantics in Santali. Santali exhibits both root-derived verbs and stem-derived verbs formed from already categorized nouns or adjectives. In the case of stem-derivation, Santali verbalizes any categorial or phrasal stem productively by assigning a change-of-state meaning. This dissertation proposes a feature-based account to analyze this phenomenon where the verbalizer carries a [FIENT] feature that encodes the transition event assigning the change-of-state interpretation to its complement and yielding inchoative and causative interpretation. The third question addresses the internal structure of adjectives, a category whose presence has been reported to be uncertain in the typological literature. Using specific diagnostics the dissertation first establishes that Santali possesses adjectives as a composite category formed through adjectivization of both roots and stems. Root-derived adjectives are idiosyncratic, lack overt morphological adjectivizers, and are formed low in the derivation. Stem-derived adjectives, in contrast, are regular and compositional, marked by the overt adjectivizer -ih(aa). This chapter also demonstrates the structural asymmetry in the stem-derived adjectivization by showing how Santali adjectivizers can merge with extended functional projections like NumP and DP in the nominals domain, while it is restricted to the vP-level in the verbal domain. This asymmetry shows how categorization is input sensitive and the selectional restriction of categorizers to merge at different structural points may depend on input categories. The findings of this dissertation unveils several theoretical implications. Firstly, morphologically simplex units can also carry derivational complexity as categories can contain complex internal structures to be formed at various derivational heights. Secondly, regular semantics on productive categorization can be a result of the feature present on the categorizer head. Thirdly, categorization is also input sensitive selecting different structural heights as the complement depending on the input category, as we learn from Santali adjectivization. This also means that even when the categorization system of a language shows extreme fluidity, it maintains certain constraints in the derivational operation. Since words are uniformly formed using the merge of specific categorizers, merge can be taken as the single fundamental operation sufficient for category formation in syntax cross-linguistically.
abstracts.010104: Reiss (2026) gives Universal Grammar two roles. In its modest role, UG is a background commitment of Chomskyan I-language inquiry: anyone modelling individual internal grammars with universal primitives is committed, explicitly or implicitly, to such a postulate. In its stronger role, UG is the condition under which data from French, Japanese, or Icelandic can bear on English, so that anyone who denies UG lacks grounds for importing analytic categories across languages. I grant the local stipulation for Chomskyan inquiry, but I deny that inquiry into individual internal grammatical knowledge as such requires UG. I accept the evidential burden but reject the exclusivity. Evidence travels by bridge principles, scoped warrants that specify a projection target, the profile connecting observed and projected features, the diagnostics that locate it, and the defeaters that limit its scope. The test separates three questions the chapter runs together: whether human languages form an inquiry domain, when evidence can travel between them, and whether UG is the only licence for that travel. Some warrants may be Chomskyan; others are causal-historical, phonetic-perceptual, typological, cultural-transmission, or institutional. Applied to Reiss’s French-English any case, the French contrast is only a cue until English-internal diagnostics and a support profile are supplied. Historical-comparative reconstruction supplies a worked counterexample to the unscoped claim: common descent and regular correspondence license bounded vertical evidential transfer without UG as the transfer warrant. The same discipline makes public standards, corpus profiles, typological comparanda, and norm-governed varieties legitimate targets when their projections are declared. UG may license some I-language inferences; it doesn’t own the need for warrant.
abstracts.010105: This paper takes up a hitherto unnoted phenomenon in Korean in which the distal demonstrative (DEM) “ku” occurs modifying an adjective phrase (AP), seemingly violating the well-established weight-based adjective ordering restriction (AOR), namely, ‘heavy N modifier > light N modifier > N’. I show that such occurrence of “ku”, which I call KU, is not a run-of-the-mill DEM, and I explain its behavior by calling it ‘a cognitive indexical DEM’. The upshot of the analysis will be that KU selects for an AP and locates the property denoted by its complement in the mental domain of the speaker, pointing to it as if it were visible to the speaker, contributing a speaker comment. To implement this idea within a formal syntactic framework, I propose a tripartite Split-DP analysis which builds on Laenzlinger’s (2005) analysis of French AOR. By doing so, I offer a Rizzian (Rizzi 1997) cartographic analysis which captures the relative surface ordering between N dependents in Korean without violating the universal AOR mentioned above. The proposed analysis will be shown to capture the syntactic, semantic, and phonological properties of KU in comparison with the more “ordinary” DEM “ku”. It also has implications for the syntax, semantics, and pragmatics of DEMs in other languages including Slovenian and English. [Published in 2016; updated in 2026 with some typos fixed. See also Ch. 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Kim 2019 “The Syntax and Semantics of Noun Modifiers and the Theory of Universal Grammar: A Korean Perspective”.]
abstracts.010106: This paper uses low sluicing in Turkish as a diagnostic for the timing of ellipsis licensing and structural case assignment. In low sluicing, wh-remnants bear case, auxiliary and tense morphology, but structural cases such as accusative and genitive fail to survive the ellipsis, even though they are present on the correlate in the antecedent clause. I argue that this disconnectivity cannot be reduced to a copular clause source: low sluicing allows multiple wh-remnants and adjunct remnants, and it is island-sensitive. Instead, I propose that low sluicing has a full clausal source, but that the ellipsis-licensing head renders its complement inaccessible for later case computation. Under a dependent case approach, this prevents wh-remnants from entering the configurational relations required for accusative or genitive case assignment, causing them to surface with unmarked nominative case. The analysis shows that ellipsis licensing can affect syntactic computation and provides new evidence for a configurational theory of structural case.
abstracts.010107: A substance-free logical analysis is given concerning the mid vowel alternation in Menominee, one of the frequently mentioned cases in the studies of vowel harmony. The analysis consists of only rules, which are composed of Search (identification) and Change (modification). Three ordered rules, each of which is more general than the previous one, are proposed to deal with the phenomenon that the pertinent segments i, u, and æ are not a natural class in the given language (due to the existence of a). Should this proposal be valid, it testifies the capacity of Search and Change. Moreover, it is worthwhile to test the method portrayed with other language phenomena whose condition is similar to that of Menominee.
abstracts.010108: In response to Futrell & Mahowald’s (2025) paper on the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) in linguistics, Sripada et al. (2026) strikingly argue that LLMs “illuminate” the mechanisms underlying what Chomsky calls the creative aspect of language use (CALU). Such illumination promises, they argue, to bring this once-intractable problem under the heel of scientific inquiry by advancing our understanding of the mechanisms by which individuals select situation-appropriate expressions from an unbounded class of expressions. Sripada et al. draw attention to an important, foundational issue in generative linguistics, but their paper mischaracterizes CALU. The mischaracterization turns principally on the notion of stimulus-independence and how this relates to the capacity for unbounded linguistic production. These comments seek to correct this mischaracterization by showing that the problem of CALU is deeper and more distinctive than they let on. Likewise, misunderstandings of Chomsky’s invocation of CALU are clarified.
abstracts.010109: This document consists of the first five chapters of a projected textbook for Maximum Entropy Optimality Theory, a.k.a. “MaxEnt”. The text is directed to beginners (i.e. to linguists who are new to MaxEnt) and is meant as a “how-to” book, more pedagogical than polemical. The book is rooted in our view that there are many linguists who are in possession of gradient data (e.g. from observations of free variation, corpora, or experiments) and wish to develop a rigorous generative analysis of their findings — but lack an appropriate formal framework for doing so. We feel that MaxEnt is a very useful such framework, and hope to make it more accessible to researchers by making it easy to learn, and by offering practical advice based on our own research experience. We show how MaxEnt can be done effectively using Excel spreadsheets, and offer example analyses along with spreadsheet implementations. Chapter contents: Chapter 1: Purpose and orientation Chapter 2: The analysis of variation in outputs Case study: Lenition in Khalkha Mongolian Chapter 3: Using MaxEnt to study lexical frequency-matching Case study: Nasal substitution in Tagalog Chapter 4: The MaxEnt math Chapter 5: Research technique Statistical analysis, building a grammar, finding data1 Future chapters: (6) phonotactics, (7) learning, (8) fields other than phonology, (9) discussion of MaxEnt as a theory. We would be grateful for feedback, including suggestions for citation (bhayes@humnet.ucla.edu, moore.cantwell@ucla.edu).
abstracts.010110: Our textbook extract, "Guide to Analysis in MaxEnt Optimality Theory, Chapters 1 and 2," just posted on LingBuzz, makes use of Excel spreadsheets to teach and implement MaxEnt analyses. This zip file includes the spreadsheets.
abstracts.010111: Second language learners often acquire substantial vocabulary and a working knowledge of grammatical rules without achieving fluent spoken production. This gap has motivated research on how patterned units shape language use. Construction grammar, the lexical approach, and formulaic-language research all emphasize the role of patterned units in fluent production, but they do not, taken together, provide a unified pedagogical method organized around such units. This paper develops the pedagogical application of Frames for second language instruction. Frames treats the frame family, a cluster of patterned expressions sharing a communicative function, as the primary unit of instruction and uses massed, varied exposure as its main mode of delivery. A frame is defined operationally as a scaffold with one or more variable slots; a slot is a position where the filler may vary without changing the frame's communicative function. Frame families are organized by functional role rather than grammatical category. The central prediction is that focused exposure to a frame family enables learners to produce fluent variants of that family with novel fillers drawn from vocabulary they already know. The broader theoretical status of frames as units of linguistic representation is not adjudicated here; the present article argues only that frame families can be operationalized as pedagogical units and that their instructional value should be tested through learner outcomes.
abstracts.010112: This paper proposes an event-scaled model of second language fluency assessment. It does not attempt to redefine fluency. It adopts the companion account of fluency as communicative integration: the preservation and carry-forward of event-state across linked communicative frames despite local incoherence. The present paper asks how that construct can be operationalized in second language testing. The proposed model distinguishes three scales of assessment: immediate frame functionality, local inter-frame coherence, and global event-state coherence. Immediate frame functionality tests whether the learner can perform a necessary communicative function in a single frame or bounded response. Local inter-frame coherence tests whether the learner can carry event-state into the directly adjacent explanatory or action frame. Global event-state coherence tests whether the learner can preserve event-state across a non-adjacent sequence where later meaning depends on earlier information. The paper argues that assessment should not be built from activities or topics such as shopping, school, hobbies, money, or transportation. Those are testing contexts. The assessed units are communicative functions: locating [person/place/object], going to [place], needing [object/help/action], wanting [object/state/action], asking for [information/action/permission], understanding [quantity/time/sequence], refusing [offer/request/action], explaining [reason/cause/result], and repairing [misunderstanding/error]. The paper positions this model against existing fluency measures, then identifies Wang Anshi’s 王安石 jingyi 經義 reform as the deeper source of the competence model. Wang developed jingyi because competency testing was systematically failing to produce competent graduates: the examination system rewarded local polish, formal display, and performative competence while failing to distinguish rencai 人才 from bucai 不才. The present paper adapts jingyi to modern language testing for the same reason and toward the same goal. Event-scaled fluency assessment is a modern communicative extension of jingyi: a test of whether learners possess true domain competence, shown by the preservation and synthesis of meaning across discontinuity, rather than merely local fluency
abstracts.010113: Standard accounts of fluency face a classification problem. If fluency is defined by speech rate, pausing, repair behavior, automaticity, vocabulary coverage, native-like production, domain knowledge, or interactional ease, a native-speaking child who preserves a story-state despite missed words may be classified as less fluent than an adult second-language listener who recognizes more words but loses the event relation. This paper argues that such measures are local proxies, not the phenomenon itself. Fluency is communicative integration: the preservation of global event-coherence despite local incoherence. Coherence means the minimum event-state required for the next communicative frame to attach. The ordinary case is decisive: the same verbal form, What's up?, can function as a friendly greeting when said casually to a friend, a genuine request for information when said in response to visible concern, or an aggressive confrontation when said with hostile posture and tone. The words remain constant; only the surrounding frame cluster changes, and with it the communicative event. Across child comprehension, adult L2 listening, technical explanation, scripted production, nonverbal uptake, and damaged signal, fluency is shown by whether event-state survives and can be carried forward.
abstracts.010114: Second language transfer is often described as the carryover of L1 grammar, but persistent idiom transfer, fossilization, and striking asymmetries between learner populations suggest that the transferred unit is neither a rule nor a word. This paper extends Frame Class theory to cross-linguistic acquisition by treating frames—event-anchored sentence patterns with fixed material, variable slots, and membership in frame classes—as the units speakers carry across languages.
