In the domain of semantics, such universals are often explained by appeal to general information-theoretic and cognitive facts, from efficient communication to ease of learning. This paper expands the range of the ease of learning explanation through a case study of monotone quantifiers. While most existing studies compare expressions which either do or do not satisfy a given universal property, we here define a metric for measuring monotonicity in degrees. A computational experiment shows that this degree correlates well with ease of learning, providing a finer-grained explanation in the ease of learning tradition.
abstracts.010183: This study examines the association between invitation message tone and student participation in digitally mediated learning environments. Using a field-based quasi-experimental design, 40 students in the Philippines were assigned through an alternating allocation procedure to receive either a formal, context-rich invitation or a brief informal message directing them to the same online task. Participation was measured through link activation, task completion, and response timing using automated digital tracking. Results showed higher completion rates and faster response patterns in the formal message condition. Completion reached 100% in the formal condition compared to 50% in the informal condition (χ²(1, N = 40) = 13.33, p < .001, V = .58). These findings show that message structure is associated with how learners respond to academic requests in digitally mediated environments. While limited by a small sample size and context-specific design, the study provides applied evidence consistent with principles of transactional distance and teaching presence. The findings suggest that low-effort improvements in communication design may support participation in asynchronous open and distance learning systems.
abstracts.010184: This paper examines the functional-head theory in syntax, i.e. the claim that grammatical meanings are represented as heads in syntax, in much the same way as contentive heads (verbs and nouns). It starts out from the presumption that the functional-head theory can be expected to predict typical head behaviour of grammatical elements, especially with respect to the core head properties: hyperonym status, distributional identity, obligatoriness, idioselection. These general predictions do not seem to be supported by the cross-linguistic evidence, so I go on to discuss additional motivations for the functional-head theory. In practice, the functional-head theory has not been justified in terms of typical head behaviour, but in rather different ways. I present some alternatives to the widely adopted functional-head notation, and then I offer a general discussion of how one might justify general theories in syntax. My conclusion that the functional-head theory appears to be wrong is not very certain, but rather than assume its correctness, future research should formulate it in a clearly testable way and find robust empirical evidence to determine whether it is correct or not.
abstracts.010185: This dissertation investigates the morphosyntax and acquisition of imperative clauses in Italian, arguing for a low structural analysis in which imperatives are radically reduced structures which do not comprise the CP layer, but only vP and a few other projections in the vP periphery in the sense of Belletti (2004). This proposal resolves a tension coming directly from acquisition data: traditionally, imperatives are assumed to target the CP layer, yet positive second person singular imperatives emerge as among the first verbal forms in child development, while CP becomes available only in later acquisitional stages, captured under the Growing Trees framework (Friedmann et al., 2021). This work is organized in four chapters. Chapter 1 offers a review of the state of the art on imperative clauses. It comprises the typological, morphosyntactic, and theoretical dimensions, focusing on the main lines of research in the generative literature and identifying their empirical and theoretical gaps. Chapter 2 presents two corpus studies on Early Italian and a series of experiments on Language Models. It emerges that positive second person singular imperatives are first-stage structures in the Growing Trees sense and that infinitival imperatives (Negative Imperatives, Generic Imperatives, and a-Imperatives) are virtually absent from early spontaneous production. This developmental asymmetry calls for a structural explanation: the proposal is that realis vs. irrealis constitutes the default aspectual opposition, instantiated in early child language through structurally reduced forms (past participle and imperative respectively), while other aspectual specifications emerge later. Chapter 3 formalizes a low analysis of core imperatives (second person singular forms), deriving the full cluster of their morphosyntactic properties under a mechanism of radical structural reduction à la Cecchetto and Donati (2022), and extends the analysis to suppletive forms and to a range of other languages, namely Spanish, Catalan, French, English, Danish, Swedish, and Norwegian. Chapter 4 provides a structural analysis of the three infinitival imperative types, arguing that each instantiates the same low architecture with a different aspectual specification, AspIrrealis, AspGeneric/Progressive, and AspInchoative/Ingressive respectively, and that their interaction with two types of arbitrary pronouns in the sense of Cinque (1988) and Roberts (2019) derives their subject interpretation, sentential force, and syntactic restrictions without further stipulations. The analysis motivates the postulation of a clause-type squish, inspired from Ross’s (1972) category squish and Lowe’s (2019) notion of prototype: a structural continuum along which imperative forms are ordered from a prototypical core to increasingly peripheral instantiations, with direct consequences for learnability and for the theory of clause types.
abstracts.010186: This paper connects two seemingly unrelated phenomena discussed in the literature and offers a unified account: (i) Why must modal adverbs (e.g., English "probably") be positive and behave like Positive Polarity Items (PPIs) (see Bellert 1977, Nilsen 2004, Piñon 2009, Wolf 2015)? (ii) Why do corrective constructions (e.g., Chinese "bìng bù", English "not p but q") obligatorily involve propositional negation (see Toosarvandani 2014, Yuan and Liu 2025, Wu 2025, Zhang 2025)? I argue that modal adverbs and corrective constructions are speaker-oriented, Common Ground (CG)-management operators, signaling two speech acts distinct from assertions: proposals and rejections. (i) Based on a proposition p’s being sufficiently likely in speaker S’s epistemic worlds, S uses a modal adverb to propose p, supporting (i.e., expressing a bias toward), but not requiring, its being considered for inclusion in the CG. (ii) Speaker S uses a corrective construction to reject (i.e., negate) a proposition p, thereby requiring its exclusion from the CG. The speaker’s support (bias) and requirement can be modeled as existential and universal modality.
abstracts.010187: This study examined the mediating role of academic stress in the relationship between second language (L2) comprehension difficulty and test anxiety among early-stage Filipino university students in an English-medium instructional context. Using survey data from 80 undergraduate entrepreneurship students, the study employed correlational and mediation analyses with bootstrapped confidence intervals to examine the proposed relationships among variables. The results indicated that greater L2 academic comprehension difficulty was associated with higher levels of academic stress, which in turn was strongly related to increased test anxiety. Mediation analysis revealed that academic stress partially mediated the relationship between comprehension difficulty and test anxiety, as the direct association between comprehension difficulty and test anxiety was substantially reduced when academic stress was included in the model. These findings highlight academic stress as a key psychological mechanism through which linguistic challenges in English-medium instruction translate into test-related anxiety. The study contributes to educational psychology literature by clarifying the L2–stress–anxiety pathway among university students in non-native English contexts. Practically, the results underscore the importance of instructional and support interventions that integrate academic language development with stress-management strategies to reduce test anxiety and promote more effective learning experiences in English-medium higher education settings.
abstracts.010188: Tone-segment asymmetry has been a frequently discussed topic in linguistic typology where tone has been argued to demonstrate properties that are rarely observed in segmental systems. This study asks whether this typological asymmetry corresponds to a systematic difference in learnability, and thus whether learning biases may contribute to the observed typological distribution. We conducted three artificial language learning experiments examining phonological counting, a non-local phonological process that has been attested for tone but not for segments. The results show that the learning profiles of tonal and segmental counting rules closely mirror the typological distribution: segmental counting patterns, which are typologically rare, are consistently harder to learn. This learning asymmetry holds across different participant populations and generalizes across both consonantal and vowel features, suggesting that it reflects a robust and systematic bias. The findings provide experimental evidence that learning biases may contribute to the typological skew between tonal and segmental systems.
abstracts.010189: The paper reports the results of four experiments on adjectival fragments and sluicing in English and German. The primary purpose of these experiments was to test the predictions of the Syntactic Question Approach (SQA) to clausal ellipsis. This analysis adopts a conservative view of the syntax of clausal ellipsis, as it denies that remnants must undergo A'-movement to escape the ellipsis site, denies that ellipsis repairs island violations, and permits ellipsis sites to be syntactically anisomorphic to their antecedents. The SQA maintains instead that observed ellipsis-specific restrictions arise from constraints governing ellipsis recoverability. However, like most sententialist theories of ellipsis, the development of the SQA was informed by informally collected acceptability judgment data, which are known to often be underinformative and unreliable for the purpose of analyzing ellipsis. By conducting experiments on adjectival frag-ments, we test various configurations in which, depending on the analysis, the remnant of ellipsis may or may not have undergone left-branch extraction (LBE) from within the ellipsis site. We find that, of the several sententialist analyses we consider, our results are most compatible with (a version of) the SQA, which therefore provides new empirical support for this approach. Specifically, we find evidence that island-violating LBE is not repaired by ellipsis, that LBE can be evaded by using an anisomorphic ellipsis site, and that non-wh remnants do not undergo ellipsis-driven A'- movement. In addition, by comparing English and German, we find evidence for two strategies for recovering ellipsis sites: one that only compares the meanings of ellipsis site and its antecedent, and one which compares their syntactic structures. Which strategy is employed appears to depend on whether or not the ellipsis remnant displays particular morphosyntactic cues.
abstracts.010190: About the politics that underlie the language endangerment.
abstracts.010191: The verbal morphology of Classical Tibetan is notoriously complex, where a com- bination of concatenative and non-concatenative processes create paradigms of stem alternants with opaque many-to-many form-function mappings, where TAM features appear to be ex- poned by overlapping and discontinuous phonological material. This paper represents the first attempt at providing a generative, decompositional analysis of the most morphophonologi- cally complex Classical Tibetan verb paradigm (illustrated with √kab ‘to cover’), and of its di- achronic development into Themchen, a modern Amdo Tibetic variety. This analysis uses the Nanosyntax (NS) framework, where I argue that the lexicalisation algorithm can generate the paradigm’s overlapping and discontinuous exponence for free. Overall, this paper presents a case study for giving a decompositional analysis to phenomena that appear to resist it, and the utility of decompositional models that admit an intervening level of representation between form and function. By applying NS to data that it has not seen before, this paper also explores the consequences for prefix-suffix interaction within NS.
abstracts.010192: This paper argues that syntactic locality is sensitive to linear order rather than c-command. The argument comes from English locative inversion, where a locative PP raises to subject position and a DP pivot remains postverbal. Using secondary predicates as fixed VP-internal landmarks, I show that the pivot must be postposed in grammatical instances of locative inversion. Crucially, this requirement holds not only when the DP underlyingly c-commands the PP, but also when the PP is structurally higher than the DP. Pivot postposing therefore cannot merely be a strategy for removing a structurally intervening DP. Instead, I propose that pivot postposing is a strategy for removing a linearly preceding intervener. I propose that Attract Closest is governed by Left-bracket Closeness: among the accessible goals in a probe’s search domain, the closest is the one whose left bracket is leftmost in the linearized representation of the search domain. On this analysis, an in-situ DP blocks PP raising whenever it precedes the PP, independent of their c-command relations. Postposing demotes the DP by placing its pronounced occurrence after the PP, making the PP leftmost within the search domain of T's EPP-bearing probe. I show that this strongly precedence-sensitive account succeeds where competing locality metrics overgenerate, including c-command-based locality, path-based locality, and a weakly precedence-sensitive metric that uses precedence only as a tie-breaker when potential goals do not c-command one another. I show that the proposal predicts a previously unobserved restriction on subextraction: a PP may be topicalized out of a DP pivot, but cannot undergo locative inversion from within that DP. This contrast supports both Left-bracket Closeness and an analysis of the fronted PP in locative inversion as undergoing movement subject to A-locality. Questions and comments are welcome.
abstracts.010193: We discuss the benefits of incorporating oscillatory neural mechanisms into the study of bilingual production errors and their traditionally documented timing signatures (e.g., event-related potentials), which can offer new implementational-level constraints for theories of bilingualism. We argue that a recent neural model of language, ROSE, can offer a neurocomputational account of syntactic transfer in bilingual production, capturing some of its formal properties and the scope of morphosyntactic sequencing failure modes. We take as a case study cross-linguistic influence (CLI) and attendant theories of functional inhibition/competition, and present these as being driven by specific oscillatory failure modes during L2 sentence planning. We argue that modeling CLI in this way not only offers the kinds of linking hypotheses ROSE was built to encourage, but also licenses the exploration of more spatiotemporally complex biomarkers of non native processing than more commonly discussed neural signatures.
abstracts.010194: This paper argues for a two-step model of spell-out in which morphological linearization precedes the insertion of phonological material. The empirical basis of our argument comes from a detailed examination of interrogative clitics in the Tsimshianic languages of northwest North America. In particular, we show that in Sm’algyax (Coast Tsimshian) interrogative clitics consistently linearize immediately to the left of the final DP in the root clause, thus constituting a typologically rare case of penultimate or “second-last position” clitics. We show that no combination of syntax and prosody can derive this pattern, since Sm’algyax clitics show tritropic behaviour: they are subject to distinct syntactic, morphological and phonological conditions. Instead, we propose that the observed distribution requires a linearization mechanism in which clitics come lexically specified with features that regulate their ordering relative to other constituents in a post-syntactic, pre-phonological component of the grammar. This modular approach allows us to maintain a strictly derivational model of spell-out while accounting for the distinctive linearization properties of “special” clitics.
abstracts.010195: This paper introduces Cross-Linguistic Compositional Analysis (CLCA), a reproducible methodology for discovering systematic semantic constraints by analyzing how genetically unrelated languages structure complex conceptual domains. CLCA treats each language as an independent experiment in conceptual engineering: rather than comparing words or grammar, it compares the compositional patterns languages use to construct meaning within a domain, allowing structural regularities to emerge without theoretical pre-specification. Applied to truth-related meaning across sixteen languages from thirteen independent lineages (twelve language families and one isolate), CLCA identifies robust candidate cross-linguistic regularities. In the current sample, all sixteen languages examined show blocking of direct morphological causation of character traits (16/16 convergence across unrelated families), strong directional asymmetries favoring positive over negative inchoatives, and a spontaneously emerging preference for revelation constructions over transformation constructions. These findings serve as illustrative evidence that the protocol detects genuine cross-linguistic structure. CLCA is implemented in two independent protocol variants. CLCA_A uses naive prompts with no domain seeding; CLCA-1.1 uses domain-seeded prompts with explicit coverage auditing. Cross-methodology comparison shows convergence on all five core universals despite radically different prompt architectures, providing strong evidence that the findings reflect linguistic structure rather than prompt-design artifacts. Within-protocol reproducibility testing across all 16 languages shows 75–100% concept-level coverage on G-phase semantic dimensions and 64–83% on HIGH-confidence candidate universals after within-model adjudication; the core structural findings reproduce uniformly across runs.
abstracts.010196: This study examines the morphosyntactic and functional encoding of agent-oriented modality in a maximally diverse sample of languages from North America. Focusing on necessity, obligation, ability, and desire, we show that agent-oriented modality is expressed through a wide range of construction types, including tense-aspect-mood morphology, modal verbs, non-verbal formatives, and complex clauses. We show that clustering the constructions by their formal properties yields three groups that align closely with the modal functions of necessity, ability, and desire. We further show that the constructions encoding different modal functions tend to differ in their morphosyntactic profiles, with strong necessity and obligation in particular showing systematic associations with tense marking, and weak and strong necessity with mood marking, respectively. These findings suggest that agent-oriented modality is not a uniform grammatical category, but a structured functional domain whose subtypes recruit material from different areas of grammar. The study contributes to a typological understanding of modality by combining constructional detail and an autotypologizing approach to cross-linguistic comparison
abstracts.010197: Bare nominals in many articleless languages present an interesting case within the typology of (in)definiteness. On one hand, they pattern with indefinites in that they can be used to talk about a discourse-novel individual that non-uniquely satisfies their descriptive content. At the same time, they pattern with definites in that one cannot felicitously use two identical bare nominals in the same context to talk about different individuals. This behavior of bare nominals is challenging for the theory of nominal meaning, as the null hypothesis is that such nominals, lacking any (in)definite counterparts, should freely be used in definite and indefinite contexts. In this dissertation, I provide a novel account for this phenomenon. Developing my analysis from a case study on Russian, I argue that the null hypothesis is in fact right, and semantically, bare nominals are neutral in terms of (in)definiteness (or, alternatively, they are indefinites that do not convey any “anti- definite” content); the observed definite-like behavior of bare nominals is due to an independent discourse-level principle that I call Unambiguity Constraint: a nominal cannot be used to introduce or pick out a discourse referent i if there is a familiar discourse referent j that maps onto another satisfier of that nominal. I show that this constraint not only manages to explain the observed “definiteness effects” but also makes independent predictions leading to novel generalizations about the distribution of introductory and anaphoric uses of bare nominals. I also compare my analysis with previous approaches to bare nominals, arguing that it manages to balance out between different extremes that make the latter either underpredict or overpredict the distribution of bare nominals. Finally, I show that my analysis has a cross-linguistic potential: judging from preliminary data, bare nominals in at least five more articleless languages are compatible with it. I also discuss challenging cases of indefinites that can be used twice in the same sentence to talk about different individuals, and argue that with certain assumptions made, the UC-based approach can account for them as well.
abstracts.010198: I outline the semantics of verification and examine its interaction with de re ascriptions. Verification sentences are analysed as having a layered structure comprising two unary operators, VER and ACT, represented as VER(ACT(p)). The operator VER establishes a link to a verification event in which agent X has established the truth of p in the actual world, while ACT renders the proposition pre-verified, that is, open to verification or falsifica­tion. Standard accounts of the de re versus de dicto distinction maintain that, in contexts of belief and desire, de re attitudes involve ontological commitments to the existence of objects in the actual world. Within a Davidsonian framework, events are treated as spatiotemporal par­ticulars. Accordingly, sentences of the type VER(ACT(p)), which posit the existence of verifi­cation events in the actual world, pattern with de re constructions. On this basis, lexical markers of VER, such as English ‘indeed’, ‘really’, ‘in fact’, and Russian ‘dejstvitel’no’, ‘na samom dele’, may be analysed as de re modal elements conveying a meaning of epistemic ne­cessity. A distinct class of discourse markers includes English ‘certainly’ and ‘naturally’, and Russian ‘razumeetsja’ and ‘estestvenno’, which introduce the operator AFF and signal that the speaker’s expectations are fulfilled. These two classes of operators display different seman­tic properties: markers of certainty do not entail that p is verified de re, whereas VER markers do not encode speaker certainty. The operator AFF may take scope over VER, yielding the configuration AFF(VER(ACT(p))), which is well-formed, whereas the inverse order VER(AFF(ACT(p))) is ill-formed. The proposed analysis accounts for two empirical generali­sations. First, VER is invariably realised overtly at the phonetic level. Second, counterfactual constructions require components that are pre-verified or verified and exclude anti-veridical markers in the protasis. This constraint supports the view that, within the metaphysics im­plicit in natural language, counterfactual worlds are treated as real and are capable of hosting verification events.
abstracts.010199: Plain futurates—bare-verb or simple-present sentences that assert a scheduled future event—raise a version of Aristotle’s puzzle of future contingents: how can a modal-free sentence make a determinate, assertable claim about an event whose truth is not yet settled? A prominent answer posits a covert future-oriented modal that does silently what will does overtly. This paper argues against that answer and sketches an alternative. Drawing on Mandarin and English data, we show that plain futurates systematically fail the standard diagnostics for covert modality. We then argue that a modal-free description analysis, on which a futurate merely describes a currently-holding schedule, is too weak to capture the speaker’s commitment to the event’s occurrence. As an alternative, we propose that a plain futurate asserts a simple proposition and presupposes that the speaker’s knowledge is causally sufficientfor it, and we motivate this direction by highlighting a connection between plain futurates and dispositional statements.
abstracts.010200: The number of possible binary trees is a function of the number of leaves in the tree. The growth of this function coincides with the series of Catalan numbers, a numerical sequence with many applications in the domain of enumerative combinatorics. As Collins (2022) recognizes, this numerical sequence specifies a theoretical limit on possible ways a string can be parsed via binary Merge. In this paper, I demonstrate that the nanosyntactic Lexicalization Algorithm (Starke 2018, DeClercq et al. 2025) bounds the number of possible outputs of derivations building and externalizing structure in a single Workspace exactly to the Catalan numbers. I then discuss how this result enables a mathematical characterization of the power of a generative grammar building observable linguistic objects from a given selection of input elements. By determining the space of possibilities open in an abstract derivational system, it becomes possible to quantitatively study the role of the independent factors that determine how languages fill this space. From this perspective, the Catalan numbers emerge as fundamental to the understanding of morphosyntactic variation as the result of the interaction of the First and the Third factor (Chomsky2005).
abstracts.010201: Two-way agreement alternatives are familiar (this family has/have travelled all night), but larger systems (with multiple agreement alternatives) are rare and remain poorly understood. Focusing on German, Norwegian and Lithuanian, we see how metonyms and their interactions induce agreement alternatives. We focus on two types: instrument-for-player metonymy and entity-for-eventuality metonymy. In Norwegian, nouns like bratsj‘viola’ can take pronouns based on the player’s gender. And Norwegian‘pancake sentences’, where subjects like pannekaker ‘pancakes’ take neuter singular agreement, illustrate entity-for-eventuality metonymy. These patterns are then analyzed using the Agreement Hierarchy (to capture differences between targets) and the Hierarchy of Agreement Sources (to rank possible agreements according to their degree of generalized semantic agreement). Lithuanian data confirm our findings, revealing similar agreement patterns in a different morphosyntactic environment. The distribution of these metonymy-induced patterns can be integrated into the typology of agreement alternatives, and without additional machinery. Our analysis also yields testable predictions for further investigation.
abstracts.010202: Social media has become a significant space for public discourse, allowing individuals to express opinions and attitudes toward sensitive social issues, including gender-based violence against women. This study investigates gendered linguistic differences in online discourse by examining male and female comments addressing gender-based violence on X (Twitter) and Instagram. The study analyzes a dataset of 30 comments, equally divided between male and female users, collected from four social media posts. A triangulation mixed-methods approach is adopted, combining qualitative and quantitative analysis to identify recurring linguistic patterns. The analysis draws on Lakoff’s (1975) Deficit Model, Tannen’s (1990) Difference Model, and Zimmerman and West’s (1975) Dominance Model, alongside an examination of morphological and syntactic features. The findings reveal both similarities and differences between male and female discourse. Female comments demonstrate a higher frequency of features associated with Lakoff’s Deficit Model, particularly empty adjectives, hedges, and hyper-politeness, while male comments show greater use of intensifiers and emphatic punctuation. In accordance with Tannen’s Difference Model, male discourse is more frequently associated with orders, conflict, and status-oriented language, whereas female discourse emphasizes feelings, understanding, intimacy, and support. Morphologically and syntactically, both groups display considerable similarities, particularly in tense marking, derivation, compounding, indicative mood, finite clauses, main clauses, and active voice. The findings suggest that gendered linguistic patterns persist in digital discourse while also demonstrating considerable overlap between male and female language use.
abstracts.010203: This paper argues that the quantifiers for all and both can occur in different positions in the three closely related languages English, German, and Yiddish. Such differences have to be taken into consideration in the explanation of ungrammatical cases, as briefly exemplified here. All these languages allow these two quantifiers to be in the DP-layer. However, they vary as regards the predeterminer and the postdeterminer positions. Since Yiddish is the most tolerant language – it allows both quantifiers to occur in all three positions, the restrictions in the other languages can presumably not involve a strong account.
abstracts.010204: Eliminativist usage-based and classical generative speech production models differ fundamentally in two respects: (i) the nature of speech representations and (ii) the locus of linguistic knowledge. In this dissertation, I ask what levels of abstraction and detail are present in speech representations and whether a lexicon of detailed speech memories is sufficient to explain a speaker’s linguistic knowledge of their language. I investigate these questions using phonetic, phonological, experimental, and computational evidence from two understudied Pakistani languages, Punjabi and Mankiyali. First, I present evidence from Punjabi that lexical representations can be completely covert, containing information that is not present in any experienced realization of a lexical item. I then demonstrate that, given an appropriately structured learning architecture, a learner can acquire covert speech representations efficiently. At the same time, a pilot study provides preliminary evidence that talker-specific phonetic and socially indexed information from recent linguistic experience is retained and reflected in subsequent production. Crucially, the same lexical items used to motivate covert representations also appear to be represented at a richly detailed episodic level. Turning to the locus of linguistic knowledge, I present acoustic data from a production experiment in Mankiyali, showing that the neutralization of a phonological contrast can be phonetically complete. I then use simulations of exemplar accumulation to examine whether a lexicon of detailed speech memories can account for the stable realization of such patterns. In these simulations, once the production and similarity biases define a stable target for an acoustic parameter, introducing exemplars with different values cannot by itself shift that target. A persistent shift in a category's optimal acoustic realization instead seems to require recalibration of the biases shaping production, motivating higher-order linguistic knowledge that operates beyond stored speech memories. Taken together, these findings challenge both eliminativist usage-based models, which reduce linguistic knowledge to accumulated exemplars, and classical generative models, which exclude fine-grained phonetic and social detail from linguistic competence. I argue for a hybrid architecture in which speakers retain detailed episodic memories, maintain abstract categories that may diverge substantially from experience, and possess higher-order knowledge that regulates their joint influence on speech production.
abstracts.010205: The distribution of upper limit effects suggests that an expression’s evaluation time cannot be bound independently from its evaluation world. Specifically, even in cases where worlds and times can be non-locally bound (which implies the availability of mechanisms with object-language quantification or equivalent power), both coordinates must be bound by the same (non-local) antecedent. From this, I conclude that the mechanism manipulating worlds and times in natural language is less expressive than a mechanism that manipulates independent object language variables that range over worlds and times. At most, the mechanism that binds worlds and times can express binding of evaluation indices (i.e. world-time pairs).
abstracts.010206: There are many approaches to locality, which differ in how they answer a central question: where do locality constraints originate? All available theories successfully explain specific subsets of the data, yet none captures the full range of locality phenomena. This suggests a “division of labour” among locality accounts, whereby variation in locality effects (within and across languages) is partitioned into distinct explanatory domains. This observation raises two possibilities: either “locality effects” comprise ontologically distinct phenomena stemming from heterogeneous sources, or there is a common denominator linking phenomena such as strong and weak islands, superiority effects, and subject–object asymmetries in A’-dependencies. If the latter is correct, a fundamental question arises: why has no unified account emerged? If these effects share an underlying basis, one might expect a unified theoretical framework to capture them. The persistence of this gap remains largely unaddressed in the literature. This thesis addresses this issue by developing a framework that seeks to explain why locality effects are multifaceted and resistant to a single overarching explanation. The core proposal is that locality effects arise from the interaction between purely linguistic factors and cognitive dynamics that extend beyond the language faculty. Most (if not all) locality-related phenomena are argued to result from the interplay between cognitive mechanisms responsible for language processing and the grammatical representations underlying them. This interaction is located at the Interface, understood as the point of interaction between grammar (conceived as a set of mental representations and their combinatory rules) and the domain-general principles and mechanisms through which language emerges and is put to use (Chomsky et al. 2023). In pursuing these questions, the dissertation offers novel insights into specific cases, including argument–adjunct asymmetries in extraction from English weak and strong islands and intervention effects in Spanish object relative clauses, both investigated experimentally. In the final chapter, the long-standing issue posed by the (subject part of the) CED is addressed theoretically.
abstracts.010207: A central question in formal semantics concerns the division of labor between lexical semantics and the compositional system. Given a particular inference pattern, we can ask whether it is encoded in the lexicon or whether it arises from a particular syntactic interaction between different compositional ingredients. This question is especially important in the domain of plural predication, where there are competing lexical and syntactic accounts for a variety of phenomena. This dissertation argues, via a detailed investigation of cumulative inferences, reciprocal alternations and the interpretation of `together', for a syntactic approach according to which these core inferences in plural predication result from different scope interactions between a limited set of syntactic operator. The dissertation therefore argues for a more impoverished lexicon and a richer syntax in the domain of plural predication. The scope-based account faces an immediate explanatory challenge: while lexical analyses appeal to lexical generalizations to capture the distribution of readings in each construction, the scope-based account appears to overgenerate unattested readings. I show that these lexical stipulations can be replaced by independently motivated grammatical constraints that cut across different constructions. More specifically, I propose that two such constraints play a key role in plural predication: (i) a generalized economy constraint, inspired by Fox's (2000) scope economy, which rules out LFs when they can be proven to be equivalent to simpler LFs, and (ii) a constraint that requires implicit arguments to take lowest scope (Fodor and Fodor, 1980). The result is a framework in which the different ingredients of plural predication are in principle free to take scope in different positions, as long as they don't violate these independently needed constraints. Finally, the scope-based account has some broader architectural consequences. The first consequence concerns the nature of economy constraints in the grammar. I show that in order to predict the desired distribution of readings, the generalized economy constraint has to be evaluated relative to an encapsulated system which only has access to some of the information that is needed to compute truth-conditions. My account therefore provides a new domain where we see evidence for a modular deductive system (Fox, 2000; Gayewski, 2002; Fox and Hackl, 2006; Chierchia, 2013, a.o.). The second consequence concerns the division of labor between the lexicon and the syntax. I suggest that the impoverished role of the lexicon in plural predication might reflect broader constraints on what kinds of meanings can be encoded in a single lexical item.
abstracts.010208: The paper examines wh-in-situ in Japanese and argues for a position that is in between wholesale LF wh-movement approaches, where all in-situ wh-phrases in Japanese undergo movement in LF, and the treatments where there is no LF wh-movement in Japanese at all by arguing that some, but not all wh-in-situ questions in Japanese involve LF wh-movement. Regarding when Japanese has LF wh-movement, Takahashi (1993) argues that in some cases, wh-scrambling in Japanese involves true overt wh-movement. I show that a rather intricate paradigm regarding wh-island and superiority effects with Japanese wh-in-situ can be accounted for if Japanese has LF wh-movement only in the contexts where Takahashi (1993) claims Japanese has overt wh-movement. The paper also establishes a parallel with wh-questions in French, providing a uniform treatment of Japanese and French, where (LF) wh-movement, Agree, and unselective binding are all involved in question formation, with Agree being clause-bounded, and unselective binding, a semantic operation, being available only after the +wh-C establishes a syntactic relationship with a wh-phrase, through either Agree or wh-movement. The discussion in the paper, which establishes the existence of LF superiority effects, also has consequences for our understanding of superiority and wh-island effects.
abstracts.010209: Bracketed notation is a standard, compact method for representing syntactic structures. Yet as structural depth increases—especially within high-density cartographic frameworks—standard linear bracketed representations rapidly become unreadable. While graphic tree diagrams resolve this readability issue, their implementation presents severe practical challenges in mainstream word processors (e.g., Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs), where manual drawing tools create fragile layouts and embedded static images hamper real-time editing and collaboration. It must be acknowledged that this note introduces Indented Bracketed Representation (IBR): a spatial bracketed representation, not as a replacement of tree diagrams, that aims at rendering standard bracketed notation as readable, tree-like structures using simple indentation and line-break rules. IBR generalizes typographical conveniences visible in Rizzi & Cinque’ (2016) “Functional categories and syntactic theory”, Annual Review of Linguistics, 2(1), 139-163. Consequently, IBR requires no external graphical engines; it preserves full editable text functionality across word processing software; it maintains strict 1:1 structural isomorphism with standard bracketed notation, and it offers direct upward compatibility with LaTeX tree packages such as forest and tikz-qtree.
abstracts.010210: Language contact is a crucial factor determining language change. This study defines a novel methodology to quantify the extent of its relevance, testing it on the distribution of 23 syntactic features in the Italian dialectal environment. Two sets of data are compared, representing two diachronic stages separated by 70-90 years. This allows to estimate for each feature (i) the amount of change attested in this timespan, (ii) the amount of contact attested at the beginning of the period considered. A simple regression analysis shows that contact accounts for up to 66% (R2 = 0.66; r = 0.812) of the diachronic variation, a highly significant result. Further post-hoc analyses indicate that some features change more/less than contact would predict. In this respect, the decisive factor is the structural compatibility among the languages in contact, defined as the degree of partial intra-linguistic overlap that feeds cross-linguistic influence in the attested contact situations (Hulk & Müller 2000). Given an equal amount of contact, features that are subject to more instances of intra-linguistic overlaps change more than others. Other factors, such as borrowability scales and areal asymmetries, do not play a significant role. This second result underlines the relevance for contact-induced change of individual-level processes active within multilingual speakers.
abstracts.010211: The question of how young children interpret disjunctive words like English “or” has become a topic of increased attention in the recent developmental semantic/pragmatic literature. We present a thematic overview of the past half century of research on children’s acquisition of the meaning of disjunction, from the Piagetian era in the 1940s to the most recent experimental pragmatics studies of disjunction. Along the way, we highlight ways in which children differ from adults in their interpretations of disjunction, as well as ongoing debates about the sources of these interpretations, with the hope that a historical perspective may shed light on these recent debates.
abstracts.010212: This paper presents novel evidence from two Northern Italian dialects supporting a movement-based analysis of Negative Doubling , in which a single-negation reading arises from the co-occurrence of a negative marker and one or more negative indefinites (Zeijlstra 2004). Under this approach, sentential negation is base-merged with the negative indefinite and subsequently splits from it during the derivation (Blanchette 2015; Tubau et al. 2024; Presotto et al. submitted). This analysis makes two empirical predictions that are not expected under Agree-based accounts (Haegeman & Lohndal 2010; Manzini & Pescarini 2024; Zeijlstra 2004, 2022). First, the base-generated constituent containing both the sentential negator and the negative indefinite should indeed be able to surface as a single constituent. Second, because the sentential negator occupies a different structural position when doubling a negative indefinite than when it is the sole exponent of sentential negation, this contrast may be reflected in morphological alternations. We show that both predictions are borne out in two Northern Italian dialects, providing new evidence for a movement-based analysis of Negative Doubling and shedding light on its underlying derivational mechanics.
abstracts.010213: Biolinguistics, to define it in a single phrase, is the study of language that takes its biological underpinnings seriously. This short book out-lines the basic tenets of a biolinguistic approach framed in the form of five ‘foundational questions’. While often associated with generative investigations of language, biolinguistics is not—and should not be—just another term for generative grammar; biolinguistic approaches to the scientific study of human language will thus be put in a richer context by inspecting and dissecting the foundational questions, with par-ticular reference to cognitive approaches from generative and non-generative perspectives alike. The organizing distinction developed here is between ‘cognitive linguistics in the narrow sense’ (nativist, hence largely generative) and ‘cognitive linguistics in the broad sense’ (usage-based or emergentist, i.e. definitely non-generative). As such, the book can be seen as a primer for cognitive at-large approaches to the study of human language on biolinguistic foundations. This first chapter presents the basic notion and the dynamic field of biolinguistics somewhat historically, provides relevant theoretical and conceptual backgrounds, introduces the five foundational questions and their eponymous problems, and sets the stage for what is to come.
abstracts.010214: The paper proposes a novel approach to the mixed agreement vs. case assignment pattern in Slavic numerals and juxtaposes the LFG formalization of this approach with the earlier Minimimalist analysis presented in detail in Concord is Insatiable Agree: Heterogeneous Case and Phi Patterns in Slavic and Finnic .
abstracts.010215: Grammatical case is sometimes viewed as dispensable in linguistic theory. The most detailed attempt at relegating case from grammar is that of Pesetsky 2013 (“Russian case morphology and the syntactic categories", MIT Press), where case marking is argued to be category flagging; for example, the accusative on a noun is taken to be the result of a verb flagging the noun with category V. This paper demonstrates that category flagging is real, but distinct from case marking. The main phenomenon under examination is category flagging by Slavic prepositions, where P-flagging is demonstrably dissociated from case marking. Other possible instances of category flagging include N- and V-flagging in languages such as Shipibo, and Numeral flagging in Slavic and Iranian languages.
abstracts.010216: This study investigates the realization of word-initial /p/ in English consonant clusters, focusing on the apparent contrast between clusters such as /pr/ and /pl/, where /p/ is consistently realized, and clusters such as /ps/, /pn/, and /pt/, where /p/ is typically absent. Using a systematic analysis of 2,586 entries from the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, the study examines the relationship between /p/ realization and the phonological class of the following segment. The results show a strong association between /p/ realization and following-segment sonority: /p/ is retained consistently in /pr/ and /pl/ clusters, while it is overwhelmingly absent in the core /ps/, /pn/, and /pt/ groups. A Fisher’s exact test confirms that the observed association is statistically significant. Rare and variable forms, including pshaw, pshew, and pschent, are examined separately as potential counterexamples. The findings are consistent with the Sonority Sequencing Principle and with established accounts of English phonotactics and the historical adaptation of consonant clusters. The study does not propose a new phonological law, but provides a corpus-based examination of the distribution of initial /p/ realization and identifies areas requiring further investigation.
abstracts.010217: This study investigates the impact of learners’ first language on their detection of indirect positive evidence presented in their second language while learning the plural morphology of an additional foreign language. The goal is to explore an alternative approach to learning foreign language grammars. The participants were 43 native Thai-speaking and 42 native Spanish-speaking learners of Mandarin who had advanced proficiency in second language English. They were divided into experimental and control groups and learned 12 Mandarin nouns in their singular form over 2 consecutive days. Only the experimental group was exposed to indirect positive evidence that provided evidence of the unmarked plural feature in Mandarin. After the learning phase, participants’ knowledge of the learned words was tested using singular and plural prompts. Followup questions were asked to investigate the basis of participants’ responses. The results showed that six Thai and three Spanish participants detected and used the indirect positive evidence. This finding suggests that language learners differ in their ability to adopt and use indirect positive evidence as a function of their first language background.
abstracts.010218: Polish and Czech both have “conjoined quadruplets”: sets of four paradigms that differ in exactly two cases. In this paper, I compare how Distributed Morphology and Nanosyntax account for these patterns, which include multiple configurations identified as problematic for Nanosyntax by Janků (2022) and others. Since both theories must relegate some of the patterns to unproductive morphology, mere ability to account for all of the attested patterns cannot distinguish them. Instead, I compare the theories’ ability to account for measures of productivity like frequency, acquisition, and behavioral patterns. Accounting for the full range of attested phenomena requires speakers to store generalizations over their lexicon in a pattern-matching module that enforces the shape of lexical entries and can be applied productively but is not active in formal derivations. The nature of lexical representations in Nanosyntax requires a much more powerful pattern-matching module to account for the attested phenomena than does Distributed Morphology. These gradient patterns, often ignored in theoretical analyses, thus provide valuable sources of data for evaluating morphological theories.
abstracts.010219: Russian masculine nouns may take a number of diminutive suffixes, and Russian speakers follow a number of gradient statistical generalizations over nouns’ phonological properties in deciding which diminutive to assign to existing and novel words (Polivanova 2008, Gouskova et al. 2015). In a corpus study, I show that Russian diminutive allomorphy is also sensitive to two morphological properties: a noun’s inflectional stress pattern and its plural suffix. Moreover, speakers productively extend these generalizations alongside the phonological ones in a nonce word study. I propose that speakers store these generalizations in the form of gradient constraints over the cooccurrence of morphological markers on underlying forms. This has implications for morphological theory: theories of allomorphy must be flexible enough to allow words to have two independently varying inflectional markers accessible to one and the same pattern-matching module.
abstracts.010220: Generative syntax standardly assumes that T universally hosts the EPP (Chomsky 1995, 2000), yet cross-linguistic evidence reveals substantial variation in which functional head exhibits syntactic centrality and morphological prominence. This paper develops the Morphosyntactic Pivot Hypothesis (MPH), proposing that the EPP bundle is hosted not universally by T but by the morphosyntactic pivot: the functional head independently identified through convergent syntactic diagnostics (coordination, complementizer selection, ellipsis, subject position, extraction, freezing) and morphological criteria (obligatoriness, paradigmatic richness, productivity, generality). Applying this Biphasic Identification Protocol to six typologically diverse core languages — five via original fieldwork (English, Italian, Swahili, Hindi-Urdu, Balti) and one from published description (Warlpiri) — uncovers hierarchical parametric organization in pivot identity: T (English), Mood (Italian), Agr (Swahili), Asp (Hindi-Urdu), Asp/Evid (Balti), and an auxiliary-complex Agr (Warlpiri). This variation is organized by two logically dependent parameters bearing an ontological/computational asymmetry: φ-Availability, whether the pivot bears φ-features at all, and, only where φ is available, φ-Interpretability, whether those features are semantically active at LF — existence necessarily precedes computation over what exists, reducing four combinatorial possibilities to three attested types. The pivots possessing iφ-features license pro-drop through matching-based Bimodal Agree whereas the pivots possessing uφ-features triggers valuation-based Unimodal Agree, blocking pro-drop and requiring expletives; in contrast, pivots with nφ-features satisfy the EPP through aspectual or evidential anchoring, independent of φ-dependencies entirely. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on an 82-language sample from 21 distinct families validate this architecture. PCA reveals an exceptionally dominant first component (PC1 = 96.60% of variance; jackknife SD = 0.176%) and discrete typological clustering rather than continuous gradation. The hand-coded classification is independently corroborated against Universal Dependencies treebank data which has been built over two decades by independent annotators without reference to MPH. The UD test recovers φ-availability at 97.5% and φ-interpretability at 95.0% accuracy. Every residual misclassification falls into one of two pre-specified failure modes — a prediction which was genuinely at risk of being falsified but was not. The framework accounts for multiple morphosyntactic phenomena from a single parametric axis. Case systems, agreement, subject licensing, expletive distribution, and pro-drop all fall from the hierarchical organization of the locus of the EPP. It derives typological macro-variation from φ-state of the pivot. It provides testable predictions for acquisition and diachronic change, including agreement morphology that outlasts the interpretability which once licensed it.
abstracts.010221: The aim of this paper is to provide a formalization of Dependency Grammars (DGs), one that may be useful to dependency linguists with different formalization needs and with different theoretical backgrounds. The formalization is set within the Model-Theoretic Syntax paradigm, as assumed in most current DGs. The proposed formalism is used in an analysis of a small fragment of English, corresponding roughly to that treated with a “feature-based dependency grammar formalism” in Gibson 2025 ( Syntax: A Cognitive Approach , MIT Press), but extending it with more explicit analyses of coordination (including coordination of unlike categories) and long-distance dependencies. Numerous empirical and theoretical advantages of the current model-theoretic approach over the rule-based approach proposed there are pointed out. A note on different versions: the differences between versions v1–v4 are very minor, mostly editorial, but v5 corrects a certain deficiency of the translation procedure in Appendix B (see (B7) and text below it) and the current version adds a reference to a paper applying MTDG to the task of modelling gradient grammaticality .
abstracts.010222: There exist among various Sinitic dialects a group of Alveolo-palatal fricatives that are so close in terms of phonetic attributes to either [tʃ] group consonants or [tɕ] group consonants that they were not identified approriately and not transcribed with suitable IPA symbols during past field surveys. One of the reasons is so far there is no defined phonetic features for the forgotten sibilants. Middle Chinese rhyme books kept records of the sibilants, i.e. Group Zhuang initials (莊组声纽), however heretofore they are not yet deciphered with correctly designated phonetic features. This paper rediscovers and identifies phonetic features for this group of sibilants. In the process this group of sibilants are identified at the end of the initials with presence of upper vocal tract occlusion which serve as medials of glottal stop for characters under Group Zhuang initials with 2nd Deng in the Middle Chinese rhyme tables. Key words: Palatalized alveoro-palatal fricatives [tɕʲ] group consonants Group Zhuang initials Upper vocal tract occlusion 在国内一些方言里存在着这样一组舌面龈腭擦音,因为其在语音特征上非常接近于舌叶擦音[tʃ]组或舌面擦音[tɕ]组,所以在过往的语言点调查中没有被正确识别和用合适的国际音标来标音。原因可以追溯到至今国内语言学界尚未有对其语音特征进行过描述。中古音韵书记录了这一组擦音,即莊组声纽,但其至今尚未有正确的构拟音。 本文对这一组有咝擦音的语音特征进行了辨别和确认,在过程中发现此组声母含有上声道阻塞的特征,也因此推测出了《韵镜》的二等具有喉塞音作为介音的语音特征。 关键词:颚化的舌面龈腭擦音 [tɕʲ]组擦音 莊组声纽 上声道阻塞
abstracts.010223: Previously the author has deciphered that 2nd Deng from Yunjing designates a glottal medial in relevant syllables of Middle Chinese rhyme books. Generally, there is little chance for word-internal glottle stops to be avilable to form CʔV syllables. The author observed there are unique waveforms of vocal fry(even series of single pulse fry, with damped pulse characteristics) phonation among vowels of words of 2nd Deng . Infered from this observation, by exploring words of 2nd Deng under non-Zhuang initials, large volumes of sounds containing phonation of vocal fry are identified among sounds from branches of Chinese dialects of Yue, Min, Hakka and Wu. [ɐ̰] and other vowels with vocal fry phonation had been functioning among Middle Chinese words under 2nd Deng, constrastive to the same catergory of rhymes with modal voice among words under 1st Deng. Aided with research results over glottal stops and creaky voice phonation it is concluded that all those words of non-Zhuang initials under 2nd Deng form CʔV syllables and contain glottal medials which are solely phonetic perpception cued by low F0 of vowels with vocal fry phonation. Key word: 2nd Deng Glottal medial Vocal fry(even series of single pulse fry, with damped pulse characteristics) 作者之前破解了《韵镜》里二等的语音性质是以喉塞清音[ʔ]作为介音。一般认为,缘于汉语声韵调的特点,在常见主干音节CV结构中在元音之前,存在喉塞清音的可能性很低。作者观察到吴方言下属音系中个别中古音二等例字其元音的声波波形为气泡音,以此为线索,以中古音非莊组声纽下麻韵江耕韵佳韵庚等等二等韵系字作为参考,成功地在闽方言粤方言客家话吴方言等下属诸多音系的二等例字发音中找到了气泡音(均匀单脉冲连续波气泡音) 发声态。作为一类较为特殊的发声态,气泡音应曾广泛地存在于中古音汉语音系中,非莊组二等韵系的主元音应以气泡音作为发声态,其与中古音中发声态为常态的一等韵系两两形成对立,由此解决了中古音中一等韵系二等韵系的拟音难题。基于中古音韵图中韵系的排列以及跟随莊组声纽的韵系也为二等,并借鉴国际语音学界对嘎裂声和喉塞音的研究成果,可以推导出中古音二等须处理为喉塞介音。在非莊组声纽下二等韵系例字中,该类喉塞介音在音节中的位置处于声母和发声态为气泡音的元音之间,此类喉塞介音主要是通过对特征声学指标提示的感知方式来实现。 关键词:《韵镜》二等 喉塞介音 气泡音发声态
abstracts.010224: The mainstream reconstruction of Qieyun sibilants—specifically the jing (精) group, zhang (章) group, and zhuang (莊) group—posits them as alveolar fricatives, Alveolo-palatal fricatives, and lamino-postalveloar or apical postalveloar fricatives, respectively. However, while studying the third and fourth Deng as well as chongniu (重纽) in Yunjing (《韵镜》), the author proposes that the zhang group should be reconstructed as lamino-alveolar fricatives,transcibed as [sʲ], the jing group as a labialized lamino-alveolar fricatives[(sʲ)w], and the zhuang initials as palatalized lamino-alveolar fricatives [(sʲ)j],. Through an analysis of relevant sounds databases, it was found that these three sets of sibilant fricatives are either partially or fully preserved in most Min, Yue (Cantonese), and Hakka dialectal varieties across Fujian, Guangdong, Hainan, and Taiwan etc.. They also persist to varying degrees in dialects within Guangxi, as well as in Wu, Hui, and Jin dialects. Just as palatalized alveolo-palatal fricatives do , there exist among Chinese dialects 2 types of palatalized lamino-alveolar fricatives, both types attain upper vocal tract occlusion which serve as glottal medials. 切韵齿音精组章组莊组的拟音主流认为是舌尖前擦音[s]、舌面前擦音[ɕ]以及舌叶擦音[ʃ]或卷舌音[ʂ]及其塞擦音。作者在研究《韵镜》三等四等以及重纽过程中发现章组书母拟音为舌叶齿龈擦音,可标识为[sʲ],精组心母拟音为唇化舌叶齿龈擦音[(sʲ)w],莊组生母声纽拟音为颚化舌叶齿龈擦音[(sʲ)j]。经对相关语音库数据分析研究后发现,这3组有咝擦音或部分或完整地留存在福建广东海南台湾区域内的大多数语言点的闽方言粤方言和客家话中以及不同程度地留存在广西区域内的语言点和吴方言赣方言徽方言晋方言中。而颚化舌叶齿龈擦音[(sʲ)j]在共时音中也如颚化舌面前擦音[ɕj]一样也分为第1类和第2类,2类颚化擦音中均留存着上声道阻塞。因为历时音中出现了第2类的颚化舌叶齿龈擦音,因此切韵中的莊组和章组得以合并为三十六字母中的照组。 关键词:切韵齿音 舌叶齿龈擦音 唇化舌叶齿龈擦音 颚化舌叶齿龈擦音 上声道阻塞
abstracts.010225: This paper reveals that Phags-pa Chinese partly conserved 2nd deng phonological features of Qieyun Middle Chinese, i.e., vocal fry 2nd deng and Zhuang initial 2nd deng,transcribed with letters designating glottal medial & upper vocal tract occlusion. Phags-pa letter ꡨ is used for transcribing vocal fry 2nd deng sysllables, Letter ꡜ, together with ꡞ forms segment ꡜꡞ to represent independent upper vocal tract occlusion, which has a phonetic value of northern Wu dialect pronunciation of Chinese word “one(一)” . There is co-occurrence constraint of segment ꡜꡞ,so we can deduce sibilants of Phags-pa Chinese shall be laminal alveolar fricatives and alveolo-palatal fricatives. Laminal alveolar fricatives, with ꡜꡞ form initial & medial of 2nd deng of Zhao group,the latter, with ꡜꡞ form initial & medial of pseudo-Zhuang group. ꡜꡞ as syllabic nucleus can also co-occur with non-sibilant initials to form syllables. As a peculiar phonetic segment, ꡜꡞ is conserved among Ming Mandarin Chinese, transcribed as ě rushengshen (ě入声甚) by Nicolas Trigault in Xiru Ermu Zi. With the same co-occurrence constraint of ě rushengshen we can deduce Ming Mandarin Chinese has laminal alveolar Fricatives and alveolo-palatal fricatives as its sibilants. ě rushengshen, as syllabic nucleus can also co-occur with non-sibilant initials to form syllables whose archaic sounds are still retained among various dialects across China. This paper also discusses how Phags-pa Chinese phonetic notation principle likely originated from the Chinese transcription methods used by Tibetan scholars during the Tang and Five Dynasties period, and how Apico-Palatal fricative entered the phonological system of Ming Mandarin through the mixing of Northeastern Chinese dialects at the end of the Ming Dynasty—brought along with the Manchu conquest—and subsequently spread to mandarin dialects and other chinese phonological systems during Qing Dynasty period. Ultimately, this mixed dialect replaced Ming Mandarin Chinese and evolved into the modern common language of China. abstracts.010226: During the investigation of Chinese dialect speech databases, it is discovered that in southeastern dialects, a set of voiced fricatives is preserved in the pronunciation of the Yu initial (喻母) and Ri initial (日母) characters,should be identitied as voiced palatal fricative & labialized voiced palatal fricative,and a voiced fricative with a similar manner of articulation but a more anterior release position. Based on a comparative analysis of Yu initials transcriptions in the Menggu Ziyun and Dunhuang Sino-Tibetan materials, the retained pronunciations of Yu initials characters in other Chinese dialects, and the topological position of the Yu initials in the Yunjing, the author proposes that the Middle Chinese Yi initials(以母) should be reconstructed as labialized voiced palatal fricative, Yun initials(云母) reconstructed as voiced palatal fricative,Ri initials(日母)reconstructed as a voiced anterior laminal alveolar fricative, distinct from [z], [ʒ], and [ʑ]. Given the numerous instances of variant readings (异读) between Yi initial and Ding initial (定母) in the Guangyun, and based on archaeological philological findings such as the theory that "Yu si initial originates from Ding initial" (喻四归定), it can be inferred that labialized voiced palatal fricative (the reconstructed pronunciation of Yi initial) evolved from voiced palatal africate, therefore, the latter is the reconstructed pronunciation of Ding initial. Furthermore, since the initials of Zhi group (知组) are in complementary distribution with the third and fourth division (三四等) initials of Duan group (端组), it can be inferred that the Middle Chinese initials of Zhi group correspond to sounds of palatal africate group. Based on the phonetic transcription records in the Dunhuang Chinese-Tibetan transcriptional materials, it can be inferred that although the majority of Duan group initials (端组) in the Northwestern dialect of the Tang and Five Dynasties period had already evolved into dental/alveolar plosives, a small number of labialized voiced palatal africate still remained. At the same time, this paper examines the transcription methods of the Middle Chinese Yu initial (喻母), Ri initial (日母), and the lingual sounds in the Dunhuang Chinese-Tibetan transcriptional materials and the Menggu Ziyun (蒙古字韵). In addition, this paper also explores the reconstructed pronunciations of the four rhymes Zhi (支), Zhi(脂), Zhi(之), and Wei(微) under Zhi rhyme group (止摄) in the Qieyun system: Zhi (支) rhyme is apical vowel of Yu initials, Zhi(之) rhyme is apical vowel of Ri initial, Zhi(脂) rhyme is apical vowel of Shu and Xin initials(书母、心母), Wei(微) rhyme is close front unrounded vowel [i]. The Grade III final of the zhi rhyme group is precisely the fricative vowel /iɿ/ or /iz/ commonly found in Wu dialects. Apart from its retention in Chinese dialects, it is also recorded in Dunhuang Tibetan-Chinese transcriptions, the Menggu Ziyun (Phags-pa Script Dictionary), and the Xiru Ermu Zi (西儒耳目资), where it is transcribed using the Tibetan letter ཨེ, the 'Phags-pa letters ꡠ、ꡭ, and the Latin letter ei respectively. This paper also discusses when the e initial(额母) entered the Middle Chinese phonological system and its subsequent evolution, and based on this, identifies the phonological characteristics of Tang dynasty official language and its influence on Chinese dialect phonologies.
abstracts.010227: The paper demonstrates representing pronomial anaphora in the orthodox first-order predicate logic with the completely standard syntax and semantics. Specifically, we show how to represent not yet resolved pronouns in conventional logical formulas, and then record the result of their resolution (coindexing). Our proposal is static, simply-typed, minimalist, with the orthodox quantification, binding and scope. It relies on the 1920s logic, and applies classically and intuitionistically -- in particular, treating implication as is. It is inspired by and extensively relies on intuitionistic Skolemization. We demonstrate our approach on intra- and inter-sentential pronomial anaphora; bound-variable anaphora; conditional, relative-clause and proportional quantifier donkey sentences; quantificational subordination. The approach aims to separate out pragmatic concerns from meaning composition: being able to map a syntactic structure to a logical formula representing the meaning, phrase-by-phrase and clause-by-clause, without prior coindexing and regardless of context. Pronoun resolution is to be done in the next, pragmatic step, based on the obtained formulas. Although coindexing is delegated to pragmatics, the logical formulas constrain the coindexing, helping the resolution and delivering predictions, of unavailability of particular antecedents.
abstracts.010229: Kartvelian languages are famous for their exuberant consonant onset clusters that violate sonority sequencing principles, notably nasal onsets. In reality, there is substantial variation amongst them to what extent they exhibit such onsets. This paper will propose that variation amongst nasal onsets in the family derives not only from retention from the protolanguage but from separate processes of nasal onset deletion in Megrelian, nasal onset epenthesis in Laz, and a process of morphophonological reanalysis called ‘M-mobile’ in Georgian.
abstracts.010230: This thesis explores Czech polar questions and their inability to license negative concord items (NCIs) when negated. Following Zeijlstra (2004, 2022), we take negative concord to be an instance of syntactic agreement where all negative elements agree with a covert negative operator. The syntactic view of the matter is further suggested by data from long-distance scrambling and scrambling from an embedded predicate within the main clause. However, data also further suggest that movement is not at play in interrogative polar questions and the lack of NC. For this reason, we turn to how negation behaves broadly in polar questions and conclude that its nature may be expletive, i.e. not bringing any negative force, which is also supported cross-linguistically, notably by the Modern Greek min/dhen split (Tsiakmakis, 2025). Based on these observations, we analyze polar questions as having two possible merge sites of negation. Crucially, in interrogative questions, this merge site is proposed above the propositional TP layer in the left periphery, where it cannot enter into the agreement relation with the negative operator and yields an epistemic interpretation which surfaces as speaker bias. Unlike declarative and embedded polar questions, which retain a low negation and license NCIs normally, interrogative questions thus lack the low negation required for negative concord.
abstracts.010231: As in Collins (2024), going back at least to Chomsky .(1957), short passives must contain a syntactically present deleted/silent agent.
abstracts.010232: *** Please share any comments or feedback with me via email: omri.amiraz@ugent.be *** Indirect scalar inferences are generally assumed to be derived by the same mechanism of implicature calculation that generates direct scalar inferences, whether this mechanism is pragmatic or grammatical in nature. However, this study reveals a critical distinction within indirect scalar inferences, identifying two distinct types: (i) those resembling direct scalar inferences in being defeasible or absent in certain embedded environments; and (ii) those that do not exhibit the characteristic context dependence of implicatures. I propose that the latter type of indirect scalar inferences should be considered a phenomenon sui generis. These inferences do not arise from implicature calculation but rather stem from an existential presupposition triggered by certain negative focus constructions. Because of their presuppositional nature, they persist even in downward-entailing environments and in echo denial. To capture the relation between the type of negative construction and the indirect scalar inference it gives rise to, this paper introduces a classification of negative constructions based on their focus sensitivity. It is argued that presuppositional indirect scalar inferences arise only in constructions that conventionally require association with narrow focus. This generalization is supported by cross-linguistic evidence from nine languages that employ a wide range of negative constructions.
abstracts.010233: It may be strange to begin a paper with a list of what it does not provide. Yet we have, depending how one views it, no positive results to report. We have found no new pattern of acquisition, and we offer no new account of any particular tense-related phenomenon in any language. What we hope to do instead is pose questions that, to our knowledge, have not received attention in the literature. The broad form of the question is all too familiar: how do speakers of a language—say, English—come to possess the grammatical knowledge that they demonstrate? The questions that guide this paper are narrow instances of this broad one, narrowed in three ways. First, they concern three particular languages: Japanese, English, and Russian. Second, they concern tenses specifically, and more specifically still, constructions containing embedded tenses. Third, they concern the semantics of tense. The learning challenge of interest to us is not merely that the learner must come to know, of certain structures, that they are grammatical or ungrammatical; the learner must come to know what meanings the relevant structures can and cannot have. For instance, one acquiring English must learn that certain instances of embedded past tense permit simultaneous readings, while one acquiring Japanese must learn that they do not. The evidence bearing on such knowledge must consist of a kind of pairing between sentences and the situations they are used to describe, and it is from such pairings (in tandem with their existing grammatical beliefs) that a learner must operate. Before we proceed, we must make it clear that our intended contribution is not specific to the semantics of tense. The issues that we explore are general to the acquisition of any piece of semantic knowledge. We choose embedded tense as a case study. Any answer to a question about acquisition must begin with explicit assumptions about the learner. The learning framework we describe operates locally (both with respect to individual utterances and individual hypotheses) in a sense that we describe and defend below (Section 3); with supporting evidence drawn in part from the experimental literature on children's word learning. A further assumption we highlight concerns where learning begins. Drawing on evidence from Hollebrandse (2000) and Demirdache and Lungu (2011) we assume that children carry an initial belief that the past tense is indexical while the present tense is vacuous—a state which matches none of our three target grammars. The challenge, then, is to arrive at the (adult) grammars of Japanese, English, and Russian from this starting point using our local learning procedure. Our finding, such as it is, is that the challenge can be met: for each of our languages there is a path from the initial state to the target grammar, provided that certain hypotheses are available to the learner and that certain critical constructions are sufficiently attested in the input. Identifying those critical inputs is, we think, one of the primary contributions of the paper. This is because the inputs that the logic of our account singles out are not necessarily the ones that inspection of the adult grammars would intuitively suggest, and perhaps only come into focus when semantics and acquisition are considered together.
abstracts.010234: Computational generative grammar is a branch of modern linguistics stipulating that all theories and hypotheses must be justified by showing that the data follows from the theory. Due to the adverse complexity profile this level of rigor can only be reached with the aid of computational techniques.
abstracts.010235: GK 框架与奇迹信条（Miracle Creed）框架是近期最简方案最前沿的探索理 论之一，本文旨在对两个框架的理论背景、修正演化及其应用做一个简单的介绍。现今 Chomsky 前沿理论最核心的思想是“理论极简性”，而两个框架在消除一些前代理论的特设独立操作，充分运用第三因素给出一套即满足“理论极简性”又具有跨语言普遍性的理论框架正是践行了这个思想。同时，文中也会探讨两个框架在汉语部分问题的可行性。
abstracts.010236: This work is a collection of syntactic and morphological observations on the Frisian language of the 17th and 18th centuries. The observations presented here were collected as I read through all Frisian texts of this period for my two anthologies of Frisian literature of this period. If the Dutch language of these centuries is already severely understudied, one can imagine how much worse this is for a minority language like Frisian. The lay-out of the present work is quite simple. The observations are classified by syntactic category. The relevant example sentences are given, glossed, translated and it is briefly explained how these examples contrast with Modern Frisian. The first draft of this work was written in Frisian, but the present version was rewritten in English, because Frisian studies need all the help they can get, and who knows whether this work catches somebody’s fancy.
abstracts.010237: An unexpected sloppy reading of proper names is observed, and its idiosyncratic properties are listed.
abstracts.010238: I show that the approach to the distinct binding properties of A vs. Ā movement proposed by Sauerland (1998, 2004), Ruys (2000), and especially van Urk (2015) derives the Ban on Improper Movement (the generalization that Ā movement cannot feed A movement). I argue that this is a good result because the Ban on Improper Movement makes correct predictions, and moreover alternative generalizations like the Generalized Ban on Improper Movement/Williams Cycle and the Generalized A-after-Ā Constraint fail to generate certain kinds of attested syntactic phenomena (e.g. raising to object in some languages, Ā-movement-fed long-distance agreement).
abstracts.010239: I suggest that neg-raising may arise through a general mechanism by which negative utterances are enriched to convey positive information. Concretely, I explore whether the inference from ¬P(φ) to P(¬φ) can be explained by assuming that ¬P(φ) addresses a question like { P(φ), P(¬φ) }, which presupposes ¬P(φ) → P(¬φ). I present evidence in favour of this conjecture, but also identify some challenges that an account of neg-raising based on this model would need to address.
abstracts.010240: Formal semantics typically assumes that the interpretation relation linking a linguistic unit to its denotation is functional, treating ambiguity—especially structural ambiguity—as a phenomenon to be resolved grammatically. However, if ambiguity were fully resolved within the linguistic system, widespread and well-documented misunderstandings would not arise. We instead model the interpretation relation as non-functional in the strict mathematical sense. Accordingly, ⟦·⟧ᴵ is redefined as a function that collects the set of possible denotations of a given linguistic unit under a relation I, while disambiguation is handled pragmatically via a choice function γ. Misunderstanding arises when γ differs across interlocutors. We further argue that constituency ambiguities motivate flattened semantic representations: ⟦·⟧ᴵ operates over LCA(S), and FA* computes type-filtered sets of denotations. The full characterization of γ is left as an open research program.
abstracts.010243: Interpreting quality can shape how an asylum applicant's account is understood, while UK inspection and guidance documents continue to identify challenges involving language matching, interpreter preparation and quality assurance. This pilot study operationalises translation literacy as explicit reflection on translation choices, semantic range, alternatives, evidence, consequences and evaluation. Twenty-one Arabic-English bilingual adults completed unguided pre- and post-framework translation-evaluation tasks after guided exposure either to TRACE, a five-step mnemonic reflection scaffold, or to an active structured control checklist. Eighty-four responses were scored on a six-dimension rubric by the original marker and three independent blinded raters; analyses used the mean of the four ratings. TRACE did not produce a statistically significant advantage over control on combined change scores (TRACE +1.48/24; control +2.33/24; U=47.0, p=.597). Alternatives showed the clearest TRACE-aligned descriptive pattern, but the between-group change difference was non-significant. The findings therefore do not establish TRACE superiority or a general causal effect of structured reflection.
