They instead identify a feasible measurement approach and hypotheses for larger, better-balanced studies using professional interpreters, delayed retention testing and spoken high-stakes tasks.
abstracts.010244: This study is concerned with the so-called clausal demonstrative in Czech -- the morphologically invariable demonstrative "to", which is morphologically related to the ordinary nominal demonstrative, but differs from it in that it attaches to finite clauses. Based on an informal corpus study, I distinguish three different uses of the clausal demonstrative -- the topic-related use, the focus-related use (akin to clefts), and the thetic use. The theoretical proposal has a syntactic and a semantic part. In syntax, the clausal demonstrative lexically encodes an array of left-peripheral heads (Top-Foc-Fin), each of which corresponds to one use type. The semantic proposal relies on the idea that the clausal demonstrative inherits the core property of the nominal demonstrative: it establishes a relation (typically identity) between the (propositional) denotation of the demonstrative's complement and a contextually salient (propositional) referent.
abstracts.010245: In this paper, I argue that Mandarin verb doubling (VD) with locative and directional spatial phrases (SpXPs) provides evidence for a division of labour between syntax and postsyntax in the derivation of doubling effects. The central empirical diagnostic comes from the distribution of SpXPs and from their effects on event interpretation. When a predicate selects locative or directional material as a complement, the selected SpXP patterns differently from an ordinary modifier, revealing a complement–modifier asymmetry. This pattern extends recent analyses of Mandarin VD (Lai 2021; Lai 2024; Yan 2025; Meadows and Yan 2023), which focus primarily on doubling configurations in which this asymmetry is not at issue. Building on the view that predicate fronting can permit multiple copy realisation (Landau 2006), I propose that locative and directional VD are derived by predicate fronting in syntax, followed by postsyntactic operations that determine which portions of the higher and lower copies are pronounced. This analysis predicts the range of Mandarin VD patterns involving SpXPs and other types of postverbal ma- terial.
abstracts.010246: Previous literature has investigated how quantificational sentences like 'Most of the dots are blue' are understood, using visual tasks which force participants to estimate numbers of dots. In this paper, we report two experiments which show that a participant's performance on a task involving the quantifier Most can be predicted by their performance on a `baseline' task which does not involve Most. Furthermore, this task does not need to be visual: an auditory task can be used to establish this prediction. We argue that this phenomenon is partly explained by different speakers sharing a specific, stable way of understanding the quantifier Most involving a subtraction operator. Because different speakers all represent Most this way, each of their behaviors is predictable, once that speaker's general acuity in non-linguistic number cognition is determined. We draw some consequences for the theories of linguistic meaning.
abstracts.010247: Asante Twi is a language where numerals and mass nouns may freely combine without the need for a classifier or container phrase. Other languages with this feature, such as Yudja and Nez Perce treat every noun as grammatically count and are considered to be the same type according to Chierchia’s 2021 typology of mass-count systems. Against the predictions of this typology, Asante Twi has nouns that are notionally count and grammatically mass, called object-mass nouns. These nouns are likely a result of the decaying noun class system. Furthermore, the mass-count system of Asante Twi more closely resembles English, despite the difference in how the two languages treat numeral-noun constructions. Ultimately, the whole mass-count system should be considered to make predictions on the existence of object-mass nouns in a language.
abstracts.010248: This paper proposes a universal account of counting constructions. The observable variation in such constructions can be categorized into four possible systems resulting from parametric variation of two linguistic properties - NP[+/-pred] (whether the NP starts out as a predicate or a kind term) and Card/CL (whether cardinal and classifier heads are fused). The four systems show different patterns vis-à-vis overt occurrence of number-marking plurals (of the English type) and numeral classifiers - they are either obligatorily complementary, or obligatorily absent, or they obligatorily co-occur. The first two systems have been extensively studied, and the third has been argued to be impossible. This paper introduces novel data from Khasi, which exhibits such a system. Independent support for the proposed typology comes from languages where the cardinal and classifier form a complex morphological unit. In one such language, Ch’ol, numeral classifiers are not grammatically compatible with borrowed Spanish cardinals, supporting that they too are cardinal/classifier units but morphologically non-transparent.
abstracts.010249: This paper develops a unified analysis of definite and demonstrative descriptions, arguing that reference is decomposable into a small set of semantically independent building blocks: uniqueness in a restricted situation, an anaphoric index, a deictic relation, and anti-uniqueness in a larger situation. Drawing on original fieldwork data from Mizo, I show that cross-linguistic variation in definite and demonstrative expressions (henceforth D-expressions) reflects different ways of distributing these components across the nominal spine. A key finding is that what distinguishes a demonstrative description is not deictic value per se, but an anti-uniqueness presupposition. The Mizo data make this transparent: several determiner morphemes encode deictic properties, yet without the anti-uniqueness component, such determiners yield definite rather than demonstrative descriptions. In Mizo, D-expressions appear in two morphological configurations, NP-D and D-NP-D, which diverge in precisely two distributional properties: compatibility with globally unique descriptions (such as the sun) and the ability to be used contrastively (as in X while Y ). I argue that this split reduces to anti-uniqueness: its presence renders an expression incompatible with globally unique descriptions and licenses contrastive use, while its absence has the opposite effect (Robinson 2005; Dayal and Jiang 2022; Dayal in prep). Within the proposed framework,the D-NP-D configuration is maximally specified, combining anti-uniqueness (contributed by the pre-nominal morpheme) with the remaining components supplied by the post-nominal D; it is this combination, rather than the demonstrative category as such, that is semantically maximal. The analysis extends cross-linguistically to Akan and Bangla, showing that while all three languages share the same division of labor between reference, indexicality, deixis, and antiuniqueness, they differ in how these components are morphosyntactically realized. The proposed decomposition also bears on the distinction between this and that in English (Elbourne 2008): I tentatively explore the possibility that the two differ in whether an anaphoric index is encoded, with this patterning with Mizo deictic expressions in lacking one, though a full treatment is left for future work. The paper advances two central claims: anti-uniqueness is an independent semantic ingredient rather than a pragmatic by-product of deixis or anaphora, and the traditional opposition between definites and demonstratives reflects different combinations of independently available reference-building mechanisms.
abstracts.010250: Using formal parameters and universal cartography, it is possible to account for linguistic variation in Chinese dialects, which display systematic microvariation within a common core grammar. This is particularly useful for the teaching of Chinese as a second language, as there is a growing interest in Chinese, not only in standard Mandarin but also in Cantonese which is immensely popular in the West and mainland China. As cartography seeks a universal word order from which language-specific parameter-settings are derived, the following schemata can account for Chinese dialects: 1) C(omp) Subj(ect) T(ense) Adv(erb) V(erb)-Aff(ix) Obj(ect) S(entence)F(inal)P(article) 2) Possessor Poss Dem(onstrative) Num(ber) Q(uantifier) Cl(assifier) Adj(ective) N(oun) In the clausal (1) and nominal (2) domains, the head-initiality of Chinese correlates with commonly spoken languages like English and Romance, which facilitates the acquisition of Chinese by many foreigners. Furthermore, these schemata permit a systematic account of the microvariation between Chinese dialects, since while Mandarin and Cantonese share forms for the same categories (e.g. C: 因爲because... 所以and so..., 雖然although... 但是/係but..., 如果if... 就then...; T: 會will/shall, 應該should, 要must, 想want; V-aff: completive aspectual 了/咗, anterior aspectual 過, stative aspectual 著/住; Poss: 的/嘅, Dem: 這/呢(proximal), 那/嗰(distal)), dialectal variation can be classified in three types: 1) dialectal forms exist in Cantonese but not in Mandarin e.g. progressive V-aff 緊(3) 2) different word order, namely Cantonese postverbal adverbs and Mandarin preverbal ones (先’before’(4), 多’more’(5), 少’less’(6)) 3) new constructions, like Cantonese classifiers heading noun phrases denoting articles, which indicates Cl-to-Poss movement (7): 3)外邊 响度 落-緊 雨 / 外面 正在 下 雨 outside AUX fall-PROG rain outside AUX fall rain ‘It is raining outside.’ (Cantonese/Mandarin) 4)我哋 行 先 / 我們 先 走 we go first we first go ‘Let’s go first.’ (Cantonese/Mandarin) 5a) 我哋 諗-住 再 住 多 三 日 we think-ASP again live more three day 5b) 我們 想-著 再 多 住 三 天 we think-ASP again more live three day ‘We are thinking of staying for three more days.’(Cantonese(5a)/Mandarin(5b)) 6a) 我 俾 少 十 分 嗰 個 學生 I give less ten mark that CL student 6b) 我 少 給 那 個 學生 十 分 I less give that CL student ten mark ‘I gave ten marks less to that student.’ (Cantonese(6a)/Mandarin(6b)) 7a) 架 車 阻-住 個 出口 CL car block-ASP CL exit 7b) 這 輛 車 阻-著 出口 this CL car block-ASP exit ‘The car is blocking the exit.’ (Cantonese(7a)/Mandarin(7b)) Based on these examples, the dialectal parametric setting for Cantonese can be represented thus: 8) C Subj T Adv V-Aff(緊) Obj Adv (多/少/先) SFP 9) Possessor Poss(CL-D) Dem Num Q Cl Adj N
abstracts.010251: This is a paper that passed the MPhil to PhD viva upgrade process. It is part of my work in progress PhD thesis. It deals with the morphosyntax of tense, aspect, and aktionsart of my dialect, Hasawi Arabic. I argue that by scrutinizing the morphosyntax of auxiliary verbs with lexical verbs, one could arrive at the morphosyntactic structure (1), where tense is higher than aspect, and aspect is higher than aktionsart. I show how this is reflected in Hasawi Arabic's morphosyntax by templatic morphology. Being a viva upgrade paper and a work in progress, this paper suffers from several drawbacks, one of which is a lack of literature review on the morphosyntax of Arabic verbs. Comments and scathing criticism are welcome.
abstracts.010252: Using formal parameters and universal cartography, it is possible to account for linguistic variation in Chinese dialects, which display systematic microvariation within a common core grammar. This is particularly useful for the teaching of Chinese as a second language, as there is a growing interest in Chinese, not only in standard Mandarin but also in Cantonese which is immensely popular in the West and mainland China. As cartography seeks a universal word order from which language-specific parameter-settings are derived, the following schemata can account for Chinese dialects: 1) C(omp) Subj(ect) T(ense) Adv(erb) V(erb)-Aff(ix) Obj(ect) S(entence)F(inal)P(article) 2) Possessor Poss Dem(onstrative) Num(ber) Q(uantifier) Cl(assifier) Adj(ective) N(oun) In the clausal (1) and nominal (2) domains, the head-initiality of Chinese correlates with commonly spoken languages like English and Romance, which facilitates the acquisition of Chinese by many foreigners. Furthermore, these schemata permit a systematic account of the microvariation between Chinese dialects, since while Mandarin and Cantonese share forms for the same categories (e.g. C: 因爲because... 所以and so..., 雖然although... 但是/係but..., 如果if... 就then...; T: 會will/shall, 應該should, 要must, 想want; V-aff: completive aspectual 了/咗, anterior aspectual 過, stative aspectual 著/住; Poss: 的/嘅, Dem: 這/呢(proximal), 那/嗰(distal)), dialectal variation can be classified in three types: 1) dialectal forms exist in Cantonese but not in Mandarin e.g. progressive V-aff 緊(3) 2) different word order, namely Cantonese postverbal adverbs and Mandarin preverbal ones (先’before’(4), 多’more’(5), 少’less’(6)) 3) new constructions, like Cantonese classifiers heading noun phrases denoting articles, which indicates Cl-to-Poss movement (7): 3) 外邊 响度 落-緊 雨 / 外面 正在 下 雨 outside AUX fall-PROG rain outside AUX fall rain ‘It is raining outside.’ (Cantonese/Mandarin) 4) 我哋 行 先 / 我們 先 走 we go first we first go ‘Let’s go first.’ (Cantonese/Mandarin) 5a) 我哋 諗-住 再 住 多 三 日 we think-ASP again live more three day 5b) 我們 想-著 再 多 住 三 天 we think-ASP again more live three day ‘We are thinking of staying for three more days.’(Cantonese(5a)/Mandarin(5b)) 6a) 我 俾 少 十 分 嗰 個 學生 I give less ten mark that CL student 6b) 我 少 給 那 個 學生 十 分 I less give that CL student ten mark ‘I gave ten marks less to that student.’ (Cantonese(6a)/Mandarin(6b)) 7a) 架 車 阻-住 個 出口 CL car block-ASP CL exit 7b) 這 輛 車 阻-著 出口 this CL car block-ASP exit ‘The car is blocking the exit.’ (Cantonese(7a)/Mandarin(7b)) Based on these examples, the dialectal parametric setting for Cantonese can be represented thus: 8) C Subj T Adv V-Aff(緊) Obj Adv (多/少/先) SFP 9) Possessor Poss(CL-D) Dem Num Q Cl Adj N
abstracts.010253: English lexical causatives typically entail result realization when used with a perfective aspect. A subset of these predicates, known as defeasible causatives, form an exception: with non-volitional subjects, they yield a culminating reading and entail the result, whereas with volitional subjects, they also allow a zero result non-culminating reading, in which the result is merely implicated and can be cancelled. This correlation between volitionality and the zero result non-culminating reading (V-ZR correlation) is captured by Demirdache and Martin’s (2015) Agent Control Hypothesis (ACH). Most existing accounts adopt a result cancellation approach, assuming a single result-encoding predicate underlying both readings. Drawing on new data from Mandarin and English, I argue against this assumption and propose instead a dual event structure approach: the culminating reading involves an achievement predicate, which encodes a result, while the zero result non-culminating reading involves an activity or accomplishment predicate, which does not. This view, also advocated by Piñón (2014), leaves open why the zero result non-culminating reading typically requires a volitional subject. I address this question by developing a causal-model-based account.
abstracts.010254: Transition points, the beginnings and ends of events, are linguistically significant, as they figure prominently in predicate classification. This work studies how transition points are represented in language and proposes the One Transition Point Hypothesis (OTPH), which states that each event can linguistically encode at most one transition point, thereby ruling out the cooccurrence of both transition points in the same structure. I derive this hypothesis by building on Travis’s (1991, 2002, 2005, 2010) proposal of an inner Asp head, which I argue is responsible for licensing both transition points. This analysis carries significant implications for predicate classification as well as for θ-role assignment.
abstracts.010255: div.a { text-indent: 50px; } [This is a slightly modified version of the dissertation available on ProQuest. Please refer to this version for citation.] Quantifier doubling is a ubiquitous phenomenon in natural languages that raises important issues for the syntax-semantics interface. Quantifier doubling refers to cases where two quantifier expressions occur in a sentence, but apparently only one is interpreted as logical quantification. For instance, in languages like Cantonese, Mandarin, Vietnamese, among others, “John only bought lamb only” may mean ‘John only bought lamb.’ This is referred to as “exclusive doubling” (focus particle concord). A form-meaning mismatch is found, which raises an issue of how syntax is mapped onto semantics. More generally, there is an intuitive sense that quantifier doubling is “redundant”: if one suffices, why two? This dissertation motivates a novel view on the mapping between syntax and semantics to provide a principled explanation for quantifier doubling, with a special focus on the doubling of exclusive focus particles. I hypothesize that quantifier doubling is a parametric strategy for languages to realize complex meaning structures with meaning pieces in distinct dimensions of (not-)at-issueness. Specifically, quantifier doubling is a syntactic manifestation (“syntacticization”) of quantification structures that are otherwise lexicalized as a whole in languages without doubling. Based on East Asian, Southeast Asian and West African languages including Cantonese, Mandarin, Vietnamese, and Yorùbá, I argue that exclusive doubling instantiates scalar focus structures. Specifically, one particle encodes at-issue exclusivity, such as the adverbial particle zinghai `only' in Cantonese, while the other particle `only’ contributes a not-at-issue scalar component that ranks the prejacent lower than excluded alternatives on a contextually salient scale, such as the sentence-final particle (SFP) zaa3 in Cantonese. In other words, both particles in exclusive doubling are not semantically vacuous: they have focus-sensitive contributions, though on two separate dimensions of (not-)at-issueness. Therefore, exclusive doubling is neither redundant nor purely syntactic, but reflects a structured division of semantic labor. Moreover, I discuss how alternatives can be accessed and the consequences for intervention effects. I argue for a syntactio-semantic dependency in exclusive doubling. The scalar operator and the exclusive operator share the same quantificational domain, which is the alternative set they quantify over. I propose a co-indexation approach for alternative accessing. The quantificational domains of the exclusive and scalar operators, which are the alternative sets, are co-indexed via syntactic Agree that transmits indices. This approach receives support from a radical immediate scope constraint that underlies the intervention effects in doubling of adverbial particles with SFPs, and the locality of (c)overt movement in doubling of adverbial particles with adfocal particles. Precisely, only truth-condition-altering quantificational elements that intervene between the scope of the two particles trigger intervention effects in exclusive doubling, but non-truth-conditional focus operators do not. These quantifier-only intervention effects speak against a syntactic minimality account and a semantic alternative-based account, and call for a semantic account that draws on illicit scopal configurations that follow from the co-indexation approach. I also discuss the role of witnessability of quantifiers in creating a widest scope that escapes intervention effects. The implications are that higher operators may have multiple pathways to access lower alternatives, and moreover the notion of “intervention effects” is best understood as a descriptive label for a heterogeneous set of phenomena spanning syntax and semantics. Last but not least, I address the locus of quantification in the clausal and nominal domains. I demonstrate that both A-quantification (clausal) and D-quantification (nominal) are available strategies for natural language to express exclusives, but the choice is parameterized. Concretely, adverbial exclusive particles in Vietnamese carry the semantic import, whereas in Yorùbá it is the adfocal exclusive particles that carry the semantic exclusion. The locus of scalarity shows a mirroring pattern, which is on the adfocal particles in Vietnamese but on the adverbial particles in Yorùbá. A battery of tests based on association and scopal behaviors is proposed for testing the semantic import. Applying this set of tests to other languages, I develop a parametric analysis that yields a four-way typology of exclusives, extended to languages such as Kasem where the exclusive semantics is neither encoded by adverbial nor adfocal particles, but by a null operator; and to Mandarin, where the exclusive semantics is encoded by both adverbial and adfocal particles. This four-way typology is similar to the typology of negative concord, supporting the clausal-nominal parallelism in different domains of quantification. Taken together, this dissertation offers an answer to “why doubling” by arguing that quantifier doubling distributes meaning across multiple elements while regulating their interaction through syntactio-semantic dependencies. The findings contribute to theories of quantification, focus association, and the interface between syntax and semantics. They also lay the groundwork for future research on cross-linguistic variations in focus operators and other concord phenomena.
abstracts.010256: Building on Geurts' (2019) programmatic proposal, this paper develops a commitment-based model of Scalar Implicatures (SIs) that shifts the explanatory focus from speaker intentions and mental states to the dynamics between private commitments and their social expression. The model accounts for both standard scalar inferences and cases in which speakers’ private stances remain partially opaque, offering a socially grounded alternative to intention-based accounts, with broad implications for the analysis of SIs across speech acts and the explanation of cross-cultural variation.
abstracts.010257: In this paper, we discuss optional agreement with third-person plural postverbal subjects of existential there clauses in New York City English. Data were obtained from the CUNY Corpus of New York City English, (CUNY-CoNYCE), an approximately two-million word corpus of extemporaneous speech from 202 participants raised in the New York City Dialect region (Tortora et al. 2025). The results of our study, along with the native-speaker grammaticality judgments of the author(s), suggest that both singular and plural verbal agreement is freely available for speakers of NYC English with 3pl postverbal subjects of existential clauses. We model the syntax of this optionally-realized agreement in terms of a single grammatical system—i.e., not as the result of multiple competing grammars (e.g., Kroch 1989, a.o.)—based in the Strong Minimalist Thesis (SMT) (Chomsky 2021; 2024). Ultimately, we analyze this instance of variable agreement as the result of the grammar allowing for multiple interpretable outputs generated in the narrow syntax. Additionally, this system permits language users’ extragrammatical preferences to constrain the frequency of use of optional forms based on interaction with variables such as tense. We provide a novel set of tools for analyzing cases of intra-speaker variation that cannot be clearly attributed to underlying multilectalism.
abstracts.010258: AXIS2026-M1 (v2) operationalizes the transition from paleographic character components to clausal syntax in Chinese, introducing the Four Pins (四拼) Pipeline: Pinyin (拼音) --> Pinyi (拼義) --> Pinzi (拼字) --> Pinzhi (拼枝). The paper replaces abstract phonological operators with a testable ZTVC (Zero / Tone / Consonant / Vowel) shift analysis and introduces the M7 Clausal Assembler to contrast paratactic Chinese clausal chaining against Germanic hypotaxis. Includes worked case studies on the gǔ (鼓) percussion continuum, the dòu (逗) spatio-temporal pauses, the jū/jù (居) postural shifts, the architectural distinction between zhì (製) and zuò (做), the self-referential bìng/pīn (并 --> 併 --> 拼 --> 摒) cycle, and the cross-linguistic Twin-Idiom Bridge linking jiéjū (拮据) morpheme-by-morpheme to "hand-to-mouth" and "credit crunch." (Note: This unified edition supersedes and retires working papers AXIS2026-M1 v1 and AXIS2026-M2).
abstracts.010259: Traditional Chinese phonology reconstructs the Middle Chinese Lai initial(来母) as the alveolar lateral approximant [l]. However, this reconstruction fails to account for its classification as a "tongue sound" (sheyin 舌音) in the Yunjing and for its distributional property of lacking chongniu doublets. This paper examines the phonological classification of Middle Chinese tongue sounds and proposes that the Lai initial should instead be reconstructed as the palatal lateral approximant [ʎ]. An articulatory analysis of [ʎ] indicates that it developed from the voiced palatal affricate [dʝ]. Drawing on previous scholarship regarding the palatalization mechanism of the Jian initial(见母), this study further demonstrates that the Middle Chinese Qun initial [ɡ] could likewise derive from [dʝ]. On this basis, the paper proposes a mechanism to account for the alternation between the Jian and Lai initials: certain characters classified under the Lai or Jian initials in the fanqie system of the Qieyun in fact shared the initial [dʝ] in Old Chinese, thereby obviating the need for the traditional *kl- cluster hypothesis. The affricate [dʝ] corresponds to the Middle Chinese Cheng initial. Its complementary counterpart, the Ding initial, is reconstructed as the labialized voiced palatal affricate [dʝʷ]. The sound [dʝʷ] could follow an analogous evolutionary path, diverging into the Qun initial of Division IV [ɡy] and the velar lateral approximant [ʟ], the latter being the proposed reconstruction for the Middle Chinese Xia initial(匣母). This provides an explanation for the classical dictum that "the third-division Yun initial belongs to the Xia initial" (yu san gui xia 喻三归匣): characters classified under the Yun or Xia initials in the Qieyun fanqie system shared the initial [dʝʷ] in Old Chinese.
abstracts.010261: This paper investigates why some predicates are compatible with quantification over parts of singular individuals, while others are not. For example, Most of the trail is narrow is acceptable, but #Most of the trail is short is not. I propose a constraint on quantification over parts, which derives the contrast between quantification-compatible and quantification-resistant predicates from an independently motivated pragmatic principle banning contextual equivalence among scalar alternatives. This analysis explains when and why quantification over parts of singular individuals gives rise to infelicity, and it naturally extends to the phenomenon of quantification compatibility in collective predication, known as the gather/numerous distinction.
abstracts.010262: This study examines changes in secondary school students' perception of the difficulty of Chinese Sign Language (CSL), and analyzes the suggestions proposed by participants. Through a questionnaire survey, data on sign language awareness were collected from 184 secondary school students. The results indicate that although most students had been exposed to sign language through online platforms, public welfare activities, and other channels, their perception of its difficulty shifted noticeably after exposure to basic sign language linguistics. Notably, students commonly reported that their unfamiliarity with sign language stemmed primarily from a lack of formal learning platforms.
abstracts.010263: This paper focuses on a series of puzzles in the semantics of the so-called subjective attitudes, zooming in on the behavior of English ﬁnd combined with small clause complements. Find-verbs, as we will call them, have been important in understanding subjectivity in natural language: they select for subjective complements (Q ﬁnds humans 3entertaining/#mortal) and their very existence was often used as an argument in favor of treating subjective predicates (e.g., entertaining but not mortal) as having a special semantics. To this end, ﬁnd-verbs have been largely regarded as subjective counterparts of think-verbs. Focusing on English ﬁnd, we challenge this view and show that ﬁnd exhibits a distinguished linguistic proﬁle not shared by think, including subject-predicate asymmetries in the embedded clause, the lack of referential opacity and the similarity to emotive factives, aspectual class and the acquaintance requirement. We propose a principled account of these seemingly unrelated properties by appealing to the small clause syntax and the lexical semantics of ﬁnd, including its argument structure and the nature of eventuality it describes. We argue that some idiosyncratic features of ﬁnd follow naturally once it’s seen within a broader context of what we dub ‘characterizing verbs’, which express evaluation and take structured proposition arguments. We further show that, based on the interpretation of referential DPs in its scope, ﬁnd is best understood as a knowledge verb, not as a belief verb. Finally, we establish that several properties of ﬁnd are due to the fact that it is an achievement predicate describing a complex event of judgment formation caused by an event of encounter. We remain deliberately agnostic about the exact nature of the attitude ﬁnd encodes: our account is compatible both with views under which ﬁnd encodes a belief and with views under which ﬁnd encodes a non-cognitive, affective state. By treating ﬁnd ﬁrst and foremost as a verb, and not only as a litmus test for subjectivity, we aim to emphasize the importance of linguistic data for the debates in philosophy of language and to contribute to the burgeoning research agenda on the ﬁne-grained semantics of attitude predicates.
abstracts.010264: This paper investigates the syntax of present active participles in Polish, morphologically similar forms that nevertheless split into agreeing and invariant types. Agreeing participles show full φ-agreement and appear in adjectival environments, while invariant participles lack agreement and function as adverbial, converb-like modifiers. Despite this contrast, both types retain core verbal properties, including argument structure and aspectual interpretation. I argue that this split does not reflect a categorial distinction between verbs and adjectives. Instead, both participle types are derived from the same verbal structure and the difference follows from the presence or absence of an additional φ-probe and from structural position. Agreement is licensed by syntactic Agree, not by recategorization to adjective. Adopting a feature-driven minimalist approach, I propose that non-categorial features such as φ can provide labels under the Labeling Algorithm, making an adjectival head unnecessary. Present active participles will therefore be defined as "centaur" constructions, showing properties of multiple categories, which however does not entail syntactic category change.
abstracts.010265: Abstract: This article develops a theory of syntactic selection and adjunction (based on Zeijlstra 20920) in which labeling follows directly from Merge and feature percolation, rather than from an independent labeling algorithm. Syntactic objects carry two types of formal features: independent features, which determine categorial status, and dependent features, which encode syntactic dependencies. When two objects merge, matching independent and dependent features under sisterhood do not percolate, whereas all other features do. This derives projection by selection while also accounting for adjunction: adjuncts are analyzed as elements that select their hosts while preserving their categorial status. Extending the analysis to PPs and clausal arguments yields a restricted theory of c-selection in which verbs syntactically select DPs (including nominalized clauses), whereas PPs and non-nominalized clauses function as predicate modifiers that select the verbal expressions they combine with. Finally, the proposal unifies local selection with long-distance Agree. Whereas independent features cannot percolate beyond their maximal projections, dependent features may percolate until they enter a local sisterhood relation with a matching independent feature. Upward Agree thus reduces to postponed local selection. The resulting architecture provides a unified account of labeling, selection, adjunction, and Agree.
abstracts.010266: The philosophy of language, along with formal-logical methods of analytic philosophy and formal semantics, is a relatively young field of inquiry in linguistics, despite being deeply rooted in philosophy since ancient times. The aim of this thesis is to identify and provide, using philosophical argument and logical formulations respectively, the ontological status of modality and indexes as seen in natural language use and their implied truth-conditions. The design follows a descriptive-analytical pattern, with a methodology of tackling each linguistic category and sub-category individually – starting by presenting their best arguments to-date, their detailed critiques and shortcomings, my own approach to the issues, followed by the resulting formal representations and their emergent constraints on meaning. The outcome of this analysis is a distinctly formulated schema of the tackled linguistic phenomena and their implications on their undiluted logical forms prior to the introduction of any context, with the implications of what this signifies for human cognition and the ontology of language, opening the path to further research and establishing the key role of semantics within such inquiries.
abstracts.010267: This article gives an analysis of Mandarin Chinese third tone sandhi. We focus on the foundations of third tone sandhi by concentrating on strings of digits and lists, commonly referred to as 'unstructured' strings, whose sandhi patterns are not influenced by morphosyntactic structure. We introduce data from a series of elicitation experiments that show, contrary to popular belief, that such strings in fact manifest internal structure and vary radically in terms of the sandhi patterns they exhibit. We analyze a variety of these patterns using a combination of Match Theory and Stochastic Optimality Theory. The former enables the description of the interplay between sandhi domains, metrical feet, and the aforementioned structural properties of the strings, while the latter is a probabilistic model well-suited for modeling interactions among competing factors of different strengths and describing the asymmetric patterns of variation like those found in our empirical data.
abstracts.010268: This paper presents a unified Optimality Theoretic analysis of left-dominant word-level tone sandhi in Shanghainese. The proposal consists of a single constraint hierarchy capable of accounting for the disparate sandhi behavior initiated by the language's five lexical tones. By appealing to one basic faithfulness condition and one correspondence constraint that formalizes a familiar rightward shifting pattern, the analysis can account for the major tone melodies induced by each of the five tones—from disyllables to tetrasyllabic expressions—with five additional markedness conditions that regulate only tone melodies in general, including an avoidance of adjacent High tones and an avoidance of melody reversal. One additional contour-faithfulness constraint extends the grammar's coverage to accurately predict the monosyllabic citation forms for each tone from its underlying representation.
abstracts.010269: This contribution discusses strict negative concord, frequently considered a major argument for Upward Agree whereby feature-defective probes are c-commanded by feature-complete goals. By focusing on the interaction between long-distance scrambling and negative concord in Russian, I formulate a challenge for Upward Agree. The facts are then shown to be trivially compatible with Downward Agree whereby probes c-command goals.
abstracts.010270: An in-situ wh-question is generally considered degraded if the wh-phrase is preceded by a focus phrase, a phenomenon known as ‘focus intervention effects’. In syntax and semantics, focus intervention effects have been considered crucial evidence for various grammatical approaches to wh-in-situ questions. However, the degradedness of sentences involving focus intervention effects has long been disputed, especially in the face of pragmatic manipulations on wh-phrases and focus phrases. The present study reports three experiments probing the role of two pragmatic factors in focus intervention effects: the givenness of a focus phrase and the linguistic informativity of a wh-phrase, using both acceptability judgment and self-paced reading tasks. The experimental results show that linguistic informativity does not influence focus intervention effects, whereas focus givenness leads to a facilitation effect in both tasks. However, the facilitation does not completely eliminate focus intervention effects. Based on these findings, we reaffirm the relevance of grammatical approaches to focus intervention effects developed in the syntax and the semantics tradition while also acknowledging the partial role of pragmatics.
abstracts.010271: Northern Toussian (ISO: tsp; Glottocode: nort2787) is a minority Niger-Congo lan- guage spoken in southwest Burkina Faso by the Toussian people. The Toussian languages are of uncertain genetic affiliation—they were originally classified as Gur (Mabia) languages, but the classification of the family has been disputed (Prost 1964, Naden 1989, Miehe 2012, Güldemann 2018). While there is adequate evidence to consider the Toussian languages to be Niger Congo, there has not been sufficient research to confidently assign it to a particular branch of the Niger-Congo family tree. This is much the same situation of the other so-called “peripheral Gur” languages like the Senoufo, Tiéfo, and Samu families, as well as the language Viemo. More precise classification of these languages not only requires historical linguistic work on Gur and each of these groups individually, but also consideration of the relationship of certain members of the Adamawa family, some of which have been shown to share many features in common with Gur languages (Kleinewillinghöfer 1996).
abstracts.010272: This paper explores the connection between the opacity of phases and their status as spellout domains. Based on evidence from West Circassian, I argue that while a subset of phases are salient prosodic domains, syntactic opacity is not a consequence of transfer to PF, but of standard conditions on locality. Furthermore, the relation between phasehood and prosodic constituency holds only partially: some phases are not salient prosodic domains. West Circassian provides a compelling illustration of this mismatch due its polysynthetic profile. On the one hand, a complex syntactic constituent is identifiable as a prosodic domain due to being pronounced as a single prosodic word. On the other, the connection between syntactic opacity and locality constraints is demonstrated by dynamic phasehood which is connected to the licensing of polysynthetic phi-agreement.
abstracts.010273: In this paper, I discuss two approaches to selective opacity: the Missing Triggers Approach (van Urk 2015, Longenbaugh 2019, Grano and Lasnik 2018, a.m.o.) and the Level Embedding Approach (Williams 2003, 2011, Poole 2022, Meadows 2023, Egressy 2025, 2026, a.o.). I provide new data from Georgian that corroborates a key challenge for the Missing Triggers Approach (Meadows 2023, 2024): it requires additional constraints on possible orderings of feature triggers that do not follow from the phase theory on its own. The Level Embedding Approach faces challenges too: besides issues of hyperraising and intermediate phases (see Meadows 2023 for discussion), none of the existing implementations are fully compatible with recent developments in theories of clausal embedding, which suggest that there are two different paths of how embedded clauses can combine with matrix verbs (Bondarenko 2020, Özyıldız 2020, Roberts 2020, Bochnak and Hanink 2021, Bondarenko 2022, Özyıldız and Uegaki 2023, 2024, a.o.). Since assumptions about how clauses are embedded are critical to the Level Embedding Approach, it is important to see if the two strands of research can be reconciled with each other. In this paper, I show that they can: that the framework in which clauses are treated as predicates of entities that modify either the event argument of the verb or its nominal argument (Kratzer 2006, 2016, Moulton 2009, Bogal-Allbritten 2016, Elliott 2020, a.o.) naturally allows for Late Merge (Lebeaux 1988) and Wholesale Late Merge (Takahashi and Hulsey 2009) of clausal complements, in line with the late-insertion requirement of the Level Embedding Approach. My proposal makes a prediction: that we should see selective opacity effects regardless of whether the clause combines by modifying the nominal argument or the event argument of the verb. I examine the case of Georgian, and show that this prediction is borne out.
abstracts.010274: The Williams Cycle (Williams 2003) generalizes the correlation between a clause’s relative size and its selective opacity. Most previous accounts (Keine 2020, Poole 2022; Meadows 2023) maintain Phase Theory (Chomsky 2001) to explain reflexes of successive cyclicity, and propose an independent mechanism to derive Williams Cycle effects. I propose a unified analysis of Williams Cycle effects and successive cyclicity.Under my unified constraint, probing must proceed along well-formed functional sequence fragments. When cross-clausal subextraction proceeds successive cyclically, Williams Cycle effects are obviated. When successive cyclicity is unavailable, the clause’s movement to an equal-sized matrix projection feeds subextraction, but subextraction obeys the Williams Cycle.
abstracts.010275: Was magnitude estimation necessary to establish acceptability judgments as serious linguistic measurements? I separate Bard, Robertson, and Sorace's broader case for graded acceptability from the narrower claim that magnitude estimation improves on simpler formal tasks. Using public method-comparison data from Sprouse, Schütze, and Almeida (2013) and Sprouse and Almeida (2017), I compare magnitude estimation with Likert, forced-choice, and yes/no judgments. The primary analysis follows a charter fixed before outcome analysis. I find a strong common item-level signal and the bounded Likert curvature that motivates magnitude estimation, but no systematic practical advantage unique to magnitude estimation in endpoint, prediction, or decision diagnostics. A post-outcome multiverse of 162 specifications confirms the result. Four 2017 rank-based forced-choice models show small incremental predictive gains, but these don't generalize to raw-scale models, yes/no judgments, or the 2013 data. The results preserve Bard et al.'s broader contribution (i.e., the formal measurement of graded acceptability) while weakening the case that magnitude estimation has a general practical advantage for the contrasts examined.
abstracts.010276: This study reflects on my work between 2013 (PhD) and 2023 through the lens of form-meaning mismatches. It discusses cases of syncretism and fusion, doubling and multiple exponence, as well as zero-to-one and one-to-zero mismatches, drawing on data from degree morphology, negation and derivational morphology. I show how two central tools of Nanosyntax (Starke 2009, Caha 2009), namely decomposition into syntactico-semantic features and phrasal lexicalisation, allow to account for these phenomena. The study argues that form-meaning mismatches do not require exceptional mechanisms, but follow naturally from the way hierarchically organised feature structures are packaged and stored as lexical items. The same architecture underlies cases in which form and meaning appear to correspond one-to-one. Form-meaning mismatches are nevertheless particularly revealing, as they provide a clear window onto the underlying structure of language.
abstracts.010277: This paper examines long-distance wh-dependencies in Haryanvi, an Indo-Aryan language of northern India, and in particular the construction in which the element "ke" appears in the matrix clause while the interrogative phrase remains in situ in the embedded clause. Haryanvi patterns with Hindi-Urdu in allowing two strategies for forming a long-distance wh-dependency: the wh-phrase may move into the matrix clause, or it may stay in the subordinate clause, in which case "ke" surfaces preverbally in the matrix clause. Drawing on data elicited from native speakers, I establish that the Haryanvi construction obeys the generalisations that have been reported for Hindi-Urdu: the scope of any number of embedded wh-phrases can be extended, a scope marker and a true wh-phrase cannot occur in the same clause, a scope marker must appear in every intervening clause, and the matrix clause can contain neither the sentential expletive yo nor negation. Against this background I argue that "ke" is not a scope marker at all. It is a wh-expletive that questions the sentential expletive "yo," which is base-generated at the edge of the embedded CP and co-indexed with it. Both elements raise to the edge of the matrix vP, so that the surface order follows without the embedded wh-phrase taking matrix scope. The account therefore leaves the wh-in-situ character of Haryanvi and Hindi-Urdu intact. Keywords: wh-expletive, wh-scope marking, wh-in-situ, Haryanvi, Hindi-Urdu
abstracts.010278: This chapter is dedicated to the grammatical category of mood and its relation to modality. It overviews some key empirical phenomena discussed in the literature, such as existence of subjunctive clauses with distinct profiles (selected vs. optional vs. polarity subjunctives), possibility of mood marking in embedded vs. root clauses, as well as mood marking in other environments such as purpose and relative clauses. The chapter compares analyses of these phenomena under three main theoretical approaches, outlining their virtues as well as the challenges that they face: ordering source-based theories, which link the choice of mood to the presence of an ordering source in the semantics of a modal, commitment-based theories, which consider the choice of mood to depend on the truth of the embedded proposition in some dedicated set of possible worlds, and alternatives-based theories, for which mood reflects presence of obligatorily activated focus alternatives to the embedded proposition. The chapter also raises the question of what the contribution of mood morphology is, suggesting that the connection between the modal meanings and mood morphemes is indirect: mood morphemes are better viewed as exponents of agreement with higher modal-introducing elements rather than the source of modality.
abstracts.010279: In this paper we provide both support for, and a challenge to, Takahashi's (2010) proposal that a moved clausal complement must involve a DP structure headed by a covert determiner. Based on data from Georgian, we show that (i) bare CPs cannot move to the left—topicalization in the language is restricted to DPs, just like in English; (ii) CPs can move to the right, and in fact must do so when they are not encapsulated in the DP structure. We argue that rightwards extraposition of CPs is semantically vacuous and driven purely by a constraint on linearization: Georgian CPs are head-initial, while VPs are head-final, and thus remaining in situ would lead to the violation of the Final-Over-Final Constraint (FOFC) (Biberauer et al. 2009a,b, Biberauer and Sheehan 2012, a.o.). For this reason, Georgian bare CPs must vacuously move to conform to the FOFC. We discuss the implications of this conclusion for the ban on bare CP movement leftwards.
abstracts.010280: This study focuses on the syntax-semantic mismatches arising from the doubling of exclusive focus particles ‘only’ in Vietnamese: (i) adverbial chỉ with adfocal mỗi and with (ii) sentence-final particle (SFP) thôi . Despite multiple occurrences, only one particle is interpreted as the exclusive operator. Following the operator-particle approach, I propose that only adverbial chỉ is the operator, which establishes different syntactic dependencies with mỗi and thôi that are truth-conditionally void: (i) covert movement triggered by focus [FOC] features in adverbial-adfocal doubling, and (ii) syntactic Agree with exclusive [EXCL] features in adverbial-SFP doubling. The non-uniformity is supported by their distinct locality profiles and (non-)sensitivity to intervention by quantificational elements. Furthermore, I argue that focus and quantificational elements constitute different featural classes for minimality-based intervention.
abstracts.010281: Proposes some new uses for an old idea (Butt (1993, 1995), Bhatt (2005), Legate (2005), Baker and Willie (2010)): that if X Agrees with Y and Y Agrees with Z, X should be taken for all syntactic and morphological purposes to be in an Agree relation with Z. I refer to the relation between X and Z as 'agreement by proxy', and argue that recognizing agreement by proxy allows for very simple statements on the conditions on locality of Agree. The resulting theory derives a version of the ban on improper movement and on A-movement out of CPs, and predicts correctly that these bans can be circumvented under the right circumstances. It also derives a version of the notion of 'phase unlocking', and accounts for some facts about the interaction of long-distance movement with agreement in Passamaquoddy-Wolastoqey (Algonquian).
abstracts.010282: Diagrams in lexical semantics come in all shapes and sizes, but there is currently no good understanding of the design space that allows for this variety. This paper derives that space from the combination of a small number of graphic and semantic parameters, thereby contributing to our insight in this increasingly common visual metalanguage in linguistics and related disciplines concerned with meaning.
abstracts.010283: Noam Chomsky and his colleagues have proposed that human languages are basically designed for construction of inner thoughts so that individual humans can plan ahead, thus giving selectional advantage to the species. The sound part of language in this view is ancillary, it is meant only for the externalization of thought. Call it a ‘thought-only’ view of language. We challenge this view by showing that the thought-only conception of language cannot accommodate the referential function of languages. We probe the issue with a focus on what philosophers call Singular Terms that enable a language-user to pick out, identify, and draw attention to an individual object. The presence of singular terms in a human language not only gives a shape to human thoughts about individuals, it ensures that such thoughts are shared between conspecifics. Since such sharing cannot be accomplished without explicit articulation, the sound of singular terms is essential for human language, it is not ‘ancillary.’
abstracts.010284: I defend the following three claims under the assumptions of Logical Phonology: with n binary features, Universal Grammar makes available an inventory of 3^n segments; there are 3^n natural classes; and the cardinality of each natural class is 3^k, 0 ≤ k ≤ n, where k is the number of features unspecified in the natural class description. An additional result is that the only member of a singleton natural class must be a fully specified segment.[This is pretty much the final version that has appeared in Radical: https://radical.cnrs.fr/reiss-3n-segments-and-3n-natural-classes-each-of-cardinality-3k/]
abstracts.010285: As has been noted in the literature, a reciprocal pronoun can have two or more separate antecedents simultaneously, as in "Tom shouted and Mary cried each other's names", contradicting all previous accounts of the syntax and semantics of reciprocals. This fact and some related observations are shown to motivate a representationalist theory of the syntax-semantics interface in which the semantic representation of each lexical item is a set of elementary predications and semantic composition is allowed to involve taking the union of such sets.
abstracts.010286: Existing research has repeatedly observed the tendency for English loanwords to cluster in the masculine gender across different recipient languages, yet the origin of this pattern remains difficult to determine, as fixed morphological rules and default assignments are frequently analysed together. This study proposes the Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio (FSDR) to quantify the degree of reliance on fixed derivational suffixes across different genders, and to distinguish between morphological anchoring and free-choice in distribution. By examining 1,832 Latvian noun lemma types, the results reveal a significant FSDR asymmetry within the loanword system: feminine loanwords rely significantly more on fixed derivational suffixes, while masculine loanwords are more concentrated in the free-choice zone. This pattern exhibits loanword specificity and has become more pronounced in contemporary usage. FSDR therefore provides a quantitative framework for testing default gender and shows how masculine default can be activated and reinforced under language contact.
abstracts.010287: Balkan languages are known for the use of the finite verb in control contexts, unlike Romance and Germanic languages. However, both Albanian and Aromanian varieties (Southern Albania) also present non-finite verbal forms in dependent clauses, in alternance with finite structures. Thus, Tosk/ standard Albanian shows both finite clauses in control contexts, and, in some contexts, a participial construction introduced by the prepositions për ‘for’, pa ‘without’, tu/ duke for the gerund. In Gheg variety all dependent contexts include an invariant form of the verbal base preceded by the preposition me ‘with’. Aromanian, like Tosk Albanian and Romanian, selects finite constructions in alternation with infinitives introduced by the preposition di ‘of’ or ti ‘for’. The article analyzes these data in keeping with recent papers by Chomsky which develop a Strong Minimalist approach to syntax.
abstracts.010288: Real-time language processing relies on a capacity-limited working memory system to encode and maintain (extra-)linguistic information. Prior research shows that structural information is rapidly used to distinguish targets from distractors in memory access, but the exact mechanisms underpinning this remain unclear. Here we consider two hypotheses. One is that structurally prominent, target representations are actively maintained in a privileged, focal attentional state that allows rapid, direct access. Another possibility is that structural prominence serves as a retrieval cue to distinguish target representations stored in a passive, non-focal state. These hypotheses can be distinguished by determining the relative time course of memory access to targets vs. distractors. To do this, we conducted a secondary analysis of a published dataset that measured the looking behavior during the online resolution of the structurally constrained Turkish local reciprocal birbirleri in a visual world paradigm. Bayesian analyses on gaze proportions and new fixations show evidence for reliable and faster access to targets relative to distractors. We interpret this as evidence for a functional divide within linguistic memory that is shaped by hierarchical syntactic structure, whereby structurally prominent target items are held in a privileged focal state, while distractors that lack this privileged status are accessed via a slower retrieval mechanism.
abstracts.010289: [This is part of a larger project to build a formal grammar of Japanese.] I propose phonosyntax as part of the phonological component, in which phonological strings are recursively merged to build the input for prosody. The proposal is motivated by merge-sensitive phonological processes, including a recursive accent rule and an opaque segmental process, and by a preceding theory of semantics. I put forth formal definitions of two phonological processes that exemplify this merge-based subcomponent of phonology, namely, concatenation and $-propagation. The former accounts for joining of two phonological strings, a phenomenon found in virtually all languages. The latter accounts for stress assignment of Tokyo Japanese. As a consequence of these proposals, I suggest from both phonological and semantic perspectives that some aspects of what has been called syntax may be better understood as part of phonology.
abstracts.010290: In this paper, we analyze the appearance of the 1>2SG suffix on the infinitival paradigm in Modern Hungarian. This development is challenging for the existing accounts of verbal agreement in Hungarian because the 1>2SG suffix has originally been restricted to the finite paradigm. We argue that the full gamut empirical facts can be accounted for by recourse to three competing grammars for agreeing infinitives: N (where infinitivals are nominal), Vdeficient (where infinitivals are verbal, with a paradigm gap in cell 1>2SG) and V full (where infinitives are verbal, with no paradigm gap.) This results in there being two tribes of Modern Hungarian speakers: Tribe 1 (where N and Vdeficient compete very discreetly) and Tribe 2 (where Vfull is crowding N out). Grammar N is in line with É. Kiss’s (2002) proposal; whereas Grammars V can be plausibly modelled in moderately revised versions of Den Dikken’s (2004) and Bárány’s (2017) system (both of which were originally developed with the finite paradigm in mind). Finally, we argue that the failure of the innovative paradigm (Vfull) to spread fast and wide is due to three factors: (i) the relatively minor advantage offered by Vfull to its alternatives, (ii) the fact that infinitival agreement in general is fading in the language and (iii) the spread of the Balkan subjunctive, which provides a more established outlet for the verbalization of subordination.
abstracts.010291: The nativism and empiricism dispute in cognitive science turns on a disagreement about the domain-specificity or domain-generality of language’s biological basis. Biolinguists tend to adopt the former perspective, whereas competing approaches like usage-based approaches tend to adopt the latter. Where Large Language Models (LLMs) have been held up as theories or proxies for theories of human language acquisition or use, they have tended to be used in support of the view that these models provide an existence proof of natural language’s domain-general learnability. This paper reviews the dispute and argues that LLMs nevertheless fail to adjudicate nativism and empiricism. In short order, LLMs circumvent challenges relevant to language acquisition by human children in ways that reduce their significance to a theory of human language. These turn principally on an LLM’s relation to its environment during (pre- and post-) training, including the curation of domain-specific data on its behalf and its closure from extraneous environmental stimuli. It is argued that the hypothesis space that LLMs traverse during training is somewhat constrained by human engineers in virtue of this relation. In the same vein, it is argued that the Poverty of the Stimulus Argument to which LLMs are often aimed is not, in its form of most interest to linguists, an argument concerning the availability of data in the child’s environment, and the use of LLMs to this end miss the point.
abstracts.010292: Nastase et al. (2026) argue that large language models (LLMs) may illuminate language processing because both rely on distributed, context-sensitive representations shaped by statistical learning. Their rejection of simple cortical "boxology" is persuasive, and they articulate a strong case for the value of LLM-brain alignment research. The key question is what kind of inference LLM-brain alignment licenses. My claim here will be narrow: representational alignment can in principle constrain mechanistic hypotheses, but it does not by itself identify a mechanism. Nastase et al. acknowledge that an encoding model can capture features represented in neural activity without establishing a shared architecture or algorithm. Yet the authors sometime move from alignment to "shared computational principles" and ultimately to LLMs as mechanistic models of natural language. Indeed, their methodological caveat that alignment does not establish a shared architecture or algorithm sits uneasily with their conclusion that LLMs might instantiate the same computational principles as biological brains and provide a "fully mechanistic model" of language. I discuss what I consider to be problems of logical, causal, and computational underdetermination in Nastase et al.'s (2026) proposal.
abstracts.010294: "Taskmaster" is a British game show where contestants attempt to complete a series of challenges. "Syntaxmaster" is a linguistic version of one of the tasks from S12E4 [ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_oXhJqhVB0 ]. Ultimately, the goal of the game is to decipher a message. But this is just a pretext to get students to retrieve important syntactic concepts. The deciphering is done by pairing linguistic concepts or definitions with data that illustrate them. Each concept is assigned to a symbol, while each data point is assigned a letter. By pairing each concept with the data that exemplifies it, the players arrive at a cipher that decodes the message. For example, let's say that the message to be decoded contains the symbol "♠." This symbol is associated with the following definition: "An anaphor must be c-commanded by its antecedent." In order to figure out which letter "♠" corresponds to, the players must inspect a set of sentences and converge on a pair of sentences like "Mary praised herself" vs. "*Mary's grandparents praised herself." Assuming further that these data are associated with the letter "S," players will, then, have uncovered part of the cipher, so that they are now able to translate the "♠" symbol in the coded message into an "S." The game is highly adaptable. The instructor can create their own "[insert subfield]master." The questions/concepts and the data can be changed too, so the level of the difficulty can be easily modulated. The message and cipher, needless to say, can be changed as well. Click on "PDF" to download an instantiation of the game, implemented as "Syntaxmaster." .tex versions of these files, but with minimal formatting, so that you can easily create your own version, can be downloaded here: [ https://www.overleaf.com/read/rhjtpdyqfcpr#3abd32 ]. Second version (2026 09 14): some typos corrected.
abstracts.010295: Equipollent and privative feature specifications are formally compared. A bijection is proven between consistent and complete equipollent and privative segments, grounding the intuition that under- and contradictory specifications have no equivalent in privative systems. However, it is shown that there exists no isomorphism between equipollent and privative natural classes, grounding the intuition that the former defines natural classes inexpressible in the latter.
abstracts.010296: This paper develops a unified analysis of cardinal expressions, challenging the assumed complementarity between number marking and numeral classifiers (Chierchia 1998; Borer 2005). Drawing on original fieldwork data from Khasi, I show that functional plural marking and individuating numeral classifiers obligatorily co-occur in counting constructions. I argue that this pattern follows once the two are assigned distinct grammatical functions: number marking encodes grammatical number, while classifiers provide the atomic structure required for counting. Building on the Nominal Mapping Parameter (Chierchia 1998), I propose that counting universally requires classifiers and derive cross-linguistic variation from two parameters. The Nominal Mapping Parameter determines noun denotation and the availability of #-based number marking, while a Card/CL Bundling Parameter (Giorgi & Pianesi 1997; Pylkkänen 2002) determines whether Card and CL are projected separately or bundled into a single complex head. Their interaction derives four attested counting systems, exemplified by Mandarin, English, Khasi, and Dëne Sųłiné. I further extend the analysis to apparent classifier optionality and mismatches between morphological and semantic plurality, suggesting that these may follow from the interaction of Economy and syntactic-semantic symmetry (Swart & Farkas 2010). The paper argues that classifiers are a universal component of cardinal composition and that number marking and numeral classification reflect independent dimensions of cross-linguistic variation.
abstracts.010297: After a long period of neglect, the discipline has rediscovered the importance of fieldwork in the last few decades and significantly increased fieldworking activities. The present contribution is concerned with the fact that the renewed interest in fieldwork and data from fieldwork has largely failed to recognize that not all fieldwork is created equal. There is an obvious difference between a chapter on the basic case system of language X that is based on 30 years of continued and extensive work with a particular community, and a brief statement that is based on the first stay in a community lasting only a few hours or days. Ignoring this difference risks trivializing fieldwork whenever one is confronted with statements based on fieldwork data. Things become quite problematic when publications based on fieldwork make claims with regard to highly conspicuous and marked phenomena, such as the claim that a language’s dominant word order is OSV (making it one of only four such languages currently listed in the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS)), or that the language in question has very long, morphologically complex words. The current contribution provides short case studies on two languages for which exactly these claims have been made: Oceanic Tobati (OSV word order) and West Bomberai Iha (‘exuberantly inflected verbs’). In both instances, the publications give no indication whatsoever of the data basis for their claims.
abstracts.010298: The article discusses the history of lexical borrowings into Arabic. It breaks down the history of this process into five basic periods: pre-Islamic and early Islamic times, Omayyads-Abbasids (seventh-thirteenth centuries), the Ottoman Yoke (fifteenth-eighteenth centuries), the Arabic Renaissance and European Colonialism (nineteenth, early twentieth century), and the technological era (1970s-present). During each period radical changes in Arabic lexicon, including changes in borrowings into the Arabic language, took place. The author gives numerous examples and considers a variety of donor languages (ranging from other Semitic languages and Turkish to a number of Indo-European languages, including Persian and later various Western European languages). This work studies different strategies for assimilating new words (including loan translations (calques) and various phonological and morphological adaptions). The author also shows that many loanwords have been borrowed by linguists, writers and other intellectuals, who were looking for alternative to borrowing ways that have not always met the phonological and morphological norms of the Arabic language. While studying the history of borrowings into Arabic, the author touches upon the question about the wholeness of the Arabic language as a part of Arabic nationalism. She also attempts to analyze the character of future borrowings into Arabic. The significance of this article is not covering all the history of borrowings into Arabic and summing up numerous works devoted to specific aspects of the given topic. It can be used for academic research and teaching by linguists, historians and specialists in the Arabic studies.
abstracts.010299: This study proposes a unified morphosyntactic–semantic account of the suffixal form -re found in the EMJ realis paradigm — the so-called izenkei — and related phenomena. It argues that -re is a contextual allomorph of the inflexional suffix -ru, which marks a clause as [0PAST, +ACTUAL-WORLD-COMMITMENT] and thereby presents the eventuality expressed by that clause as belonging to the actual world lato sensu. It surfaces as -re when the clause is set as a premise. This premise-setting environment is supplied overtly by the suffixes -ba [+CONDITIONAL] and -do(mo) [+CONCESSIVE], and covertly by the phonologically null suffix -Ø [+PREM(ISE-SETTING)] in the =koso type of kakari-musubi. Thus, the focus particle =koso does not itself condition the allomorphy -ru → -re, but merely focalises a constituent not containing the finite predicate within a clause already set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. In the =zo/=namu type, by contrast, a clause with a topic–comment articulation is first constructed, and its topic constituent containing the finite predicate is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM(INAL)] so that it can be treated as a topic NP. The focus particle =zo or =namu is then added to the comment. The resulting construction is analysed as a COPULA-LESS INVERTED PSEUDO-CLEFT in which the comment/focus precedes the nominalised topic/background without the intervention of the pseudo-copula =n-ari. This pseudo-cleft has two further types: the =ka type and the =ya type. The distribution of the focus particles is simple: in an interrogative clause, =ka is selected if an interrogative phrase constitutes the focus, whereas =ya is selected if a non-interrogative phrase constitutes the focus; in a declarative clause, =zo/=namu is selected. Cross-linguistically, Spanish and Portuguese provide close structural parallels to the =zo/=namu, =ya and =ka types. The =koso type, by contrast, contains no such nominalised topic phrase containing a finite predicate and is therefore NOT a PSEUDO-CLEFT. NOR does there seem to be any syntactic evidence that it is an IT-CLEFT. Finally, the absence of a special predicate form with the focus particles =ha and =mo follows from the set-based nature of their focalisation, which presupposes a contextually relevant set rather than a clause set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. Furthermore, in these constructions, no constituent containing a finite predicate constitutes the topic, and hence no such constituent is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM] to form a topic NP. Accordingly, the particles themselves do not determine the predicate forms. Rather, the configuration is constructed FIRST and only THEN determines both the predicate form and which focus particle may occur. Traditional particle–predicate concord called kakari-musubi is therefore reanalysed as a surface correspondence between two consequences of the same independently constructed structure.
abstracts.010300: Recent work on number has shown that number features may be distributed across different layers of nominal structure. Akan provides a revealing case: multiple number morphemes can occur within a single nominal and differ in their distribution and interpretation. This paper argues that these patterns reflect a split nominal architecture in which number is distributed across three functional heads: a low nominalizing head, a higher renominalizing head associated with humanness, and a Num head. Each plural morpheme realizes a distinct structural position and may make a different semantic contribution. The analysis provides new evidence for split number in Niger-Congo languages.
abstracts.010301: Common sense is prone to error, especially when it comes to scientific matters. “Ergativity” is a concept fraught with bias. Not every language that appears to be ergative actually is one. SHIPIBO is a very good example. It is a DIFFERENTIALLY-marked-subject/argument language, mistakenly considered to be ergative. This SQUIB is the answer to reviews of "Ergativity, properly aligned". [typo-reduced version v.1.3]
abstracts.010302: The interaction between modality and evidentiality has received considerable attention, but much less is known about the interaction between modality and speech-act operators. This paper argues that this interface is crucial to understanding how evaluative meanings arise with epistemic modals, particularly in non-information-seeking interrogatives and exclamatives. We develop an account of modal bias as a manipulable component of modal meaning and propose that question and exclamative operators can themselves act as bias manipulators. The empirical domain is Italian epistemic future, whose exceptional flexibility makes visible the mechanisms underlying this interaction. Building on previous work, we analyze the \textbf{Italian future} as a universal epistemic modal with no default bias, rather than as an evidential or a marker of subjective credence. Its flexibility derives from a metaevaluative layer at which the speaker’s evaluation of the prejacent is encoded and can be modified. The analysis distinguishes two mechanisms of negative bias: in `mica' future questions, bias emerges through the interaction of modality, QUES and the particle; in future exclamatives, it is introduced directly by EXCL. More generally, the paper argues that speech-act operators participate in semantic composition with modal meaning by manipulating its metaevaluative dimension, while remaining distinct from modality itself.
abstracts.010303: This version introduces the devil child from Golding's final chapter as the subject of Tuami's carving, names the unspeakable remainder for the first time in this paper, and points to the companion papers for its full development. Closes with the claim that what the haft carries is what the representational project will spend the rest of its history trying to return to. The structural and linguistic dimensions of this argument are developed in the companion papers already available on this server: "Pictures and Figures: Golding, Halliday, and the Stratum Closest to Being" grounds the claim in Halliday's Systemic Functional Grammar and Golding's narrative enactment of pre-representational consciousness; "The Sail and the Wind: Why Proximity Is Not Access" develops the empirical case through gerontolinguistic research on aging and developmental research on dreaming. Readers encountering the trilogy for the first time may find it useful to begin with either companion paper before returning to the more abstract philosophical argument made here. This paper is the first of three companion papers developing the connected argument about Being, representation, and the conditions under which human beings can access the pre-representational ground of experience. The argument begins here with the philosophical and epochal case: tracing an arc from pre-Socratic immediacy through Cartesian modernity to artificial intelligence, the paper argues that AI represents the completion of the Western representational project — the first technology to externalize not the products of human cognition but the generative loop itself, without embodied ground behind it.
abstracts.010304: This is part I of the book: "Explorations in Old Frisian Syntax". It offers a brief introduction to the various facets of the linguistic study of Old Frisian.
abstracts.010305: This is part II of the book: "Explorations in Old Frisian Syntax". It contains observations about prepositions, postpositions and verb particles in Old Frisian. The book consists of five parts, which have been uploaded separately. The five parts are: I. A Broad Outline of Old Frisian II. The PP in Old Frisian III. The NP in Old Frisian IV. The VP in Old Frisian V. The AP in Old Frisian
abstracts.010306: Though profane imprecations like F*** you! have received no attention in formal semantics, we might expect our theory of linguistic meaning to have something to say about such common expressions. In this paper, I discuss the nature of the meanings of profane quasi-verbs (Quang 1971) that function syntactically like f*** in the example above, and I provide a formal model that can account for some important aspects of their meaning and conversational use. This analysis throws light on the role of social relations in semantics and pragmatics.
abstracts.010307: This is part III of the book: "Explorations in Old Frisian Syntax". It offers observations about the NP in Old Frisian. The book consists of five parts, which have been uploaded separately. The five parts are: I. A Broad Outline of Old Frisian. II. The PP in Old Frisian. III. The NP in Old Frisian. IV. The VP in Old Frisian. V. The AP in Old Frisian.
