The book consists of five parts, which have been uploaded separately. The five parts are: I. A Broad Outline of Old Frisian. II. The PP in Old Frisian. III. The NP in Old Frisian. IV. The VP in Old Frisian. V. The AP in Old Frisian.
abstracts.010309: This is part V of the book: "Explorations in Old Frisian Syntax". It offers observations about the NP in Old Frisian. The book consists of five parts, which have been uploaded separately. The five parts are: I. A Broad Outline of Old Frisian. II. The PP in Old Frisian. III. The NP in Old Frisian. IV. The VP in Old Frisian. V. The AP in Old Frisian.
abstracts.010310: Several languages display Qualitative Binominal Noun Phrases (QBNPs), i.e. binominal structures where the first noun phrase encodes an evaluation by the speaker of the referent denoted by the second noun phrase, and at the same time conveys the emotional state of the speaker. An example of such a structure is given in (1), which conveys the fact that the speaker is annoyed by a professor, for whatever reason. (1) That idiot of a professor has disappeared again! We argue that Italian provides evidence for the existence of (at least) three different classes of Expressive Nouns (EN), which differ from each other in terms of (i) semantic and pragmatic contribution to the proposition, (ii) syntactic distribution, and (iii) concord patterns. The QBNPs we discuss feature ENs such as cazzo ‘dick’, merda ‘shit’, and stronzo ‘turd’ (2). We propose that the different ENs we identify occupy different syntactic positions, i.e. they can occur in the specifier of a functional projection hosting evaluative adjectives or in the Deg-head hosted in the extended projection of such functional projection. We also propose that the expressive component of these ENs is determined by both their syntactic position and the degree to which they are grammaticalised. More specifically, we argue that their different behaviour with respect to concord derives from their morpho-syntactic structure, namely from the hypothesis that ENs can be semi-lexical to different degrees, and from the EN having or not having interpretable ϕ-features that can be either valued or unvalued. As for the prepositional element occurring between ENs and RNs, we propose that it is a context-dependent realisation of a morphosyntactic structure that is formally and functionally similar to adjectival concord markers.
abstracts.010311: We examine an apparent case of a variable-flavor attitude predicate, the verb kä in Äiwoo, which can receive ‘think’, ‘say’, or ‘want’ translations. We argue that this verb denotes linguistic production, which may be mental or physical (thus capturing its use in doxastic and assertive reports). Its use for bouletic reports arises from combining it with an overt priority modal (the prefix nä-) in the embedded clause, whose semantic contribution can be independently established from its use in unembedded contexts.
abstracts.010312: The way that the author has framed the problem of multilingualism has presented us with a dilemma. Just as during an earlier expansion of scholarship and learning – when East Asia and Europe each needed their lingua franca – today’s global imperative for a language of international communication has selected English. At the same time as English-language venues have become the indispensable tool of research and cross-cultural discussion in almost every discipline, they have also suffered the effects of an impending corruption, particularly in academia. More than for any other major or cross-national language, publication in English, in print and online, has become the favoured channel for propagating a new genre of pseudo-science and anti-scientific critique of the advances of the Enlightenment. Depending on the prospects for greater plurality, a shift towards a new international linguistic multi-polarity may not be as impractical as it once appeared to be. Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development (2026) 47, 3: 1950-1952.
abstracts.010313: In this paper, I inspect two types of readings that emerge in a range of environments, such as in negative imperatives, under 'not want', under 'fear', etc.: (i) ABSTAIN readings, which convey willingness to prevent someone from intentionally engaging in some kind of act, and (ii) AVOID readings, which convey willingness to prevent a potentially unintended outcome. The ABSTAIN vs. AVOID distinction has a variety of grammatical reflexes cross-linguistically, e.g., anti-/re-licensing of 'some'-indefinites in English: 'Don't call anyone!' (which asks the addressee to abstain from intentionally engaging in the activity of calling some person or other) vs. 'Don't (accidentally) call someone!' (which cautions the addressee against accidentally calling some person or other). I will focus on perfective vs. imperfective aspect and distribution of indefinites in Russian. I will argue that the relevant complements in ABSTAIN vs. AVOID cases have distinct compositional structures: there is a situation layer in AVOID, but not in ABSTAIN cases. This will allow us to explain the relevant Russian facts about aspect and indefinites, but will also establish a framework for building accounts of grammatical reflexes of the ABSTAIN vs. AVOID distinction cross-linguistically. The choice between the two compositional structures in the environments at hand is then driven by global pragmatic considerations about preventing unwanted scenarios, yielding the diverging inferences about intentional vs. accidental actions arising in the two cases.
abstracts.010314: As a child growing up in a triglossic society such as Hong Kong, my native intuitions in Chinese are shared between standard literary Mandarin and the Cantonese vernacular, which has proven to be useful to my research in comparative parametric syntax and teaching Chinese as a foreign language. Applying formal parameters based on universal cartography, the main dialectal differences between Cantonese and Mandarin can be classified in three types: 1) functional categories with different selectional properties 2) different word order of the same lexical items 3) syntactic operations that occur in certain dialects but not in others. This paper provides an outline of how my triglossic upbringing laid the foundation for my current work in linguistic research and language teaching.
abstracts.010315: This book follows up on the seminal work by Bobaljik, who proposed a containment relation among the positive, comparative and superlative degrees. The starting point of our work was the observation that some languages provide a much richer morphology: we discovered cases where the comparative is derived from the positive by the addition of two or even three independent suffixes, while in other cases the comparative is not derived from the positive, but from a shorter, truncated form of the positive. We argue that the full morphological complexity can be derived by unifying the original claim that the superlative syntactically contains the comparative, and the comparative syntactically contains the positive with a more fine-grained decomposition, using the ingredients familiar from the semantics research distinguishing scales, standards of comparison, measure phrases, etc. Specifically, we argue for a syntactic representation consisting of two scales, with the comparative showing both scales and the positive only one, along the lines of Kennedy and Levin’s 2008 work. Each scale is in turn represented syntactically by the same four features of standard of comparison, dimension of the scale (e.g., size or speed), direction of the scale (positive vs. negative, as in fast vs. slow) and perhaps a measure phrase (which we call ‘distance’). We show that this combination yields exactly the rich morpho-syntactic patterns observed.
abstracts.010316: The apparent negative polarity behavior seen with 'much' and 'many' is a side effect of a licensing requirement holding of the silent AMOUNT or NUMBER that they cooccur with, much as in Kayne (2021) on 'long'. The overall conclusion is that negative polarity is not a primitive of the language faculty, at least not in the kind of cases discussed. Silent elements and their licensing requirements are more fundamental.
abstracts.010317: Old Iranian languages display patterns of relativization that do not fit neatly into existing accounts. This thesis examines free relatives and correlatives, primarily in Old Avestan, with comparative evidence from Old Persian and Young Avestan. Its first chapter addresses a basic methodological problem: how can we reliably classify constructions in ancient and low-resource languages when interpretations are uncertain and native-speaker judgments unavailable? It develops a replicable algorithm that moves from formal schema induction to typological comparison and the testing of structural and interpretive predictions. Using this method, the Old Avestan data are situated within the cross-linguistic typology of headless and head-internal free relatives, correlatives, and related constructions. The comparison establishes these patterns as grammatical constructions in their own right, rather than variants of postnominal relative clauses, and motivates expanding the cross-linguistics typology of free relatives to include non-interrogative-based forms. The thesis also proposes a novel analysis of free relatives at the syntax-semantics interface. Its central advantage is that it derives the maximalizing semantics of free relatives without recourse to empty categories or silent operators. It further examines Old Avestan generalizing relative clauses and relates their generalizing expressions to Negative Polarity and Free Choice Items. The surveys of Old Persian and Young Avestan show that these constructions are less productive and less varied outside Old Avestan.
abstracts.010318: Restrictions on clitic combinations are generally in place when a ditransitive is expressed with both direct object and indirect object clitics. The best-studied such restrictions involve local persons, as in classic person-case constraint (PCC) effects—e.g., in French, banning combinations of local person DO clitics with IO clitics (strong PCC). Many languages also impose restrictions on combinations of 3rd person clitics (*3-on-3). Spanish, for instance, bans combinations of 3rd dative + 3rd accusative, requiring the dative to be replaced by the so-called “spurious se” (Perlmutter 1971). These two types of restrictions have typically been attributed to separate grammatical rules, if not entirely separate components of the grammar. However, in recent work, Pancheva and Zubizarreta (2018) have proposed a partial unification of *3-on-3 and classic PCC, treating both as grounded in syntactic licensing principles. This theory predicts a typological interaction: 3-on- 3 restrictions will be found only in certain languages that also constrain combinations including local persons. In this paper, I argue that this prediction is false. In Ubykh (NW Caucasian), no restriction is imposed on clitic combinations involving local persons--there is no PCC effect of any type--but 3-on-3 combinations show clitic opacity effects reminiscent of spurious se. Capturing this pattern requires grammatical rules for the 3-on-3 context that are not grounded in PCC syntax, thus making a case for the independence of the two types of ditransitive person restrictions more generally.
abstracts.010319: We investigate the tough-construction in Thai, focusing on two exceptional properties. First, Thai tough-constructions may involve a potentially unconstrained dependency, and second, the gap in the embedded clause can be in the subject position. While these facts superficially support a heterogeneous view of tough-constructions across the world’s languages, on closer inspection, we come to a different conclusion. We argue that unconstrained dependencies and subject gaps are not a function of Thai tough-constructions, but instead reflect the fact that Thai has an undiagnosed broad subject position. Once controlled for, Thai tough-constructions look surprisingly like other well-documented cases. Ultimately, we are concerned not with variation in tough-constructions, but rather crosslinguistic similarities.
abstracts.010320: Although the Austronesian family is widely regarded as a hotspot for antipassive constructions, a closer investigation of 53 languages from Taiwan and Maritime Southeast Asia challenges this view. Philippine-type Austronesian languages have often been analyzed as exhibiting an alternation between a basic transitive construction and a corresponding antipassive. Yet when established typological criteria are applied consistently to the constructions commonly referred to as Actor Voice, genuine antipassives prove to be rare in western Austronesian. We further demonstrate how these putative antipassives form a continuum of semitransitives, characterized by a general decrease in semantic transitivity while often still featuring a patient that retains various traits of a core argument. Not only does this cline enhance our understanding of how antipassive-like constructions may develop over time, but it also suggests that syntactic intransitivity is not necessarily the endpoint of discourse-driven changes that reduce clausal transitivity. Moreover, it undermines the prevalent ergative view of western Austronesian languages and lends new support to accusative and symmetrical voice analyses, both maintaining that Austronesian-style voice does not alter clausal transitivity. The Austronesian pseudo antipassives thus underscore the importance of approaching typological classifications with caution and situating language-specific analyses within the broader typological literature.
abstracts.010321: What must a neural system be capable of to implement language? Current research annotates stimuli with linguistic variables and tests which electrodes, voxels, or language-model layers predict neural activity. Yet predictive success leaves neural mechanisms under-constrained, and candidate composition rules may fail to preserve distinctions natural language requires. Here, we show that algebraic properties of language can constrain this search space by specifying invariants that candidate mechanisms must preserve, such as non-associative hierarchical grouping, binding that ignores the order of its parts, recursive closure, access to substructures, semantic role compatibility, and transitions through structured workspaces. This constraint-led approach is termed the Neural Admissibility Program (NAP). To illustrate it, syntactic structure building is analyzed algebraically and candidate mechanisms are proposed for each requirement: content-addressable workspace memory (e.g., expander Hopfield networks), graph-structured transient dynamics for scheduling structure-building operations (e.g., stable heteroclinic channels), and a phase-coupled sealing operation that records grouping. Simulations then show that a corrected form of the Marcolli–Berwick entropy-optimized binding gate preserves grouping only within a narrow band of commitment. As an alternative, we propose a novel neural binding operation we term ‘Meld’: two constituent populations converge through shared synapses, integrate sublinearly, and saturate. Meld is, to our knowledge, the closest neurally plausible composition law to the syntactic Merge computation. It preserves every invariant the NAP demands, is built from operations cortex is known to perform, and recovers hierarchical structure at every depth and temperature tested, decoding bracketing to within a few points of the best-performing rival law (ordered role-filler) while remaining order-blind. It predicts that the effective dimensionality of population activity separates alternative bracketings and that the composite depends on how far its constituents disagree. Importantly, the laws that decode bracketing most accurately are a priori inadmissible, indicating that neural decoding accuracy alone cannot adjudicate between mechanisms. By specifying how neural dynamics can remain faithful to linguistic structure, the NAP changes the criterion by which neural implementations of cognition are evaluated.
abstracts.010322: We propose a formal syntactic analysis of the Latin construction at the origin of Romance perfect tenses with a have-auxiliary, arguing that the Latin construction ‘habere + NP.acc + PaPa.acc’ is a grammatically passive structure in which habere ‘have’ is the main verb, selecting a small clause with the accusative NP as subject and the participle as predicate. Drawing on Myler’s (2016) analysis of have and insights from the literature on stative passives and the internal structure of participles, we show that the participles in these constructions may denote event and state tokens, and that different semantic readings of the construction correspond to a single syntactic structure. On the basis of this analysis, we develop a new account of the rise of analytic perfect tenses in Romance. We argue that the trigger for reanalysis was an independent change in the nominal domain — the emergence of a D-layer and in particular the grammaticalization of definite articles — which forced reanalysis specifically in contexts involving inalienably possessed direct objects. Once established in this critical context, the construction spread to new environments, including, for the first time, intransitive verbs.
abstracts.010323: The goal of this work is to provide a description and an in-depth analysis of the main configurations in which nominal ellipsis and verbal ellipsis are licensed in Romanian. Chapter I provides a motivation for the choice of nominal and verbal Following previous bibliography, I focus on a particular family of elliptical types, namely elliptical structures which (i) are derived by PF-deletion and (ii) are tied to a particular licensing element; this class includes elliptical phenomena like sluicing, VP-ellipsis and nominal ellipsis. Chapter II discusses at length the differences between these phenomena and other types of surface anaphora (such as gapping and stripping). Chapters III and IV are devoted to the in-depth study of verbal and nominal ellipsis, and chapter V summarizes the results and puts them into a larger perspective. [This book is a revised version of my 2013 PhD dissertation (Types of Ellipsis in Romanian. The Interpretation of Structures containing Ellipsis Sites and the Syntactic Licensing of Ellipsis), jointly supervised by professors Gabriela Pană Dindelegan (University of Bucharest) and Ian Roberts (University of Cambridge). I defended this dissertation in November 2013 at the University of Bucharest, and published the monograph in 2019 with Bucharest University Press.]
abstracts.010324: This work proposes a mechanistic model of sound change based on pressure-resistance dynamics and tipping-point behaviour. It explains how small phonetic biases can accumulate, stall, or suddenly accelerate, producing the historical patterns seen in vowel shifts, rhoticity loss, and regional diffusion, etc. The mechanism links sociophonetic evolution and offers a unified framework for understanding when and why sound change progresses. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22712648 The full licence information is available on the Zenodo DOI page linked above
abstracts.010325: Approximators such as approximately or exactly have been analyzed either as operators that manipulate a numeral's denotation, or as devices that select a granularity level at which the numeral is interpreted. A single numeral, however, can host several approximating devices at once. In Ukrainian, an overt adverb, a preposition, an indefinite, and approximative inversion may co-occur with one numeral, yet the result conveys the same interval as any one alone, differing only in an intensified hedging effect. Pragmatic halo theories correctly predict that imprecision in such cases does not compound, but fail to rule out mixed-precision stacks like approximately exactly; granularity-based accounts predict that stacking is infelicitous altogether. I propose an approach where a single mechanism derives the idempotence of same-precision stacking alongside the phenomena prior views miss. I argue that a bare numeral introduces a family of resolution descriptions—the precision levels at which it may be read—and approximators function like indefinites and definites over this family: approximately restricts it to its non-exact members without choosing among them, and exactly retrieves the unique exact member. Stacking is then intersection of conditions, idempotent for same-precision devices and contradictory for mixed-precision ones. I implement the account in effect-driven semantics and lift it to probabilistic dynamic semantics. Treating the choice of resolution as uncertain yields an interpretation peaked at the numeral; roundness and magnitude phenomena then reduce to how the prior over resolutions varies with it. The mixed-precision clash is rescued in discourse as an instance of ordinary anaphora.
abstracts.010326: Messapic is an Indo-European language attested in inscriptions from pre-Roman Apulia. Its possible relationship with the prehistoric ancestor of Albanian remains disputed. Messapic bilia and Albanian bijë, both meaning “daughter”, offer a noteworthy comparison, but the limited corpus does not yet support a secure classification based on regular sound correspondences and shared morphological innovations. This review considers three claims often presented together: that Messapic and Albanian are related, that Messapic was Albanian’s closest ancient relative, and that Messapic can establish the age of Albanian. The first is uncontroversial at the broad Indo-European level; a particularly close relationship is plausible but not established; the third claim does not follow. The earliest surviving Albanian texts are late medieval, whereas the spoken language has a much older prehistory.
abstracts.010327: In several languages, when a head agrees with a conjoined phrase, it may express either the sum of the features of all conjuncts (i.e., full agreement) or the features of only a subset of conjuncts (i.e., partial agreement). Investigations into (partial) agreement with conjunction have played a crucial role in linguistic theorizing of agreement. Here we aim to contribute to this literature by experimentally investigating verbal agreement strategies with coordinate and disjunctive subjects in Turkish. Using three acceptability judgment tasks, we test the availability of partial verbal agreement with preverbal and postverbal coordinate subjects and preverbal disjunctive subjects. For coordinate subjects, we find that full agreement is the most acceptable strategy, while partial agreement with the last (or second) conjunct ‘I’ is somewhat available in both word orders. For disjunctive subjects, acceptability is overall degraded, suggesting a grammatical gap in assigning number with disjunction. Nevertheless, similar to coordination, full agreement remains the most acceptable option, followed by partial agreement with the last conjunct.
abstracts.010328: I show that reflexives in DP-sized Right Node Raising pivots can have strict readings, just like pronouns in the same environment. Certain properties of these examples preclude an elliptical analysis of Right Node Raising. A multidominant analysis of these examples follows if we assume strict readings come from a referential reading of these reflexives and pronouns. This paper thus supports a treatment of reflexives that distinguish referential from bound readings. Reflexives are like pronouns, except they have to satisfy Condition A. (This paper is titled "Rediscovering referential reflexives with Right Node Raising" in its later iterations.)
abstracts.010329: Proto-Indo-European featured a complex system of accentual and ablaut paradigms. In this paper, I outline a proposal for the development of accentual mobility in Pre-PIE. The accent-ablaut system is mostly described as a morphologically conditioned, but its diachronic origin is likely phonetic. Based on the behavior of the most archaic lexical and morphological layer, root nouns and verbs, I argue that ending morphemes with heavy syllables attracted stress, which results in accentual mobility. While the rule was not phonetically active in PIE, it leaves traces and allows us to explain some forms that were difficult to explain. The rule also provides a simple phonetic motivation for a complex morphophonological system of PIE accentual mobility.
abstracts.010330: In Latin phonology and poetry, so-called s impurum refers chiefly to word-initial s + stop clusters, e.g. in stā.re ‘to stand’. When preceded by a vowel, the cluster is heterosyllabic, e.g. /re + stāre/ res.tā.re ‘to remain’. To make sense of this apparent inconsistency, Cser (2012) posits that this medial s is “extrasyllabic” but that a stipulation prohibiting extrasyllabic segments from neighboring a nucleus obliges it to become a coda via “leftward resyllabification.” Parker (2002:9) considers this contrivance “painful.” Rejecting the inherently exceptional “extrasyllabic” analysis of s impurum, this paper proposes an exception-free Optimality Theoretic (OT) account relying solely on necessary, cross-linguistic generalizations. Hierarchically arranged, these constraints collaboratively drive the syllabification of every s, each syllabification being the best fit for its respective environment. Notably, the constraint hierarchy never references the segment [s]. A testament to the robust coherence and parsimony of this analysis, the same constraint hierarchy—without modifications or stipulations—(1) accounts for the exceptional behavior of other clusters (ps, mn); (2) elucidates the seemingly exceptional effect of x on meter; and (3) refutes the supposed “unknowability” of whether the purportedly extrasyllabic, “trapped” [s] in e.g. dexter [dekster] ‘right’ is an onset or coda (Cser 2016). Additionally, the paper critiques the argumentation underpinning the extrasyllabicity account by identifying several overlapping fallacies that undermine the hypothesis. The study also examines why Latin poets avoided s impurum in “non-neutral” positions, e.g. un.de.#ski.at (in Lucretius) vs. nul.la#s.pēs (Catullus), speculating on the cognitive and sociolinguistic benefits afforded by the avoidance of this superficially ambiguous structure. Though poets avoided non-neutral s impurum, their distinct preferences for syllabifying it as an onset vs. coda are depicted here in terms of the optimal output of – very simply – two ways to rank the same constraint set. The analysis underscores the importance of prioritizing necessary generalizations over ad hoc stipulations in phonological analysis and offers insights into a dilemma faced by the poets. Demonstrating economy, elegance, and intuitive appeal, the proposed OT approach dispels the pejorative taint traditionally associated with s "impurum" and illustrates that its syllabification ceases to be a curiosity when examined through the lens of OT tableaux.
abstracts.010331: It has recently been argued that scalar implicatures are presuppositional; e.g. that the inference of the sentence "some students passed the test" that not all students passed the test is a presupposition of the sentence (Bassi et al., 2021). A known challenge to this approach is that scalar implicatures do not intuitively feel like presuppositions, and, more concretely, do not pass a well known test that diagnoses presuppositional content; the "Hey, wait a minute! I didn't know that..." test (Shanon 1976, von Fintel 2004). We offer a new way of thinking about this diagnostic that renders the fact that it does not seem to target implicatures unproblematic for their presuppositional analysis.
abstracts.010332: In this paper, we examine the status of the syntactic projection of the implicit external argument in short periphrastic passive derivations in Spanish. To do this, we apply tests mainly from Collins (2005, 2024) concerning the licensing of agent-oriented secondary depictive predicates, the argument control of big PRO subjects of embedded clauses, the binding of reflexive pronominals, and the non-anaphoric status of non-reflexive pronominals. The results of these tests, placed in a theoretical context of a Minimalist framework (e.g., Chomsky 2021; Chomsky et al. 2023), strongly endorse a view in which the external argument is syntactically-projected in the Spanish short passive. We additionally present novel evidence from Spanish that the reflexive pronominal elements licensed in Spanish short passives cannot plausibly be exempt logophors. In accordance with these theoretical and empirical considerations, we straightforwardly adopt Collins’ (2005, 2024) smuggling approach to the Spanish passive. We further show that several notable properties of the Spanish passive are naturally explained under this smuggling analysis, such as the preverbal, nominative status of the structural subject, the obligatory agreement in phi-features between the participial verb and the subject, and the impossibility of inalienable-possession readings of the short passive, as noted by MacDonald (2017).
abstracts.010333: Previous work has reported that several Armenian varieties show ejective or glottalized stops, a claim with significant implications for the reconstruction of the Proto-Indo-European stop system. This paper reviews the historical, dialectological, and phonetic evidence for ejective, glottalized, and breathy-voiced stops in Armenian, finding that these claims largely rest on unreliable impressionistic reports. To provide an empirical assessment, we present preliminary acoustic data from field recordings of three native speakers of the Janik subdialect of Hamshen Armenian. This variety has previously been reported to possess glottalized / ejective stops, and we additionally test whether its historical voiced series is realized with breathy phonation. We conducted an exploratory acoustic analysis by extracting fundamental frequency (F0) trajectories and Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPP) values at the vowel onset following target plosives. Our initial findings yield no clear evidence of full glottal closure or severe aperiodicity associated with glottalization or ejectivity, nor of the laryngeal slackness associated with breathy voice. Instead, the target tokens predominantly exhibit high-falling F0 trajectories and CPP values characteristic of modal voice. While further large-scale articulatory and statistical work is needed, these preliminary results suggest that where non-modal phonation or ejectivity does occur in Armenian, it is likely sporadic or paralinguistic, offering little support for the existence of a stable ejective, glottalized, or breathy-voiced series.
abstracts.010334: In Persian, anti-rogative predicates can select for an embedded clause with the polarity particle aya in certain contexts. We characterize these contexts as non-veridical, and we propose that the particle does not introduce a polar question: the ke aya-complement denotes a unique proposition and conveys that the latter is positively or negatively decided in the attitude state of the selecting anti-rogative predicate. In veridical contexts, the ke aya-complement is ruled out by the competition of the corresponding declarative complement, which conveys positive decidedness and thus determines strictly more informative truth conditions. In non-veridical contexts, however, the informativeness competition is suspended and ke aya-complements are allowed. We argue that the polar complement interpretation constitutes a weakening of the interpretation of aya as the polar question operator.
abstracts.010335: Frequency matching has been proposed as a central principle underlying phonological knowledge and learning. A central example comes from Hungarian vowel harmony, where stems with back vowels followed by neutral vowel(s) show structurally-conditioned lexical variation in whether they take back or front suffixes. In wug tests, Hungarian speakers show evidence of internalizing this structural conditioning, often taken as evidence of speakers internalizing a probabilistic grammar. This article critically analyzes the Frequency Matching Hypothesis and argues that the appearance of frequency matching emerges from variation across speaker vocabularies and from averaging over categories that may not reflect those internalized by speakers. I suggest that the central question of lexical variation is how learners discover its structural conditioning and propose a learning theory, in the form of an independently-motivated learning model, for that question. Assuming just variation across speaker vocabularies, the model exhibits the appearance of frequency matching. The model matches wug test results as well as previously proposed probabilistic grammars, predicts a diachronic shift in Hungarian vowel transparency, and explains a surprising lack of token-level variation in Hungarian vowel harmony.
abstracts.010336: A reader who encounters the companion papers without this piece will find rigorous argument: convergence across Halliday's linguistics, gerontolinguistic evidence, phenomenological philosophy, developmental psychology. The argument stands on its own. But what precedes it is the encounter that made the argument findable at all — a man in an apartment, three years into living inside cultural difference, reading a novel about the first men who held hafts, and feeling something arrive that the categories he had spent his career building could not hold. The haft was always resting in a hand. The password was always waiting in the ivory. What the years built was the capacity to feel it when it arrived.
abstracts.010337: This paper examines several understudied and unusual types of copular constructions in Polish, in which the copula agrees with the predicate rather than the subject. It argues that this seemingly unexpected agreement pattern follows from a well-known principle: the controller of agreement is the highest accessible phrase in the domain of agreement. This conclusion is defended against appearances, which suggest that the controller of agreement is not the highest accessible phrase in the constructions at hand. In the process, the paper advances several theoretical claims, including the proposal that the demonstrative found in the subject position in such constructions is structurally reduced and lacks a case projection, that certain non-agreeing leftmost phrases are base-generated above TP, and that there are two flavours of Pred in Polish, including a highly defective Pred which combines with nominal predicates in the nominative instead of the usual instrumental of predication. The paper also reports the discovery of long-distance agreement in Polish, apparently not noted so far in the context of Slavic.
abstracts.010338: This note discusses some recent findings in Nacireman phonology. This language makes suprasegmental use of overtones on each syllable to encode lexical meaning. This typologically unusual feature is integrated into several morphological alternations in the language.
abstracts.010339: In this paper I present a novel observation on reciprocal equatives (henceforth, RE) in Mandarin: a reciprocal equative, when embedded under a necessity modal or a predicate of desire, gives rise to an unexpected, at-least-equal-to interpretation (henceforth, ≥-interpretation). I show that the meaning of a modal sentence or a desire report of this kind may be derived through the postulation of two covert operators: one is akin to at least and serves to weaken the meaning of the embedded RE; the other is an exhaustification operator, which gives rise to the inference of sufficiency. Along with Alonso-Ovalle and Hirsch’s (2022) analysis, the proposal draws a connection between the sufficiency modal construction (e.g., To get good cheese, you only have to go to the North Ends) and examples of embedded reciprocal equatives investigated in this paper. To the extent that the proposal is on the right track, it provides further support for the postulation of a semantic weakening operator in natural language meaning composition and sheds light on the issue how this weakening operation may be constrained (e.g., Alonso-Ovalle and Hirsch, 2022; Crniˇc, 2011; Schwarz, 2005).
abstracts.010340: This thesis presents a comparative study of composite A'/A constructions and develops a syntactic analysis for investigating such constructions cross-linguistically. In many languages, phrasal movement falls into two types with mutually exclusive properties: A-movement (e.g. passivization) and A'-movement (e.g. wh-movement, topicalization). Some languages, however, exhibit movement that combines properties associated with both types. In recent featural approaches, such derivations have commonly been analyzed as involving a composite [A'/A] probe, suggesting that phrasal movement can be triggered by a fused [A'/A] probe and thereby form an A'/A chain. The thesis systematically compares composite constructions in fifteen languages from nine language families, including Dinka Bor extraction, Mandarin Chinese BEI passives and TP-internal topics/foci, Khanty passives, promotion to pivot in Balinese and Malagasy, as well Hyperraising, and long-distance agreement in various languages. I ask whether A'/A constructions exhibit arbitrary combinations of A'- and A-properties or whether these properties follow predictable distributions. I show that only a small number of A'/A mixtures is attested cross-linguistically and that these follow a highly systematic pattern: some A'- and A-properties consistently cluster together, while others allow more variation. Based on these findings, I develop a unified syntax of composite [A'/A] probes that differs from existing accounts in proposing that there is no such thing as "composite A'/A movement". Although [A] and [A'] features may combine on a single probe and jointly search for a goal, the resulting movement chain is either an A-chain or an A'-chain, never a mixed chain. I therefore reconceptualize the traditional binary A'/A distinction as a finer-grained, tripartite system involving three interacting factors: i) the probing head ([A'], [A], or [A'/A]), ii) the movement chain (A or A'), and iii) the location of the probing head in the syntactic spine (on C or below). Each factor determines a distinct subset of A'- and A-properties. Their different combinations give rise to what I term a construction-specific A'/A signature, which predicts the particular combination of properties associated with a given construction. While natural language permits only a limited number of such signatures, this set is larger than the traditional binary A'/A distinction. I apply the A'/A signature analysis to established [A'/A] probe accounts in Dinka Bor, Mandarin Chinese, and Khanty, and extend it to Hyperraising, long-distance agreement, and promotion to pivot in Balinese and Malagasy. The analysis captures the composite nature of these constructions while maintaining a unified account of their properties. Beyond the analysis of A'/A signatures, the thesis addresses broader questions concerning the emergence of composite [A'/A] probes, the implications of a featural approach to phrasal movement, the nature of A'- and A-movement, and the role of comparative syntax.
abstracts.010341: In Spanish ad sensum agreement, semantically-plural, but grammatically-singular subjects, of the form [DP1 [de NP2/DP2]] 'DP1 of NP2/DP2' (e.g. la mayoría de los triunfadores ‘the majority of the winners’), agree with a singular or plural verb. Previous accounts identify a ‘head N’ responsible for agreement, but cannot explain variable agreement. We couch our proposal within Distributed Morphology (DM), with number encoded and valued semantically and morphologically, following research on DP-internal gender (e.g. Kramer 2016, Puškar 2018). We propose that conflicting semantic and morphological number within the DP triggers Count, an alternative agreement mechanism that calculates a plural ratio diacritic for variable production based on feature values. We test our hypothesis comparing predicted rates of singular and plural verb agreement generated by Count with attested data in the Corpus del Español (CdE). Statistical analysis reveals that the variables in our proposal are significant predictors of variable agreement observed in the data.
abstracts.010342: An asylum answer may be judged evasive before anyone establishes whether the applicant understood the question. This article uses Grice's Cooperative Principle to examine how a judgement about an answer's relevance, detail or expression becomes a judgement about the speaker's truthfulness. I call this movement pragmatic credibility migration. Drawing on research into asylum communication and four published UK decisions, I distinguish misunderstanding, limited knowledge, interpreting error and the later misreading of a record. I argue that assessors should identify the proposition attributed to an applicant, show how the record supports it and address any explanation for the apparent difficulty. Communicative safety names the conditions in which uncertainty and correction can be examined as evidence without deciding credibility in advance.
abstracts.010343: A description built on a superordinate category term (an animal perched on a branch) does not pick out its members evenly: some come to mind more readily than others. This paper separates three conditions under which such a description meets two candidate referents differing in typicality, according to whether the full description is satisfied by both, by the atypical candidate only, or by the typical candidate only. These conditions support different interpretations of the same choice response and therefore require separate analysis. Forced-choice referent selection is the appropriate primary instrument for comparing them, but choice alone cannot separate a candidate rejected as false from one rejected as a worse fit, so judgment data remain necessary. Picture-based versions add a further confound: the restricting detail must be visually recoverable before it can override anything. An existing image-based study is described as a worked instance. No new results are reported.
abstracts.010344: This is a brief (informal) reply to Pullum(2026c), which is a review of Postal(2025). [09-23 update: added some literature details into the last remark, also corrected some mistaken dates, e.g. Marr(2010), not 2011] [09-24 update: more literature details added] [10-04 update: fixed some terminological issues] [Disclaimer: this is a work in progress, I'm posting it early so that I can expose the arguments to criticism and revise it iteratively]
abstracts.010345: Children are remarkable word learners, who exploit a variety of information sources — syntax, others’ attention and intention, general expectations about communication — to learn otherwise hidden meanings. Here we explore the learning of presupposition triggers, a ubiquitous but special class of words whose meanings cannot be learned from the usual information sources. In their syntactic distribution, they overlap with presupposition-free counterparts, and their meaning includes information that everyone in the conversation takes for granted, making it unattended and uninformative by definition. How, then, do children figure out that this information is part of a word’s meaning, let alone that it is presupposed? We decompose the problem of presupposition learning into two components: discovery (registering that the presupposed content is part of the word’s meaning) and packaging (determining that it is presupposed rather than asserted). If all the child ever encountered were typical uses of triggers, the problem of discovery might indeed be unsolvable. We propose that presuppositions are instead discovered from atypical, informative uses. The packaging problem, in contrast, is solved using typical uses, with various sources of evidence bearing on it. Separating discovery from packaging makes the problem tractable and yields predictions about the course of learning, the evidence that drives it, and the intermediate meanings learners may entertain. Beyond development, the decomposition relocates the hard question, from how meanings get assigned their dimension to how presupposed content becomes representable at all. It offers an instructive test case for psychological accounts that tie word learning to communicative usefulness.
abstracts.010346: Clausal nominalizations, which combine nominal properties externally with verbal properties internally, have often been understood as involving a nominal layer above the clausal content (Borsley & Kornfilt 2000; Kornfilt & Whitman 2011). Research based on this assumption proposes that the nominal layer consists of a determiner element D that nominalizes the clause structure rather than an n (or N). In this paper, I argue that clausal nominalizations do not always require a DP layer. Furthermore, I demonstrate that TP-nominalizations by nP do exist. I support both claims by examining nominalized complement clauses in the Tupí-Guaraní language Ka(g)wahíva. I show that complement clauses in this language are nominalized through nP, and do not have any additional nominal projections. Moreover, the clausal content consists solely of a TP. The first finding parallels clausal nominalization in Japanese and the Mongolic language Khalkha (Nasu et al. 2024; Lim 2025), while the second finding has only been argued for the Bantu language Oshiwambo (Lee & Ndapo 2025).
abstracts.010347: Jacobson (2016) observes that fragment answers (e.g., Q: Which linguist is on the committee? A: Jill ) must denote elements in the restrictor of the wh -phrase in the question immediately preceding them, while the corresponding element in an overtly clausal answer, possibly elided via VP-ellipsis, does not. This fact presents a challenge for an analysis of F ragments a s C lausal E llipsis, or FACE, according to which fragment answers are full clauses in which movement of the overt fragment to a left-peripheral position, followed by ellipsis of the vacated TP, silences everything but the moving fragment itself (cf. Merchant 2005 and references therein). This is because, prima facie , it is unclear what properties of movement and ellipsis might conspire to give rise to Jacobson's observation. We show that current FACE-compatible proposals for deriving this observation suffer from conceptual or empirical problems, and offer our own FACE-saving alternative, which we argue overcomes these problems.
abstracts.010348: This paper focuses on pronouns in the Norwegian dialects spoken in the Nord-Jæren region, a geographic area in Rogaland county on the Norwegian West Coast. We present a data set focusing on three variants of the 3rd person feminine singular object pronoun ("her"): hu, 'na and henna. We raise the question how these three variants fit into pronominal typologies such as Cardinaletti & Starke's (1996, 1999) classification of pronouns as clitic, weak and strong. We present a survey where participants (n=822) were asked to choose which of the three pronouns fits best in a given sentence. The survey results indicate that 'na is the unmarked form, whereas hu and henna are preferred in a subset of contexts, such as the topic position and the complement position of a copula verb. The overall data are indicative of a markedness hierarchy (from least marked to most marked): 'na < hu < henna. Within this markedness hierarchy, both hu and henna pattern as strong pronouns in the sense of Cardinaletti & Starke (1996, 1999), whereas 'na qualifies as a weak pronoun. These generalizations lay the groundwork for further exploration into the morphosyntactic properties of the Nord-Jæren dialects, which bears on the question of how pronominal systems are organized cross-linguistically, particularly whether languages can have more than one pronominal paradigm that classifies as strong.
abstracts.010349: The same copular syntax that yields the tradition's favorite truth condition, \textit{snow is white}, yields the animal rights movement's favorite slogan, \textit{meat is murder}. We argue that the difference between the two lives in a single parameter of the \textit{evaluation}, temperature, and that the term is not a metaphor: the parameter so named is literally the one that Harmonic Grammar and maximum entropy phonotactics fit to gradient acceptability data. The attention mechanism of transformers runs at the fixed temperature $1/\sqrt{d}$, and deployed language models expose a second instance of the same parameter to their users as the sampling knob. Grammaticality stars, analytic truths, thematic role assignment, anaphora resolution, and rhetorical force are readouts of one Gibbs competition at different operating points. We work through the mechanism on \textit{meat is murder} and its political cousins \textit{property is theft} and \textit{taxation is theft}, and on anaphora resolution in \textit{he beat him} discourses and Winograd schemas. A small experiment on a deployed model tells the two sites of the parameter apart: the sampling knob leaves the reading of \textit{meat is murder} untouched at every setting, the evaluation instruction flips it, and the model's refusal, when it refuses, localizes at the one taught boundary the analysis predicts. A self-contained appendix develops the machinery -- Gibbs distributions, annealing, energy landscapes, softmax, regularization -- assuming nothing beyond linear algebra and one-variable calculus.
abstracts.010350: This squib revisits the claim that causative predicates uniformly trigger subjunctive complements in Catalan (Rigau, 1981; Quer, 1998). While canonical causatives such as fer ‘make’ require subjunctive clauses, causative recordar ‘remind’ permits the indicative. We argue that mood selection is sensitive not simply to the causative semantics, but to the structural relation between the causative predicate and the embedded proposition. Whereas fer directly embeds the propositional content, recordar introduces it indirectly through a further embedded predicate that is a part of a periphrastic structure. We suggest that this layered structure fits well into the locality effects of subjunctive selection (Quer, 1998) which, in turn, predict the possibility of indicative in clausal complements of recordar.
abstracts.010351: **Joint work with Franco Liu** Much recent work on definiteness has assumed that definite descriptions come in two types, weak and strong. Weak definites make use of a simple situation-relative uniqueness operator; strong definites add to this a variable available to dynamic binding. Drawing on evidence from Mandarin, Jenks (2018) influentially proposed that strong definites but not weak definites can serve as donkey anaphors. We show that this claim is incorrect for Mandarin as well as for German and English. Certain special cases of donkey anaphora nevertheless have diagnostic value for the distinction between weak and strong definites. We discuss two. First, in structures where there is no dynamic quantifier available to serve as an antecedent, strong definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. Second, in so-called bishop sentences, the uniqueness requirement of the weak definite is not met; in these cases weak definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. We apply these tests to definites in German, English, and Mandarin. Our results indicate that English the and Mandarin bare nouns are always weak definites, but also that important aspects of crosslinguistic variation with respect to weak definites remain to be explained.
abstracts.010352: Nicholas Shea’s *Concepts at the Interface* (2024) identifies concepts with temporary working memory (WM) labels: ‘two-ended’ devices connected to stored information at one end and composing with other labels at the other. I argue that this framework cannot yet account for linguistic understanding. First, Shea’s theory requires stable categorical mechanisms to track category identity over time, although he is officially neutral as to their nature. Second, even granting such mechanisms, neither they nor his temporary WM labels can provide the needed compositional vehicles. The empirical evidence I review converges on the need for stable, freely compositional vehicles that I call ‘G-concepts’. On the view developed here, G-concepts—stable symbols individuated by their compositional role—compose into thoughts and bear word meaning, while ‘S-concepts’—stable representations that underwrite categorization—orient the mind toward the world. The Hybrid view preserves Shea’s interface insight while providing the compositional resources needed for linguistic cognition.
abstracts.010353: I see the concern about AI and the future of scientific fields such as pure mathematics and linguistics somewhat differently. AI opens new perspectives much more than it closes disciplines—everything is a matter of a standpoint. (This comment was submitted to Terence Tao’s moderated blog on September 22, 2026, but has not been published there yet: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/11/a-severe-misalignment-of-ai-in-mathematics/)
abstracts.010354: We make the double claim that the domain of Content (‘lexical meaning’) is not a constituent, ‎but a Span, and that the search for atomic Content is contingent on phonological representations. ‎We argue for such a dependency based on properties of (so-called) Hebrew complex prepositions, ‎such as ʕal jed-ej (múzika), ‘by (music)’ (lit ‘on hands of music’). The sequence P+N(+X) in ‎Modern Hebrew (MH) as well as in Biblical Hebrew and interim periods comprises hundreds of ‎attested tokens with rich idiosyncratic Content. However, the phonological, prosodic, Content, and ‎syntactic properties of P+N(+X) combinations do not align, with N forming a constituent with its ‎complement that excludes P (jedej muzika), but with Content and phonological properties ‎associated with the non-constituent P+N (ʕal jedej) arguing for the syntactic structure [ P [ N ‎DP/X]] in which Content can be associated with the non-constituent P-N, a Span. To affirm that ‎conclusion, we discuss and dismiss on empirical grounds several alternative analyses, among ‎which (i) the view that P+N are an instance of a possibly complex P; (ii) the possibility that N ‎incorporates into P; (iii) the possibility that Content is associated not with the sequence P-N, but ‎with N alone in the context of a designated P. ‎

abstracts.010356: In this thesis, we investigate the multifaceted uses of the Cantonese particle sin. Firstly, we argue with historical evidence that the temporal sin derives the question focus sin and the scalar sin separately. Secondly, we argue that the formulations of temporal sin derives question-focus by type-shifting: while temporal sin arranges the sequence of two propositions, question sin arranges the sequence of two questions. Then we argue that semantics of scalar sin gives a long presupposition between its prejacent p and a contextually salient expectation r. It combines with various exclusive particles by predicate modification. Decomposing the scalar and the exclusive components resolve the directionality puzzle: a single sin can associate with various exclusive particles, which can have either directionality.
abstracts.010357: In this thesis, we investigate the multifaceted uses of the Cantonese particle sin (先). Firstly, we argue with historical evidence that the temporal sin derives the question focus sin and the scalar sin separately. Secondly, we argue that the formulations of temporal sin derives question-focus by type-shifting: while temporal sin arranges the sequence of two propositions, question sin arranges the sequence of two questions. Then we argue that semantics of scalar sin gives a long presupposition between its prejacent p and a contextually salient expectation r. It combines with various exclusive particles by predicate modification. Decomposing the scalar and the exclusive components resolve the directionality puzzle: a single sin can associate with various exclusive particles, which can have either directionality.
abstracts.010358: The goal of this paper is to investigate the structural distinctions that exist between prefixoids and prefixes in modern Dutch, with an empirical focus on inseparable complex verbs (ICVs). Adopting a derivational, separationist approach to the syntaxmorphology interface (Distributed Morphology), we maintain that the fundamental difference between prefixoids and prefixes is that the former are clitics while the latter are initially merged with roots lower in the first phase (vP) prior to when these complex predicates are labeled (by v). As clitics, prefixoids are adjoined to the left-edge of the first phase (with the phase head v). Our theoretical claims are further substantiated by data extracted from the Dutch Celex Lexicon, providing a detailed assessment of the categorical status of the stem that prefixoids and prefixes attach to, their ability to contribute a resultative interpretation, and their potential effects on the argument structure of the ICV.
abstracts.010359: This revised version of my doctoral dissertation was published nearly four decades ago in 1988 and available on my website since 2010 (https://crlao.cnrs.fr/membres/waltraud-paul/). The reason for posting it now on lingbuzz with its much larger audience is the renewed interest by neurolinguists in the data set extensively discussed in my thesis. Here’s the background. Chinese has verb-object phrases (VOP) whose meaning can be compositional or non-compositional: bō ‘remove’ pí ‘skin’ = ‘peel’, kāi ‘open’ dāo ‘knife’ = ‘operate (on)’. Given their phrasal status, the verb can bear aspectual suffixes and the object can be modified; only the latter shows some constraints in the case of idiomatic VOPs. The patient of the VOP as a whole (i.e. the fruit to be peeled, the person to be operated on) must not follow the VOP, due to the Phrase Structure Condition, a general principle of Chinese syntax (cf. C.-T. James Huang 1982, ch. 2). Instead, it can occur in preverbal position, preceded by bǎ (still misanalysed as a preposition in Paul 1988), gěi ‘to, for’ or gēn ‘with’. The particular form for encoding the patient needs to be specified in the lexicon, both for compositional and non-compositional VOPs. Against this background, the thesis uses a fine-grained analysis of VOPs as a red thread to explore different core domains of Chinese syntax. Notwithstanding the myriad of syntactic arguments in favour of the phrasal status of VOPs, they are still often considered verbs, i.e. words (V°), which for mysterious reasons can be “separated” (e.g. by an aspectual suffix on the verb: V-Asp O), hence the label "separable verbs". These contrast with so-called "inseparable verbs", i.e. bona fide compound verbs (V°) such as chū ‘produce’- bǎn ‘printing.plate’ = ‘publish’ ([chū-(*Asp) bǎn] -Asp) . The main reason for the incorrect analysis as words (V°) seems to be the often observed non-compositionality of meaning and the (mis)assumption of an isomorphism between syntax and semantics. Neurolinguistic research now (mis) takes these so-called “separable verbs” (i.e. VO-phrases) as representative of the morphological domain and performs different experiments, inter alia with the aim to challenge the distinctness between morphology and syntax via the obtained neural responses (cf. as the most recent example Yu et al 2026 and similar studies cited there: https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70220). Unsurprisingly, the results are often not very conclusive and quite a lot of speculations are offered in terms of explanation. However, no-one goes back to their initial experimental design and realizes that their purported words are in fact phrases.
abstracts.010360: This paper is a state of the art paper on the linguistic phenomenon ‘semi-lexicality’. We discuss what a semi-lexical item is, namely an item which is typically considered to be from a lexical, open class (noun, verb, adjective) but which shows morphosyntactic and/or semantic properties that are usually associated with elements from functional, closed classes (quantifiers, auxiliaries, et cetera), and its theoretical relevance for the field of generative linguistics. In the first part of the paper, we relate the notion of semi-lexicality within generative linguistics to the notions of fuzziness and gradience in the fields of cognitive and functional linguistics. In the second part, we discuss earlier and later approaches to semi-lexicality within the generative framework. In the third part, we discuss the connection between grammaticalization and semi-lexicality, with a particular focus on recent generative approaches which explicitly tie these two notions together in one formal analysis.
abstracts.010361: This dissertation examines verbal number agreement with disjunctive subjects. Whereas disjunctions, like indefinites, are known to freely take existential scope above other sentential operators — even out of environments from which scope-taking is typically blocked — I show that scope readings are more limited in sentences where disjoined singular subjects control plural agreement. In particular, I argue that plural-agreeing SG-SG disjunctions must take existential scope within a polar question or beneath a downward-entailing or quantificational operator. I call this pattern Ivlieva’s Generalization based on Ivlieva (2012, 2013). While Ivlieva’s findings conflict with other existing accounts of disjunctive agreement, I present data — primarily from English, but also from Spanish, German, and Romanian — that strengthen the case that plural agreement with disjunctive subjects is semantically restricted. The cross-linguistic convergence of evidence indicates that the restricted distribution of plural disjunctive agreement owes to more general properties of disjunction and agreement rather than language-internal factors. I show that disjoined singular subjects that control singular verbal agreement, as well as disjoined plural subjects that control plural verbal agreement, display none of the same semantic restrictions. That agreement morphology correlates with semantic environment may seem surprising under a feature-copying view of agreement, but I show that the pattern becomes more familiar once we compare the distribution of plural-agreeing disjunction to that of other semantically marked indefinites, such as negative polarity items and epistemic indefinites. Though the empirical signature of each class of words is slightly different, considering plural-agreeing disjunction within the larger typology of indefinites (e.g., Haspelmath 1997) makes its distribution less anomalous. Compared to these other marked indefinites, the difference with plural-agreeing disjunction is that its distributional restrictions correlate with a reflex external to the nominal (namely, the verbal agreement) rather than with a lexical alternation within the nominal itself. I also show that the semantic environments where plural-agreeing disjunction can take existential scope strongly resemble the environments that block cross-sentential anaphora to indefinites. In light of these cross-domain connections, I present a formal account using tools from Giannakidou (1998, 2011)’s analysis of NPIs and Kamp and Reyle (1993)’s Discourse Representation Theory (DRT). In my account, the morpheme that is responsible for plural agreement with disjunction also restricts how the disjunction can existentially quantify over the disjunctive alternatives. Finally, I reconcile Ivlieva’s Generalization with past studies reporting that verbal agreement with disjoined subjects is simply unpredictable, rather than sensitive to semantic environment, as I argue it is. These previous studies primarily examine sentences where disjunction appears in matrix clauses without any overt quantification, and tend not to control for pragmatic context. I show that controlling for context allows us to better predict when singular and plural disjunctive agreement will be possible. Further, I argue that in some contexts, covert modality can provide the licensing environment that plural disjunctive agreement requires.
abstracts.010362: It is a near-consensus view in the semantic literature that the interaction between quantificational DPs and intensional operators does not give rise to wide-scope opaque readings of intensional sentences; namely, readings in which a DP in a sentence outscopes an intensional operator while its restrictor is evaluated opaquely, in the operator’s domain of quantification. In a dissent, Szabó (2010, 2011) presents a set of intensional sentences—cutting across the three primary intensional environments: attitudes, modals and tense—argued to exemplify exactly this reading, and deduces from the apparent generality of the data that an unrestricted bare quantification mechanism is in charge of accounting for it. We argue that the phenomenon is not as general as claimed, illustrating that Szabó’s wide-scope opaque reading arises for modal sentences only when the modal they contain is embedded in a relative clause, and the determiner under which the relative clause itself is embedded scopes over that modal, while the NP heading the relative clause is interpreted opaquely. We then argue that the problematic reading can thus be derived without non-standard scoping mechanisms, as the byproduct of reconstruction into intensional relative clauses. Since reconstruction effects are strictly constrained, our approach makes testable predictions regarding the distribution of Szabó’s reading with modals, which are corroborated. While we focus only on Szabó’s examples with modals, we conclude by outlining the kind of approach we believe will prove to be most fruitful in accounting for rest of the data.
abstracts.010363: At-issueness is a key concept in semantics and pragmatics, distinguishing the main point of an utterance from background information. However, there is no consensus on how at-issueness should be defined or diagnosed, given that different diagnostics for at-issueness align with different definitions and rely on different assumptions about properties of at-issue content. This paper presents an experimental comparison of five diagnostics of at-issueness, applied to the contents of non-restrictive relative clauses and the complements of clause-embedding predicates. The results are mixed: While some comparisons of the results of diagnostics reveal differences, suggesting that the diagnostics are not interchangeable, other comparisons yield more consistent results. The paper develops several hypotheses about factors that may lead different diagnostics to give different results and cautions against concluding that differences between the results of two diagnostics means that they probe distinct underlying properties (cf., Snider 2017a; Koev 2018).
abstracts.010364: Weak Crossover (WCO) describes the fact that movement dependencies like "which boy_1 did his_1 mother scold?" are unacceptable on the intended bound reading. Reviving and updating an old idea due to Eddy Ruys (1994), this paper proposes that WCO effects in overt-movement dependencies are a byproduct of a principle of competition between semantically equivalent structures: the WCO structure loses to an equivalent structure that involves shorter movement dependencies. I'll present a series of arguments for this theory, based on both new data as well as known facts which have thus far escaped analysis in the literature on crossover. The theory also offers a relatively simple explanation for why A-movement is immune to crossover effects.
abstracts.010365: Syntactic movement and its relation to syntactic islands is a core tenet within linguistics. However, the existence of said islands affecting the grammaticality of movement presents a challenge for connecting the two while modeling syntactic movement under internal merge within the minimalist program. Most approaches modeling island effects through PIC present several flaws, presenting both theoretical inconsistencies with the minimalist program, and limited empirical coverage of linguistic data. Departing from a new mathematical model of merge that is not labelless and that includes group theory and its related symmetries, PIC together with formal properties of the minimalist program such as ciclicity and c-command are derived from it while most categorical island constraints are reduced to symmetry breaking. The relabelling proposal presented here is supported by a mathematical model that reduces the additional formal machinery of the minimalist program, an analysis of syntactic movement in small clauses, case assignment in partial indirect questions, general distribution properties of syntax and sluicing. The results under the present model of merge suggest that categorical island effects on syntactic movement emerge as a result of symmetry breaking between either the two copies, or the copies and the resulting label of the higher copy landing site.
abstracts.010366: This chapter argues that the basic architecture of minimalist syntax does not need to be expanded to be consistent with the existence of variation of the kind that is of interest to sociolinguists: the core mechanisms of Merge and Agree, together with the ways that features are assumed to enter into dependencies are sufficient to provide an elegant model of such variation. The question then is whether social meanings are to be incorporated into such a feature checking mechanism, which is clearly technically possible and has been suggested in the literature. I suggest the answer to this should be no, and advocate for a stronger position, where social meanings are interpretations of structure, rather than being part of the grammat- ical representation itself, as more in keeping with the broader goals of minimalist syntax as an autonomous system with as few primitives as possible.
abstracts.010367: Classical Phase Theory suffers from a number of conceptual problems, which I sketch out here. Layered Derivation approaches (e.g. Zwart 2009, 2017) solve some, but not all of these. I suggest that rethinking the core syntactic operation, so that it is not set-theoretic Merge, but rather part-theoretic Subjoin, following Adger (2025), provides a new and improved perspective on these issues.
abstracts.010368: Attempts to classify spoken Arabic dialects based on distinct reflexes of consonant phonemes are known to employ a mixture of parameters, which often conflate linguistic and non-linguistic facts. This article advances an alternative, theory-informed perspective of segmental typology, one that takes phonological properties as the object of investigation. Under this approach, various classi-ficatory systems are legitimate; and we utilize a typological scheme within the framework of feature geometry. A minimalist model designed to account for segment-internal representations produces neat typologies of the Arabic consonants that vary across dialects, namely qāf, ǧīm, kāf, ḍād, interdentals, rhotic, and pharyngeals. Cognates for each of these are analyzed in a typology based on a few monovalent contrastive features. A key benefit of the proposed typologies is that the featural compositions of the various cognates give grounds for their behavior, in terms of contrasts and phonological activity, and potentially in diachronic processes as well. At a more general level, property-based typology is a promising line of research that helps us understand and categorize purely linguistic facts across languages or language varieties.
abstracts.010369: The R sound exhibits considerable variability both across and within Arabic dialects; one that covers place and manner of articulation, as well as the notorious emphatic-plain distinction. Some R phones are in contrastive distribution, while others are contextually conditioned or free variants. This article aims to establish the underlying R phonemes in the spoken varieties of Arabic, evidence of which is sought in R’s dialect-specific phonological behavior: in minimal pair contrasts, distributional phenomena, loanword phonology, and phonological processes that target or are triggered by R. Investigation of such evidence reveals four major patterns based on the nature and number of R phonemes, consequently classifying Arabic dialects into four types: the split-R dialects (primarily Maghrebi and Egyptian dialect groups), the emphatic-R dialects (the Levantine group), the plain-R dialects (the Gulf group together with most peripheral dialects), and the uvular-R dialects (the qeltu-dialects of Mesopotamia). The analysis employs a minimalist, contrast-based model of feature geometry to characterize aspects of the attested R’s – such as emphatic-ness, coronality, dorsality, and sonority – and shows that the typology is directly mirrored in the representation. This has theoretical implications as well. Diverse rhotic representations within closely related language varieties demonstrate that distinctive features should not be interpreted as rigidly as is often assumed, and call attention to the semi-arbitrary relationship between phonetics and phonology.
abstracts.010370: The present paper investigates a type of broad-subject construction in Egyptian Arabic in which an adjective or participial structurally qualifies the head noun (or subject) but logically qualifies a subsequent noun, as in ir-raagil [il-ħilwiin banaat-u] 'the man the beautiful.PL his daughters'. This Adjectival Relative Construction is interesting in that it incorporates properties of both relative clauses and adjectival phrases. I evaluate the main analytical approaches in the literature and conclude that it must be analyzed as a hybrid type of nominal modifier that has adjectival and relative characteristics. Binding to the head noun is accomplished through a semantically motivated resumptive pronoun.
abstracts.010371: In the speech of some educated Cairenes, the coronal stops /t d tˤ dˤ/ acquire a secondary palatal articulation before high front vowels and glides, resulting in [tj] or [dj]. Based on first-hand data, this article provides a detailed phonetic and phonological investigation of this palatalization process in an attempt to fill a descriptive gap in the literature on Cairene Arabic. By examining the full range of triggers, targets, and potential blockers, I demonstrate that this is a phonetic coarticulatory effect, and that it should be distinguished from phonological assimilation. I also explore the hypothesis that this process – characterized as a sound change in progress – has been phonologized in a different sociolect of Cairene Arabic.
abstracts.010372: This note makes two points concerning the prediction of Fox (2007) according to which disjunction should end up as conjunction in the absence of a conjunctive alternative. The first point is that Fox’s theory only makes this prediction when the disjuncts are not logically mutually exclusive. The second one is that, when the first point is taken together with Singh’s (2008) claim that "or" requires that its arguments be mutually exclusive, it may become possible to analyze both "and" and "or" as disjunctions with no conjunctive alternative, potentially explaining the homogeneous behavior of "and".
abstracts.010373: This. paper uses the technology developed in Johnson and Postal (1980) ARC PAIR GRAMMAR, to deal inter alia with facts which have totally befudled French grammarians since the 19th century. To my knowledge day, in 2026, there remains no alternate treatment to that in the listed paper.
abstracts.010374: Focus constructions in Igbo feature a set of subject/non-subject asymmetries. Subject focus constructions lack both the left peripheral morphology and the tonal reflex of A′-movement which are present when a non-subject is focused. I argue that these asymmetries diagnose neither a lack of left peripheral structure, nor a lack of A′-movement in subject focus clauses – focused subjects move to the CP layer. The surface differences reflect the fact that non-subjects, but not subjects, undergo successive cyclic A′-movement from the edge of the vP, and subjects, but not non-subjects, move from a position linearly adjacent to the complementizer domain. This proposal provides support for the existence of A′-movement reflexes at the vP edge, implicating a clause-medial phase, and C-trace effects at PF.
abstracts.010375: Several theories of reduplication have attempted to accommodate the typologically rare option of syllable copying, arguably attested in Yidiɲ (mu.la-mu.la.ri ‘initiated men’, ŋa.lal-ŋa.lal ‘big ones’). We revisit the pattern, concluding that it does not support the traditional characterization. Rather, Yidiɲ reduplication targets morphological roots most of the time, and truncates roots longer than two syllables after the second vowel. The theory of reduplication best suited for this type of pattern is Serial Template Satisfaction, which we modify to allow only segmental and morphological copying. The shape of templates is mediated partly by prespecification at the UR level and partly by markedness constraints. This theory is compared with two alternatives: Base-Reduplicant Correspondence Theory (BRCT) and Morphological Doubling Theory (MDT). We argue that BRCT has difficulties with opacity in Yidiɲ reduplication, while MDT cannot characterize the basic phonological generalizations about the shape of the reduplicative affix or the bracketing paradoxes in verbal reduplication.
abstracts.010376: This dissertation investigates how the grammar expresses defeated expectations through matrix and embedded wh-exclamatives, such as “Wow, how smart Maria is!” and “George is surprised at how smart Maria is”. It asks two central questions. First, why do wh-exclamatives morphosyntactically resemble wh-interrogatives cross-linguistically, while behaving differently from both interrogatives and declaratives? Second, what is the role of negation in wh-exclamatives when it appears redundant, not reversing the truth value of the sentence? I show that wh-exclamatives are not merely exclamatory uses of declaratives or interrogatives, and I disentangle the speech act of exclamation from the clause type of wh-exclamatives. I argue that the resemblance between wh-exclamatives and wh-interrogatives is not accidental: exclamatives are built from interrogatives plus “surprise” (or a predicate with an equivalent meaning). A wh-exclamative expresses the surprise of the speaker (for root exclamatives) or the attitude holder (for embedded exclamatives) at the answer to the question. I propose that the structure of root exclamatives is “wow-type particle + Q”, where “wow” a speaker-anchored “surprise/amaze/can’t believe”, and that of embedded exclamatives “surprise-type predicate + Q”. This accounts for their interrogative-like morphosyntax without reducing them to questions semantically: a question asks for an answer, whereas an exclamative expresses or describes surprise at an answer. The analysis has consequences for question embedding. Following Grimshaw (1979), I argue that embedded exclamatives must be distinguished from embedded interrogatives, and that the typology of clause-embedding predicates must therefore be expanded.
