Predicates such as “wonder” embed interrogatives but not exclamatives; predicates such as “surprise”, “amaze”, and “cannot believe” embed exclamatives but not genuine interrogatives; and predicates such as “know”, “tell”, and “find out” can embed both. I predict that the latter, on their exclamative use, contain a covert surprise-type predicate, and I provide several empirical arguments that support this prediction. Furthermore, I introduce a paradigm showing that declarative and question-embedding “surprise” as well as matrix exclamatives all have different discourse contributions. I argue that surprise-type predicates need to have access to their prejacent question/set of propositions, and thus that answerhood operators should not be applied to the question complement before it composes with the predicate. I also discuss the puzzling absence of polar and alternative whether-exclamatives. The second part of the dissertation turns to a cross-linguistically recurrent negation in wh-exclamatives, which I call Cover Negation (e.g., How often have I (not) watched this series! ). Examining the phenomenon cross-linguistically, I show that this negation is not expletive and has certain cross-linguistically recurring properties: it resists stress, does not license negative polarity items, permits positive polarity items, often appears with a discourse-initial “and” or “wh all”-type material, and is blocked by relative-clause complementizers. I argue that Cover Negation contributes a coverage reading: the speaker is surprised that the actual wh-values instantiate sufficiently many contextually salient categories. Formally, it performs complementation over a contextual cover, a structured set of categories in the wh-domain. I discuss other corners of the grammar where such a wh-domain is attested. The broader conclusion is that exclamatives are not peripheral expressive constructions. They illuminate how clause types are built from one another, how embedding predicates interact with questions, how language expresses or describes surprise, how negation can operate over structured alternatives, and how wh-domains are organized into contextually salient categories.
abstracts.010377: I show that the complementizer “pu” in Northern Greek is not always restricted to factive complements and can trigger an anti-factive inference. This contrasts with Standard Modern Greek “pu”, but is in line with other Greek dialects where “pu” is a generic realis—rather than a factive—complementizer (Nicholas 1998). I show that similar inferences arise with the complementizer “pos”. I argue that the incompatibility of “pu” with the definite article is independent of factivity (contra Roussou 1992, 1994), since it persists in dialects where “pu” is not factive, and since *to pos is also ungrammatical, in addition to *to pu (Angelopoulos & Tsilia 2026). I suggest that “pu” and “pos” share a question feature, inherited from their wh-uses, which contributes speaker-side questioning of the embedded proposition. This teaches us that “pu” is not always factive, that “oti” and “pos” are not in free variation, and that the explanation of *to pu cannot be tied to factivity.
abstracts.010378: A'ingae (ISO 639-3: con) has three evaluative morphemes (the augmentative -ʔu/-ʔ AUG, diminutive -ʔvi DMN, and ambivalent -ʔkhu AMV) which can be used either as nominal modifiers or as adjectivizers. Across the two functions, the segmental phonology of the evaluatives stays constant, but their stress assignment differs—the nominal modifiers stress the second syllable to their left, while the adjectivizers preserve underlying stress (if present), and stress the preceding syllable otherwise. To account for both their similarities and differences, I propose that the A'ingae evaluatives realize complex feature bundles. The modifiers expone [AUG, EVAL], [DMN, EVAL], [AMV, EVAL], and the adjectivizers expone [AUG, a], [DMN, a], [AMV, a]. The features [AUG], [DMN], and [AMV] shared across the two functions capture their segmental content. The function-specific features ([EVAL] and [a]) capture their distinct stress assignment patterns. Thus, the A'ingae data demonstrate that morphological exponence may involve not only segmental content, but also phonological processes (Hockett, 1954; Anderson, 1992; Sande, 2020; Sande, Jenks, and Inkelas, 2020), and that the realization of any single morpheme may stem from a non-trivial interplay of elements introduced by different features.
abstracts.010379: LLMs have been studied in recent linguistics as potential models of humans’ linguistic abilities. Here we discuss an entirely different use of AI, namely as a co-scientist, to help construct and assess linguistic theories (we refer to the result as “Co-Linguistics”). Since the 1960s, linguistics has developed theories that are in principle mathematically formalizable, often in the language of formal language theory or model theory. The AI revolution in mathematics will thus have consequences in linguistics—but with an essential twist: proving new theorems is rarely the linguist’s goal. Rather, one seeks to find the best set of axioms to derive empirical statements. AI could accelerate research by making existing theories fully explicit, by comparing competing theories, and more ambitiously, by proposing new theories (in machine learning, this relates to “program induction”). It will also help assess theories by accelerating the identification and test of crucial predictions, thanks to unparalleled access to data (in machine learning, this relates to “active learning”). While the cycle from theory evaluation to theory construction may give rise to recursive and possibly autonomous improvement of linguistic theories, humans remain central: linguists provide scientific directions and evaluate theories conceptually, and experimental participants are needed to assess empirical predictions that are outside the reach of LLMs. Illustrations and proofs of concept are available at https://tinyurl.com/colinguistics.
abstracts.010380: Human language allows for virtually limitless productivity. Why, then, are certain perfectly-comprehensible sentences (e.g., *The boy dragged the girl the box) deemed ungrammatical by native speakers? Here, we test the prediction of Construction Grammar accounts (c.f., Categorical Grammar accounts) that grammatical acceptability is probabilistically affected by the compatibility between the meaning (semantics) of the construction (e.g., [AGENT] [ACTION] [RECPIENT] [PATIENT]) and (a) the nouns (e.g., "The boy sent the girl the package" is more grammatical than "*The boy sent Chicago the package"; Studies 1,3,5) and (b) the speaker’s intended meaning in context (e.g., the team in the Chicago office > the geographic location; Studies 2,4,6). Across a series of six large (N=100) pre-registered studies, we find that (in all but one case), both of these factors significantly affect English speakers’ rated acceptability of sentences, across the transitive and periphrastic causative (e.g., "The clown made the man laugh" vs *"The clown laughed the man"); the to- and double-object dative (e.g., "The girl said something to the boy" vs "*The girl said the boy something") and the active/passive (e.g., "The book cost $10" vs "*$10 was cost by the book"). These findings constitute support for Construction Grammar approaches, under which this type of grammatical acceptability results from a probabilistic semantic clash, and against Categorical Grammar accounts, which can explain graded (as opposed to categorical) ungrammaticality only via some kind of add-on.
abstracts.010381: This paper examines a case of future temporal reference in Khalkha Mongolian (Eastern branch, Mongolic) that occurs in the absence of overt future morphology. When VPs are inflected solely with the tense morpheme -nA, either a present or future reading can arise, leading past descriptions of the language to characterize -nA as a non-past tense. However, the distribution of -nA raises questions for current semantic theories of the future: if a modal semantics is necessary for future temporal reference due to the uncertainty of future eventualities, does the tense morpheme give rise to the future-shifted readings on its own, or is a modal operator (covertly) present? I present novel empirical evidence that such a modal operator appears covertly alongside -nA, which I reclassify as a present tense due to its interactions with the Aktionsarten and aspect. While this modal is covert in affirmative sentences with -nA, I show that it is overtly realized under negation as the morpheme -kh. The availability of both present and future readings is traced to an ambiguity between two underlying structures: one that is future-oriented, and one that is present-oriented. In the future-oriented structure, future temporal reference stems from the presence of a covert modal operator and covert prospective aspect. Altogether, I argue that a modal analysis of future reference is needed, even when no modal appears on the surface.
abstracts.010384: Stress in (Beijing) Mandarin, or the lack thereof, is a topic under much debate in the literature. Retroflex lenition, an optional phenomenon occurred in fast speech, provides insight into prosodically weak positions in the language. Neutral-tone syllables, on the other hand, have been traditionally analyzed as unstressed. My paper discusses that the neutral-tone syllables and prosodically weak positions predicted by retroflex lenition involve different levels of (un)stress, and that the distribution of neutral-tone syllables does not affect prosodic structures in the language. Detailed analysis of the interaction between neutral-tone syllables and retroflex lenition is constructed under the Harmonic Grammar framework.
abstracts.010385: Whether Mandarin has phonemic stress has been a controversial topic in the field. Previous literature researches the phonetic evidence of stress in the language but to less avail because of the influence of tone. In my paper, I examine data from retroflex lenition from a phonological angle, arguing that the language is best analyzed with foot structures. I propose a prosodic hierarchy that allows level skipping and foot recursion. I then analyze the phenomenon under the Harmonic Grammar framework and propose an updated Match constraint that unifies morphosyntactic structures' prosodic parsing.
abstracts.010386: This study presents a reproducible framework for quantitative cross-linguistic comparison that integrates Python-based natural language processing and R-based statistical modeling. Using a corpus of 1,860 Wikipedia articles across five languages (English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German), the study extracts lexical, syntactic, and semantic features from multilingual texts. Semantic representations are generated using LaBSE Transformer embeddings, while traditional linguistic indicators capture lexical diversity and syntactic complexity. PERMANOVA results indicate that language accounts for a substantial proportion of variation in the feature space, whereas text length contributes comparatively little. Pairwise distance analyses identify Chinese as a clear outlier and English and Spanish as the closest language pair. A Mantel test further reveals a significant correlation between lexical-syntactic and semantic distance matrices, suggesting that traditional linguistic measures align with modern embedding-based representations. Mixed-effects models confirm the robustness of language effects after controlling for text length and sampling stage. The proposed framework provides a scalable and reproducible approach to quantitative typology, multilingual corpus analysis, and computational linguistic research.
abstracts.010387: We present MLFD-5, a multilingual dataset of lexical, syntactic, and semantic features extracted from 1,860 Wikipedia articles in English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German. Each document is annotated with lexical diversity measures (Type-Token Ratio, MTLD, Shannon entropy, and hapax ratio), syntactic measures derived from Universal Dependencies parsing, and 768-dimensional LaBSE semantic embeddings. The dataset is designed to facilitate reproducible cross-linguistic research by integrating interpretable linguistic indicators with Transformer-based semantic representations. Validation analyses demonstrate substantial linguistic structure in the dataset. PERMANOVA shows that language explains 35.8% of the variance in the feature space, whereas text length accounts for only 3.5%. A Mantel test reveals a significant correlation between lexical-syntactic and semantic distance matrices (r = 0.467, p = 0.001). Mixed-effects models further confirm robust language-specific effects after controlling for document length and sampling stage. MLFD-5 is publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub, together with all processing code and documentation. The dataset provides a reusable resource for quantitative typology, corpus linguistics, multilingual NLP, and cross-linguistic semantic analysis. 【1-b977d1】
abstracts.010388: Collective predication, part quantification by items like ‘both’ and ‘each’, and homogeneity provide evidence that conjunctions denote complex objects (Link, 1983; Schwarzschild, 1994; Križ, 2015). The starting point of this squib is that all of these three phenomena have counterparts with disjunction: collective predication and floating quantifiers (see also Schmitt, 2026, on similar data in German): “Heads or tails are equally likely”; “A or B both could win the race”; but also homogeneity under existential modals, the classic profile of Free Choice disjunctions (Goldstein, 2019). I also observe that the parallel goes as far as encompassing homogeneity removal: adding floating ‘each’ or ‘both’ to a Free Choice disjunction preserves its positive entailments, but under wide scope negation gives rise to a “not each”/“not both” meaning, rather than the “none”/“neither”, double prohibition profile familiar from disjunctions under negated possibility modals. On these grounds, I argue that Free Choice amounts to homogeneous distributivity over sets of alternatives. The availability of this operation, like that of other operations of closure over alternatives, is constrained by an economy principle: it is blocked whenever the same (positive) truth conditions can be achieved by replacing ‘or’ with sum-forming ‘and’ and deleting the alternative-level distributive operator in the local domain of comparison, the smallest node at which the alternative argument of this operation is saturated. This can be seen as an instance of Meyer’s (2013; 2014; 2015) more general Efficiency requirement that an LF have no simpler equivalent competitor. The constraint I propose predicts alternative-level distributivity to be allowed in sentences with possibility modals, but not in sentences with necessity modals or with non-modal predicates. Crucially, the distribution of floating ‘each’ and ‘both’ tracks that of covert distributivity over alternatives, making visible the restriction that the economy principle imposes on it: ‘each’ and ‘both’, too, are licensed in sentences with possibility modals, but not in sentences with necessity modals or non-modal predicates (and Schmitt, 2026, reports similar data for ‘jeweils’ in German). While floating part quantifiers have the same licensing conditions as distributivity over alternatives, they are also correctly predicted to affect the global truth conditions: as is familiar from the literature on homogeneity they “flatten” the truth conditions of an otherwise trivalent sentence (Schwarzschild, 1994; Löbner, 2000; Križ, 2015). Besides alternative-level distributivity and overt ‘each’ and ‘both’, this constraint also regulates existential closure but systematically leaves it available, since, as I show, the corresponding conjunctive competitor systematically isn’t equivalent to it. Distributivity over alternatives, where licensed, and existential closure together derive the range of readings associated with disjunction in non-modal sentences as well as with possibility and necessity modals, including their interaction with negation.
abstracts.010389: This article argues that Amorite exhibits substantial structural affinity with Classical Arabic and that, in several phonological, morphological, and grammatical features, Arabic provides closer correspondences to Amorite than later stages of Hebrew and other Canaanite languages. Drawing on Amorite personal names, loanwords, and the recently published Amorite–Akkadian bilingual tablets, the study examines vowel structure, interdental consonants, nominal case marking, verbal prefixes, derivational patterns, and selected lexical correspondences. The analysis distinguishes linguistic classification from structural resemblance: placing Amorite within Northwest Semitic does not make it Canaanite by default or preclude close parallels with Arabic. Particular attention is given to the preservation of older features and to the absence of the Canaanite vowel shift in Western Amorite. These observations are integrated into an account of linguistic conservatism that explains why Classical Arabic can illuminate important aspects of Amorite structure. The article concludes that the Amorite–Arabic relationship is supported by a coherent constellation of linguistic correspondences rather than isolated lexical similarities, and that Arabic constitutes an important comparative reference for interpreting Amorite evidence.
abstracts.010390: Traditional macro-comparative linguistics has historically struggled with stochastic acoustic noise and subjective lexical alignments. This study resolves these vulnerabilities through an automated, data-first computational framework, aggregating 568,820 phonetic forms across 7,791 global languages using Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment. The algorithmic pipeline extracted 75,107 distinct transitional events, isolating 3,606 universal diachronic sound-change laws driven by physical articulatory economy and directional asymmetry. Applying these optimized transition matrices within an outgroup-filtered Bayesian framework yielded a 96.4% posterior probability favoring linguistic monogenesis under a Dual-Trunk topological architecture. Intermediate trunk telemetry confirmed clean signal resolution for Proto-African (H = 5.85 bits) and Proto-Eurasian (A = 0.78,logL = −14,208.4), while isolating Sahul drift in Proto-Oceanic as an outgroup variability parameter. Spatial mapping of global phonemic entropy decay localized the theoretical Urheimat to the East African Rift (3.8◦ N,36.2◦ E), providing independent linguistic corroboration for Upper Paleolithic out-of-Africa migration patterns (r = −0.892). Ultimately, time-stratified dynamic multi-sequence alignment across 16 intermediate proto-ancestors reconstructs de novo multi-syllabic master roots, establishing a mathematically rigorous baseline for deep-time diachronic reconstruction.
abstracts.010391: My previous studies have demonstrated that current AI systems can readily assist users in performing questionable research practices (QRPs) when prompted to do so. This paper shifts the focus from documenting the problem to developing a solution. Five experiments tested whether custom instructions---short texts that users can paste into their AI settings---can serve as a "vaccine" against AI-assisted QRPs in Gemini. Experiment 1 found that both a conceptual-level instruction (referring to QRPs in general) and a behavior-list instruction (enumerating specific prohibited practices) reduced Gemini's willingness to p-hack from 100% to 0% across 30 trials each. With 30 pre-registered follow-up trials, the behavior-list instruction maintained a 0% execution rate across 60 trials in total, placing the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on its execution rate below 5%. Experiments 2a&b showed that the same instruction generalized to optional stopping, post-hoc outlier exclusion and data fabrication by blocking these requests in all 20 out of 20 trials for each task, though it failed to block a missing value imputation request in one out of 20 trials. Experiments 3a&b demonstrated that the custom instruction written in English remained effective when the user's prompt was in Japanese. Taken together, the results show that a very simple, user-level intervention can (almost) categorically eliminate a wide range of AI-assisted QRPs under the tested conditions. The vaccine is provided in a copy-and-pastable format for immediate use.
abstracts.010392: This book investigates the encoding of perspective in natural language, by looking specifically at the class of attitude report known as de se reports. In a de se report, the attitude holder entertains a thought about herself from a first personal perspective. So in a typical context, ‘Ali believes that she wrote an interesting article’ reports that Ali has the thought, “I wrote an interesting article”. Exactly how this perspective on the self is integrated into the truth conditions of de se reports is a matter of long-standing debate. The book approaches this question in two parts. First, I argue that de se construal is mediated by a dedicated grammatical mechanism established at LF, known as ‘de se binding’. Evidence for this is drawn from a detailed study of counterfactual attitudes such as imagine, marshalling data from a variety of languages. Next, I show that the classical rendition of de se binding suffers from a number of problems. I develop a new semantics for de se that maintains de se binding, but which overcomes the challenges faced by previous approaches. The resulting picture serves as an affirmation of ‘de se exceptionalism’ – the view that there is something distinctive about attitudes about the self as a mental phenomenon, and that this distinctiveness is apparent in how such attitudes are encoded in the grammar.
abstracts.010393: Not every language that appears to be an ergative language actually is one. However, if it is a language with ergative alignment, the absolutive is the case of the grammatical subject, regardless of transitivity. Pseudo-ergative languages must not be confused with ergative languages; otherwise, the very confusions to which typologists have become accustomed arise. [corrected bibliography; included: marked-S languages; with a few cosmetic touch-ups]
abstracts.010396: This paper discusses loanwords in the Kanien’kéha (a.k.a. Mohawk) language in the dialect of the Kahnawà:ke community south of Montreal. This dialect is termed Kahnawa’kéha. The main contribution of the paper is a list of loanwords in different semantic categories. It also discusses the influence of language revitalization activities on the use of loanwords. These have caused some loanwords that were formerly in common use to be replaced by words with entirely Kanien’kéha roots; other loanwords have remained in daily use by most speakers of the language. There are also intermediate cases, where a given loanword continues to be used by a significant number of speakers, while others have abandoned it in favour of a purely Kanien’kéha word. Thus, there is a kind of tug of war between efforts to rid the local dialect of loanwords, and the desire of some speakers to retain a minority of frequently used loanwords. The paper builds on earlier work on Kanien’kéha loanwords. It represents a good-faith attempt by a well-informed local observer with linguistic training to describe the current use of loanwords in the community. It concludes with an informal survey of language “purification” activities across the globe.
abstracts.010397: Robust results from psycholinguistic research show that in the processing of a negative sentence, the subject passes through an initial stage in which they entertain the prejacent of negation. In this short paper, I point out a parallelism between the two-step simulation account, motivated by this evidence, and the dynamic semantic analysis of negative sentences by Heim (1983), where context update by the prejacent is an intermediate step. I then propose, building on Krifka (2013), that each step of the recursive update of negative sentences introduces a propositional discourse referent, and I explore the possibility that the "prejacent" discourse referent, when sufficiently salient, can be exploited to support exceptional anaphora to an antecedent embedded in the prejacent.
abstracts.010398: Allama Nasir Hunzai’s works present the suffix cited as -ik in descriptive grammars under the label tabʿīz, called kāf-e tabʿīz in Burushaski Jawahir Paray. This documentary comparison examines three grammatical tables and twelve dictionary records alongside Berger’s and Yoshioka’s descriptions. All 34 rows supply a form in the third column, including rows whose singular and plural are written alike. In 17 of the 24 rows with differently written singular and plural, the third-column form begins with the plural exactly as written; this written relation does not identify a morphological base. Eleven dictionary headwords carry the category label; seven receive direct glosses rendered here as ‘some’, ‘a few’ or ‘certain’. These findings document an author’s grammatical presentation, rather than speakers’ acceptance or a new semantic analysis. A comparison with forty identified tokens in Berger’s Hunza texts does not decide between indefinite-plural and subset readings, or rule out a contextual-quantification possibility considered here. The contribution is a documentary account of the category’s labels, paradigm arrangement and non-uniformities, with limits on the semantic inferences these support.
abstracts.010399: Certain structural domains restrict syntactic movement, a phenomenon termed the island effect. Although traditionally considered a class of syntactic constraints, island effects have been attributed by some to the clash between the discourse backgrounded status of the island domain and the foregrounding function of movements. Although previous work supports a correlation between the discourse backgroundedness of structures and their islandhood, it is unclear whether island effects can be entirely reduced to a discourse constraint as some previous studies suggest. In this study, we provide evidence against this reductionist version of the discourse accounts of island. Specifically, using the island satiation effect as an experimental manipulation, we show that island effects ameliorate after repeated exposure, but there is no corresponding reduction in perceived backgroundedness of the island domains. This result demonstrates a dissociation between the satiation of island effects and any change in the perceived discourse backgroundedness of the island domain, challenging a core prediction of the discourse-only account of islands.
abstracts.010400: This doctoral dissertation deals with the syntax (and semantics) of German experiencer-object verbs like _gefallen_ ‘to appeal to’ or _freuen_ ‘to please’, which realise the experiencer of a psychological state as their object. Experiencer-object verbs are widely held to show peculiar behaviour, i.a. with respect to argument ordering preferences and reflexive binding options (backward binding), a view which is rejected here for German. The work presents three experimental studies on argument ordering preferences and one on binding options, along with additional discussion. The experimental results speak against theories of German clausal syntax assuming that arguments have to combine with the predicate in a predicate-specific order and equating this order with the normal one, and against predicate-based binding theories, binding theories relying on a hierarchy of grammatical functions and all accounts detaching surface order and configurational syntax. The analysis assumes that reflexive binding of German _sich_ ‘REFL’ requires c-command, that arguments can be base-generated freely in any order in the German midfield, and that argument ordering preferences are determined by violable weighted constraints (implemented in a Maximum Entropy Grammar). Case- or grammatical-function-based constraints are not needed. The widespread idea that (dative-object) experiencer-object verbs are unaccusatives is rejected. While the heterogeneity of accusative-object experiencer-object verbs is well-established, the experiments and additional discussions demonstrate that dative-object experiencer-object verbs are not a homogeneous class in German either, both semantically and in terms of their ordering preferences.
abstracts.010401: When we rehearse a sentence silently, such as ‘Hi, what’s up?’ before greeting a friend, the brain runs much of the machinery of speaking without moving a muscle. This paper asks, from a linguistic perspective, how a machine could turn that silent speech into words. We propose a framework in two parts. The first is a measurement programme that moves from overt to covert speech in controlled steps. Phonemes are first mapped while they are spoken aloud (data-A). Articulatory and laryngeal layers are then removed one at a time to isolate the neural correlates of individual distinctive features (data-B). Finally, the same items are only imagined (data-C). The second part is an inference cascade. Noisy, phoneme-level neural evidence is resolved by successive layers of linguistic knowledge: phonotactics, prosodic timing, the lexicon, morphosyntax, semantics, and discourse. A worked example shows how the fragmentary signal H..y, w…tz ..p converges on a single utterance. We argue that the phoneme is the right unit for decoding because of duality of patterning: a small, closed inventory generates an open-ended vocabulary. This architecture converges with that of current speech neuroprostheses, which pair phoneme decoders with language models and have recently begun to decode inner speech. The linguistic analysis adds three cautions that such systems rarely state. Inner speech may be condensed rather than merely noisy. A strong language model can end up writing the speaker’s sentence for them. And only inner speech addressed to someone should be decoded at all. I welcome reviews or comments on this work, as well as collaborations.
abstracts.010402: The research presented in this paper aims to explore the articulation of patients with bifurcated tongues. It focuses on three aspects: spontaneous articulation, controlled articulation, and the hypothesized ability of people with split tongues - to articulate two coronal consonants simultaneously thanks to the possibility of moving the halves independently. The project involved two anonymous participants and three judges: a linguist, a Polish language teacher, and a speech-language pathologist. To verify the accuracy of patients’ articulation in spontaneous speech, a list of generic, open questions was designed. To verify their controlled articulation, the author made use of a pronunciation test recommended by a fellow speech-language pathologist. To measure the ability to coarticulate coronal consonants, a special test was designed by the author. Prior to the research itself, the participants were provided with the consonantal pairs and asked to train the coarticulation for a period of a week or two. The participants answered the questions on the list, followed the instructions of the controlled articulation test, and attempted to pronounce the consonantal pairs given to them a few times. The attempts were recorded and sent to the judges, who then independently verified the first two parts. The author then gathered their opinions and compared them. The third part of the research, the coarticulation test, was verified by the author. The research found out that spontaneous speech in the participants was mostly intelligible, with some distortions to their sibilants and the consonant [r]. Their controlled speech was practically perfect. The participants also managed to pronounce ten of the 38 consonantal pairs. The author then described the achieved pairs and proposed IPA symbols for them, which concluded the research.
abstracts.010403: Building on the author's previous series of studies on Middle Chinese sound categories and rhyme categories, this paper reorganizes and improves the reconstruction of the Qieyun rhyme headings. Previous research has revealed the existence in Middle Chinese of vocal fry phonation, the coexistence of rounded and unrounded front vowels, and apical vowels arising from fricative categories. On this basis, and in light of existing scholarship, this paper introduces coarticulatory constraints between the medial and the rhyme nucleus, and employs Sino-Japanese readings to correct the phonetic values of the Qieyun. The study finds that Sino-Japanese Kan-on and Sino-Vietnamese readings record ě rushengshen in the Chang'an dialect of the Tang dynasty, while Go-on records vocal fry phonation of the Jiangdong Qieyun system，employing Sino-Japanese transcriptions -ei and -e, as well as Sino-Vietnamese -inh and -ê, to record the relevant sounds. Since ě rushengshen does not appear in Sino-Japanese Go-on, the watershed in the evolution of Middle Chinese is thereby clearly delineated. The discrepancy in Division II rhyming practices between the Liu Song and Qi-Liang periods, as attested in Southern Dynasties poetry and prose, warrants the inference that the vocal fry phonation attested in the Qieyun system was inherited from the Wu dialect of the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties. To verify these extraterritorial transcriptions, this paper also examines portions of the rhyme groups of the Zhongyuan Yinyun, finding that the Qiwei, Zisi, Jiama, and Chezhe rhyme groups each contain two rhyme feet of similar phonetic value. Finally, based on the reconstructed Qieyun rhyme categories and taking Wang Li's Old Chinese rhyme groups as a framework, the phonetic values of the Old Chinese rhyme groups are reconstructed. This paper also reveals that the evolution of Chinese phonology cannot be characterized as a linear historical development within a single phonological system.
abstracts.010404: This study investigates quantitatively the validity and causality of the connection between verbal agreement richness and null-subject availability that is central to the Null Subject Parameter (Rizzi, 1982). We first introduce the Verbal Agreement Syncretism Score (VASS), an information-theoretic metric that quantifies agreement syncretism directly from corpus data. We show that VASS captures the diachronic increase in syncretism in Historical English, which is significantly associated with a decline in null-subject rates. Extending the analysis to five historical and modern Germanic and Romance languages, we find the same significant inverse correlation crosslinguistically, providing evidence for a gradient connection between agreement syncretism and null-subject use. We then investigate the causal basis of this correlation through simulations. By incorporating pressures for communicative efficiency and a pragmatic markedness assumption into an adaptation of the Variational Learning framework (Yang, 2002), we reproduce the empirically observed variation in null-subject rates from differences in VASS, lending support to a causal link behind the parametric dependency. More broadly, we show that a numerical approach to parameterization makes the gradient nature of linguistic parameters empirically measurable, their development and variation quantitatively crosslinguistically trackable, and their potential causal dependencies computationally testable.
abstracts.010406: Based on the joint work primarily on Chinese with Redouane Djamouri and John Whitman (cf. references section and my website: https://crlao.cnrs.fr/membres/waltraud-paul/), this talk argues for what historical linguists have long called the “uniformitarian principle”, i.e. the assumption that the same principles that apply to synchronic grammars also apply to earlier stages of the language (cf. Walkden 2019 for the history of that term). Each synchronic stage, present and past, represents a stable system which can be acquired and hence must be consistent with the universal constraints observed for language in general. (Cf. Hale 1998, 2007; Hale & Kissock 2021, Lightfoot 2020). Not recognizing the need for a uniformitarian approach has given rise to an array of concepts currently used in diachronic syntax, some borrowed from typology: (dis)harmony, parameters, “gradual” change, change towards a goal (“cycle”, “path”), triggers for a change. The goal of this talk is to disentangle this Gordian knot. Chinese serves as an illustration and confirmation of the rich literature in the past decades showing that the concepts above have no role to play in linguistic theorizing (cf. Whitman 2001a, 2008; Whitman & Ono 2017, Paul 2024). Every acquirer creates a new I-language, i.e. there is no “transmission” of language with language being handed down from one speaker to the other (Cf. most recently Lightfoot 2020: 147: “I-languages are not objects floating smoothly through time and space”.)
abstracts.010407: This paper explores the controversial topic of wanna contraction through the lens of the syntax-prosody interface. After an overview of previous theories, it focuses on comparing two unrefuted accounts. By providing new prosodic evidence from an elicitation experiment with native speakers, the study resolves the debate in favor of Goodall’s (2021) restructuring analysis. Further theoretical implications include the claim that both exceptional case-marking (ECM) infinitives and Control infinitives embed a Complementizer Phrase (CP). A key methodological contribution of this investigation is the use of measurable phonetic correlates, such as pitch contours, to disentangle theoretically contentious linguistic topics.
abstracts.010408: Collins (2026) showed that the version of the coproduct used to implement 'movement' in Marcolli, Chomsky and Berwick (2025) did not give an adequate account of Reconstruction. Here I will propose one that does, by maintaining the full structure of 'extracted' subtrees, but managing their 'cancelled' status with some extra bookkeeping in the workspace.
abstracts.010410: This article aims to show, based on an overview of the literature, that an important theme in the study of these languages is the role of stress. Many of the phenomena in the language can be and traditionally have been understood as a result of the very dominant asymmetries between syllables that have been caused by the fact that the Germanic foot is an asymmetric trochaic and quantity-sensitive unit.
abstracts.010411: This manuscript has been written as the first version of the Coordination chapter for Carnie et al. 2027 – the 2nd edition of the Routledge Handbook of Syntax . Unfortunately, it is almost two times longer than the official space limit allows, so I will probably have to substantially shorten it for the handbook. If so, I plan to maintain two versions of this paper: a longer forever unpublished manuscript with the current title and a much shorter Coordination chapter of the handbook. (The current version 3 adds references to recent experimental work on violations of the Coordinate Structure Constraint, version 2 differs from the original version 1 only by including a funding statement.)
abstracts.010413: In a recent paper, Berg (2024) explored the typology of gender distinctions conditioned by person and number in independent pronouns, drawing on a large sample of languages. The main finding is that, although third-person pronouns are more likely to feature gender distinctions in the singular, first-person pronouns are more likely to do so in the plural, quantitatively confirming earlier observations, as discussed in Plank’s (2026) commentary on the paper and in Berg’s (2026) response. Berg (2024) relates the asymmetry between third-person and first-person pronouns to the long-standing idea that gender distinctions are less useful in singular first-person pronouns because the referent is unambiguous in language use. In this commentary, I discuss an explicit model of gender syncretism based on communicative efficiency, proposed in Storme (2022), which is conceptually close to the approach advocated by Berg (2024). I examine both the insights the model offers into Berg's findings and the limitations these findings reveal. Although the model derives the observed direction of the asymmetries, it also makes problematic predictions. In particular, it incorrectly predicts that the preference for gender-marking in plural first-person pronouns should have the form of an implicational universal, similar to Greenberg’s (1963) Universals 44 and 45. Yet the data collected by Berg (2024) does not point to an implicational universal, even under a statistical interpretation: relatively many languages in the sample distinguish gender in first-person singular but not plural pronouns, compared with languages that maintain gender distinctions in both numbers. I discuss why the generalization on gender distinctions in first-person pronouns does not have an implicational form, contrary to Greenberg’s Universals 44 and 45 about third-person pronouns. I suggest that gender distinctions are less useful in first- than in third-person pronouns overall, making communicative-efficiency pressures more susceptible to being overridden by factors such as analogical leveling in the former.
abstracts.010414: Generative linguistics typically treats grammaticality as a binary matter, attributing the gradient effects frequently observed in acceptability judgment experiments to performance factors rather than to the grammar. Yet no specific performance account has, to our knowledge, been offered for most such effects, which strengthens the case for gradient grammaticality. Gradient judgments, however, have received little systematic study in experimental syntax, and the frameworks built on existing findings are better characterized as blueprints than formalized grammars. This paper takes a step towards closing both gaps. Four acceptability judgment experiments, two in English and two in Polish, manipulated violations of two constraints: subject–verb agreement and syntactic selectional restrictions. The results show that violation costs are systematically gradient, differing by constraint and by predicate, and reliably cumulative in that two violations are generally worse than one. Crucially, however, they combine under-additively rather than by linear summation as commonly assumed. We then outline Gradient Model-Theoretic Dependency Grammar , a formally explicit, monostratal, constraint-based framework in which constraints are adorned with stochastic penalty weights and violations combine through an under-additive function. As a proof of concept, we apply it to one of our experiments to estimate weights from the judgment data and derive acceptability predictions.
abstracts.010415: An ellipsis construction known as sluicing is commonly analyzed as involving wh-movement to the left-periphery of the clause followed by deletion of TP (Merchant 2001). Such an analysis, however, cannot be directly applied to languages without obligatory wh-fronting, raising the expectation that other mechanisms are employed to derive sluicing-resembling strings in these languages. In this paper, I provide a detailed description of two sluicing-like constructions in Muira Dargwa, an under-investigated Nakh-Daghestanian language without obligatory wh-fronting, and develop an analysis for each of them. I argue that only one construction – the one that exhibits the case-connectivity effect – is derived via ellipsis. Specifically, I propose that it is derived from a cleft-like argument-focus construction, to which deletion has been applied. By contrast, a construction that exhibits the case-disconnectivity effect is in fact a copular clause with an omitted E-type subject pronoun (Evans 1977); crucially, this pronoun is missing not due to ellipsis. Thus, these findings provide new data that further supports the claim that languages without obligatory wh-fronting lack genuine sluicing, as predicted by the move-and-delete approach.
abstracts.010416: This dissertation investigates how speakers know what it means for an argument to be interpreted with a given thematic role in the context of a given event; e.g., what it means to be the patient of a stabbing event. It argues that these interpretations are not already stored as part of the lexical entry of the verb but generated compositionally in the syntax by combining an event description with an argument-introducing functional head associated with a thematic role.
abstracts.010417: This paper investigates the morpho-phonology of Sekani nouns by focusing on the dual-level behavior of the POSS suffix -è. After an evaluation of the empirical coverage and theoretical fitness of previous theories, I reconsider data from Hargus (1985) that are not addressed in the analysis by McCann (2024) and propose a new theory consisting in optimized stratal boundarization at the morpho-phonology interface. The new theory suggests that stratal affiliation on morphemes does not exist. The stratal location of morphemes is instead determined by a combination of their morpho-syntactic features and the stratal boundarization strategies of the language.
abstracts.010418: There is a joke about language competence, namely that people seem to believe that speaking a language makes you competent enough to participate in any discussion on the topic of language. Now, since language is at the core of LLMs, the joke appears easily transferable to the topic of LLMs. Thus, currently, many people who use LLMs try to improve them, speaking of AI in general, though the latter clearly goes far beyond language. The text is a reaction to the announcement of the Conference on Language Intelligence, to be held in Vienna, at the Austrian Parliament, on November 17–19, 2026. The focus is on the distinction between using and evaluating an LLM and improving its underlying model. The issues addressed are relevant to language and language studies and applications, including LLMs and AI. The discussion is structured to be of interest to linguists and non-linguists alike.
abstracts.010419: This Master Thesis investigates the morpho-syntax of Basque nominal inflection, focusing on two quantifier-article interactions: {Quantifier + Indefinite article} and {Quantifier + Definite article}. The former interaction displays a puzzle of Definiteness Ambiguity or Definiteness Unambiguity depending on the presence of certain quantifiers. The latter interaction shows ineffability in the presence of certain quantifiers. While prior work has examined quantifiers and determiners individually, less attention has been devoted to how their combination affects other components of the nominal domain, such as pre-case morphemes and demonstratives. This study aims to fill this gap by providing a unified account. My proposal for the {Quantifier + Indefinite article} interaction consists in Definiteness Underspecification to account for the pattern of Definiteness Ambiguity, and a Number Impoverishment rule to account for the pattern of Definiteness Unambiguity. My proposal for the {Quantifier + Definite article} interaction is a syntactic output optimization step with syntactic DP (Determiner Phrase) phasehood, but without morphological DP phasehood. Through new empirical and theoretical contributions, this work tries to shed light on the understanding of Basque grammar as well as on the understanding of overall morpho-syntactic theory, including issues such as agreement directionality, syntactic output optimization, modular phasehood, and directionality of allomorphy.
abstracts.010420: This paper provides a crosslinguistic investigation of unrestrictive relative pronouns as syntactic operators that condition selective Agreement opacity. I have identified two types of relative pronouns: Comp-RelPs (relative pronouns syncretic with the verbal complementizer) and else-RelPs (relative pronouns non-syncretic with the verbal complementizer). I have collected a dataset of unrestrictive relative clauses from 10 languages. The main empirical observation in the dataset is that Comp-RelPs always seem to require matching Agreement. In contrast, when it comes to else-RelPs, all logically possible agreement patterns are attested: matching Agreement, default third person Agreement, and optionality between matching or default Agreement. The proposed account consists in analyzing Comp-RelPs as a [∗REL_PRO∗] operator, i.e. a relativizing operator that requires a pro Subject in the embedded clause. Else-RelPs, however, are analyzed as a [∗REL∗] operator, i.e. a relativizing operator that does not require any pro Subject in the embedded clause.
abstracts.010421: The Person-Case Constraint (PCC) is a family of restrictions on the distribution of marked features on objects in double-object constructions. Decades of research have focused on languages where only 'phonologically weak' elements (clitics, agreement markers) are subject to the PCC effect. This has led to debates about the relative roles of syntactic and morphological/PF factors in giving rise to the PCC. In this paper we show that PCC effects are also attested in cases where neither object is phonologically weak. We make our case primarily for Atchan (Kwa), and show how it extends as well to English and other languages. Among contemporary theories of the PCC, these data support those based purely on licensing in syntax (e.g. Anagnostopoulou 2003, Béjar and Rezac 2003). They challenge theories tying the PCC tightly to the grammar of phonologically weak forms, such as Coon and Keine’s (2021) Feature Gluttony theory.
abstracts.010422: Since its inception, phase theory has changed its phase heads, its impenetrability condition and its motivation, which makes it a test case for a programmatic Minimalism in which divergent analyses are hard to compare. The question is not whether phases exist, but what they follow from. I show, under explicit assumptions, that the Phase Impenetrability Condition never enlarges the domain that search can reach, and bounds it only if every recursive spine is cut at bounded intervals: efficiency requires cuts, not their location. I argue that the location is set by the interfaces: phases close the argument domain of a predicate and the clausal domain built over it, whereas non-complements are transferred whole, as in Multiple Spell-Out. Nominals without argument structure contain no closure point, so DPs and PPs are not punctuated, and their recursion is left unbounded. The proposal is compared with minimality-based and mereological alternatives on explicit predictions.
abstracts.010423: This paper explores a phenomenon where the Degree Word (Deg) in Basque exhibits semantically vacuous positional variability. Basque Degs can be located before the adjective they modify, or one slot further to the left, i.e. prenominally. This optionality between the preadjectival and the prenominal position is restricted semantically (only augmenter Degs permit it) and syntactically (Degs cannot be scrambled across a Determiner Phrase boundary). To formally account for the phenomenon, I test syntactic, prosodic and morphological hypotheses, and I end up proposing an account consisting in morphological metathesis through an optimization step of two equally ranked Optimality Theoretic (OT) constraints. This paper can be situated within a line of research suggesting that all Free Word Order phenomena cannot be reduced to a single component of the grammar. Rather, it seems that different linguistic modules are equipped with technical devices that are able to produce scrambling.
abstracts.010424: Cataphora resolution requires a forward-looking parser to utilize linguistic cues to identify potential referents. This study examines how semantic gender, the phase c-command constraint (Huang & Lin, 2021), and the linearity constraint influence the processing of cataphoric dependencies in Chinese. We manipulated the position of the cataphoric pronoun within a prenominal relative clause such that its coreference with the head noun either complied with or violated the phase c-command constraint. Self-paced reading and eye-tracking results suggest that gender cues guide early-stage processing only when coreference is licensed by the phase c-command constraint. The linearity constraint does not block active formation of dependencies during incremental parsing, but at later stages structural violations can be overridden by semantic congruency. These findings can inform linguistic and psycholinguistic accounts of cataphora resolution.
abstracts.010425: Generative AI systems are equipped with ethical guardrails, which are supposed to block requests that can potentially cause harm. However, the robustness of these guardrails (vis-a-vis research ethics) across languages remains underexplored. Kawahara (2026b) found that Gemini (Flash Lite 3.5) generally refused to share a hypothetical manuscript under review when asked in English, but complied when asked in Japanese. Building on this finding, the current experiment asked Gemini to fabricate experimental data to supplement an underpowered study, a request that amounts to a clear case of research misconduct. Gemini executed the request in 9 out of 30 English trials (30%), whereas it did so in 17 out of 30 Japanese trials (57%), revealing a significant difference (p < .05). Moreover, among compliant responses, Japanese outputs included ethical warnings only once (1/17), whereas English outputs more frequently included warnings (5/9). These findings suggest that ethical alignment in generative AIs can be language-dependent, raising concerns that users who rely on generative AI in languages other than English may be facing heightened exposure to AI-facilitated misconduct.
abstracts.010426: Irish presents a twofold restriction on negation: it lacks constituent negation, and sentential negation can only take sentential scope; Irish employs negative clefts for constituent negation. I argue that these restrictions follow from independent conditions on the realisation of Focus. Prosodically, Irish disfavours in situ marking of narrow Focus and rather resorts to Focus-fronting. Hence, unlike in Italian, sentential negation cannot associate with a corrective Focus in its scope. Irish realises corrective Focus with cleft sentences; since constituent negation prototypically associates with corrective Focus, it is consequently relegated to negative clefts. I argue that the underlying factor in this distribution is exhaustivity, which in Irish is syntacticised by clefts: Irish realises correction as exhaustive Focus plus incompatibility with a previous assertion. I conclude with some speculations on the role of the copula in deriving the exhaustivity of clefts and discuss how exhaustivity constrains the distribution of Irish monotone decreasing expressions.
abstracts.010427: Work on reduplication has mostly developed in parallel, constraint-based terms, while serial rule-based accounts have received less attention. This paper develops Link/Copy, a derivational account that splits reduplication between link, in restricted phonology, and copy, in surface phonology. The model builds on Distributed Reduplication but embeds it in a cyclic model of the morphosyntax-phonology interface with a more restricted morphophonology. We begin from the hypothesis that the reduplicant has no segmental content until copy, and test it with three cases where reduplication interacts with infixation and allomorphy: umlaut overapplication in Chamorro, prosodically conditioned allomorphy in Nancowry, and segmentally conditioned allomorphy in Muna. Chamorro shows that umlaut overapplication can be derived without Base-Reduplicant Correspondence Theory if segmental mapping to the reduplicant is delayed. Nancowry shows that the reduplicant’s skeletal structure must be visible before a later cycle. Muna shows that segmental information must be visible too. We therefore revise link so that it establishes phonemic associations earlier, and argue that allomorphy around reduplication diagnoses operation timing and intermediate representations in morphophonology.
abstracts.010428: We propose to restore the discovery procedure to the center of linguistic inquiry. To do so, however, we must abandon the goal of constructing an optimal grammar for linguistic data but pursue a merely adequate one in a sense to be precise. We propose an abductive learning procedure that incrementally generates and evaluates grammatical hypotheses and apply it to several morpho-phonological learning problems across languages in comparison to child language development and alternative, optimization-based, learning models including neural networks. This new and renewed perspective on the discovery procedure has broad implications for the pursuit of descriptive and explanatory adequacy in the study of language and its connection to cognition.
abstracts.010429: Branan (2023) proposes that locality constraints on A-movement may be obviated if movement of the closest goal would violate antilocality, a condition which prohibits movement from being too short. This reply argues that the account is not sufficiently supported by the data, raises a number of theoretical concerns and is incompatible with the broader literature on antilocality. The inefficacy of antilocality as an explanation for the patterns discussed in the paper and the number of ancillary assumptions it requires raise concerns for the validity of antilocality constraints more generally.
abstracts.010430: This is a paper on gender and classifier marking in eight southern Dravidian languages. This paper is part of a special volume on gender and classifier marking in world languages. The full volume is freely available on the website of the Journal of Foreign Language Education (Keio University, Japan). Comments and suggestions are most welcome.
abstracts.010431: ***This manuscript has been accepted for publication in Cognitive Linguistic Studies; the version currently posted is the author‑submitted preprint prior to peer review.*** Human cognition universally supports understanding of motion events, yet languages vary in how they encode them. A key crosslinguistic difference concerns the expression of manner and path. Verb-framed languages typically encode path in the main predicate, leaving manner to optional adjuncts; satellite-framed languages express manner through the main verb and path through satellites (Talmy 1985, 2000). However, the classification of Mandarin motion constructions (MMCs) remains debated. This paper challenges the binary framework, arguing that Mandarin represents a third type, equipollent-framed language (Slobin, 2004), where both verbs contribute equally to motion event structure. MMCs involve a serial verb construction in which each verb introduces a distinct argument via separate functional v heads. This study analyzes the morphosyntactic properties of each component and of the MP complex as a whole, and examines how their syntactic structure maps onto conceptual representation, providing new evidence for the equipollent-framed hypothesis and clarifying Mandarin’s typological status.
abstracts.010432: This paper argues that English and Chinese distribute logical information differently across their grammatical surfaces, and that this difference has consequences for formal reasoning tasks. English obligatorily encodes reference, time, modality, and clause hierarchy on the surface; Chinese leaves much of this information to context, aspect, word order, and discourse coherence. The distinction is not one of expressive capacity—both languages can express what the other can express—but one of where the information is carried. We introduce the concept of formal accessibility: the degree to which a language's grammar places the logical relations required by formal reasoning on the surface, where they can be read without reconstruction. We propose, as a hypothesis, that the preference of modern formal science for English is in part a structural consequence of this difference, though historical and sociological factors are also involved. We also argue that both languages, regardless of their internal distribution, operate within the same symbolic boundary: neither reaches beyond what symbolic systems can carry. The scope of this paper is restricted throughout to written texts used for formal reasoning—primarily mathematical proof, engineering specification, and program documentation. Legal statute comparison would require separate parallel-corpus treatment and is not attempted here. The analysis does not extend to literary texts, ordinary conversation, or other registers, in which the implicitness of Chinese may function as an advantage rather than a cost.
abstracts.010433: This paper revisits the analysis of tough constructions (this book is easy to read), assuming that, unlike many recent proposals, tough predicates have a single lexical entry and take a single thematic argument. It proposes as most analyses do, that silent operator movement is involved, but targets the periphery of the adjective phrase, allowing complex predicate formation. Some reconstruction effects in French and English suggest that tough subjects can sometimes originate inside the infinitival clause. The paper explores restrictions on such movement, proposes an account of intervention effects based on extraposition, and extends the approach to pretty/heavy constructions (this box is heavy to carry), treating their infinitives as comparison-class restrictors. (a few typos in the published version are corrected here).
abstracts.010434: In the AI era, almost everybody has heard of tokens, and many know that these are the basic units of LLMs. Yet, it is hard to believe that LLMs work with tokens, specifically with token IDs, and not with words. This text explains the apparent contradiction between words and tokens with the help of ‘made from’ and ‘made of’. It does seem most natural to infer the nature of a system from what it produces; and if an LLM produces extraordinarily fluent language, we expect that inside it there must be language that comes out during communication. LLMs are made from language and, exactly like humans, are not full of words.
abstracts.010435: Much work in Distributed Morphology assumes that Impoverishment is a post-syntactic operation, applying to the output of the syntax, and thus unable to affect Agree. This paper argues that Impoverishment instead applies as soon as the context for it is met (Richards 2023), and so may be interspersed with Merge and Agree. The argument comes from the interaction of agreement with case and with Ā-features, both of which are known to disrupt agreement with the nominal that bears them, giving rise to default agreement, partial agreement, or skipping of the nominal altogether. I show that all three patterns result from a single operation, Impoverishment of φ-features in the context of a case or Ā-feature, and that they differ only in whether the rule applies on the probe, after Agree, or on the goal, before it. Chirag Dargwa (Nakh-Daghestanian) provides a timing argument for this view: the ergative causee of a periphrastic causative is skipped by the person probe, while an ergative subject bearing the same features is not, and the two differ only in when they received their case. No post-syntactic theory of Impoverishment, with or without Multiple Agree, is able to make this distinction. A unification of case discrimination and anti-agreement follows as a consequence.
abstracts.010436: Icelandic nominal declension show (acc = dat) ̸= gen syncretisms which go against Caha’s (2009) cross-linguistic pattern of of acc > gen > dat and hence seemingly violate the *ABA generalisation (Harðarson 2016; Starke 2017) . Proposals to overcome this problem have needed to either allow variation in the fseq (Harðarson 2016), or enrich the fseq (Starke 2017). Here we show that the Icelandic *ABA problem can be solved while keeping to Caha’s (2009) fseq, and without adding mechanisms to the standard theory of Nanosyntax. The key to the solution lies in the phonology of Icelandic, together with a recent reformulation of the nanosyntactic algorithm in terms of pied-piping.
abstracts.010437: Acceptability judgments are central to syntactic theory and formal acceptability experiments have made the underlying data more reliable. Yet they leave one issue open: once a sentence is placed on a rating scale, the resulting number is interpretable only relative to the other items in its experiment, not in any absolute sense. Standard items – a fixed battery of sentences validated to occupy known, approximately evenly spaced positions across the acceptability range – address this by serving as shared anchors, but such sets exist only for English (Gerbrich et al., 2019) and German (Featherston, 2009). This paper develops and validates the first standard item set for Polish with a methodological approach consisting of a two-stage design that separates set selection (three iterative norming experiments) from validation (four large-scale experiments, around 1000 participants in total). The resulting set places fifteen items at five evenly spaced, correctly ordered levels that remain stable across studies with different participants, target items, and contexts. To establish a benchmark, two further experiments were conducted using a comparable methodology to test the existing English standard items. The Polish set was found to be at least as reliable as the English one.
abstracts.010438: This paper argues that correlative constructions are sensitive to the presence of an index in their correlate. This perspective challenges existing views on which correlatives require a demonstrative (Lipták 2009). I argue that the index-based view is theoretically grounded and, further, empirically borne out: strong, index-introducing definites can serve as correlates alongside demonstratives. I propose a reanalysis on which languages appear to require demonstratives exactly when they lack a strong definite, leaving demonstratives as the only lexicalized index-introducing form. The analysis underscores the relevance of variable-binding dependencies in diagnosing index-introducing forms across languages.
abstracts.010439: This study examines structural parallels between language and music while avoiding direct equivalences between their respective units and representational systems. The comparison focuses on three domains: expectation and resolution, structural dependency and compatibility, and the interaction between recurrent patterns and creative production. Drawing on research in linguistics, music cognition, and neurocognition, the study combines theoretical discussion with linguistic and musical examples. The analyses show that both language and music exploit previously established contexts to generate expectations whose fulfilment, postponement, modification, or disruption contributes to the interpretation of unfolding sequences. Comparable organizational principles also emerge in context-sensitive structural relations and in the reuse and transformation of acquired patterns. These parallels, however, do not imply shared grammatical representations or equivalent communicative functions. Instead, the findings support a constrained comparison in which language and music remain distinct systems with domain-specific representations, while exhibiting converging principles in the organization of structure, expectation, and creative variation over time.
abstracts.010440: Descriptions of negated nominal constructions vary drastically across Mixtec languages, even between closely related varieties. This paper argues that the apparent intervarietal differences in the syntactic and morphological characteristics of negated nominals arise because three distinct constructions, all of which are superficially similar, may coexist within a single variety. A description of negation and the syntactic and morphological features of the three types of negated nominals is given for San Martín Peras Mixtec. A review of published data on eleven other Mixtec varieties shows that their negated nominals all fit relatively neatly into one of the three categories seen in San Martín Peras Mixtec but that many varieties only include description of one of the constructions. These findings emphasize the need for more thorough descriptive and comparative work on negated nominals in Mixtec, and they provide researchers with a set of syntactic features to consider in investigations of other Mixtec languages.
abstracts.010441: This paper discusses various approaches to head movement in HPSG. It points out that the cyclic verb trace causes problems with coordinated verbs in initial position and discusses non-cyclic approaches. Restricting the conjunctions in coordination structures is explored as well. The interaction of verb fronting with apparent multiple frontings (V3) in German is discussed and it is pointed out that this causes problems to approaches assuming a different architecture of the fronting mechanism in HPSG (elements of SLASH of type sign. Finally an implicational constraint is proposed that rules out coordinations in head-complement structures.
abstracts.010442: This article investigates the meaning of Mandarin sentences with wǎngwǎng, an adverb commonly translated as ‘often’ or ‘usually’. Empirical observations of wǎngwǎng range from proportional quantification and conditional probability to regularity, stability, and predictability. We argue that wǎngwǎng-sentences combine an extensional prevalence requirement with a non-accidental, projectable interpretation, a characteristic property of descriptive generic generalizations. Specifically, we propose a two-dimensional analysis: (i) wǎngwǎng contributes a contextually high prevalence relation between a restriction and a nuclear scope; and (ii) the resulting prevalence pattern must be appropriately grounded in a contextually relevant causal structure in order to support projection beyond the observed cases. In this synchronic sense, wǎngwǎng-sentences exhibit an emerging generic profile while retaining an overt prevalence requirement not shared by generic sentences in general. The analysis connects existing discussions of wǎngwǎng in the Chinese literature on proportionality and regularity with causal approaches to genericity, and clarifies the division of labor between extensional prevalence and causal grounding.
abstracts.010443: This work investigates Chinese particle hekuang (‘let alone’), which exhibits an intriguing interaction with the even-like scalar use of dou (scalar dou). We highlight two important but underexplored empirical observations. First, hekuang typically co-occurs with scalar dou. Second, a hekuang-sentence is reminiscent of a rhetorical question. Drawing on these observations and a degree-QUD-based perspective on scalar particles (e.g., Greenberg 2018, Zhang 2022’s work on English even, and Chen and Greenberg 2022, Zhang 2026a’s work on Chinese dou), we propose that hekuang marks a speech act that carries a rhetorical, persuasive effect. ‘p hekuang q’ can be paraphrased as ‘given p, which maximally resolves the contextually salient degree QUD, isn’t q evidently true’. It thus persuades interlocutors to accept the truth of an implied q.
abstracts.010444: [This paper condenses work that is spread across several chapters of my dissertation, and offers a unified and improved discussion of the theoretical implications of the proposal. Feedback is more than welcome!] Two vastly held assumptions in the syntactic literature of the past few decades are that movement is always triggered by a step of Agree, and that agreement probes can be relativized as searching for particular φ-features. If we combine these two, a so-far mostly unnoticed prediction is derived: we should expect to find instances of movement that are not strictly DP-local (i.e., they can target a lower DP instead of one closer to the probe), but otherwise have all properties of A-movement, and none of Ā-movement. I argue that this is a welcome prediction, as it is empirically borne out: movement to specTP in Äiwoo shows exactly this combination of properties.
abstracts.010445: This paper proposes that Tamil phonotactics shape words toward the sound contour of ōm (ஓம்): a clean, unobstructed opening and a close that settles on a sustained sonorant rather than stopping abruptly. The evidence is threefold. The Tolkāppiyam permits words to end only in vowels or in sonorant consonants (nasals, liquids, semivowels), never in stops. Words may not begin with liquids, retroflexes or consonant clusters. And Tamil modulates loanwords to meet both conditions (Rāma → Irāmaṉ, loka → ulakam, rājan → aracaṉ, with j → c and a vowel added before r). The hypothesis is descriptive and testable against Tamil dictionaries and texts. The contour is named after ōṅkāram, whose a-u-m structure it shares. It takes no position on the origin of Om itself. Predictions and falsification criteria are stated so that the hypothesis can be confirmed or rejected by future work.
abstracts.010446: There’s an attractive view in social ontology on which a group is identical to its members. It has its defenders, but seems felled by a simple objection resting on plausible assumptions about the semantics of plural partitives—assumptions built into standard plural logic. We argue the assumptions are false: whether something counts as ‘one of’ a plurality turns on how that plurality is carved up, a sensitivity the standard regimentation misses. We propose and defend a cover-based semantics that captures it, blocks the objection, and earns its keep on independent grounds. The same account answers a parallel, wellknown objection to composition as identity. Our view thus bears both on the logic and meaning of plurals and on debates in metaphysics.
abstracts.010447: Synthetic linguistic data have become increasingly prominent in linguistic research, from the analysis of large collections of AI-generated texts to controlled experiments investigating grammatical and lexical preferences. This glossary entry extends Bresnan’s (2016) distinction between the linguistic garden and the bush by introducing an artificial plant nursery as a metaphor for synthetic data. We distinguish between synthetic bush data, consisting primarily of corpus-like collections of model-generated language, and synthetic garden data, in which model outputs are elicited under controlled conditions to investigate specific linguistic hypotheses. We argue that synthetic data constitute a distinct object of linguistic investigation: comparing them with natural language data can reveal both shared patterns and divergences, but their interpretation requires careful consideration of the conditions under which they are generated.
abstracts.010448: This article (BA) tackles language contact at the Volga-Kama region.
abstracts.010449: Kawahara (2026) found that Gemini complies with a request for data fabrication in 17 out of 30 trials (57%). In this note, I briefly report the results of three follow-up experiments conducted nine days after Kawahara (2026), which all failed to replicate this result. The most plausible explanation is an unannounced change in the safeguard mechanisms.
abstracts.010450: Lakota has been described as a language in which adnominal modification is realized by a postnominal stative verb (SV). Lakota SVs can function predicatively without a copula, and their attributive use is subject to various constraints that are not typically observed for property words used with a copula, such as adjectives in familiar languages. Among these constraints is their inability to be chained, coordinated, contrasted, or modified within a referring expression. This study investigates the motivation for these constraints and provides evidence that, while a postnominal SV semantically assigns an attributive property to a noun, syntactically it does not function as a modifier of the noun. Instead, the adjacent N and SV constitute a complex stative expression and stand in a syntactic relationship inherited from the copredication and co-dependency between a clause-final N and SV functioning predicatively. This analysis accounts for the constraints, elucidates several outstanding issues in Lakota morphosyntax, and suggests a typologically novel (i.e., previously undescribed) strategy of assigning an attributive property within a referring expression.
abstracts.010451: This study systematically examines the regular patterns of Swahili perception verbs evolving from concrete sensory actions to abstract cognitive functions, revealing the primary mechanisms involved in this developmental pathway. The research materials were collected and analyzed through dictionary searches, literature reviews, and interviews with native speakers. The findings indicate that all five-sense verbs in Swahili project into the cognitive domain: Visual verbs (e.g., "ona", "angalia", and "tazama") have developed rich cognitive meanings such as "understand", "think", and "judge"; auditory verbs (e.g., "sikia") have derived meanings like "know" and "perceive"; while tactile ("gusa"), olfactory ("nusa"), and gustatory ("onja") verbs have extended to cognitive functions such as "move emotionally" and "feel". The semantic extension of Swahili perception verbs into the cognitive domain, along with the language's unique reliance on sensory experiences when conceptualizing internal states, reflects the coexistence of universality and individuality in language. This study unveils the cognitive principles underlying lexical meanings and their cultural conceptualizations in language.
abstracts.010452: Russian Dative-Infinitive-Structures (DIS) have been a matter of debate, with focus on such issues as mono vs. bi-clausality, modal flavour, TAM features and case-marking. I argue that all contextual realizations of Russian DIS sentences express a single flavour in root indicative clauses — alethic modality and exhibit the constraint on perfect infinitives in non-negative clauses. The Perfective Infinitive Constraint is canceled in other varieties of DIS sentences which do not express alethic meanings and are realized in irrealis or usual contexts. These asymmetries are explained by the fact that root DIS declaratives unlike irrealis DIS clauses have deictic tense. On formal accounts, deictic tense comes from the TP layer above the infinitive phrase, and the illocutionary force and modal flavour come from the upper CP layer above the TP. Root DIS declaratives enter the derivation as bi-clausal but undergo restructuring as the border between TP and VP is removed. The dative subjects of DIS sentences are raised out of the embedded infinitival clause and lack the animacy condition. The syntax and semantics of DIS sentences are valued across an overtly similar sentence pattern with embedded infinitives ― Dative-Predicative-Structures (DPS). I argue that Russian DPS sentences are control structures that implement a different mechanism of case assignment. Russian infinitival clauses by default retain deictic tense: this factor overrides the control versus raising distinction, but some types of both control and restructuring predicates block deictic tense for semantic reasons.
abstracts.010453: Nominal constituents of the form that kind of table allow both subkind and existential readings. According to Carl-son (Linguistics and Philosophy 1(3), 1977, 413–456; Reference to Kinds in English.
