Doctoral dissertation, Uni-versity of Massachusetts, Amherst 1977, published in 1980 by Garland Press) both of these readings involve a unique underlying syntactic configuration and a unique denotation for the noun kind. This analysis cannot be ex-tended to the Romanian acest fel de masă ‘this kind of table’, which is fully acceptable and colloquial on the exis-tential reading, but unacceptable (or only marginally accepted by certain speakers) on the subkind reading. In addi-tion to bringing up the existence of the atypical Romanian fel ‘kind’, I will enrich the empirical landscape of taxo-nomic nouns (which include kind, type, model, sort or species) by formulating two new crosslinguistic generaliza-tions: (i) the choice between existential and subkind readings correlates with different agreement patterns observable in Romanian and other Romance languages; (ii) in English as well as in Romance languages the necessarily quanti-ficational determiner each is only marginally acceptable in existentially interpreted nominals of the form each kind/type of NP. My solution to these problems will build on Wilkinson’s (The semantics of the common noun kind. In G. Carlson & F. Pelletier, eds. 1995, The Generic Book, 383-397) syntactic-ambiguity hypothesis, accord-ing to which the existential and subkind readings of that kind of table rely on two different syntactic structures. The theoretical contribution of the present paper is a new syntactic analysis of the structure underlying the existential reading and a corresponding semantic composition. The core syntactic assumption will be a null functional head Qual(ity), which carries the burden of the semantic composition. The theoretical advantage of this proposal is that it separates classifying meaning, which is contributed by the syntactic structure (more precisely by the Qual° head) from reference to kind-level entities, which is contributed by taxonomic nouns.
abstracts.010454: Recent research in computational linguistics has found that most long-distance linguistic dependencies are tier-based strictly 2-local (TSL-2) over their respective representations, providing a precise characterization of blocking elements in phonology and syntax. A subset of the well-known syntactic island effects have been claimed to be one such class of blockers, explaining their superficial diversity via a common computational basis. This article revisits the TSL-2 analysis of islands in light of subsequent work on other types of syntactic locality constraints and on the treatment of gradient blocking. It finds that the TSL-2 islands display variation and gradience of the sort found in other syntactic blockers, while those islands which are not TSL-2 can be distinguished in this regard. Several directions are suggested for future research on islands and other syntactic locality phenomena.
abstracts.010455: This dissertation aims to establish a tight bound on the computational complexity of case and agreement dependencies in syntax, that is, the class of possible formal patterns which they exemplify. Such dependencies are shown to be modeled well by a tree-based generalization of of tier-based strictly 2-local (TSL-2) formal languages, mirroring past results on long-distance phonotactics and syntactic movement. This characterization has several important consequences. First, TSL-2 is a highly restrictive formal class, ruling out many unnatural and presumably impossible patterns whose absence is left unexplained by earlier, string-based classifications of syntactic patterns. Second, the range of patterns it can express aligns closely with well-known cross-linguistic generalizations and points of variation, unifying many phenomena previously handled by distinct theoretical mechanisms. Third, TSL-2 patterns can be computed by simple, cognitively plausible pattern-detection mechanisms, explaining why it is that language makes use of these and not others. Finally, the class of TSL-2 patterns is in principle efficiently learnable, providing a crucial hint into how human children learn languages so effortlessly, and by extension, how we might design artificial systems that do the same. All necessary background on subregular formal languages and their application to syntax is included, though some familiarity with Minimalist syntax is assumed. As such, this dissertation may also serve as an introduction to subregular complexity for both theoretical and computational linguists alike.
abstracts.010456: It has been an ongoing effort in Generative Phonology to explain how the unique Root & Pattern morphology of Semitic languages follows from more cross-linguistic principles. This paper applies the same approach to a phonological pattern that also seems to be unique to Semitic languages, namely “Geminate Transfer”: the realization of an expected C1C2VC2 sequence as C1C1VC2. Focusing on the pattern as it is manifested in the Modern South Arabian language Mehri, the paper follows Bendjaballah and Ségéral (2013) in designating the C1C1VC2 realization as a repair, rather than an alternative, to C1C2VC2. At the same time, it follows Rose (2000) in regarding the phenomenon as the ultimate expression of a universal OCP constraint against sequences of similar (though not necessarily identical) consonants separated by a vowel. An OT account is provided that crucially covers an aspect of the facts that was not treated by Bendjaballah & Ségéral, while also arguing for their skelettal – as opposed to prosodic – conceptualization of the template. Finally, it is claimed that the phenomenon occurs only in Semitic because of the special morphological make-up of Semitic languages.
abstracts.010457: Eliminativist theories of speech production and perception locate linguistic knowledge exclusively within detailed episodic speech representations and their interactions. This paper examines the tenability of that commitment. Through a series of exemplar based computational simulations modeling the contextual neutralization of phonemic vowel nasality over time for an individual speaker, I explore what is required for eliminativist models to predict both phonetically complete and incomplete neutralization. The simulations show that, with the appropriate weighting of competing production biases of anticipatory nasalization and morphological similarity, eliminativist models can successfully produce phonetically incomplete neutralization. While token frequency manipulations and socially weighted encoding of exemplar memories can achieve phonetically complete neutralization, they introduce questionable empirical predictions and over-generate the predicted types of neutralization. Adjusting the relative strength of production biases provides an alternative solution by regulating the degree of neutralization while keeping the production optimum bounded by the competing phonetic targets of production biases. I argue that permitting learned, language-specific production-bias weights provides a more explanatorily adequate account of neutralization than the frequency-based or socially weighted encoding approaches examined here. Crucially, this account requires a form of linguistic knowledge that extends beyond the network of episodic speech representations and their interactions.
abstracts.010458: The Romanian noun fel 'kind' is puzzling insofar as it allows the existential reading of DPs of the form acest fel de masă ‘this kind of table’, but disallows the subkind reading.
abstracts.010459: In this paper, we will compare the syntax of English tough-movement with that of its translational equivalent in German. We will see that, on the one hand, the syntax of the German construction is very different: there is no A′-movement involved but rather A-movement and restructuring; additionally, the adjective is merged as an adjunct to the infinitival clause rather than being the head that selects it; on the other hand, we will see that one can observe similar restrictions on the placement of experiencers. We will argue that this suggests that many of the proposals that have been made to account for experiencer intervention in English cannot be applied to German. Instead, we will argue that the restrictions follow from independent properties of German such as (i) the constituency that obtains if German tough-movement essentially receives the same analysis as the modal passive and (ii) a general adjacency requirement on verb clusters.
abstracts.010460: This paper investigates the diachronic development of the Venetan progressive construction formed with drio (‘behind’) and an infinitive. While this construction has traditionally been described as a prepositional infinitive, I argue that its historical evolution calls into question the prepositional status of drio and the nominal nature of the infinitive it introduces. Building on minimalist assumptions about labeling and agreement, the analysis proposes that early stages of the construction involved a nominalized infinitive embedded under a PP, with nominalization arising through agreement rather than categorial recategorization. Diachronically, the loss of nominal layers and of overt determiner realization leads to the reanalysis of drio as an aspectual head and to the emergence of a purely verbal progressive structure in Modern (Central) Venetan. The paper further situates the Venetan pattern within a broader cross-linguistic perspective, drawing parallels with Danish and Quebec French progressive constructions and argues that the instability of nominalized infinitives provides a principled explanation for their loss. More generally, I propose that nominalization effects can be derived without recourse to costly recategorization operations and that minoritized languages such as Venetan offer particularly transparent evidence for diachronic change.
abstracts.010461: This study investigates stochastic knowledge of French demonym formation, focusing on lexical propensity, phonological nasal clash, and extralinguistic knowledge. In an online forced-choice experiment, 27 native speakers of Metropolitan French and 26 native speakers of Quebec French selected demonyms for 17 nonce toponyms, first without and then with geographical labels referring to French regions. Baseline suffix propensity was the strongest predictor of choice. The varieties differed in their preference orderings: Metropolitan French speakers favoured -ois, whereas Quebec French speakers favoured -ien. Geographical labels modestly increased the selection of -ien and -éen relative to -ois among Metropolitan French speakers, but no credible geographical effect was established among Quebec French speakers. Nasal-final toponyms showed a weak tendency to disfavour nasal suffixes, except for -ien in Quebec French. A MaxEnt analysis of Metropolitan French responses compared lexical-propensity constraints weighted using existing demonym data with a hypothetical, evenly spaced weight profile. The latter more closely approximated the experimental distribution, suggesting sensitivity to abstract suffix typicality rather than direct reproduction of lexical frequencies. These findings support a probabilistic account of word formation in which lexical propensity predominates, while phonological and geographical cues make weaker, context-dependent contributions.
abstracts.010462: Classical Latin counts a syllable with a short vowel as heavy (“long by position”, positione longa) when the vowel is followed by two consonants, unless these are a stop and a liquid (muta cum liquida), before which it may remain light. Phonological theory expresses this by assigning a mora to the coda consonant, but leaves open why listeners of quantitative verse equated that mora with the second half of a long vowel. This article proposes that, in careful speech and the recitation of verse, the second mora of such a syllable, closed by the first of the two consonants, rested on a phase that followed the vowel and shared some of its properties (voicing, resonance or airflow), and that this similarity made the equivalence possible. The clearest form of this phase is a brief transitional vocoid into which a coda consonant was released before a heterorganic consonant: ărma [arᵊ.ma]. Too weak to form a syllable, the vocoid together with the preceding consonant made up the second mora. Where the typology excludes such a vocoid, in homorganic clusters and geminates, or where the coda is s or final -m, the same role was played by the sustained body of the coda itself or, in voiceless stop geminates, probably by a laryngeal phase of the preaspiration type; a stop before a homorganic consonant may have had one as well or merged with the following consonant. Typological parallels support the proposed realizations. Weaknesses of the proposal and first corpus tests are discussed.
abstracts.010463: Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.
abstracts.010464: Este trabajo examina la distribución de la voz media en español desde una perspectiva cuantitativa basada en corpus, combinando un enfoque conceptual con un análisis de las alternancias de diátesis asociadas a las construcciones medias. Los datos proceden de ADESSE, una base de datos sintáctico-semántica construida sobre el corpus ARTHUS, que incluye 158 624 cláusulas correspondientes a 4011 verbos. En una primera fase se analiza la asociación de la voz media con distintos dominios conceptuales, agrupados en las clases Emoción, Espacial, Cambio, Atribución y Otras. Los resultados confirman una especial afinidad de la voz media con los dominios espacial, emocional y de cambio. En una segunda fase se identifican y cuantifican distintos tipos de alternancias de diátesis documentadas con la voz media: anticausativas, antipasivas, alternancias activa-media con estructuras intransitivas y transitivas, y casos de media tantum. El análisis muestra que la alternancia anticausativa constituye el patrón más frecuente y productivo, especialmente en los dominios espacial y de cambio, mientras que las alternancias antipasivas y las construcciones medias transitivas se concentran principalmente en otras clases semánticas. Se concluye que la distribución de la voz media no depende exclusivamente de propiedades conceptuales generales, sino también de la frecuencia y productividad de determinadas alternancias de diátesis, que contribuyen decisivamente a estructurar su comportamiento en el uso. Abstract: This study examines the distribution of the middle voice in Spanish from a quantitative, corpus-based perspective, combining a conceptual approach with an analysis of the diathesis alternations associated with middle constructions. The data are drawn from ADESSE, a syntactic-semantic database built upon the ARTHUS corpus, which comprises 158,624 clauses corresponding to 4,011 verbs. In the first phase, the association of the middle voice with various conceptual domains—grouped into the categories of Emotion, Spatial, Change, Attribution and Others—is analysed. The results confirm a particular affinity between the middle voice and the spatial, emotional and change domains. In a second phase, different types of diathesis alternations documented with the middle voice are identified and quantified: anticausative, antipassive, active–middle alternations with intransitive and transitive structures, and cases of ‘media tantum’. The analysis shows that anticausative alternation constitutes the most frequent and productive pattern, particularly in the spatial and change domains, whilst antipassive alternations and transitive middle constructions are mainly concentrated in other semantic classes. It is concluded that the distribution of the middle voice does not depend exclusively on general conceptual properties, but also on the frequency and productivity of certain diathesis alternations, which play a decisive role in shaping its behaviour in usage.
abstracts.010465: Some grammars give a word two syntactic functions at once. The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language treats some in take some as both the determiner and the head of its noun phrase, and rich in the rich as both modifier and head, a fusion of functions that Payne et al. (2007) defend. The simpler alternative is that the word is just the head. I argue that a second function needs evidence of form that varies with it rather than with the word, and test for such evidence with the grammar’s own diagnostics and new corpus data. For the modifier function, there’s none. For the determiner function, there’s one fact, that no adjective comes before a bare determinative outside a few exclamations, but the comparison is close, and on balance, it doesn’t justify the extra function. Fused relatives such as whoever told you that are different: they relativize subjects, they have no infinitival forms, and in usage, the case of whoever answers to its function inside the clause. There a second function is favoured, though not forced. Keeping a category, heading a phrase, and taking a reading from context are things a head with no second function can do, not evidence of one.
abstracts.010466: Paycheck pronouns have often been presented as a challenge to dynamic semantic accounts of pronominal anaphora. In this paper, I present new data suggesting that discourse relations play an essential role in the availability of paycheck pronouns. I thus argue for a discourse coherence-based account of paycheck anaphora. I present a new analysis of paycheck pronouns using Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) that accounts for the distribution of paycheck pronouns through independently motivated constraints on discourse relations. In developing this analysis, I demonstrate that by incorporating discourse coherence insights into the analysis, dynamic semantic approaches are more than able to account for paycheck pronouns.
abstracts.010468: Tigrinya (Ethiopia and Eritrea; Semitic) has a well-behaved head-final verbal domain that canonically displays S-O-V-Aux word order. A notable exception is found in so-called cleft constructions, where the verbal copula appears in a clause-medial position, between a focused constituent (FOC) and a presupposed relative clause (RC). I argue that this non-canonical FOC-cop-RC word order is derived from a head-final specificational copula construction by way of predicate fronting. This approach preserves the head-finality of the language and offers an account for some otherwise exceptional case and agreement patterns.
abstracts.010469: The article proposes a new term, postmortonyms, denoting names assigned to unidentified deceased individuals. Drawing on an exemplary semantic onomastic analysis of 220 postmortonyms from multiple cultures, the study explores the motivations, structures, and functions of these bynames, distinct from posthumous names, deadnames, and necronyms. The research demonstrates that postmortonyms often incorporate details such as location or distinguishing features, which serve investigative, communicative, and memorial purposes. The analysis highlights the phenomenon of polyonymy, in which temporary names coexist with potential authentic identities, and discusses the broader cultural and legal contexts that influence naming practices for the nameless dead. The research is a preliminary study, and the findings provide a foundation for further research on the conceptualization of death and naming across cultures.
abstracts.010470: Prompt engineering adapts large language models (LLMs) to specific tasks by designing their inputs, without modifying pretrained parameters. Researchers in the field of linguistics and speech-language pathology use the Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) software to analyze functional language use and language disorders. However, transcription of language samples for SALT analysis requires intensive coding procedures, creating a barrier to efficient SALT language sample analysis (LSA). In three stages, this study developed and tested the capabilities of prompt-engineered large language models in annotation of SALT bound morphemes. In the first stage, five prompt versions were compared using GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna on 12 synthetic mixed-convention transcripts to determine the optimal engineering strategy. Using the highest-performing prompt in stage 1, stage 2 evaluated nine different LLM configurations on the same transcript set, to select the best-performing models. Paired with prompt v5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 3.6 Flash advanced to stage 3 final testing, where they were tested on 18 held-out mixed-convention transcripts (1,889 utterances) and 30 single-convention transcripts (1,800 utterances) per model. Performance was measured by morpheme-level micro F1, precision, and recall. GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 97.81% micro F1 on the mixed-convention transcripts, compared with 90.60% for Gemini, whose score was lowered by two structurally invalid responses; on the transcripts Gemini returned in valid format, the two models were similarly accurate (Sol 97.72% vs. Gemini 97.97%). Sol returned valid output for all 48 final transcripts. These findings demonstrate the potential of prompt-engineered LLMs for automated bound-morpheme annotation. Further validation on authentic language samples is necessary before implementation in research or clinical settings.
abstracts.010471: Intensified response particles such as English "absolutely" and German "voll" (lit. 'full' ≈ 'totally/absolutely') have been analyzed as degree modifiers of assertion (Greenberg & Wolf 2019): they strengthen a response by marking maximal speaker commitment to an anaphorically retrieved proposition. We test whether maximal commitment alone captures their distribution. Two acceptability experiments on English and German show that these particles are degraded relative to neutral response particles in plain factual-positive confirmations, whereas this disadvantage is absent or substantially reduced in evaluative contexts. Factual-negative contexts reveal further language-specific asymmetries. These findings show that commitment strength alone is insufficient. We propose, as a first account, that intensified response particles express contrastive commitment: maximal alignment with a proposition relative to a salient incompatible alternative. The results thus motivate a discourse-sensitive analysis of response particle intensification, while leaving open whether polarity opposition fully characterizes the relevant licensing condition.
abstracts.010472: This paper proposes a novel syntactic analysis of English resultative constructions within the framework of modern Minimalist syntax (Chomsky 2024; Kitahara and Seely 2025). Challenging traditional Small Clause analyses, we argue that the result predicate is accommodated within a functional phrase, PredP (Bowers 1993), separating the state-holder from the main verb's direct object position. Combined with the FormCopy operation and Minimal Search, our model accounts for the long-standing WH-extraction asymmetry between paint-type and consider-type resultatives. Specifically, we demonstrate that consider-type verbs lack a lexical object position (DP2), preventing FormCopy from generating the required search path for WH-extraction. This structural difference naturally derives the extraction restriction without positing ad-hoc constraints, offering a unified account of syntactic relations and semantic interpretations in resultative constructions.
abstracts.010473: The extraction of bare wh-adjuncts from whether-clauses is a prototypical instance of weak-island violation and has traditionally been treated as ungrammatical. This paper presents novel experimental evidence that challenges this generalisation. We show that English speakers fully accept adjunct extraction from whether-islands when these are introduced by a discourse context that licenses reconstruction of the extractee within the embedded clause. By contrast, the same contextual manipulation produces no amelioration in strong islands, whose extraction remains overwhelmingly rejected. Building on these findings, we advance two claims. First, adjunct extraction from whether-clauses is grammatically licit and its perceived degradation arises from a domain-general preference for shorter dependencies, which can be overridden by appropriate discourse context. Second, the differential sensitivity of strong and weak islands to the same manipulation bears directly on the broader debate concerning the source of locality effects. In particular, we argue that the weak and strong islands considered here have distinct sources: strong-island effects reflect a grammatically encoded constraint on extraction, whereas weak-island effects emerge from the interaction between grammatical representations and domain-general factors. In the conclusion, we suggest that this interpretation is compatible with approaches that place at least some locality effects at the interface between grammar and external systems, in line with the broader explanatory goals of Minimalism.
abstracts.010474: Perception-production asymmetries have been modelled through representational or grammatical non-isomorphism. We identify a further architectural property of multi-level OT that drives such mismatches. Formalizing a recently reported asymmetry in L2 tonal acquisition, we show that asymmetric patterns can arise despite complete isomorphism across modalities. Depending on the input, the same undominated mapping constraints may drastically narrow the candidate set in one modality before lower-ranked constraints apply, while leaving sufficient candidates in the other modality for those constraints to determine the outcome. Thus, perception-production asymmetries can emerge from the architecture of a single grammar, without requiring separate grammatical systems across modalities.
